tf.f: The Pitchford thesis argues that every current account deficit is a serious problem.

tf.t: Wealth is distributed much more unequally than income in Australia.
The GST is regressive, because low-income households spend a larger share of their income.
tf.f: The GST is a progressive tax.

tf.t: The social wage includes government-provided services such as Medicare, public education and public housing.
A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality; 1 means perfect inequality.
tf.f: A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect inequality.

tf.t: Inequality can provide incentives to work, study and take risks.
Women, on average, earn less than men in Australia.
Ecologically sustainable development means meeting the needs of today without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A negative externality means the market produces too much, because the external cost is ignored.
tf.f: A negative externality means the market produces too little of a good.

tf.t: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable.
Because people can use public goods without paying, private firms underproduce them, so governments provide them.
tf.f: The free rider problem means private firms will overproduce public goods.

tf.t: Full employment does not mean zero unemployment; it is unemployment at about the NAIRU.
Objectives can conflict, such as faster growth raising inflation and the current account deficit.
tf.f: Economic objectives never conflict, so a government can always achieve all of them at once.

tf.t: Macroeconomic policies aim to stabilise the business cycle by managing aggregate demand.
Fiscal policy is set by the Federal Government through the budget; monetary policy is set by the RBA.
tf.f: Fiscal policy is set by the Reserve Bank.

tf.t: The budget outcome is government revenue minus government spending.
An expansionary stance adds to aggregate demand, for example through a larger deficit or smaller surplus.
tf.f: An expansionary budget stance means the government is reducing its deficit.

tf.t: Automatic stabilisers increase the deficit in a downturn without any new decision by the government.
The cyclical component changes with the business cycle; the structural balance reflects the government's policy settings.
tf.f: The structural budget balance changes automatically with the business cycle.

tf.t: Selling Commonwealth Government Securities is the main way the government finances a deficit.
The RBA Monetary Policy Board sets the target for the cash rate.
The RBA sets the cash rate target; banks set their own lending rates, which usually follow the cash rate.
tf.f: The RBA sets the interest rates banks charge on home loans.

tf.t: Changes in the cash rate affect the economy with long and variable lags.
A cut in the cash rate tends to make the Australian dollar depreciate, as Australian assets become less attractive.
tf.f: A cut in the cash rate tends to make the Australian dollar appreciate.

tf.t: Monetary policy aims for inflation of 2 to 3 per cent and the maximum sustainable level of employment.
Microeconomic reform aims to raise efficiency and productivity, shifting aggregate supply to the right.
Competition policy aims to increase competition, for example by stopping price fixing and the misuse of market power.
tf.f: Competition policy aims to protect large firms from new competitors.

tf.t: The Fair Work Commission sets the national minimum wage and modern award wages in its Annual Wage Review.
Enterprise agreements are negotiated between an employer and its employees; the Fair Work Commission approves them.
tf.f: Enterprise agreements are set by the Fair Work Commission for each industry.

tf.t: Education and training programs can reduce structural unemployment by matching workers' skills to the jobs available.
An emissions trading scheme caps total emissions and lets firms buy and sell permits.
Under the Paris Agreement each country sets its own target (its nationally determined contribution).
tf.f: The Paris Agreement sets legally binding emission cuts for each country, chosen by the UN.

tf.t: Australia has a legislated target of net zero emissions by 2050.
Time lags, global influences and political constraints all limit how well economic policies work.
Monetary policy has the shorter implementation lag: the cash rate can change at any meeting, while budget changes take time to plan and legislate.
tf.f: Fiscal policy has a shorter implementation lag than monetary policy.

tf.t: Scarcity exists because people's wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
tf.f: Opportunity cost is the money price paid for a good.

tf.t: Consumers, producers and governments are the economic agents that make economic decisions.
The cost–benefit principle says a choice is worth making when its marginal benefit is at least as great as its marginal cost.
tf.f: The cost–benefit principle says a choice is worth making whenever its total benefit is positive.

tf.t: An incentive can have unintended consequences that work against the aim of the policy.
Behavioural economics challenges that assumption: cognitive biases and ethical concerns shape real decisions.
tf.f: Behavioural economics assumes that people always make rational, self-interested decisions.

tf.t: Microeconomics studies individual markets, while macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole.
The four factors of production are land (natural resources), labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Wages are the income earned by labour; interest is the income earned by capital.
tf.f: Interest is the factor income earned by labour.

tf.t: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce, how much to produce and how to distribute production.
In a free market economy, consumers' spending and the price mechanism decide what is produced.
tf.f: In a free market economy, a central planning authority decides what is produced.

tf.t: Australia is a mixed market economy.
That is money as a medium of exchange; as a store of value, money can be saved and spent later.
tf.f: Money acting as a store of value means it is accepted in exchange for goods and services.

tf.t: A production possibilities frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology.
A point inside the frontier shows unemployed resources; a point outside it cannot be reached with current resources.
tf.f: A point outside the production possibilities frontier shows unemployed resources.

tf.t: Moving along the frontier to produce more of one good has an opportunity cost: less of the other good.
An improvement in technology shifts the frontier outwards.
tf.f: An improvement in technology shifts the production possibilities frontier inwards.

tf.t: Producing more capital goods today can allow an economy to produce more of both goods in the future.
In the circular flow of income, households supply factors of production and businesses pay them factor incomes.
Exports are an injection; imports are a leakage.
tf.f: Exports are a leakage from the circular flow of income.

tf.t: The economy is in equilibrium when S + T + M = I + G + X.
When leakages are greater than injections, national income falls.
tf.f: When leakages are greater than injections, national income rises.

tf.t: The financial sector links saving, a leakage, with investment, an injection.
GDP is the total market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy in a period.
The peak is the highest point; the trough is the lowest point.
tf.f: The trough is the highest point of the business cycle.

tf.t: During an expansion, unemployment usually falls and inflationary pressures build.
During a contraction, tax revenue falls and spending on income support rises.
tf.f: During a contraction, government tax revenue rises and welfare spending falls.

tf.t: A fall in demand for exports can start a downturn in the business cycle.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses contribute to GDP through the goods and services they produce and the people they employ.
Prices signal to producers and consumers when a good has become more or less scarce.
The rationing function means a scarce good goes to those willing and able to pay the price.
tf.f: The rationing function of price means everyone gets an equal share of a good.

tf.t: Secure property rights and enforceable contracts encourage people to invest and trade.
Labour is traded in factor markets; goods and services are traded in product markets.
tf.f: Labour is traded in product markets.

tf.t: The law of demand states that, other things equal, a rise in price leads to a fall in the quantity demanded.
A change in a good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve.
tf.f: A change in a good's own price shifts its demand curve.

tf.t: A rise in the price of a substitute increases the demand for a good.
A rise in the price of a complement decreases the demand for a good.
tf.f: A rise in the price of a complement increases the demand for a good.

tf.t: Effective demand is the desire for a good backed by the ability and willingness to pay.
The supply curve slopes upwards because higher prices make it profitable to produce more.
An improvement in technology lowers costs and increases supply, shifting the supply curve right.
tf.f: An improvement in technology decreases supply.

tf.t: A rise in the cost of the factors of production decreases supply.
A rise in a good's own price causes an expansion of the quantity supplied, a movement along the curve.
tf.f: A rise in a good's own price is an increase in supply.

tf.t: At equilibrium, the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
When the price is above equilibrium, there is a surplus.
tf.f: When the price is above equilibrium, there is a shortage.

tf.t: An increase in demand, with supply unchanged, raises both the equilibrium price and quantity.
A decrease in supply raises the equilibrium price and lowers the equilibrium quantity.
tf.f: A decrease in supply lowers the equilibrium price.

tf.t: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.
When demand is price elastic, a price rise reduces total revenue.
tf.f: When demand is price elastic, a price rise increases total revenue.

tf.t: Goods with few close substitutes, such as necessities, tend to have price inelastic demand.
Demand usually becomes more elastic over time, as buyers find substitutes.
tf.f: Demand usually becomes less elastic over time.

tf.t: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is vertical.
Supply is usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run.
Spare capacity makes supply more elastic, because firms can raise output quickly.
tf.f: Spare capacity makes supply less elastic.

tf.t: A perfectly elastic supply curve is horizontal.
Perishable goods that cannot be stored tend to have inelastic supply.
tf.f: Goods that perish quickly have very elastic supply.

tf.t: In perfect competition, firms are price takers.
A monopoly has one seller; an oligopoly is dominated by a few large firms.
tf.f: An oligopoly is a market with one seller.

tf.t: Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products, with low barriers to entry.
Higher market concentration usually gives firms more pricing power, so prices tend to rise.
tf.f: Higher market concentration usually leads to lower prices for consumers.

tf.t: Network effects make a digital platform more valuable to each user as more people use it.
A negative externality is a cost borne by third parties who are not part of the transaction.
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable.
tf.f: Public goods are rival and excludable.

tf.t: Merit goods, such as education, tend to be under-consumed when left to the market.
Collusion is an abuse of market power that raises prices for consumers.
tf.f: Collusion between firms benefits consumers through lower prices.

tf.t: Asymmetric information occurs when one party to a transaction knows more than the other.
A common-pool resource, such as a fish stock, is rival but hard to exclude people from.
tf.f: A common-pool resource is non-rival.

tf.t: Land held communally or under native title generally cannot be mortgaged, which can make it harder for some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses to borrow.
A binding price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price and causes a shortage.
A floor below equilibrium has no effect; a binding floor is set above equilibrium and causes a surplus.
tf.f: A price floor set below the equilibrium price causes a surplus.

tf.t: A nudge changes how choices are presented without banning options or changing prices.
Government intervention can fail, for example through unintended consequences or rent-seeking.
tf.f: Government intervention always improves the allocation of resources.

tf.t: When demand is price inelastic, consumers bear most of the burden of a per-unit tax.
MPC + MPS = 1.
If the MPC is 0.9, the MPS is 0.1.
tf.f: If the MPC is 0.9, the MPS is 0.9.

tf.t: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that each extra unit consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before.
Demand for an inferior good falls as incomes rise.
tf.f: Demand for an inferior good rises as incomes rise.

tf.t: For a Veblen good, demand can rise when its price rises, because a high price signals status.
A sludge adds friction that makes beneficial choices harder, such as cancelling a subscription.
tf.f: A sludge makes it easier for consumers to make choices that benefit them.

tf.t: More affordable and available childcare tends to increase the supply of labour.
Geographic mobility is the ability to move between places; occupational mobility is the ability to change jobs or occupations.
tf.f: Geographic mobility of labour is the ability of workers to change occupations.

tf.t: Inflexible workplaces and inadequate leave entitlements can discourage people from joining the workforce.
Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs as well as explicit costs from revenue.
Accounting profit is usually larger, because economic profit also subtracts implicit (opportunity) costs.
tf.f: Accounting profit is usually smaller than economic profit.

tf.t: Productivity is output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked.
Capital deepening means increasing the amount of capital per worker.
tf.f: Capital deepening means hiring more workers.

tf.t: The technical optimum is the level of output at which long-run average cost is lowest.
Diseconomies of scale cause long-run average cost to rise as a firm grows beyond its technical optimum.
tf.f: Diseconomies of scale cause long-run average cost to fall as a firm grows.

tf.t: The Fair Work Commission sets Australia's national minimum wage each year.
Flexible working hours are a non-wage benefit.
tf.f: Flexible working hours are a wage benefit.

tf.t: A fall in the cost of capital relative to labour can reduce businesses' demand for labour.
The financial sector channels funds from savers to borrowers.
Employers must pay the superannuation guarantee, 12 per cent of ordinary earnings from 1 July 2025.
tf.f: Superannuation contributions are voluntary for Australian employers.

tf.t: Banks, insurers, fund managers and the central bank are types of financial intermediaries.
A share gives its owner part-ownership of a company.
Companies raise funds when new shares are issued in the primary market; secondary trading is between investors.
tf.f: Companies raise new funds each time their shares are traded on the secondary market.

tf.t: An initial public offering takes place in the primary share market.
The interest rate is the price of money: the cost of credit and the return on savings.
An increase in saving increases the supply of loanable funds, which lowers the interest rate.
tf.f: An increase in household saving increases the demand for loanable funds.

tf.t: Riskier borrowers usually pay higher interest rates.
A rise in interest rates raises repayments and reduces how much buyers can borrow, making housing less affordable.
tf.f: A rise in interest rates makes housing more affordable for new buyers.

tf.t: Governments borrow in the debt market by issuing bonds.
The roles of government include redistribution, reallocation, stabilisation and correcting market failure.
A budget deficit occurs when spending is greater than revenue; a surplus is when revenue is greater.
tf.f: A budget surplus occurs when government spending is greater than revenue.

tf.t: A nudge uses insights about behaviour to encourage a choice without forcing it.
Privatisation is the sale of a government business to private owners; nationalisation is the reverse.
tf.f: Privatisation is the government taking ownership of a private business.

tf.t: Individual income tax is the largest source of Australian Government revenue.
The GST is an indirect tax on spending.
tf.f: The GST is a direct tax.

tf.t: The legal incidence of a tax is on whoever must pay it to the government.
A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from people on low incomes.
tf.f: A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from people on high incomes.

tf.t: Simplicity, fairness and efficiency are features of a good tax.
Social security and welfare is the largest area of Australian Government spending.
Building a hospital is non-recurrent (capital) spending; running it is recurrent spending.
tf.f: Building a new hospital is recurrent government spending.

tf.t: The NDIS, aged care and health are among the fastest-growing areas of Australian Government spending.
Trade based on comparative advantage lets countries produce more from the same resources.
China is Australia's largest two-way trading partner.
tf.f: The United States is Australia's largest two-way trading partner.

tf.t: Mineral and energy resources make up the largest share of Australia's goods exports.
A trade surplus occurs when exports are greater than imports.
tf.f: A trade surplus occurs when imports are greater than exports.

tf.t: From at least the 1700s, before European colonisation, Yolŋu people in Arnhem Land traded with fishermen from Makassar, who sold the trepang they collected to China.
Foreign debt must be repaid with interest, while foreign equity earns dividends and profits for its overseas owners.
The United States is the largest source of foreign investment in Australia.
tf.f: China is the largest source of foreign investment in Australia.

tf.t: Australian companies borrowing from overseas banks add to Australia's foreign debt.
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another.
The Australian dollar has depreciated, because each A$1 buys fewer US dollars.
tf.f: If A$1 falls from US$0.70 to US$0.65, the Australian dollar has appreciated.

tf.t: If A$1 = US$0.65, a US$650 item costs A$1,000.
The balance of payments records all economic transactions between Australian residents and the rest of the world.
Exports are recorded in the current account; the financial account records investment and borrowing.
tf.f: Exports of beef are recorded in the financial account.

items.q: How can the government decrease inflationary pressures in the Australian economy?

e.why: Higher taxes leave households and firms with less to spend, reducing demand and the pressure on prices.

not.B: A deficit adds to demand.
not.C: A depreciation makes imports dearer, adding to inflation, and the government does not set a floating exchange rate.
not.D: More government spending adds to demand.

items.q: How are the foreign company dividends paid to Australian investors recorded on Australia’s Balance of Payments?
o: As a debit on the current account
As a credit on the current account
As a debit on the capital and financial account
As a credit on the capital and financial account

e.why: Dividends are income from investment, recorded in the income part of the current account. Money flowing into Australia is a credit.

not.A: Money received is a credit, not a debit.
not.C: Dividends are income, not a capital or financial transaction.
not.D: It is a credit, but income belongs in the current account.

items.q: Which indicators are used to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI)?
o: Population growth, per capita GDP, life expectancy
Population growth, infant mortality rate, malnutrition
Life expectancy, educational attainment, per capita GDP
Current account balance, infant mortality rate, educational attainment

e.why: The HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income per person.

not.A: Population growth is not part of the HDI.
not.B: None of these three is used in the HDI.
not.D: The current account balance and infant mortality are not used in the HDI.

items.q: Which action by the Reserve Bank would stimulate the economy in an economic downturn?
o: Selling government securities in the cash market
Buying government securities in the cash market
Selling foreign currencies on the foreign exchange market
Buying foreign currencies on the foreign exchange market

e.why: Buying securities puts cash into the banking system, lowering the cash rate and encouraging borrowing and spending.

not.A: Selling securities removes cash and raises interest rates.
not.C: Selling foreign currency means buying Australian dollars, which raises the dollar and hurts exporters.
not.D: Buying foreign currency affects the exchange rate; the main tool for stimulating the economy is the cash rate.

items.q: The table shows data for a nation’s terms of trade. Which of the following statements about this nation’s terms of trade is correct?
o: They improved from Year 1 through to Year 3.
They deteriorated from Year 1 through to Year 3.
They deteriorated from Year 1 to Year 2 and then improved from Year 2 to Year 3.
They improved from Year 1 to Year 2 and then deteriorated from Year 2 to Year 3.

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Year 1 = 100; Year 2 = 110 ÷ 106 × 100 = 103.8; Year 3 = 115 ÷ 110 × 100 = 104.5. It rises each year.

not.B: Export prices rose faster than import prices throughout.
not.C: There was no deterioration in either period.
not.D: The index rose again from Year 2 (103.8) to Year 3 (104.5).

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. Given the changes in the data from Year 1 to Year 2 and from Year 2 to Year 3, what can be concluded about this economy?
o: The inflation rate has decreased and the volume of exports has fallen.
The inflation rate has increased and the economy is less internationally competitive.
The inflation rate has increased and the price of exports has increased at a faster rate than the price of imports.
The inflation rate has decreased and the price of exports has decreased at a faster rate than the price of imports.

e.why: Inflation fell from 8.3% (120 to 130) to 3.8% (130 to 135). The terms of trade index fell each year, so export prices were falling relative to import prices.

not.A: Inflation did fall, but the terms of trade measure prices, not the volume of exports.
not.B: Inflation decreased.
not.C: Inflation decreased, and falling terms of trade mean export prices lagged import prices.

items.q: Which of the following statements best describes the implementation and impact of economic policies?
o: Microeconomic policy is quickly implemented through the annual budget.
Microeconomic policy shifts the aggregate demand curve to improve productivity.
Monetary policy is quicker to implement than fiscal policy but takes longer to affect economic activity.
Monetary policy is slower to implement than fiscal policy and is quicker to affect economic activity.

e.why: The Reserve Bank can change the cash rate at a monthly meeting, but it takes 6 to 18 months to work through to spending. Fiscal changes are slower to pass but act on demand more directly.

not.A: Microeconomic reform is slow and is not mainly delivered through the Budget.
not.B: Microeconomic policy works on aggregate supply.
not.D: This is the reverse of the true pattern.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. What is the value of net foreign equity as a percentage of real GDP?

e.why: Net foreign liabilities = net foreign debt + net foreign equity, so equity = 780 − 550 = $230bn. As a share of GDP: 230 ÷ 1120 = 20.5%.

not.B: 30.3% does not come from these figures.
not.C: 49.1% is net foreign debt as a share of GDP (550 ÷ 1120).
not.D: 69.6% is net foreign liabilities as a share of GDP (780 ÷ 1120).

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to improve Australia’s international competitiveness?
o: An increase in domestic interest rates
An improvement in the terms of trade
An increase in the value of the Australian dollar

e.why: Structural change moves resources into more efficient industries, lowering costs and raising productivity.

not.B: Higher interest rates raise costs and push the dollar up.
not.C: The terms of trade measure prices received, not how competitive firms are.
not.D: A higher dollar makes exports dearer.

items.q: The graph shows the impact of the introduction of a tariff. Which of the following describes the impact of introducing this tariff?
o: Government revenue increased by the rectangle GHQ3Q2.
Resource allocation improved as the demand for imported products contracted from QQ1 to Q2 Q3 .
Consumers’ real income improved as the supply of locally made products expanded from Q to Q2.
Resources were reallocated from importers to local producers as imports fell from QQ1 to Q2 Q3 .

e.why: The tariff raises the price from P to P1. Local production expands from Q to Q2 and imports shrink from QQ1 to Q2Q3, so resources move towards local producers.

not.A: Tariff revenue is the tariff (P to P1) times imports (Q2 to Q3): the rectangle EFHG.
not.B: Protecting less efficient producers worsens the allocation of resources.
not.C: Consumers pay a higher price, so their real income falls.

items.q: What is the most likely impact of an appreciation of the Australian dollar?
o: Lower import prices and an increase in net foreign debt
Higher export prices and a deterioration of the terms of trade
An improvement in the current account deficit and an increase in inflation
A decrease in capital inflows and a decline in international competitiveness

e.why: A higher dollar makes Australian assets dearer for foreign investors and Australian goods dearer for foreign buyers.

not.A: Import prices do fall, but an appreciation reduces the value of foreign currency debt.
not.B: The terms of trade are measured from price indexes and do not deteriorate because of an appreciation.
not.C: An appreciation tends to worsen the current account and lower inflation.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. According to the data, which statement is correct for this economy?
o: Real GDP has increased and the quality of life has improved.
Real GDP has increased and the quality of life has declined.
Real GDP has decreased and the quality of life has improved.
Real GDP has decreased and the quality of life has declined.

e.why: Real GDP: Year 1 = 6000 ÷ 130 × 100 = 4615; Year 2 = 6800 ÷ 150 × 100 = 4533. It decreased. The HDI rose from 0.61 to 0.76, so quality of life improved.

not.A: Real GDP fell once the rise in prices is removed.
not.B: Real GDP fell and the HDI rose.
not.D: The HDI rose.

items.q: The table shows the Gini coefficient for Country A and Country B over three years. Which statement is correct given the data in the table?
o: The Lorenz curve for Country A is moving closer to the line of equality.
The Lorenz curve for Country B is moving away from the line of equality.
The Lorenz curve for Country A is further away from the line of equality than the Lorenz curve for Country B.
The Lorenz curve for Country B is further away from the line of equality than the Lorenz curve for Country A.

e.why: A higher Gini coefficient means a Lorenz curve further from the line of equality. Country B's coefficient is higher than Country A's in every year.

not.A: Country A's coefficient is rising, so its curve is moving away from equality.
not.B: Country B's coefficient is falling, so its curve is moving closer to equality.
not.C: Country A's coefficient is lower in every year.

items.q: The graph shows aggregate demand and aggregate supply curves for an economy. Other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to shift the aggregate supply curve from AS0 to AS1?
o: Increasing the rate of company taxation
Reducing tax incentives for research and development

e.why: AS has shifted to the right. Deregulating labour markets makes labour more flexible and productive, lowering production costs.

not.B: More regulation raises firms' costs.
not.C: Higher company tax reduces investment and supply.
not.D: Less support for research slows productivity growth.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to occur when the Australian government finances a budget deficit by borrowing from overseas?
o: The current account deficit will rise.

e.why: Interest on overseas borrowing is paid to foreigners, adding to the income deficit on the current account.

not.A: Borrowing overseas avoids pressure on domestic interest rates.
not.B: The money supply does not fall.
not.D: Funds flowing in raise demand for the dollar, which would appreciate.

items.q: Which of the following occurs when the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) increases?
o: The value of the multiplier increases and the equilibrium level of income falls.
The value of the multiplier increases and the equilibrium level of income rises.
The value of the multiplier decreases and the equilibrium level of income rises.
The value of the multiplier decreases and the equilibrium level of income falls.

e.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). A higher MPC means more of each dollar is re-spent, so the multiplier and equilibrium income both rise.

not.A: A larger multiplier raises income.
not.C: A higher MPC increases the multiplier.
not.D: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: The graph shows the demand and supply for Australian dollars ($A). Which of the following would cause the supply curve to shift from S0 to S1?
o: Increased demand for foreign assets by Australians
Decreased demand for foreign imports by Australians
Decreased demand for Australian assets by foreigners
Increased demand for Australian exports by foreigners

e.why: Supply of Australian dollars has increased. Australians buying foreign assets must sell dollars to obtain foreign currency.

not.B: Fewer imports reduce the supply of dollars.
not.C: Foreigners' demand for Australian assets affects the demand for dollars.
not.D: Export demand affects the demand for dollars.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. What would be the new equilibrium level of income (Y) in Year 4, if consumption (C) in this economy increases to $300m in Year 4 and the MPC remains constant?

e.why: Each 100 of extra income raises consumption by 50, so MPC = 0.5. Consumption rises by 100 (200 to 300), which needs income to rise by 200: Y = 600 + 200 = $800m.

not.A: $200m is the rise in income, not its new level.
not.B: $600m is the Year 3 level.
not.C: $700m adds only 100, which would mean an MPC of 1.

items.q: How would the size of the labour force and the rate of unemployment be affected if people retrenched from their jobs did not actively seek employment?
o: The labour force would be smaller and the unemployment rate would be lower.
The labour force would be smaller and the unemployment rate would be higher.
There would be no change in the labour force and the unemployment rate would be higher.
The labour force would be smaller and there would be no change in the unemployment rate.

e.why: People who do not look for work are not counted as unemployed or in the labour force, so the labour force shrinks by the jobs lost. The number unemployed is unchanged but is now a larger share of a smaller labour force.

not.A: The rate rises because the labour force is smaller.
not.C: The labour force shrinks because these people have left it.
not.D: The same number of unemployed in a smaller labour force is a higher rate.

items.q: Which of the following is a feature of a decentralised labour market?
o: A more flexible dispute resolution process to address wage claims
Minimum wage levels automatically adjusted to changes in the cost of living
Bargaining between unions and government to set pay and working conditions
Collective bargaining to set national benchmarks for pay and working conditions

e.why: In a decentralised system disputes and pay claims are settled at the workplace, which allows more flexible arrangements.

not.B: Automatic cost-of-living adjustments belong to centralised wage fixing.
not.C: Bargaining between unions and government is centralised.
not.D: National benchmarks are a feature of a centralised system.

items.q: Which of the following economic objectives can best be achieved simultaneously with economic growth?

e.why: Producing more output needs more workers, so growth and employment rise together.

not.A: Strong growth tends to push prices up.
not.B: Strong growth draws in imports, worsening the external balance.
not.D: More production usually means more resource use and pollution.

items.q: Which of the following microeconomic reforms is most likely to relate to a product market?
o: Reduction in marginal income tax rates
Deregulation of the Australian financial system
Introduction of the National Competition Policy

e.why: National Competition Policy increased competition among firms selling goods and services.

not.A: Labour is a factor of production, so this is a factor market.
not.B: Income tax changes affect incentives to work, a labour market matter.
not.C: Finance (capital) is a factor market.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. According to the information in the table, which statement is correct for the economy if it has a floating exchange rate?
o: There is a deficit of $225bn on the balance of goods and services.
There is a surplus of $140bn on the capital and financial account.
There is a surplus of $950bn on the current account.
There is a deficit of $10bn on the capital account.

e.why: Current account = (500 − 540) − 70 − 115 + 85 = −140. With a floating rate this is matched by a $140bn surplus on the capital and financial account.

not.A: Goods and services = −40 − 70 = −$110bn; $225bn also includes net income.
not.C: The current account is in deficit by $140bn.
not.D: Capital transfers of +30 are a surplus on the capital account.

items.q: The graph shows an economy in equilibrium at We. Qe Labour What will be the impact if the government set a minimum wage of W1?
o: The demand for labour will increase.
The labour force participation rate will fall.
There will be an increase in unemployment.
Firms will demand less labour at every wage rate.

e.why: At W1, above the equilibrium wage, more people want to work than firms want to employ. The gap is unemployment.

not.A: A higher wage reduces the quantity of labour demanded.
not.B: A higher wage attracts more people into the labour force.
not.D: The demand curve does not shift; firms move along it to a lower quantity.

items.q: Which of the following policies would lead to a rise in the natural rate of unemployment?
o: An increase in official interest rates
A decreased emphasis on wage decentralisation
A reduction in protection of manufacturing industries

e.why: Removing protection forces uncompetitive manufacturers to close. Their workers' skills do not match the jobs available, raising structural unemployment.

not.A: Interest rates affect cyclical unemployment.
not.B: Government spending affects cyclical unemployment.
not.C: A change in how wages are set does not displace workers in the way that removing protection does.

items.q: Which international organisation is responsible for maintaining international financial stability?
o: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development

e.why: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and lends to countries in financial crisis.

not.A: The World Bank funds development.
not.B: The WTO oversees trade rules.
not.D: The OECD is a policy forum.

items.q: The table shows Consumer Price Index (CPI) data by expenditure group for an economy. According to the data, which CPI expenditure group contributes most to the inflation rate?

e.why: Contribution = weight × price rise. Food 30 × 10 = 300; Health 10 × 30 = 300; Housing 15 × 25 = 375; Clothing 20 × 20 = 400. Clothing is the largest.

not.A: Food has the largest weight but the smallest price rise (300).
not.B: Health has the largest price rise but the smallest weight (300).
not.C: Housing contributes 375, less than Clothing.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase Australia’s international competitiveness?
o: Structural change and higher interest rates in Australia
Lower labour costs and improved infrastructure in Australia
Lower inflation in Australia and reduced import quotas on foreign cars
Productivity growth in Australia and appreciation of the Australian dollar

e.why: Lower labour costs and better infrastructure both reduce the cost of producing and moving Australian goods.

not.A: Higher interest rates raise firms' costs and push the dollar up.
not.C: Smaller import quotas are more protection, which reduces pressure to be efficient.
not.D: An appreciation makes exports dearer, offsetting the productivity gain.

items.q: Which of the following government policies is most likely to reduce the size of a negative externality?
o: Abolition of national park entry fees
Lowering rebates on sustainable energy sources
Reducing tax concessions on car parking spaces in the city

e.why: Cheap city parking encourages driving. Removing the tax concession makes driving in dearer, reducing congestion and pollution.

not.A: Cheaper petrol encourages more driving.
not.B: Free entry increases visitor numbers and damage to parks.
not.C: Smaller rebates discourage clean energy.

items.q: The graph shows that the Australian economy has moved from point X to point Y. Which policy mix is the most appropriate for this economy?
o: The Reserve Bank buys government securities and the Federal Government implements an expansionary budget.
The Reserve Bank sells government securities and the Federal Government implements an expansionary budget.
The Reserve Bank buys government securities and the Federal Government implements a contractionary budget.
The Reserve Bank sells government securities and the Federal Government implements a contractionary budget.

e.why: From X to Y the economy is heading into a downturn. Buying securities lowers interest rates and an expansionary budget adds to demand.

not.B: Selling securities raises interest rates, working against the budget.
not.C: A contractionary budget would deepen the downturn.
not.D: Both would deepen the downturn.

items.q: Which of the following policies is most likely to result in a decrease in demand inflation and an increase in cost inflation?
o: A decrease in non-discretionary government expenditure and loose monetary policy
An increase in non-discretionary government expenditure and increased import tariffs
An increase in discretionary government expenditure and a reduction in subsidies to producers
A decrease in discretionary government expenditure and a depreciation of the domestic currency

e.why: Less discretionary spending reduces demand. A depreciation makes imported goods and inputs dearer, raising costs.

not.A: Loose monetary policy adds to demand inflation.
not.B: More government spending adds to demand inflation.
not.C: More discretionary spending adds to demand inflation.

items.q: The table shows selected data for a hypothetical economy. What is the value of the multiplier?

e.why: Each year consumption rises by 100 and saving by 100, so income rises by 200 and MPC = 0.5. Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 2.

not.A: 0.2 does not come from these figures.
not.B: 0.5 is the MPC, not the multiplier.
not.C: A multiplier of 1 would mean nothing is re-spent.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to occur when a budget deficit is funded by selling new government securities?
o: Private sector borrowing costs will rise.
Private sector investment levels will increase.

e.why: The government competes with firms for the same pool of savings, pushing interest rates up (crowding out).

not.A: Borrowing existing savings does not create money.
not.B: Selling securities at home does not directly raise the current account deficit.
not.D: Higher borrowing costs reduce private investment.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to shift both the aggregate demand and aggregate supply curve to the right?
o: An increase in investment and a reduction in subsidies to producers
An increase in the budget deficit and a decrease in the cost of labour
An increase in the productivity of labour and an increase in interest rates
An increase in the budget surplus and an increase in the cost of raw materials

e.why: A larger budget deficit adds to demand (AD right). Cheaper labour lowers production costs (AS right).

not.A: Lower subsidies raise producers' costs, shifting AS left.
not.C: Higher interest rates shift AD left.
not.D: Both shift the curves to the left.

items.q: Which statement best describes public goods?
o: They are provided at zero marginal costs.
Property rights tend to be easily defined.

e.why: Public goods are non-rival: once provided, an extra user adds nothing to the cost.

not.B: No one can be excluded, so property rights are hard to define.
not.C: They are not sold, so they have no price.
not.D: They are non-rival and non-excludable.

items.q: Which scenario best demonstrates the benefits of a fixed exchange rate system?
o: A country experiencing a recession fixes its currency to that of a country in which interest rates are low.
A country experiencing a boom fixes its currency to that of a country experiencing a recession.
A country experiencing a recession fixes its exchange rate above the equilibrium rate.
A country experiencing a boom fixes its exchange rate below the equilibrium rate.

e.why: NESA accepted both A and D. In A, tying the currency to one with low interest rates brings lower rates to an economy in recession. In D, a rate held below equilibrium keeps exports competitive.

not.B: Tying a booming economy to one in recession would bring lower interest rates and add to the boom.
not.C: A rate above equilibrium makes exports dearer, deepening the recession.

items.q: The table shows the human development index (HDI) values for two countries. Which statement is most consistent with the HDI data given?
o: Adult literacy rates are higher in Country A than in Country B.
The level of urbanisation is greater in Country A than Country B.
The population growth rate in Country A is higher than in Country B.
Public institutions are more developed in Country A than in Country B.

e.why: Countries with a low HDI are less developed, and less developed countries typically have high birth rates.

not.A: Literacy is part of the HDI, so it is lower in Country A.
not.B: Urbanisation is higher in developed countries.
not.D: Institutions are weaker in less developed countries.

items.q: The table shows selected data on the composition of Australia’s GDP by industry. Which of the following is most likely to explain the trends in the table?
o: A decline in rural population and increased global demand for commodities
Greater financial integration and reduced levels of protection for Australian manufacturers
The deterioration of tourism infrastructure and the discovery of new mineral deposits outside Australia
The rise of efficient manufacturers in developing economies and an increase in the demand for agricultural products

e.why: Services have grown as finance and other services became globally integrated, and manufacturing has shrunk as tariffs were removed.

not.A: Stronger commodity demand would raise mining's share, not lower it.
not.C: Poorer tourism infrastructure would not produce a rise in services.
not.D: Stronger demand for farm products would raise agriculture's share.

items.q: The diagram refers to the distribution of income and wealth in a hypothetical economy. According to the diagram, which statement is correct for this economy?
o: Wealth has a higher Gini coefficient than income and the distribution of wealth is more unequal than the distribution of income.
Income has a higher Gini coefficient than wealth and the distribution of income is more unequal than the distribution of wealth.
Wealth has a lower Gini coefficient than income and the distribution of wealth is more unequal than the distribution of income.
Income has a higher Gini coefficient than wealth and the distribution of income is more equal than the distribution of wealth.

e.why: The wealth curve is further from the line of equality than the income curve. A curve further out means more inequality and a higher Gini coefficient.

not.B: The income curve is closer to the line of equality.
not.C: A more unequal distribution has a higher, not lower, Gini coefficient.
not.D: Income is more equal, so it has the lower Gini coefficient.

items.q: What would be the likely impact on an economy if the government increased quotas on imported cars?
o: The domestic price of cars would increase.
The market share of domestic producers would decline.
The supply of cars in the domestic market would decrease.
Foreign producers would find it more difficult to access the domestic market.

e.why: A larger quota lets more imported cars in, so local producers hold a smaller share of the market.

not.A: More supply lowers the price.
not.C: The supply of cars increases.
not.D: A larger quota makes access easier.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to slow the process of globalisation?
o: An increase in the world price of oil
A reduction in export subsidies by advanced economies

e.why: Dearer oil raises the cost of transporting goods around the world, which discourages trade.

not.A: Workers moving more freely between countries speeds up globalisation.
not.B: Cheaper communication speeds up globalisation.
not.D: Lower export subsidies are a reduction in protection, which frees up trade.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to reduce income inequality?
o: An increase in the minimum wage
Decentralisation of the wage determination system
Lower government funding for education and training

e.why: A higher minimum wage lifts the incomes of the lowest-paid workers, narrowing the gap with higher earners.

not.B: Lower benefits reduce the incomes of the poorest households.
not.C: Decentralised bargaining tends to widen wage differences.
not.D: Less education and training reduces the earning power of lower-income people.

items.q: Which of the following policies would be most likely to reduce an economy’s non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU)?
o: Policies that increase factor market competition
Policies that decrease product market competition

e.why: More competition in labour and other factor markets makes wages and employment more flexible, reducing structural unemployment and so the NAIRU.

not.A: Fiscal policy acts on cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.B: Monetary policy acts on cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.D: Less competition makes the economy less efficient.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. Which of the following statements is true for this economy?

e.why: Injections = G + I + X = 30 + 25 + 30 = 85. Withdrawals = S + T + M = 30 + 20 + 35 = 85. They are equal, so income is in equilibrium.

not.A: Income contracts only when withdrawals exceed injections.
not.B: Both total 85.
not.C: Both total 85.

items.q: The graph shows aggregate demand and aggregate supply for an economy. All other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to shift the aggregate supply curve from AS0 to AS1?
o: An increase in unit labour costs
An increase in the economy’s national income
An appreciation of the economy’s exchange rate

e.why: AS has shifted to the left. Higher labour costs per unit of output make production dearer at every price level.

not.B: Lower inflationary expectations restrain wage claims, shifting AS right.
not.C: A change in national income is a movement along the curves, not a shift of AS.
not.D: An appreciation lowers the cost of imported inputs, shifting AS right.

items.q: Which of the following combinations is most likely to reduce Australia’s export volumes?
o: The Australian dollar depreciates and there is a recession in the US economy.
The Australian dollar appreciates and there is a recession in the US economy.
The Australian dollar depreciates and there is an expansion in the US economy.
The Australian dollar appreciates and there is an expansion in the US economy.

e.why: An appreciation makes Australian exports dearer for foreign buyers, and a US recession reduces their demand.

not.A: A depreciation makes exports cheaper, working against the effect of the recession.
not.C: Both changes increase exports.
not.D: An appreciation hurts, but a US expansion raises demand.

items.q: The table shows data for a nation’s terms of trade. All other things being equal, which of the following policy actions is most likely to reduce the economic impact of the change in the nation’s terms of trade?
o: The Reserve Bank increases interest rates.
The Government increases income tax rates.
The Reserve Bank intervenes to increase the value of the currency.

e.why: The terms of trade have fallen (110 to 105), reducing export income and economic activity. Higher government spending offsets the fall in demand.

not.A: Higher interest rates would slow the economy further.
not.B: Higher taxes would slow the economy further.
not.D: A higher currency would make exports even less competitive.

items.q: All other things being equal, households that are most likely to benefit from an increase in the Consumer Price Index are those

e.why: Asset prices such as property and shares tend to rise with inflation, so the owners' wealth keeps its real value or grows.

not.B: A fixed income buys less as prices rise.
not.C: The real value of money in the bank falls.
not.D: Pensioners are on low, largely fixed incomes that lag behind price rises.

items.q: Which of the following is an economic cost of a rise in the Gini coefficient?
o: An increase in the mobility of labour
An increase in risk-taking by entrepreneurs
An increase in government welfare support

e.why: More inequality means more low-income households needing support, which costs the government more.

not.A: Faster growth would be a benefit, not a cost.
not.B: Greater mobility of labour is a benefit of wider wage differences.
not.C: More risk-taking is a benefit of larger rewards.

items.q: The graph shows the demand for and supply of Australian dollars. Which of the following is the most likely reason for the shift in the supply curve from S0 to S1?
o: An increase in foreign imports into Australia
An increase in foreign financial investment in Australia
A reduction in the net income deficit on the current account
A decline in the international competitiveness of Australian firms

e.why: Supply of Australian dollars has decreased. A smaller net income deficit means fewer dollars are sold to pay interest and dividends overseas.

not.A: More imports mean more dollars are supplied.
not.B: Foreign investment in Australia changes the demand for dollars, not the supply.
not.D: Less competitive firms mean more imports, increasing supply.

items.q: What is the most likely impact of a rise in the level of Australia’s interest rates relative to overseas interest rates?
o: An increase in foreign investment in Australia and a depreciation of the $A
An increase in foreign investment in Australia and an appreciation of the $A
A decrease in foreign investment in Australia and a depreciation of the $A
A decrease in foreign investment in Australia and an appreciation of the $A

e.why: Higher returns in Australia attract foreign funds. Investors must buy Australian dollars, so demand rises and the dollar appreciates.

not.A: More capital inflow raises the dollar.
not.C: Higher relative rates attract investment.
not.D: The dollar does appreciate, but because foreign investment rises.

items.q: What is the impact of an economic expansion on government revenues and expenditure?
o: Both progressive taxation receipts and unemployment benefit payments increase.
Both progressive taxation receipts and unemployment benefit payments decrease.
Progressive taxation receipts decrease and unemployment benefit payments increase.
Progressive taxation receipts increase and unemployment benefit payments decrease.

e.why: In an expansion incomes rise, so more income tax is collected, and unemployment falls, so fewer benefits are paid.

not.A: Unemployment benefits fall when more people have jobs.
not.B: Tax receipts rise with incomes.
not.C: This describes a downturn.

items.q: The table shows national accounts data for Consumption (C) and National Income (Y) in $ billion for an economy. What is the new equilibrium level of income (Y) in Year 3 if investment increases by $40bn?

e.why: Income rose by 150 and consumption by 90, so MPC = 0.6 and the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. Extra income = 2.5 × 40 = 100, so Y = 300 + 100 = $400bn.

not.A: $360bn uses a multiplier of 1.5.
not.B: $367bn uses a multiplier of 1 ÷ 0.6 instead of 1 ÷ 0.4.
not.D: $420bn uses a multiplier of 3.

items.q: In which of these situations are the net foreign liabilities of an economy most likely to increase?
o: Current account deficit and currency appreciation
Current account deficit and currency depreciation
Current account surplus and currency appreciation
Current account surplus and currency depreciation

e.why: A current account deficit is financed by borrowing or selling assets, adding to liabilities. A depreciation raises the Australian dollar value of debt owed in foreign currencies.

not.A: An appreciation reduces the value of foreign currency debt.
not.C: A surplus reduces liabilities.
not.D: A surplus reduces liabilities.

items.q: The table shows Balance of Payments data for a hypothetical economy with a floating exchange rate. What is the value of the Financial Account?

e.why: Current account = −15 + 5 − 50 + 5 = −55. The capital and financial account must be +55. With a capital account of 5, the financial account is 55 − 5 = $50bn.

not.A: $45bn leaves out one of the current account items.
not.C: $55bn is the whole capital and financial account.
not.D: $60bn adds the capital account instead of subtracting it.

items.q: Which is the most appropriate macroeconomic policy mix if the Australian economy is experiencing inflationary pressures?
o: A decrease in taxation and the sale of government securities by the Reserve Bank
A decrease in government spending and the sale of government securities by the Reserve Bank
An increase in taxation and the purchase of government securities by the Reserve Bank
An increase in government spending and the purchase of government securities by the Reserve Bank

e.why: Lower government spending reduces demand, and selling securities takes cash out of the system and raises interest rates. Both are contractionary.

not.A: Lower taxes increase spending.
not.C: Buying securities lowers interest rates.
not.D: Both would add to inflation.

items.q: The following graph shows the effect of a tariff on the price and quantity of imported shirts. Assume that the world price of shirts is $10 and that the tariff is $5 per shirt. By what amount does the revenue of foreign producers of shirts decrease as a result of the tariff?

e.why: At $10: demand 400, local supply 100, imports 300, so foreign revenue is 300 × $10 = $3000. With the tariff the price is $15: demand 300, local supply 200, imports 100. Foreign producers still receive $10, so revenue is $1000. The fall is $2000.

not.A: $500 is the tariff revenue (100 × $5).
not.B: $1000 is foreign producers' revenue after the tariff, not the fall.
not.C: $1500 is what consumers pay for imports after the tariff (100 × $15).

items.q: The table shows the gross domestic product per capita (GDP/Capita) and the Human Development Index (HDI) values for two countries. What can be correctly inferred from the data in the table?
o: Country A has a lower Gini coefficient than Country B.
Country A has a higher Gini coefficient than Country B.
Country A has a lower life expectancy and lower educational attainment than Country B.
Country A has a higher life expectancy and higher educational attainment than Country B.

e.why: The HDI combines income, life expectancy and education. Country A has a lower income but a higher HDI, so it must score higher on health and education.

not.A: The HDI says nothing about how income is distributed.
not.B: The HDI says nothing about how income is distributed.
not.C: With lower income and lower health and education, A's HDI would be lower.

items.q: Which of the following methods of financing an expansionary fiscal policy will be more likely to result in higher inflation?
o: Issuing government securities for sale in the domestic market
Issuing government securities for sale to foreign investors in a foreign currency

e.why: Borrowing from the central bank creates new money to pay for the spending, adding directly to demand.

not.A: Selling assets raises funds without creating money.
not.C: Borrowing existing savings does not add to the money supply and pushes interest rates up.
not.D: Borrowing overseas does not create new money at home.

items.q: An industry that generates pollution incurs both private and social costs. What will happen to the quantity and equilibrium price when BOTH private and social costs are taken into account?
o: Both output and price will fall.
Both output and price will rise.
Output will fall and the price will rise.
Output will rise and the price will fall.

e.why: Adding the social cost to firms' costs shifts supply to the left: less is produced and the price is higher.

not.A: Higher costs raise the price.
not.B: Higher costs reduce output.
not.D: This would happen if costs fell.

items.q: Which of the following is classified as a trading bloc?
o: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)

e.why: The EU is a group of countries with free trade among members and common barriers to others.

not.A: The UN is concerned with peace, security and development.
not.C: The G20 is a forum for policy coordination.
not.D: The OECD is a policy research forum.

items.q: What was one of the objectives of the national wage system established by the Fair Work Act 2009?
o: To reduce the number of awards
To reduce the national minimum wage
To remove the safety net protection for low paid workers

e.why: The Fair Work system replaced thousands of state and federal awards with a much smaller number of modern awards.

not.B: Enterprise agreements remain central to the system.
not.C: The minimum wage is reviewed each year and was not reduced.
not.D: The safety net was kept through the National Employment Standards and modern awards.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to occur as a country becomes more economically developed?
o: Agricultural production as a share of GDP increases

e.why: Development brings better education, health and capital, all of which raise output per worker.

not.A: Education levels rise with development.
not.C: Reliance on aid falls as incomes rise.
not.D: Agriculture shrinks as a share of GDP as industry and services grow.

items.q: What are the Reserve Bank of Australia’s main objectives in implementing monetary policy?
o: Price stability and a reduction in national debt
Full employment and an increase in national savings
Full employment and a more equal distribution of income

e.why: The Reserve Bank's charter refers to the stability of the currency, full employment and the economic prosperity and welfare of the people.

not.B: National debt is a matter for fiscal policy.
not.C: National savings are not an objective of monetary policy.
not.D: Income distribution is addressed mainly through fiscal policy.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. For Year 2, which policy mix is most appropriate for policy makers focused ONLY on employment outcomes?
o: Expansionary fiscal policy and expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal policy and expansionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy and contractionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal policy and contractionary monetary policy

e.why: Output has fallen and unemployment has risen to 8%. Both policies should stimulate demand to create jobs.

not.B: Contractionary fiscal policy would cost jobs.
not.C: Contractionary monetary policy would cost jobs.
not.D: Both would raise unemployment further.

items.q: The table shows employment data for an economy. Based on the data in the table, what is the change in the labour force between Year 1 and Year 2?

e.why: Labour force = employed + unemployed. Year 1: 200 000 + 600 000 + 100 000 = 900 000. Year 2: 210 000 + 640 000 + 110 000 = 960 000. The change is 60 000.

not.A: 40 000 is the change in full-time employment only.
not.B: 50 000 is the change in total employment; the unemployed are also in the labour force.
not.D: 70 000 is the change in the working age population.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. Based on the information in the table, which of the following is correct?

e.why: Taxation (60) is greater than government expenditure (50), so the budget is in surplus.

not.A: Exports (80) exceed imports (70): a trade surplus.
not.C: Injections (40 + 50 + 80 = 170) equal leakages (40 + 60 + 70 = 170).
not.D: Injections and leakages are equal at 170.

items.q: The unemployment rate rises from 4% to 6%. What is the most likely impact on the Federal Government’s income tax revenues and social security payments?

e.why: Fewer people in work means less income tax, and more people out of work means more unemployment benefits.

not.A: Income tax revenue falls when fewer people have jobs.
not.B: Social security payments rise with unemployment.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: All other things being equal, what impact will a decrease in domestic interest rates have on consumer spending and on the household savings rate?

e.why: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so households spend more and save a smaller share of income.

not.A: Spending rises when rates fall.
not.B: A lower return on saving reduces the saving rate.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: The Reserve Bank of Australia sells government securities. What is the most likely effect on the supply of cash in Exchange Settlement accounts and on interest rates?

head: Supply of cash in Exchange Settlement accounts
Interest rates

e.why: Banks pay for the securities from their exchange settlement accounts, so cash becomes scarcer and the cash rate rises.

not.A: Less cash pushes interest rates up.
not.B: Selling securities removes cash.
not.D: Selling securities removes cash from the accounts.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy with a floating exchange rate. From the data, what is the value of exports?

rows: Balance on the capital and financial account

e.why: A capital and financial account surplus of 200 means a current account deficit of 200. Current account = X − 700 + 100 − 150 + 50 = X − 700, so X − 700 = −200 and X = $500bn.

not.A: $900bn would give a current account surplus of 200.
not.B: $700bn would give a current account balance of zero.
not.D: $300bn would give a deficit of 400.

items.q: Which of the following government policy decisions would be most suitable for achieving environmental sustainability?
o: Impose a tax on firms that cause either a positive or negative externality
Pay a subsidy to firms that cause either a positive or negative externality
Impose a tax on firms that cause a positive externality and pay a subsidy to firms that cause a negative externality
Pay a subsidy to firms that cause a positive externality and impose a tax on firms that cause a negative externality

e.why: A subsidy encourages activities with benefits to others, and a tax makes polluters pay for the costs they impose.

not.A: Taxing a positive externality discourages a beneficial activity.
not.B: Subsidising a negative externality encourages a harmful activity.
not.C: This rewards harm and penalises benefit.

items.q: Which of the following statements best applies to public goods?
o: These goods are subject to over-pricing.
There are fixed supplies of these goods.
Consumers must pay to use these goods.
Consumers can access these goods without paying directly for them.

e.why: Public goods are non-excludable: people cannot be charged at the point of use, so they are funded from taxation.

not.A: They are not priced in a market at all.
not.B: Their supply is decided by government and is not fixed.
not.C: People cannot be made to pay directly, which is why markets do not provide them.

items.q: The following diagram shows aggregate demand (AD) and aggregate supply (AS) curves for the Australian economy. All other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to cause the shift in the aggregate supply curve from AS1 to AS2?
o: An increase in the budget surplus
An increase in the minimum wage for casual workers
An increase in interest rates by the Reserve Bank of Australia

e.why: AS has shifted to the right. Higher labour productivity lowers the cost of each unit of output and raises productive capacity.

not.A: The budget balance affects aggregate demand.
not.C: A higher minimum wage raises costs, shifting AS to the left.
not.D: Interest rates affect aggregate demand.

items.q: The table shows population and employment data for an economy. Which of the following statements is correct for Year 2 compared to Year 1?
o: Year 2 has a lower participation rate and lower unemployment rate.
Year 2 has a lower participation rate and higher unemployment rate.
Year 2 has a higher participation rate and lower unemployment rate.
Year 2 has a higher participation rate and higher unemployment rate.

e.why: Year 1: labour force 24 million; participation 24 ÷ 30 = 80%; unemployment 3 ÷ 24 = 12.5%. Year 2: labour force 30 million; participation 30 ÷ 40 = 75%; unemployment 3 ÷ 30 = 10%. Both are lower.

not.B: Unemployment falls from 12.5% to 10%.
not.C: Participation falls from 80% to 75%.
not.D: Both rates fall.

items.q: All other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to cause an increase in Australia’s current account deficit?
o: A decrease in Australian overseas aid
An increase in the Federal Government’s budget surplus
An increase in the number of overseas students studying in Australia

e.why: When national savings fall short of investment, the gap is funded from overseas, and the cost of servicing that borrowing adds to the current account deficit.

not.B: Less aid means smaller secondary income debits, reducing the deficit.
not.C: A larger budget surplus adds to national savings.
not.D: Overseas students are an export of services.

items.q: The table shows the exchange rate of the Australian dollar ($A) expressed as units of foreign currency per $A. How has the exchange rate of the Australian dollar changed in Year 2 compared to Year 1?
o: It has appreciated against the Euro and depreciated against the Yen.
It has depreciated against the Euro and appreciated against the Yen.
It has appreciated against the Euro and depreciated against the $US.
It has depreciated against the Euro and appreciated against the $US.

e.why: One Australian dollar buys more euros (0.7 to 0.8), so it appreciated against the euro. It buys fewer US dollars (1.10 to 1.00), so it depreciated against the US dollar.

not.A: It buys more yen (80 to 90), so it appreciated against the yen.
not.B: It appreciated against the euro.
not.D: It appreciated against the euro and depreciated against the US dollar.

items.q: The diagram shows the impact of a subsidy paid to domestic producers on the price and quantity of beach towels. Assume that the equilibrium price of beach towels with the subsidy is $10 per towel. From the diagram, what is the subsidy (per towel) paid to domestic producers?

e.why: The subsidy is the vertical gap between the two supply curves. At the quantity of 20, producers need $12 without the subsidy (S1) but accept $10 with it (S2): a subsidy of $2.

not.B: $4 is the gap between $12 and $8, two prices on the axis, not the gap between the curves at one quantity.
not.C: $8 is a price on the axis.
not.D: $12 is a price on the axis.

items.q: An increase in investment of $5000 increases the equilibrium level of national income by $20 000. What is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

e.why: The multiplier is 20 000 ÷ 5000 = 4. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), 1 − MPC = 0.25 and MPC = 0.75.

not.A: An MPC of 0.2 gives a multiplier of 1.25.
not.B: 0.25 is the MPS.
not.D: An MPC of 0.8 gives a multiplier of 5.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to reduce Australia’s import volumes?

e.why: In a recession households and firms buy less of everything, including imports. A depreciation makes imports dearer.

not.A: A recession reduces imports, but an appreciation makes them cheaper.
not.B: A depreciation reduces imports, but an expansion raises demand for them.
not.C: Both changes increase imports.

items.q: Which of the following international organisations is most likely to be involved in financing the construction of a dam in a developing country?
o: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development

e.why: The World Bank lends to developing countries for infrastructure and development projects such as dams.

not.B: The WTO oversees trade rules and does not lend.
not.C: The IMF lends to stabilise economies in financial crisis.
not.D: The OECD is a policy forum of mostly advanced economies.

items.q: What is the most common reason given for a country to increase tariff protection?
o: To reduce the rate of domestic inflation
To lower the level of domestic interest rates

e.why: Governments most often justify tariffs as protecting local jobs from import competition.

not.A: Tariffs reduce trade volumes.
not.C: Tariffs raise prices, adding to inflation.
not.D: Tariffs have no direct effect on interest rates.

items.q: The diagram shows the Lorenz curves for Country A and Country B. Which of the following statements is most likely to explain the different income distribution in Country A and Country B?
o: Country A has higher rates of saving than Country B.
Country A has higher GDP per capita than Country B.
Country A has higher social welfare spending than Country B.
Country A has higher incentives for entrepreneurs than Country B.

e.why: Country A's curve is closer to the line of equality, so its income is more evenly shared. Higher welfare spending redistributes income to lower-income households.

not.A: Saving rates do not explain a more equal distribution.
not.B: Average income says nothing about how income is shared.
not.D: Stronger incentives for entrepreneurs usually go with wider income differences.

items.q: Which of the following statements about free trade agreements is correct?
o: They reduce trade between member countries.
They treat member and non­member countries in the same way.
They can divert trade from efficient non­member countries to inefficient member countries.
They prevent member countries entering into bilateral free trade agreements with non­members.

e.why: Preferential treatment can lead members to buy from each other even when a non-member produces more cheaply. This is trade diversion.

not.A: They increase trade between members.
not.B: Members receive preferential treatment over non-members.
not.D: Members are free to sign other agreements.

items.q: Which of the following is likely to encourage the hidden unemployed to enter the labour force?
o: An increase in the unemployment rate
An increase in marginal income tax rates
A reduction in funding of traineeship programs

e.why: Hidden unemployed people want to work but are not looking. Cheaper childcare removes a barrier for parents, so they start looking for work.

not.B: Higher unemployment discourages more people from looking.
not.C: Higher tax rates reduce the reward for working.
not.D: Less funding for traineeships removes a path into work.

items.q: Which of the following discretionary changes to taxation and transfer payments is most likely to have the greatest expansionary effect on the economy?

e.why: Lower taxes and higher transfer payments both raise household disposable income and spending.

not.A: Higher taxes offset the higher transfers.
not.B: Lower transfers offset the lower taxes.
not.D: Both changes are contractionary.

items.q: There is an increase in the minimum rate of employer superannuation contributions from 9% to 12% of wages. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this increase?

e.why: Higher compulsory contributions raise the cost of employing each worker. Firms pass higher costs on as higher prices: cost inflation.

not.B: Labour costs rise; they do not fall.
not.C: The change works through firms' costs, not through extra spending.
not.D: The main effect is on costs, not demand.

items.q: The non­accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) is most likely to be reduced by increasing

e.why: The NAIRU reflects structural unemployment. Retraining gives job seekers the skills employers need, reducing the mismatch.

not.B: Higher benefits can reduce the incentive to take a job.
not.C: Protection slows structural change; it does not make workers more employable.
not.D: Infrastructure spending mainly reduces cyclical unemployment.

items.q: Which of the following describes the market equilibrium price and output in the presence of a negative externality?

e.why: Producers ignore the external cost, so the market price is below the true social cost and too much is produced.

not.A: The price is too low because it leaves out the external cost.
not.B: Output is too high, not too low.
not.D: This describes a positive externality.

items.q: The table shows current account data for a hypothetical economy with a floating exchange rate. What is the balance on the capital account?

e.why: Current account = 100 − 120 − 140 − 40 = −200. With a floating exchange rate a current account deficit of $200 billion is matched by a surplus of $200 billion on the capital and financial account.

not.A: $160 billion leaves out net secondary income, and the balance is a surplus.
not.B: $160 billion leaves out net secondary income (−40).
not.C: The size is right, but a current account deficit is offset by a surplus.

items.q: Which of the following types of unemployment is NOT affected by the rise in mining sector activity or the decline in manufacturing sector activity?

e.why: Seasonal unemployment follows the time of year, such as fruit picking. It is not affected by the long-term shift from manufacturing to mining.

not.B: Workers moving between industries spend time between jobs.
not.C: A change in the structure of industry is the cause of structural unemployment.
not.D: Displaced manufacturing workers without the right skills can be out of work for long periods.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase a manufacturing firm’s productivity?
o: An increase in personal income tax rates
An increase in investment in capital goods
A decrease in demand by consumers for the firm’s product
A decrease in the size of the import quota for similar products

e.why: More and better machinery lets each worker produce more.

not.A: Income tax rates do not change what a firm's workers can produce.
not.C: Lower demand reduces sales, not output per worker.
not.D: A smaller quota gives more protection and less pressure to improve.

items.q: Which combination of actions by the Reserve Bank of Australia is most likely to cause a rise in the value of the Australian dollar?

e.why: Selling foreign currency means buying Australian dollars, adding to demand. A higher cash rate attracts foreign funds, also adding to demand.

not.A: Buying foreign currency means selling Australian dollars, which lowers the dollar.
not.B: A lower cash rate reduces demand for the dollar.
not.D: Both actions lower the dollar.

items.q: Which combination of changes in interest rates and the value of the Australian dollar is most likely to increase aggregate demand in the Australian economy?

e.why: Lower interest rates raise consumption and investment. A lower dollar makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, raising net exports.

not.A: Both changes reduce aggregate demand.
not.C: Lower rates help, but an appreciation reduces net exports.
not.D: A depreciation helps, but higher rates reduce spending.

items.q: There is a decline in the marginal propensity to consume (MPC). Which combination of changes in the simple multiplier and equilibrium income is most likely to result?

e.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). A lower MPC means a smaller multiplier, and with less consumption equilibrium income falls.

not.A: Both are the wrong direction.
not.C: The multiplier does fall, but so does income.
not.D: A lower MPC reduces the multiplier.

items.q: Australia’s interest rates are reduced while those of its major trading partners remain unchanged. Which combination of changes in the supply of $A and the trade weighted index is most likely to result?

e.why: Lower Australian rates lead investors to sell Australian dollars and move funds overseas. The supply of dollars rises and the dollar falls against trading partners' currencies.

not.A: A greater supply of dollars lowers the TWI.
not.B: The TWI does fall, but because supply increases.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: Which combination of actions does the Reserve Bank of Australia need to take in order to implement a contractionary monetary policy?

e.why: Selling securities takes cash out of the banking system, reducing the money supply and pushing interest rates up.

not.A: Buying securities adds cash: expansionary.
not.C: Selling securities reduces the money supply.
not.D: Buying securities increases the money supply.

items.q: Australia’s headline annual (CPI) inflation rate has fallen from 3% to 2%, while the underlying annual inflation rate remains unchanged at 3%. The divergence between these two measures of inflation is most likely due to
o: a decrease in world oil supply.
an increase in world oil supply.

e.why: More oil lowers petrol prices. Petrol is a volatile item that is counted in headline inflation but excluded from underlying.

not.A: Established house prices are not in the CPI.
not.B: Established house prices are not in the CPI.
not.C: Less oil would raise petrol prices and headline inflation.

items.q: The following table shows the volume and price of exports and imports for two years. How have the terms of trade and the volume of net exports changed between Year 1 and Year 2?

e.why: Terms of trade = export prices ÷ import prices × 100 = 110 ÷ 105 × 100 = 104.8, a rise from 100. Net export volume goes from 100 − 100 = 0 to 105 − 110 = −5, a decrease.

not.A: The terms of trade rose, but import volumes grew faster than export volumes.
not.B: Export prices rose more than import prices, so the terms of trade rose.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: The diagram shows the effect of a tariff on domestic supply (SS) and demand (DD). The free trade price is $20. The current tariff is $10. If the government reduces the tariff to $5, which combination of outcomes is correct? Tariff revenue Domestic output
