e.why: With a $10 tariff the price is $30, the no-trade equilibrium: no imports, no revenue, and local output of 100. With a $5 tariff the price is $25: local output falls to 90 and imports are 20, so revenue rises to 20 × $5 = $100.

not.A: Revenue rises, but a lower price reduces local output.
not.B: Local output falls, but revenue rises from zero.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: Which of the following is a trading bloc?
o: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)

e.why: A trading bloc is a group of countries that reduce trade barriers among themselves. The EU is the largest example.

not.B: The WTO is a global organisation that oversees trade rules.
not.C: The GATT was the global agreement that preceded the WTO.
not.D: The OECD is a policy forum, not a trade arrangement.

items.q: Of which of the following groups is Australia a member?
o: The North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)
The Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN)

e.why: Australia is one of the 19 countries (plus the EU) in the G20.

not.A: The G8 was made up of the largest advanced economies and Russia; Australia was not a member.
not.C: NAFTA covered the United States, Canada and Mexico.
not.D: ASEAN is made up of South-East Asian nations; Australia is a partner, not a member.

items.q: Which of the following would be most likely to occur if there was a recession in the domestic economy?

e.why: In a recession incomes and employment fall, so less income tax is collected.

not.A: Defence spending is not linked to the business cycle.
not.B: Transfer payments rise as more people become unemployed.
not.C: Spending falls, so GST receipts fall.

items.q: In which of the following circumstances could the International Monetary Fund (IMF) be called in to assist a country?

e.why: The IMF lends to countries that cannot meet their international payments and helps stabilise them in a financial crisis.

not.A: Trade disputes are handled by the WTO.
not.C: Investment disputes are not the IMF's role.
not.D: Infrastructure funding is the role of the World Bank.

items.q: In 1983 Australia moved from a fixed to a floating exchange rate. Which of the following has been a disadvantage of the floating exchange rate?

e.why: A floating rate moves with demand and supply every day, creating uncertainty for exporters, importers and borrowers.

not.A: Needing fewer reserves is an advantage of floating.
not.B: A floating rate does not require higher reserves.
not.D: Volatility increased, and less volatility would not be a disadvantage.

items.q: A second airport is to be built in Sydney. Which of the following best describes a positive externality likely to arise from this project?
o: Reduced job opportunities around the second airport
Increased traffic congestion around the second airport
Reduced traffic congestion around the existing airport
Increased job opportunities around the existing airport

e.why: A positive externality is a benefit to people outside the project. Diverting flights reduces congestion for people near the existing airport.

not.A: Fewer jobs would be a cost, and the new airport creates jobs.
not.B: More congestion is a negative externality.
not.D: Jobs around the existing airport are more likely to fall than rise.

items.q: An economy is operating at its natural rate of unemployment. What would be the long term effect on the unemployment rate and the participation rate of an increase in labour market flexibility?

e.why: More flexible labour markets match workers to jobs more easily, lowering structural unemployment, and offer working arrangements that draw more people into the labour force.

not.A: Flexibility lowers the natural rate of unemployment.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.
not.D: Unemployment does fall, but participation rises.

items.q: The table shows selected data for an economy. According to the data, what has happened to the consumer price index (CPI) between 2013 and 2014?
o: The CPI has fallen by less than the change in nominal GDP.
The CPI has fallen by more than the change in nominal GDP.
The CPI has risen by less than the change in nominal GDP.
The CPI has risen by more than the change in nominal GDP.

e.why: Nominal GDP rose 5% but real GDP rose 3%. The difference, about 2%, is the rise in prices, which is less than the 5% rise in nominal GDP.

not.A: Nominal GDP grew faster than real GDP, so prices rose.
not.B: Prices rose; they did not fall.
not.D: Prices rose by about 2%, less than the 5% rise in nominal GDP.

items.q: If a government stopped funding education, what would happen to the market equilibrium price and quantity of education?

e.why: Government funding acts like a subsidy that increases supply. Removing it shifts supply left, so the price rises and the quantity falls.

not.A: This is what happens when funding is increased.
not.B: A fall in supply raises the price.
not.C: A fall in supply reduces the quantity.

items.q: The graph shows the demand for, and supply of, Australian dollars. Which combination of shifts in the demand and supply curves must result in a depreciation of the Australian dollar? Demand curve shift Supply curve shift

e.why: Lower demand for the dollar and greater supply of it both push its value down, so the result is certain.

not.B: Demand left lowers the value but supply left raises it: the result is uncertain.
not.C: Both shifts raise the value of the dollar.
not.D: Demand right raises the value but supply right lowers it: the result is uncertain.

items.q: Which of the following best illustrates the effect of reduced competition on product markets?

e.why: With fewer competitors, firms have more market power: they can restrict output and charge more.

not.A: This is the effect of more competition.
not.B: Less competition raises prices.
not.C: Less competition reduces the quantity sold.

items.q: The table shows consumer price index (CPI) data for a hypothetical economy. What is the inflation rate for this economy for 2013?

not.A: 3% does not come from these figures.
not.C: 5 is the rise in index points in 2012.
not.D: 6 is the rise in index points, not a percentage.

items.q: Australia’s mining boom has resulted in a significant increase in foreign investment. Which of the following shows the effects of this increase on Australia’s Balance of Payments?

e.why: Foreign investment flowing in is a credit on the capital and financial account. The profits and interest later paid to the foreign investors are debits on the primary income account.

not.A: Inflows of investment are credits, and the income paid out is a debit.
not.B: Income paid to foreign investors is a debit.
not.C: Investment flowing into Australia is a credit.

items.q: The Reserve Bank of Australia decides to implement an expansionary monetary policy. Which of the following changes to commercial banks’ holdings of assets is most likely to occur?

head: Commercial banks’ holdings of Commonwealth Government securities
Commercial banks’ holdings of cash in exchange settlement accounts

e.why: To lower the cash rate the Reserve Bank buys government securities from the banks. Banks hold fewer securities and more cash in their exchange settlement accounts.

not.B: The banks sell securities to the Reserve Bank, so their holdings fall.
not.C: The banks receive cash for the securities, so their cash rises.
not.D: This is what happens when monetary policy is tightened.

items.q: The diagram shows the Lorenz curves for a hypothetical economy. The Lorenz curve has shifted from A to B. All other things being equal, which of the following changes might explain this shift? Change in the top marginal tax rate Change in business profits

e.why: Curve B is further from the line of equality, so inequality has increased. A lower top tax rate and higher business profits both raise the incomes of high earners.

not.B: Lower business profits reduce the incomes of high earners.
not.C: A higher top tax rate reduces inequality.
not.D: Both changes would reduce inequality.

items.q: The table shows components of the Balance of Payments for a hypothetical economy. What is the balance on the Financial Account?

rows: Components of the Balance of Payments

e.why: Current account = 10 − 20 − 5 = −15. The capital and financial account must be +15. With a capital account of 1, the financial account is 15 − 1 = $14 billion surplus.

not.A: A deficit on the current account is offset by a surplus on the financial account.
not.B: The financial account is in surplus, and 16 adds the capital account instead of subtracting it.
not.D: $16 billion adds the capital account instead of subtracting it.

items.q: Australia has a lower minimum wage for youth than for adults. Which of the following is most likely to cause an increase in youth unemployment?

e.why: If the youth wage rises and the adult wage does not, young workers become more expensive relative to adults, so employers hire fewer of them.

not.A: A higher adult wage makes young workers relatively cheaper.
not.B: No change in wages gives no reason for a change.
not.C: If both rise, the relative cost of young workers changes less.

items.q: The table shows National Accounts data for consumption (C ) and national income (Y) for a hypothetical economy. An increase in exports lifted national income by $100 million in Year 3. All other things being equal, what was the increase in exports?

e.why: Income rose by 50 and consumption by 40, so MPC = 0.8 and the multiplier is 5. The rise in exports = 100 ÷ 5 = $20 million.

not.B: $25 million would need a multiplier of 4.
not.C: $75 million does not come from the multiplier.
not.D: $80 million is the extra consumption (0.8 × 100), not the initial rise in exports.

items.q: Consider an economy in which there is a tariff of $15 in addition to the world price of $10. If the government reduces the tariff from $15 to $10, what will be the change in tariff revenue?

e.why: With a $15 tariff the price is $25, the no-trade equilibrium, so there are no imports and no revenue. With a $10 tariff the price is $20: supply 40 million, demand 60 million, imports 20 million. Revenue = 20 million × $10 = $200 million, a rise of $200 million.

not.A: $100 million would be a $5 tariff on 20 million imports.
not.C: $400 million is total spending on imports (20 million × $20).
not.D: $600 million is not tariff revenue at either tariff.

items.q: Consider an economy that operates a free trade policy. The government is proposing to introduce a $5 tariff in addition to the world price of $10. What import quota could the government introduce to have the same effect on domestic output as a $5 tariff?

e.why: A $5 tariff makes the price $15, at which local firms produce 30 million and consumers buy 70 million. Imports are 40 million, so a quota of 40 million gives the same domestic output.

not.A: 20 million is the level of imports at a price of $20.
not.B: 30 million is domestic output at $15, not the import quota.
not.D: 60 million is the level of imports under free trade (80 − 20).

items.q: Assume that foreign producers are selling canned tomatoes in Australia at below their cost of production. Domestic producers ask the government to impose a tariff on these imports. What is the most likely reason for this request?

e.why: Selling in another country below the cost of production is dumping. A tariff raises the price of the dumped goods so local producers are not driven out unfairly.

not.B: Canned tomatoes are not a defence industry.
not.C: An infant industry is new and still growing; nothing says this one is.
not.D: Jobs may be protected as a result, but the request is prompted by the below-cost pricing.

items.q: Which of the following economic policies has the shortest time lag for implementation?

e.why: The Reserve Bank can change the cash rate at a single board meeting, with effect the next day.

not.A: Fiscal measures usually wait for the Budget and need to pass Parliament.
not.C: Labour market changes need legislation and consultation.
not.D: Microeconomic reform takes years to legislate and put in place.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase gross world product?
o: Increased investment by transnational corporations in developing countries

e.why: Investment by transnational corporations brings capital, technology and jobs to developing countries, raising their output and so world output.

not.A: Higher interest rates slow spending and growth.
not.B: Migration to developing countries does not in itself raise world output.
not.C: Protection reduces trade and world output.

items.q: Which of the following could be a negative impact of foreign direct investment in an emerging economy?
o: An increase in the country’s Human Development Index from 0.6 to 0.8
An increase in the influence of transnational corporations on government regulation

e.why: Large foreign firms can pressure governments to weaken labour, tax or environmental rules in their favour.

not.A: More public goods is a benefit.
not.B: Better transport infrastructure is a benefit.
not.C: A higher HDI is an improvement in development.

items.q: Australia provides foreign aid to build schools in a developing country. This will be entered in Australia’s Balance of Payments as a

e.why: Aid tied to a capital project such as building schools is a capital transfer, recorded in the capital account. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

not.B: Primary income is earnings such as interest, dividends and wages.
not.C: Aid is not an investment, and an outflow is not a credit.
not.D: It is a debit, but secondary income records unconditional transfers, not aid for capital works.

items.q: A government wants to increase the efficiency of its domestic industries in order to improve their international competitiveness. Which combination of trade policies would be most likely to achieve this?

e.why: A larger quota lets in more imports and a smaller subsidy removes support. Both expose local firms to competition, forcing them to become more efficient.

not.A: A smaller quota is more protection.
not.B: A larger subsidy shelters firms from competition.
not.D: Both changes increase protection.

items.q: The table shows Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, inflation and unemployment rate data for an advanced economy with an inflation target of 2–3%. With reference to the data in the table, which policy response would be best for this economy?
o: Expansionary fiscal and expansionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal and contractionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal and expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal and contractionary monetary policy

e.why: Growth is strong, unemployment is falling and inflation (3.8%) is above the 2–3% target. Demand needs to be slowed by both policies.

not.A: Stimulating demand would push inflation higher.
not.B: The two policies would work against each other.
not.C: The two policies would work against each other.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to operate as an automatic stabiliser during an upswing in the Australian economy?

e.why: Income tax is progressive. As incomes rise in an upswing, people pay a higher share in tax, which automatically slows the growth of spending.

not.B: Company tax is charged at a flat rate, so it does not take a rising share of profits.
not.C: Tariff revenue is small and not designed to respond to the cycle.
not.D: The GST is a flat 10%, so it does not take a rising share of spending.

items.q: The diagram shows changes in the demand for, and supply of, Australian dollars ($A). Which of the following statements is most likely to explain the change in the equilibrium value of the $A illustrated in the diagram?
o: The $A has appreciated because of an increase in demand for Australian exports.
The $A has depreciated because of reduced microeconomic reform in the US economy.
The $A has appreciated because of a rise in the number of overseas tourists visiting Australia.
The $A has depreciated because of a rise in foreign interest rates relative to Australian interest rates.

e.why: Demand for Australian dollars has shifted to the left, lowering the equilibrium value. Higher interest rates overseas draw funds away from Australia, reducing demand for the dollar.

not.A: The dollar has depreciated, and stronger export demand would raise demand for it.
not.B: The dollar has depreciated, but less reform in the US would not reduce demand for Australian dollars.
not.C: The dollar has depreciated, and more tourists would raise demand for it.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. What is the effect of the changes from Year 1 to Year 2 on the terms of trade and international competitiveness of this economy?

e.why: Terms of trade fall from 100 to 100 ÷ 110 × 100 = 90.9. The TWI rises from 60 to 70, an appreciation, which makes exports dearer and reduces competitiveness.

not.A: Import prices rose while export prices did not, so the terms of trade fell.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.
not.D: The terms of trade did fall, but an appreciation reduces competitiveness.

items.q: Which of the following government policies would be most likely to reduce an economy’s Gini coefficient?
o: A decrease in the goods and services tax rate and a decrease in transfer payments
A decrease in expenditure on health and an increase in deregulation of the labour market
An increase in childcare subsidies for low-income earners and an increase in the highest marginal income tax rate
An increase in the income tax free threshold and a decrease in compulsory employer superannuation contributions

e.why: A lower Gini coefficient means less inequality. Childcare subsidies raise the incomes of low earners and a higher top tax rate takes more from high earners.

not.A: A lower GST helps, but cutting transfer payments hurts low-income households.
not.B: Both changes increase inequality.
not.D: A higher tax-free threshold helps, but lower superannuation contributions reduce workers' income.

items.q: A firm invests in a new, environmentally sustainable method for recycling used aluminium soft drink cans. Which of the following best describes the likely economic outcome that will result from this innovation?
o: A positive externality and a reduction in social costs
A negative externality and an increase in social costs
A positive externality and a reduction in social benefits
A negative externality and an increase in social benefits

e.why: Recycling benefits the wider community through less waste and less mining, a positive externality, and it lowers the costs society bears.

not.B: The effect on third parties is beneficial, not harmful.
not.C: A positive externality adds to social benefits.
not.D: The externality is positive.

items.q: The graph shows aggregate demand (AD) and aggregate supply (AS ) curves for an economy. Which of the following is most likely to reflect government policy designed to increase efficiency and equilibrium output?
o: AS curve shifts to the left.
AD curve shifts to the left.
AS curve shifts to the right.
AD curve shifts to the right.

e.why: Policies that raise efficiency (microeconomic reform) lower costs and increase productive capacity, shifting AS to the right and raising output.

not.A: AS shifting left means higher costs and lower output.
not.B: AD shifting left lowers output and is not about efficiency.
not.D: AD shifting right raises output but through demand, not efficiency.

items.q: The table shows labour market data for a hypothetical economy: Year 1 — unemployment rate 7%, participation rate 65%; Year 2 — unemployment rate 5%, participation rate 60%. Which of the following reasons would account for these changes from Year 1 to Year 2? (Each option gives a reason for the change in the unemployment rate, then a reason for the change in the participation rate.)
o: Global economic recession / A reduction in the number of skilled migrants
Fewer incentives to hire the long-term unemployed / Increased job training for the unemployed
Increased government spending on infrastructure / An increase in childcare subsidy payments
Increased consumer confidence / Increase in school retention rates

head: Reason for change in the unemployment rate
Reason for change in the participation rate
rows: A reduction in the number of skilled migrants
Fewer incentives to hire the long- term unemployed
Increased job training for the unemployed
An increase in childcare subsidy payments

e.why: Unemployment fell: stronger consumer confidence means more spending and more jobs. Participation fell: more young people staying at school means fewer in the labour force.

not.A: A global recession would raise unemployment.
not.B: Fewer incentives to hire the long-term unemployed would raise unemployment.
not.C: Infrastructure spending would lower unemployment, but childcare subsidies would raise participation.

items.q: Which of the following could lead to a deterioration in the structural component of Australia’s current account deficit?
o: An increase in net foreign liabilities
A decrease in portfolio investment by foreign firms
A decrease in export volumes due to a weakening global economy
An increase in imports resulting from an improvement in the terms of trade

e.why: Higher net foreign liabilities mean larger interest and dividend payments overseas every year, a long-term (structural) addition to the primary income deficit.

not.B: A change in portfolio investment is in the financial account.
not.C: A weak global economy is a cyclical influence.
not.D: A change in the terms of trade is a cyclical influence.

items.q: The table refers to a hypothetical economy. If the government wishes to raise the level of national income by $1000 in Year 4, by how much will it have to increase investment?

e.why: Saving rises by 100 for each 500 of income, so MPS = 0.2 and the multiplier is 5. To raise income by $1000, investment must rise by 1000 ÷ 5 = $200.

not.A: $100 would need a multiplier of 10.
not.C: $500 would need a multiplier of 2.
not.D: $800 is the MPC (0.8) × $1000, the extra consumption, not the investment needed.

items.q: The Reserve Bank of Australia purchases Commonwealth Government Securities in order to alter the cash rate. Which of the following is the most likely result of this decision?

e.why: Buying securities puts more cash into the banking system, lowering the cash rate. Lower rates reduce demand for the dollar (it depreciates) and raise spending (GDP rises).

not.A: These are the effects of a higher cash rate.
not.B: The dollar does depreciate, but lower rates raise GDP.
not.D: GDP does rise, but lower rates depreciate the dollar.

items.q: The table contains nominal data on the components of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for a hypothetical economy. Assume that the consumer price index for this economy increases from 100 in Year 1 to 110 in Year 2. What is the growth rate of real GDP in Year 2?

e.why: GDP = C + I + G + X − M. Year 1 = 1000; Year 2 = 550 + 250 + 300 + 200 − 200 = 1100. Real GDP in Year 2 = 1100 ÷ 110 × 100 = 1000, so real growth is 0%.

not.B: There is no real growth once the 10% rise in prices is removed.
not.C: 10% is the growth in nominal GDP.
not.D: 14% does not come from these figures.

items.q: The table refers to a hypothetical economy. Which combination of reasons is most likely to account for changes in the headline and underlying inflation rates from Year 1 to Year 3?
o: Decreased global oil production Expansionary fiscal policy
Flooding in agricultural areas Increased microeconomic reform
Increased tariffs Increased minimum wage Appreciation of the domestic

head: Reason for change in headline inflation
Reason for change in underlying inflation

e.why: Headline inflation rises while underlying falls. Floods push up food prices, a volatile item in headline only. Microeconomic reform lowers costs across the economy, reducing underlying inflation.

not.A: Lower oil production would raise headline, but expansionary fiscal policy would raise underlying inflation.
not.C: Tariffs and a higher minimum wage raise costs broadly, lifting underlying inflation.
not.D: More oil production would lower headline inflation.

items.q: The table shows Balance of Payments data for a hypothetical economy with a flexible exchange rate. Using the data above, what is the value of the capital account?

e.why: Current account = 50 − 200 + 25 = −125. Financial account = 5 + 50 + 10 + 45 = 110. The capital and financial account must total +125, so the capital account = 125 − 110 = $15 billion surplus.

not.A: The size is right, but a surplus is needed to offset the current account deficit.
not.C: $25 billion is net secondary income, not the capital account.
not.D: $25 billion is net secondary income, not the capital account.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a monetary union?

e.why: Of these, only the EU has members sharing a common currency, the euro, and a common monetary policy.

not.B: APEC is a forum for economic cooperation.
not.C: ASEAN is a trading bloc whose members keep their own currencies.
not.D: NAFTA was a free trade agreement.

items.q: Which of the following policies is mainly used to manage inflation?

e.why: The Reserve Bank uses the cash rate to keep inflation within its 2–3% target.

not.A: Fiscal policy mainly affects growth, employment and income distribution.
not.C: Competition policy is a microeconomic policy aimed at efficiency.
not.D: Labour market policy deals with wages and employment conditions.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to result in an increased budget surplus?
o: Reduced government spending and reduced taxation
Increased government spending and reduced taxation
Reduced government spending and increased taxation
Increased government spending and increased taxation

e.why: A surplus is revenue minus spending. Less spending and more tax revenue both make it larger.

not.A: Lower spending helps but lower tax revenue works against it.
not.B: Both changes reduce the surplus.
not.D: Higher revenue helps but higher spending works against it.

items.q: Other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to increase if Australia’s major trading partners experience an economic slowdown?

e.why: A slowdown overseas reduces demand for Australian exports, so output falls and unemployment rises.

not.A: Lower export demand reduces GDP growth.
not.C: Demand for exports falls.
not.D: Weaker demand reduces inflationary pressure.

items.q: A government decides to reduce tariffs on imported goods. Other things being equal, what will be the most likely impact on the domestic economy?
o: There will be a redistribution of income from importers to local producers.
There will be a redistribution of income from local producers to importers.

e.why: Lower tariffs make imports cheaper, so sales and income shift from protected local producers to importers.

not.A: Each import is taxed at a lower rate, so revenue is unlikely to rise.
not.B: A change in the tariff rate changes revenue.
not.C: This is the effect of raising tariffs.

items.q: An increase in which of the following will most likely change a Gini coefficient from 0.3 to 0.4?
o: The goods and services tax rate
Marginal income tax rates for high income earners
Tax rates levied on the profits from the sale of property

e.why: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality. The GST is regressive: it takes a larger share of income from low-income earners.

not.A: Company tax falls on profits, which go mostly to higher-income households.
not.C: Higher rates on high incomes reduce inequality.
not.D: Capital gains are earned mostly by wealthier households, so taxing them more reduces inequality.

items.q: Which of the following best describes a person experiencing frictional unemployment?
o: A university student struggling to find work during a recession
A summer fruit-picker undertaking full-time training to acquire new skills
A self-employed worker whose business has shut down and who plans to start a new business
A factory worker who is employed part-time and who is actively seeking to increase their hours of work

e.why: Frictional unemployment is the time people spend moving between jobs or businesses.

not.A: Unemployment caused by a recession is cyclical.
not.B: A person in full-time training is not looking for work, so is not in the labour force.
not.D: A part-time worker who wants more hours is underemployed.

items.q: The diagram refers to the change in the distribution of income in a hypothetical economy. Which of the following is most likely to increase as a result of the change in income inequality from Year 1 to Year 2?

e.why: In Year 2 the Lorenz curve is closer to the line of equality. Lower-income households spend a larger share of their income, so a more even distribution raises consumption.

not.B: Labour mobility is encouraged by wage differences, which have narrowed.
not.C: Risk-taking is encouraged by the prospect of high rewards, which is weaker with more equality.
not.D: Higher-income earners save more, so more equality tends to reduce saving.

items.q: A government has recently decided to increase the age of retirement. Which of the following are the most likely impacts of this decision on the labour force participation rate and taxation revenue?

head: Impact on the labour force participation rate
Impact on taxation revenue

e.why: People work for longer, so more of the working age population is in the labour force and more income is earned and taxed.

not.A: More people working means more tax revenue.
not.C: Participation rises, not falls.
not.D: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: All other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to shift the demand curve for labour from DD to D1D1?
o: An economic downturn in the global economy
An increase in the labour force participation rate
The establishment of minimum employment standards across all industries
The implementation of a decentralised method of determining employment contracts

e.why: Demand for labour has increased. Workplace bargaining links pay to productivity, and more productive labour is worth more to employers.

not.A: A global downturn reduces demand for labour.
not.B: Higher participation shifts the supply of labour, not the demand.
not.C: Minimum standards raise the cost of labour; they do not increase demand for it.

items.q: A government has changed the method of financing its budget deficit. Instead of borrowing from the domestic private sector, it will now borrow from overseas. All other things being equal, what is the most likely impact of this change on the domestic economy?

e.why: Interest on overseas borrowing is paid to foreigners, which increases the primary income deficit and so the current account deficit.

not.A: Borrowing from overseas adds to foreign debt.
not.B: The size of the deficit is not changed by how it is financed.
not.D: Less government borrowing at home eases pressure on domestic interest rates.

items.q: What is the most likely impact of an increase in the official cash rate on the domestic economy?
o: Lower inflationary expectations resulting from a depreciation of the domestic currency
Higher inflationary expectations resulting from an appreciation of the domestic currency
A redistribution of income and wealth towards those with a relatively high marginal propensity to save
A redistribution of income and wealth towards those with a relatively high marginal propensity to consume

e.why: Higher interest rates raise the incomes of savers and the costs of borrowers. Savers are those with a high marginal propensity to save.

not.A: A higher cash rate attracts funds and appreciates the currency.
not.B: A higher cash rate lowers inflationary expectations.
not.D: Borrowers, who tend to spend more of their income, lose from higher rates.

items.q: The Australian Government has received a repayment of an interest-free loan made to a developing economy. How will this be recorded in Australia’s balance of payments?
o: A debit in the secondary income account
A credit in the secondary income account
A debit in the capital and financial account
A credit in the capital and financial account

e.why: Repayment of a loan is a financial transaction, and money coming into Australia is a credit.

not.A: Secondary income records gifts and transfers, not loan repayments.
not.B: A loan repayment is not a transfer.
not.C: It belongs in this account, but an inflow is a credit.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to result in a decline in Australia’s terms of trade?

e.why: Lower demand and greater supply both push export prices down, which lowers the terms of trade.

not.B: Both changes raise export prices.
not.C: The two changes pull export prices in opposite directions.
not.D: The two changes pull export prices in opposite directions.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to allow an infant industry in Australia to benefit from globalisation?
o: An increase in Australia’s import quotas
A decrease in Australia’s levels of protection
A decrease in Australia’s regulation of transnational corporations
An increase in Australia’s recognition of international educational qualifications

e.why: Recognising overseas qualifications lets a new industry draw on skilled workers from the global labour market.

not.A: A larger quota lets in more competing imports.
not.B: Less protection exposes the industry before it is competitive.
not.C: Less regulation of transnational corporations brings stronger competitors.

items.q: The table shows selected data for a hypothetical economy. All other things being equal, how are real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the Human Development Index (HDI) most likely to change from Year 1 to Year 2?
o: Real GDP and the HDI both increase.
Real GDP and the HDI both decrease.
Real GDP decreases and the HDI increases.
Real GDP increases and the HDI decreases.

e.why: Real GDP rises from 1000 to 1500 ÷ 110 × 100 = 1364. But real GDP per person falls from $10.00 to about $9.09, and income per person is a component of the HDI.

not.A: Real GDP rises, but income per person falls.
not.B: Real GDP rises.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: An increase in which of the following is most likely to lower the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU)?

e.why: Better infrastructure raises productivity and helps workers reach jobs, reducing structural unemployment and so the NAIRU.

not.A: The cash rate affects cyclical unemployment.
not.B: Higher government spending affects cyclical unemployment.
not.D: Centralised wage fixing makes wages less flexible, which tends to raise the NAIRU.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for the Australian economy. All other things being equal, how did the purchasing power of Australian consumers change overseas and domestically from Year 1 to Year 2?

head: Purchasing power of Australians travelling overseas
Purchasing power of Australian consumers domestically

e.why: The dollar rose from US$0.70 to US$0.75, so it buys more overseas. At home prices still rose (by 1%), so each dollar buys slightly less.

not.A: Inflation is positive, so domestic purchasing power fell.
not.B: Both are the wrong direction.
not.D: A higher dollar buys more overseas.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for the Australian economy. What is the value of Australia’s Net Foreign Liabilities?

rows: Loans owed by foreigners to Australians ($ billions)
Loans owed by Australians to foreigners ($ billions)
Australian assets owned by foreigners ($ billions)
Foreign assets owned by Australians ($ billions)

e.why: Net foreign liabilities = foreign liabilities − foreign assets = (600 + 100) − (150 + 250) = $300 billion.

not.B: $400 billion is the total of foreign assets only.
not.C: $600 billion is one liability only.
not.D: $1100 billion adds all four items.

items.q: It can be argued that a public road is NOT a public good because
o: the private sector can build and maintain roads.
when one car uses the road another car can still use the road.
the road is used by both public and private forms of transport.

e.why: When more cars use a road, congestion slows everyone. One driver's use reduces the benefit to others, so the road is rival.

not.B: Who builds a good does not decide whether it is a public good.
not.C: This describes non-rivalry, which supports calling it a public good.
not.D: The type of vehicle has nothing to do with rivalry or excludability.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to be of benefit to transnational corporations?
o: Migration laws that encourage international labour mobility

e.why: Transnational corporations operate in many countries. Being able to move skilled staff between them easily lowers their costs.

not.A: Trade barriers make it harder and dearer to move goods between a firm's operations.
not.B: Differences in business cycles are not something a firm benefits from directly.
not.C: Restrictions on financial flows make it harder to invest and move profits across borders.

items.q: In theory, which of the following best describes the characteristics of a public good?

e.why: A public good cannot be withheld from people who do not pay (non-excludable), and one person's use does not reduce the amount left for others (non-rival).

not.A: Excludable and rival describes a private good.
not.B: Excludable but non-rival describes goods such as pay television.
not.C: Non-excludable but rival describes common resources such as fish stocks.

items.q: Which statement about the time lags associated with government policies is most correct?
o: Fiscal policy has a longer implementation lag than monetary policy.
Microeconomic policies have a shorter impact lag than fiscal policy.
Monetary policy has a longer impact lag than microeconomic policies.
Microeconomic policies have a shorter implementation lag than monetary policy.

e.why: Fiscal changes usually wait for the annual Budget and must pass Parliament. The Reserve Bank can change the cash rate at any board meeting.

not.B: Microeconomic reforms take years to affect the economy, longer than fiscal policy.
not.C: Microeconomic policies have the longest impact lag of all.
not.D: Microeconomic reforms need legislation and consultation, so they take far longer to implement.

items.q: An economy is experiencing high unemployment and an inflation rate below the central bank’s target rate. Which macroeconomic policy mix is best for this economy?
o: Expansionary fiscal and contractionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal and expansionary monetary policy

e.why: High unemployment and low inflation both point to weak demand. Both arms of macroeconomic policy should stimulate spending.

not.B: Contractionary policy would raise unemployment further.
not.C: The two policies would work against each other.
not.D: The two policies would work against each other.

items.q: Other things being equal, Australia’s international competitiveness would be improved by an increase in which of the following?
o: The value of the Australian dollar

e.why: Greater aggregate supply means higher productivity and lower costs, so Australian goods are cheaper relative to those of other countries.

not.A: Higher inflation makes Australian goods dearer.
not.C: More government spending adds to demand and can add to inflation.
not.D: A higher dollar makes exports dearer for foreign buyers.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a market-based policy for the management of air pollution?
o: Firms buying and selling pollution permits
Domestic regulation that forces firms to meet certain emission targets
An international treaty that specifies emission targets and is legally enforceable

e.why: Tradable permits put a price on pollution and let the market decide which firms cut emissions.

not.A: Fines are penalties set under regulation.
not.C: This is regulation, not a market.
not.D: This is an international agreement, not a market-based policy.

items.q: Which of the following would most likely be driven by fluctuations in the business cycle?
o: An increase in the GST rate
An increase in the tax free threshold
A decrease in company taxation receipts
A decrease in the top marginal income tax rate

e.why: Company profits fall in a downturn, so company tax receipts fall automatically with the cycle.

not.A: Changing the GST rate is a deliberate policy decision.
not.B: Changing the tax-free threshold is a deliberate policy decision.
not.D: Changing a tax rate is a deliberate policy decision.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to occur if the Australian government finances a budget deficit by borrowing funds in the domestic money market?
o: A rise in the Australian government’s share of foreign debt

e.why: Government borrowing adds to the demand for the limited pool of domestic savings, which pushes interest rates up (crowding out).

not.B: Borrowing existing savings does not create new money.
not.C: Higher interest rates attract foreign funds, which would appreciate the dollar.
not.D: Borrowing at home does not add to foreign debt.

items.q: A government decides to reduce the import quota for a product. Other things being equal, which of the following is most likely to occur in the domestic market?
o: The revenue of foreign producers will increase.
The domestic price of the product will increase.
Domestic firms will produce less of the product.
The market share of foreign producers will increase.

e.why: A smaller quota means fewer imports, so total supply in the market falls and the price rises.

not.A: Foreign producers sell fewer units.
not.C: A higher price leads local firms to produce more.
not.D: Foreign producers' share of the market falls.

items.q: Which of the following is the minimum requirement in order for an adult worker in Australia to receive the National Minimum Wage?
o: They are a member of a trade union.
They are covered by an industrial award.
They are covered by an enterprise agreement.

e.why: The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor for all adult employees in the national system, including those not covered by an award or agreement.

not.B: Union membership is not required.
not.C: The National Minimum Wage exists for employees not covered by an award.
not.D: It applies whether or not there is an enterprise agreement.

items.q: Which of the following must have happened if there has been a movement in Australia’s Terms of Trade from 115 to 105?
o: The value of Australia’s imports increased relative to the value of Australia’s exports.
The value of Australia’s imports decreased relative to the value of Australia’s exports.
The price of Australia’s imports increased relative to the price of Australia’s exports.
The price of Australia’s exports increased due to an appreciation in the Australian dollar.

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. A fall means import prices have risen relative to export prices.

not.A: The terms of trade measure prices, not the value (price × quantity) of trade.
not.B: The terms of trade measure prices, not values, and this is the wrong direction.
not.D: Higher export prices would raise the terms of trade.

items.q: Which of the following correctly ranks, from largest to smallest, the sources of income as a percentage of Australian household income?
o: Returns to labour, returns to enterprise, returns to land and capital, transfer payments
Returns to labour, transfer payments, returns to land and capital, returns to enterprise
Returns to labour, transfer payments, returns to enterprise, returns to land and capital
Returns to labour, returns to enterprise, transfer payments, returns to land and capital

e.why: Wages and salaries are by far the largest source, followed by government transfer payments, then rent, interest and dividends, with profit from unincorporated businesses the smallest.

not.A: Transfer payments are the second largest source, not the smallest.
not.C: Returns to land and capital are larger than returns to enterprise.
not.D: Returns to enterprise are the smallest of the four.

items.q: There is a downturn in the economy of a major importer of Australian goods and services. Which of the following is most likely to occur?
o: A depreciation of the Australian dollar
An appreciation of the Australian dollar
A revaluation of the importer’s currency
A devaluation of the importer’s currency

e.why: A downturn in a major buyer reduces demand for Australian exports and so for Australian dollars, lowering the dollar's value.

not.B: Lower demand for the dollar reduces its value.
not.C: Revaluation is a decision by a government with a fixed exchange rate, not a market outcome.
not.D: Devaluation is a decision by a government with a fixed exchange rate, not a market outcome.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for an economy. Which statement about this economy is correct?
o: It is expanding because exports are greater than imports.
It is contracting because savings are greater than taxation.
It is expanding because injections are greater than leakages.
It is contracting because leakages are greater than injections.

e.why: Injections = I + G + X = 20 + 25 + 70 = 115. Leakages = S + T + M = 35 + 30 + 60 = 125. Leakages are greater, so national income falls.

not.A: Exports do exceed imports, but total leakages still exceed total injections.
not.B: Comparing savings with taxation says nothing about the direction of the economy.
not.C: Injections (115) are less than leakages (125).

items.q: The table shows employment data for a hypothetical economy. In which year is the unemployment rate 40% and the participation rate 62.5%?

e.why: Year 2: labour force = 3 + 2 = 5 million. Unemployment rate = 2 ÷ 5 = 40%. Participation rate = 5 ÷ 8 = 62.5%.

not.A: Year 1: unemployment 1 ÷ 3 = 33%, participation 3 ÷ 5 = 60%.
not.C: Year 3: participation is 62.5% but unemployment is 3 ÷ 10 = 30%.
not.D: Year 4: unemployment is 40% but participation is 15 ÷ 20 = 75%.

items.q: The table shows consumer price index (CPI) data for a hypothetical economy. What happens to the prices of goods and services from Year 1 to Year 3?
o: They increase at a constant rate.
They increase at a decreasing rate.
They increase at an increasing rate.

e.why: Prices rise by 5% in Year 2 (100 to 105) and by 4.8% in Year 3 (105 to 110). They are still rising, but more slowly.

not.A: The CPI rises each year.
not.B: The index rises by the same number of points, but 5 points on a base of 105 is a smaller percentage.
not.D: The rate of increase falls from 5% to 4.8%.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical balance of payments data for a country. Assuming a floating exchange rate, which of the following statements is true?
o: The balance of goods and services remains constant.
The current account deficit decreases from Year 1 to Year 2.
The net errors and omissions are larger in Year 2 than in Year 1.
The capital and financial account surplus decreases from Year 1 to Year 2.

e.why: Year 1: current account = −10 − 20 − 80 + 10 = −100; capital and financial = 95; errors and omissions = 5. Year 2: current account = −10 − 30 − 85 − 5 = −130; capital and financial = 120; errors and omissions = 10.

not.A: The balance on goods and services goes from −30 to −40.
not.B: The current account deficit grows from 100 to 130.
not.D: The capital and financial account surplus grows from 95 to 120.

items.q: It can be argued that a book in a public library is NOT a public good. Which of the following explanations best supports this argument?
o: People can borrow a different book.
Only one person can read the book at a time.
Anyone can become a member of the library and borrow the book.
The contents of the book do not change regardless of the number of times it has been read.

e.why: A public good must be non-rival. While one person has the book, no one else can read it, so it is rival.

not.A: The availability of other books does not affect whether this book is rival.
not.C: Open membership suggests it is non-excludable, which supports calling it a public good.
not.D: Unchanged content suggests it is non-rival over time, which supports calling it a public good.

items.q: The table shows data for National Income (Y) and Consumption (C ) for a hypothetical economy. If the value of the multiplier is 2.5, which row in the following table shows the missing values for X and Z?

e.why: A multiplier of 2.5 means MPC = 0.6. Consumption is 100 when income is zero, so C = 100 + 0.6Y. At Y = 1000, Z = 700. When C = 1300, 0.6Y = 1200 and X = 2000.

not.A: These values do not fit an MPC of 0.6.
not.B: Z of 1100 would mean consumption above income of 1000 and an MPC of 1.
not.C: X is right, but 600 leaves out the 100 of consumption that occurs at zero income.

items.q: In 2019, one US dollar buys 1.25 Australian dollars. In 2020, one Australian dollar buys 0.75 US dollars. Which statement is most correct?
o: There is no change in the exchange rate between 2019 and 2020.
Australian exports to the US are less expensive in 2020 compared to 2019.
Goods imported from the US are more expensive in 2019 compared to 2020.
For US investors, Australian assets are more expensive to buy in 2020 compared to 2019.

e.why: In 2019, US$1 = A$1.25, so A$1 = US$0.80. In 2020, A$1 = US$0.75. The Australian dollar has fallen, so Australian exports cost Americans less.

not.A: The rate fell from US$0.80 to US$0.75.
not.C: US goods are dearer for Australians in 2020, after the depreciation, not in 2019.
not.D: A lower Australian dollar makes Australian assets cheaper for US investors.

items.q: A key objective of decentralised wage determination is to increase

e.why: Enterprise bargaining lets pay rises be traded for changes in work practices at each workplace, with the aim of lifting labour productivity.

not.A: Work-life balance may be bargained over but is not the key objective.
not.B: Decentralised bargaining tends to widen pay differences.
not.D: Full-time employment is not a direct objective of the wage system.

items.q: From which of the following would a developing economy be most likely to receive funds to build a bridge?
o: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development

e.why: The World Bank lends to developing economies for infrastructure and other development projects.

not.B: The WTO oversees trade rules and does not lend.
not.C: The IMF lends to stabilise economies in financial crisis, not to build infrastructure.
not.D: The OECD is a policy forum of mostly advanced economies.

items.q: The value of trade between countries A and B increases while the value of trade between countries A and C decreases. All other things being equal, this most likely occurred because country A
o: implemented a free trade agreement with country B.
implemented a free trade agreement with country C.
raised import tariffs on both country B and country C.
reduced import tariffs on both country B and country C.

e.why: A free trade agreement with B makes B's goods cheaper in A, so A trades more with B and diverts some trade away from C.

not.B: An agreement with C would increase trade with C.
not.C: Higher tariffs on both would reduce trade with both.
not.D: Lower tariffs on both would increase trade with both.

items.q: A reduction in a country’s company tax rate is most likely to
o: reduce the profitability of the country’s firms.
increase frictional unemployment in the country.
increase foreign direct investment in the country.

e.why: A lower company tax rate raises after-tax returns, making the country more attractive to foreign firms deciding where to invest.

not.A: More investment inflow raises demand for the currency, appreciating it.
not.B: Lower tax increases after-tax profit.
not.C: Company tax has no direct link to people moving between jobs.

items.q: A country’s central bank wishes to improve the international competitiveness of the country’s exports. Which combination of actions by the central bank is most likely to achieve this objective?

e.why: Exports become more competitive when the currency falls. Buying foreign currency means selling the domestic currency (more supply), and lower interest rates reduce demand for it.

not.A: Selling the currency lowers it, but higher interest rates push it back up.
not.B: Both actions raise the currency.
not.C: Lower rates help, but selling foreign currency means buying the domestic currency, which raises it.

items.q: Residents in a country town experience a significant slow-down in the speed of their internet service as a result of a large increase in usage from newly-connected households. The slower internet speed is most likely a result of
o: the internet being a public good.

e.why: Each extra user reduces the speed available to others. That is rivalry in consumption.

not.A: Free riding is using something without paying; these households are connected customers.
not.C: Internet access is excludable: you must pay to be connected.
not.D: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable; the internet service here is neither.

items.q: There is a significant increase in official interest rates in the United States of America (US). All other things being equal, which of the following would be true?

head: Impact on foreign exchange markets
Value of Australian dollar in terms of $US

e.why: Higher US interest rates attract funds to the US, increasing demand for US dollars. Investors sell Australian dollars to buy them, so the Australian dollar depreciates.

not.B: Demand for US dollars rises, not falls.
not.C: The Australian dollar falls, and the main effect is on demand for US dollars.
not.D: The Australian dollar depreciates against a stronger US dollar.

items.q: Country A’s Lorenz curve is closer to the line of perfect equality than Country B’s Lorenz curve. All other things being equal, which of the following is true?
o: Country A has a larger Gini coefficient than country B.
Country B has a more equitable distribution of income than country A.
Country A’s Lorenz curve will move closer to country B’s Lorenz curve if country A’s top marginal income tax rate is decreased.
Country B’s Lorenz curve will move closer to country A’s Lorenz curve if country B’s top marginal income tax rate is decreased.

e.why: Country A is more equal. Cutting A's top marginal tax rate leaves high earners with more, increasing inequality and moving A's curve out towards B's.

not.A: A curve closer to the line of equality means a smaller Gini coefficient.
not.B: Country B's curve is further from equality, so its distribution is less equitable.
not.D: Cutting B's top rate would make B more unequal, moving its curve further from A's.

items.q: An Australian company purchases a foreign company that pays a dividend to Australian shareholders. How would these transactions be recorded on Australia’s balance of payments?
o: Debit on the financial account Credit on the current account
Credit on the financial account Debit on the current account
Credit on the capital account Debit on the financial account
Debit on the capital account Credit on the current account

e.why: Buying a foreign company sends money overseas to acquire an asset: a debit on the financial account. Dividends received are primary income: a credit on the current account.

not.B: This describes a foreign company buying an Australian one.
not.C: Purchases of companies are recorded in the financial account, not the capital account, and dividends are in the current account.
not.D: The dividend is right, but the purchase belongs in the financial account.

items.q: Alex has worked full time for the last two years at her current place of work. Under Australia’s national system for determining minimum employment standards, and assuming all other things being equal, Alex is NOT guaranteed
o: four weeks annual leave per year.
notice of termination of her employment.
protection against unfair dismissal by her employer.

e.why: The National Employment Standards guarantee leave, notice of termination and redundancy pay. Protection from unfair dismissal is a separate part of the Fair Work Act with its own eligibility rules, so it is not guaranteed to every employee.

not.A: Redundancy pay is one of the National Employment Standards.
not.B: Four weeks annual leave is one of the National Employment Standards.
not.C: Notice of termination is one of the National Employment Standards.

items.q: Which change in budget outcomes from Year 1 to Year 2 represents an expansionary fiscal stance?

e.why: Moving from a $10 billion surplus to a $5 billion deficit means the budget is now adding to demand: an expansionary stance.

not.A: A larger surplus is contractionary.
not.B: A smaller deficit is less expansionary than before: a contractionary change.
not.C: Moving from deficit to surplus is contractionary.

items.q: The Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) facilitated the move from a state-based to a national system of industrial relations. Which of the following provides the best justification for this move?
o: To reduce the power of national employee unions
To reduce compliance costs for state governments
Because private sector companies employ workers in many states
Because state governments typically employ workers only in their own state

e.why: Firms that operate across state borders faced a different set of rules in each state. One national system gives them a single set.

not.A: Reducing union power was not the justification for a national system.
not.B: The costs that mattered were those of businesses, not of state governments.
not.D: State public sector workers were not the reason; many remained in state systems.

items.q: Which of the following statements about government regulation is most correct?
o: Regulations restricting the behaviour of firms can increase efficiency.
Microeconomic reform requires the removal of government regulation.
Government regulations restrict the entry of transnational corporations.

e.why: Rules such as competition law stop firms abusing market power, which makes markets work more efficiently.

not.A: Many regulations improve efficiency by correcting market failure.
not.C: Reform often replaces or improves regulation rather than removing all of it.
not.D: Regulation is not generally aimed at keeping transnational corporations out.

items.q: In Australia, returns to enterprise typically represent a lower proportion of household income than returns to labour because
o: the company tax rate is higher than some marginal personal income tax rates.
lower interest rates have significantly reduced household income from interest.
most workers are employed by firms and many family businesses make a loss or small profit.
households usually comprise at least one worker and most workers are employed by large firms.

e.why: Most people earn wages as employees. Returns to enterprise (profit) go to the smaller number who run businesses, and many small businesses earn little.

not.A: Tax rates do not explain where household income comes from.
not.B: Interest is a return to capital, not to enterprise.
not.D: Having a worker in most households explains why wages are large, but the size of the employer is not the reason profit is small.

items.q: The diagram shows the relationship between a country’s consumption and income in Year 1 and Year 2. Which of the following could explain the change from Year 1 to Year 2?
o: A fall in the unemployment rate
A fall in the goods and services tax rate

e.why: In Year 2 households consume less at every level of income. Higher interest rates reward saving and raise loan repayments, reducing consumption.

not.A: Higher asset prices make households feel wealthier and spend more.
not.C: Lower unemployment raises confidence and spending.
not.D: A lower GST makes goods cheaper and raises consumption.

items.q: The table shows economic information for a hypothetical economy. Which of the following best explains the changes in the TOT and the TWI from Year 1 to Year 2?
o: There is an increase in global demand for the goods this economy exports and imports.
The economy’s central bank increases the official cash rate relative to global interest rates.
Global demand for the goods this economy imports has increased relative to global demand for the goods this economy exports.
Global demand for the goods this economy exports has increased relative to global demand for the goods this economy imports.

e.why: Stronger world demand for this economy's exports raises export prices relative to import prices (terms of trade up) and raises demand for its currency (TWI up).

not.A: If demand rose for both exports and imports, the terms of trade would not clearly improve.
not.B: A higher cash rate would lift the TWI but would not change the terms of trade.
not.C: Stronger demand for the goods it imports would raise import prices and worsen the terms of trade.

items.q: For a particular country, the underlying inflation rate is greater than the headline inflation rate. This is most likely to have been caused by a significant
o: increase in the country’s minimum wage.

e.why: More oil production lowers petrol prices. Petrol is a volatile item counted in headline inflation but excluded from underlying, so headline falls below underlying.

not.A: Less electricity production raises power prices.
not.C: A depreciation raises import prices broadly, lifting both measures.
not.D: A higher minimum wage raises costs broadly, lifting both measures.

items.q: The table shows economic information for a hypothetical economy experiencing cyclical unemployment. The government of this hypothetical economy increases its expenditure by $1 billion. All other things being equal, what will be the consequence of this action?
o: National income will rise by $1 billion.
The rate of unemployment will equal the NAIRU.
The NAIRU will exceed the rate of unemployment.
The economy will experience a rapid increase in inflation.

rows: Change in national income (Y) required to reach full employment

e.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5, so $1 billion of spending raises income by $5 billion, exactly the amount needed for full employment. Unemployment then equals the NAIRU.

not.A: This ignores the multiplier: income rises by $5 billion.
not.C: Unemployment falls to the NAIRU, not below it.
not.D: The economy reaches full employment but does not go beyond it.

items.q: Country A and country B have flexible exchange rates and are considering forming a monetary union. Country A is currently experiencing a recession while country B is currently experiencing a boom. Which of the following is most likely to be true immediately after country A and country B form the monetary union?
o: Imported inflation will be lower in country B.
It will be cheaper for foreign tourists to visit country A.
It will be cheaper for foreign firms to acquire assets in country B.
The international competitiveness of country A’s exporters will increase.

e.why: Country B's boom would have meant a strong currency. The shared currency reflects both economies, so it is weaker than B's was, making B's assets cheaper for foreign buyers.

not.A: A weaker currency for B makes its imports dearer, raising imported inflation.
not.B: The shared currency is stronger than A's recession-weakened currency was, so visiting A costs more.
not.D: A stronger currency for A makes its exports less competitive.

items.q: The diagram shows domestic demand and supply curves for a hypothetical economy. As a result of a change in trade policy in this economy, government revenue increases by $400, the revenue of local producers declines by $1400 and the revenue of foreign producers increases by $1600. Which of the following is most likely to describe the change in trade policy that occurred?
o: A tariff of $0 has been replaced with a tariff of $2.
A tariff of $4 has been replaced with a quota of 200.
A quota of zero has been replaced with a tariff of $2.
A quota of zero has been replaced with a quota of 200.

e.why: With a quota of zero the price is $10 and local firms sell 300 (revenue $3000). With a $2 tariff the price is $8: local firms sell 200 (revenue $1600, down $1400) and 200 units are imported. Government revenue is 200 × $2 = $400, which only a tariff can produce. The 200 imports sell for $1600 in total.

not.A: Starting from free trade at $6, a $2 tariff would raise local producers' revenue, not reduce it.
not.B: A quota raises no government revenue.
not.D: A quota raises no government revenue.

items.q: Which of the following is a feature of globalisation?

e.why: Globalisation lets firms split production across countries, with each stage done where it is cheapest: the international division of labour.

not.B: Globalisation is associated with lower, not higher, protection.
not.C: More integrated markets are generally more efficient.
not.D: Globalisation is increased economic integration.

items.q: The G20 is best described as
o: a regional free-trade agreement involving Australia.
a monetary union that has adopted a common currency.
a government forum for coordination of economic policies.

e.why: The G20 brings together leaders, finance ministers and central bank governors of major economies to coordinate economic policy.

not.A: It has no preferential trade arrangements, so it is not a trading bloc.
not.B: It is global, not regional, and is not a trade agreement.
not.C: Its members keep their own currencies.

items.q: Which of the following describes a benefit of an appreciation of the Australian dollar to the Australian economy?

e.why: A higher dollar means fewer Australian dollars are needed to service and repay debt owed in foreign currencies.

not.A: A larger trade deficit is a cost of an appreciation, not a benefit.
not.B: Imports become cheaper, so import volumes rise.
not.D: An appreciation makes exports dearer, reducing competitiveness.

items.q: Which policy in Australia is least likely to be influenced by political constraints?

e.why: Monetary policy is set by the Reserve Bank, which is independent of the government, so it is the least exposed to political pressure.

not.A: Budgets must pass Parliament and are shaped by elections.
not.C: Labour market policy is legislated and strongly contested politically.
not.D: Microeconomic reform needs legislation and often faces opposition from affected groups.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of a rise in the participation rate?
o: More parents are returning to the workforce
More unemployed people are joining the defence force
More students are choosing to continue with further education

e.why: Parents returning to work move from outside the labour force into it, raising the participation rate.

not.A: Early retirees leave the labour force.
not.C: Unemployed people are already in the labour force, so taking a job does not change participation.
not.D: Full-time students are generally not in the labour force.

items.q: If there is an increase in interest rates, which of the following is most likely to happen?
o: Economic growth will decrease and consumer spending will decrease.
The money supply will increase and the rate of inflation will decrease.
Business investment will increase and consumer spending will decrease.
Unemployment will decrease and the rate of economic growth will decrease.

e.why: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and the reward for saving, so households spend less and growth slows.

not.B: Higher rates are associated with tighter money, not a larger money supply.
not.C: Consumer spending falls, but higher borrowing costs also reduce business investment.
not.D: Growth does slow, but slower growth raises unemployment.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for low wage growth in an economy?

e.why: Low unemployment means employers compete for scarce workers, which pushes wages up. It is a reason for faster, not slower, wage growth.

not.A: With low inflation, workers need and seek smaller pay rises.
not.C: Weak growth means weak demand for labour.
not.D: Without productivity gains firms cannot afford larger pay rises.

items.q: Which pair of sectors contribute most to Australia’s export income?

e.why: Mining (iron ore, coal, gas) is the largest export sector and services (education, tourism) the next largest.

not.B: Agriculture earns less than services.
not.C: This leaves out mining, the largest exporter.
not.D: Manufacturing is a small share of exports, and mining is missing.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for an economy. Which row of the table is correct for this economy?

e.why: Trade balance = X − M = 250 − 350 = −100, a deficit. Injections (I + G + X = 1000) exceed leakages (S + T + M = 850), so national income rises.

not.A: Imports exceed exports, so the trade balance is a deficit.
not.B: Imports exceed exports, and injections exceed leakages.
not.D: The deficit is right, but injections exceed leakages so growth is positive.

items.q: The central bank of a hypothetical economy reduces the cash rate. All other things being equal, what is the likely effect of this action?
o: An increase in the rate of unemployment
An appreciation of the economy’s exchange rate
An increase in the price of assets in the economy

e.why: A lower cash rate makes borrowing cheaper, which raises demand for assets such as housing and shares and lifts their prices.

not.A: Cheaper credit increases consumer spending.
not.B: More spending creates jobs, lowering unemployment.
not.C: Lower interest rates reduce demand for the currency, so it depreciates.

items.q: The following diagram shows the level of income in an economy over two years. What changes in the top marginal rate of tax and the goods and services tax (GST) would have caused this shift in the Lorenz curve from Year 1 to Year 2?

e.why: In Year 2 the Lorenz curve is closer to the line of equality, so income is more evenly shared. A higher top marginal rate takes more from high earners, and a lower GST helps low-income earners most.

not.A: A higher GST is regressive and would widen inequality.
not.C: Both changes would increase inequality.
not.D: A lower top marginal rate benefits high-income earners, widening inequality.

items.q: The table shows information for a hypothetical economy. What is the Net Foreign Liabilities for this economy as a percentage of GDP?

e.why: Net foreign liabilities = net foreign debt + net foreign equity = 900 + 100 = $1000 billion. As a share of GDP: 1000 ÷ 1800 = 55.6%.

not.A: 2.8% is the CAD as a percentage of GDP (50 ÷ 1800).
not.B: 44.4% subtracts equity from debt (800 ÷ 1800) instead of adding it.
not.C: 50% uses net foreign debt only (900 ÷ 1800).

items.q: Inflation in a hypothetical economy has decreased from 3% in Year 1 to 2% in Year 2. Based on this information, which statement is true?
o: Unemployment is at the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU).
Unemployment is below the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU).

e.why: Inflation of 2% is still positive: prices are rising, only more slowly than before (disinflation).

not.B: Falling prices would need a negative inflation rate (deflation).
not.C: Nothing is said about unemployment; if inflation is falling, unemployment is more likely above the NAIRU.
not.D: Unemployment below the NAIRU would make inflation accelerate, not slow.

items.q: The following information is for a hypothetical economy. How many people are employed part time in this economy?

not.B: 1 000 000 takes 10% of the working age population rather than of the labour force.
not.C: 4 000 000 is the number employed full time.
not.D: 4 500 000 is total employment, full time and part time.

items.q: The table shows data for national income (Y ) and savings (S) in $ billion for a hypothetical economy. All other things being equal, what is the new equilibrium level of income (Y ) in Year 3 if investment increases by $35 billion?

e.why: Income rose by 200 and saving by 50, so MPS = 0.25 and the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. Extra income = 4 × 35 = 140, so Y = 450 + 140 = $590 billion.

not.A: $497 billion uses a multiplier of 1.33, treating 0.25 as the MPC.
not.C: $600 billion does not come from a multiplier of 4.
not.D: $650 billion adds the 200 rise in income from the table, not the effect of the investment.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a fiscal policy that is both contractionary and discretionary?
o: Increased infrastructure spending in rural regions
Increased spending due to unexpectedly higher unemployment
Decreased unemployment expenditure due to higher than forecasted economic growth

e.why: Lowering the tax-free threshold is a deliberate decision (discretionary) that collects more tax and reduces spending (contractionary).

not.B: This is discretionary but expansionary.
not.C: This is an automatic stabiliser, and it is expansionary.
not.D: This is contractionary but automatic, not a decision.

items.q: The Australian government provides financial aid to build a road in a neighbouring country. Residents in Australia receive pension payments from overseas. How will these debit and credit transactions be recorded in Australia’s balance of payments?

e.why: Aid to build a road is a capital transfer, recorded as a debit in the capital account. Pensions received from overseas are transfers, recorded as a credit in secondary income.

not.A: Aid for a capital project goes in the capital account, and pensions are not primary income.
not.B: The debit is right, but pensions are a transfer (secondary income), not income earned from work or investment.
not.D: The credit is right, but aid tied to building a road is a capital transfer.

items.q: Which combination of factors is most likely to result in an increase in Australia’s Trade Weighted Index?

head: Terms of trade
Global interest rates relative to Australian interest rates

e.why: Higher terms of trade mean more export income and more demand for Australian dollars. Lower global interest rates relative to Australia's attract funds into Australia. Both raise the TWI.

not.A: Higher global interest rates draw funds out of Australia, lowering the dollar.
not.C: Both changes reduce demand for the dollar.
not.D: Relatively lower global rates help, but lower terms of trade reduce demand for the dollar.

items.q: The diagram shows the domestic demand and supply for a particular good within an economy. The world price is $3. The government is considering imposing a tariff that would have the same impact on domestic production as an import quota of 20 000 items. What is the total tariff revenue that will be generated?

e.why: A quota of 20 000 means demand exceeds domestic supply by 20 000, which happens at a price of $4 (demand 50 000, supply 30 000). The equivalent tariff is $4 − $3 = $1. Revenue = $1 × 20 000 = $20 000.

not.A: Unlike a quota, a tariff does raise revenue.
not.B: $10 000 would need imports of only 10 000.
not.D: $40 000 would be a $2 tariff on 20 000 imports, but a $2 tariff takes the price to $5, where there are no imports.

items.q: The diagram shows the domestic demand and supply for a particular good within an economy. The world price is $3. Assume the government decides to only use subsidies as a form of protection. What is the subsidy per unit that would result in no imports?

e.why: At the world price of $3 consumers demand 60 000. For no imports, local producers must supply all 60 000, which they do only if they receive $7. The subsidy is $7 − $3 = $4.

not.A: With no subsidy, producers supply only 20 000 at $3.
not.B: A $2 subsidy gives producers $5, at which they supply 40 000: imports continue.
not.C: $3 is the world price, not the gap between it and the $7 producers need.

items.q: Which of the following identifies two economic objectives of monetary policy?
o: Price stability and distribution of income

e.why: The Reserve Bank's objectives include the stability of the currency (low inflation) and the maintenance of full employment.

not.B: External stability is not an objective of monetary policy.
not.C: Distribution of income is pursued mainly through fiscal policy.
not.D: Environmental sustainability is not an objective of monetary policy.

items.q: Which international organisation is responsible for maintaining financial stability in global financial markets?

e.why: The IMF monitors the global financial system and lends to countries in crisis to maintain financial stability.

not.A: The World Bank funds long-term development.
not.B: The WTO deals with the rules of trade.
not.D: APEC is a regional forum promoting trade and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a feature of a decentralised wage determination system?
o: Wage increases are linked to inflation
Employment contracts can vary from one workplace to another

e.why: In a decentralised system wages and conditions are negotiated at each workplace, so agreements differ between workplaces.

not.A: Decentralised bargaining tends to widen wage differences.
not.B: Linking wages to inflation (indexation) is a feature of centralised wage fixing.
not.C: Government or tribunal determination of wages is the centralised system.

items.q: A developing economy is most likely to be characterised by
o: low productivity and low population growth.
low employment and low infant mortality rate.
inadequate access to education and underprovision of public goods.
inadequate access to health care and GDP dominated by the provision of services.

e.why: Developing economies lack the income and tax base to fund schools and public goods such as roads, sanitation and power.

not.A: Productivity is low, but population growth is usually high.
not.B: Infant mortality is high in developing economies.
not.D: Health care is inadequate, but their GDP is usually dominated by agriculture, not services.

items.q: A country imposes a quota on wheat imports. Assume that it does not allow any imports of wheat beyond the quota. Which of the following is most likely to occur if this country decides to reduce this quota on wheat imports?
o: Increased wheat prices within the country
Increased export revenue for foreign wheat exporters
Decreased income for wheat producers within the country
Decreased government revenue from the change in the volume of imports

e.why: A smaller quota means less wheat can be imported. Total supply in the country falls, so the price rises.

not.B: Foreign exporters sell less wheat, so their revenue falls.
not.C: Local producers sell more at a higher price, so their income rises.
not.D: A quota is a limit on quantity; unlike a tariff it does not raise revenue from each unit imported.

items.q: The table represents data for a hypothetical economy. Which of the following shows the value of the terms of trade index in Year 2 and the terms of trade trend from Year 1 to Year 2?

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Year 1: 100 ÷ 125 × 100 = 80. Year 2: 80 ÷ 160 × 100 = 50. It has decreased.

not.A: 50 is right, but that is a fall from 80.
not.C: 200 puts import prices on top: the formula is export prices over import prices.
not.D: The trend is a decrease, but 200 has the formula upside down.

items.q: A foreign business purchases the rights to sell an Australian-designed product overseas. How will this transaction be recorded in Australia’s Balance of Payments?

e.why: Selling rights such as licences and franchises is the sale of a non-produced, non-financial asset, which is recorded in the capital account; money coming into Australia is a credit. NESA accepted both B and C for this question.

not.A: Australia is selling the rights and receiving payment, which is a credit, not a debit.
