not.D: NESA did not accept this option: the sale of the rights itself is recorded as a credit in the capital account, not the financial account.

items.q: Which of the following is likely to cause a decrease in the labour force participation rate?
o: A decrease in the rate of unemployment
A decrease in the number of discouraged workers
An increase in the level of hidden unemployment
An increase in the value of transfer payments made to the unemployed

e.why: Hidden unemployed people have stopped looking for work, so they are no longer in the labour force. More of them means a lower participation rate.

not.A: Lower unemployment signals that jobs are available and tends to draw people into the labour force.
not.B: Fewer discouraged workers means more people are back in the labour force.
not.D: To receive unemployment payments people must be looking for work, which keeps them in the labour force.

items.q: The following diagram shows two aggregate demand curves for a hypothetical economy. All other things being equal, the shift from AD1 to AD2 is most likely to have been caused by an increase in
o: the cash rate of the hypothetical economy.
employment in the economy of a major trading partner.

e.why: AD2 is to the left of AD1, so aggregate demand has fallen. A higher cash rate raises borrowing costs and reduces consumption and investment.

not.A: A higher tax-free threshold leaves households more income, raising AD.
not.B: More business investment raises AD.
not.D: More employment in a trading partner raises its demand for exports, raising AD.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for the Australian economy over a two-year period. Which row of the table below best accounts for the changes in CPI and unemployment rate from Year 1 to Year 2?
o: Reduction in the cash rate Removal of government initiatives for education and training
Appreciation of the Australian Increase in domestic investment dollar
Increase in import tariffs Global economic downturn
Increase in consumer confidence An appreciation in the currency of a major trading partner

head: Reason for change in CPI
Reason for change in unemployment rate
rows: Removal of government initiatives for education and training
An appreciation in the currency of a major trading partner

e.why: The CPI rose 3% and the unemployment rate fell from 10% (200 ÷ 2000) to 5.9% (125 ÷ 2125). Stronger consumer confidence raises spending and prices. A higher currency in a trading partner makes this economy's exports cheaper there, creating jobs.

not.A: A lower cash rate could raise the CPI, but removing training programs would raise unemployment.
not.B: An appreciation makes imports cheaper, which lowers the CPI.
not.C: A global downturn would raise unemployment, not lower it.

items.q: A central bank’s monetary policy stance results in a depreciation of the economy’s exchange rate. All other things being equal, which of the following best identifies the stance and a possible effect on the economy of the depreciation in the exchange rate?
o: Expansionary Increase in the level of foreign direct investment by domestic businesses
Expansionary Increase in the cost of international borrowing
Contractionary Increase in the number of service-based exports
Contractionary Increase in the balance on the net primary income account

head: Monetary policy stance
Effect on economy
rows: Increase in the level of foreign direct investment by domestic businesses
Increase in the cost of international borrowing
Increase in the number of service-based exports
Increase in the balance on the net primary income account

e.why: Lower interest rates (an expansionary stance) reduce demand for the currency, so it depreciates. Loans in foreign currencies then cost more to service and repay in local currency.

not.A: The stance is right, but a weaker currency makes buying assets overseas more expensive.
not.C: A contractionary stance raises interest rates and appreciates the currency.
not.D: A contractionary stance would appreciate the currency, not depreciate it.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. Assume the economy is operating at the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU). Which of the following describes the most likely relationship between the changes in the economy’s real GDP growth rate and level of unemployment?
o: Lower aggregate supply leading to a reduction in dynamic efficiencies
Lower aggregate supply accompanied by a decrease in technical efficiencies
Higher aggregate demand accompanied by a decrease in underemployment
Higher aggregate demand leading to a reduction in structural unemployment

e.why: Growth rose but the unemployment rate stayed at 5.2%, the NAIRU. Stronger demand was met by existing workers getting more hours, so underemployment fell without changing the unemployment rate.

not.A: Lower aggregate supply would not produce faster growth.
not.B: Lower aggregate supply would not produce faster growth.
not.D: A fall in structural unemployment would have lowered the unemployment rate, which did not change.

items.q: A domestic economy has experienced a decline in its net foreign liabilities as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Which of the following is most likely to have increased, contributing to this decline?
o: Foreign investment into the domestic economy
Returns on international investments by domestic businesses

e.why: Higher returns on Australian-owned investments overseas increase income from abroad and the value of foreign assets, which reduces net foreign liabilities.

not.A: Higher debt servicing costs add to the current account deficit and to liabilities.
not.B: Exchange rate volatility does not in itself reduce liabilities.
not.C: More foreign investment into the economy increases foreign liabilities.

items.q: Under a floating exchange rate, the capital and financial account for an economy in Year 1 is $10.6 bn surplus. In Year 2 the current account balance is in a $3.5 bn surplus. Which of the following represents the outcome of the capital and financial account in Year 2 and the change in size of this account from Year 1 to Year 2?

head: Outcome of capital and financial account in Year 2
Change in size ($bn)

e.why: With a floating rate the two accounts offset. A current account surplus of $3.5 bn in Year 2 means a capital and financial account deficit of $3.5 bn. Moving from +10.6 to −3.5 is a change of 14.1.

not.A: It is a deficit, but 7.1 ignores the change of sign (10.6 − 3.5).
not.C: A current account surplus is matched by a capital and financial account deficit.
not.D: The change is 14.1, but the account is in deficit in Year 2.

items.q: An economy has a headline inflation rate of 2.3% while its underlying inflation rate is 2.6%. Which factor could best account for this?
o: Reduced supply of fruit due to drought
Increased demand for the domestic currency

e.why: Headline inflation is below underlying. A temporary glut of petrol lowers its price; petrol is a volatile item that is counted in headline inflation but removed from underlying.

not.A: A higher minimum wage raises costs across the economy, lifting both measures.
not.C: A drought raises fruit prices, which would push headline above underlying.
not.D: Stronger demand for the currency appreciates it, lowering import prices broadly and affecting both measures.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. All other things being equal, which statement is most likely to be true for this economy?
o: Real GDP remains unchanged due to a decrease in global economic activity.
Nominal GDP has increased due to an appreciation of the economy’s exchange rate.
Nominal GDP has increased due to a decrease in the tariff applied to imported products.
Real GDP remains unchanged due to increases in the cost of production for businesses.

e.why: Real GDP: Year 1 = 400 ÷ 100 × 100 = 400; Year 2 = 420 ÷ 105 × 100 = 400. Output is unchanged; nominal GDP rose only because prices rose 5%, which higher production costs would explain.

not.A: Real GDP is unchanged, but a global downturn does not explain a 5% rise in prices.
not.B: An appreciation makes imports cheaper and lowers prices.
not.C: Lower tariffs reduce prices; they do not raise them.

items.q: An initial increase in government spending of $10 million leads to a final increase in national income of $25 million. What is the value of marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

e.why: The multiplier is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), 1 − MPC = 0.4 and MPC = 0.6.

not.A: An MPC of 0.25 gives a multiplier of 1.33.
not.B: 0.4 is the MPS (1 ÷ 2.5).
not.D: An MPC of 0.75 gives a multiplier of 4.

items.q: At equilibrium, when there is no international trade, an economy consumes 30 000 kg of cotton. The government opens the economy to trade and introduces a tariff of $5 per kg on cotton, resulting in imports of 10 000 kg and a total consumption of 35 000 kg of cotton. The world price for cotton is $20 per kg. What is the change in the domestic production of cotton and in government revenue?

e.why: With no trade, local production equals consumption: 30 000 kg. With trade, consumption is 35 000 kg and imports are 10 000 kg, so local production is 25 000 kg, a fall of 5 000 kg. Revenue = 10 000 kg × $5 = $50 000.

not.B: $200 000 is imports × the world price ($20), which is paid to foreign producers.
not.C: 10 000 kg is the volume of imports, not the fall in local production.
not.D: Both figures are imports-based: production fell by 5 000 kg and revenue is $50 000.

items.q: The table shows exchange rate movements for the Australian economy and United States economy. All other things being equal, which of the following best accounts for the fluctuation of the exchange rate between Year 1 and Year 2?
o: There has been a depreciation of the AUD caused by an upturn in the international business cycle.
There has been a depreciation of the AUD caused by a downturn in domestic economic activity.
There has been a depreciation of the USD caused by an increase in Australia’s cash rate relative to the US cash rate.
There has been a depreciation of the USD caused by a decrease in the deficit of the net income component of the US balance of payments.

e.why: In Year 1, A$1 buys US$0.90. In Year 2, A$0.90 buys US$1, so A$1 buys about US$1.11. The Australian dollar has risen and the US dollar has fallen. Higher Australian interest rates relative to US rates attract funds into Australia.

not.A: The Australian dollar appreciated; it did not depreciate.
not.B: The Australian dollar appreciated; it did not depreciate.
not.D: The US dollar did depreciate, but a smaller US income deficit would support the US dollar, not weaken it.

items.q: The diagram shows the demand and supply curves of labour for a hypothetical economy. The government of this economy has introduced a minimum wage (Wl) set above the equilibrium wage rate (We). The introduction of this minimum wage has an impact on the Lorenz curve of this economy. The most likely impact on the Lorenz curve will be a shift
o: inwards as all employees receive a higher wage.
inwards as there is an increase in the level of employment.
outwards as all employees receive a higher wage.
outwards as there is an increase in the level of unemployment.

e.why: A minimum wage above equilibrium reduces the quantity of labour demanded, so some workers lose their jobs and their wage income. Inequality rises and the Lorenz curve moves outwards, away from the line of equality.

not.A: Not all employees gain: some lose their jobs. A shift inwards would mean less inequality.
not.B: Employment falls when the wage is set above equilibrium.
not.C: The curve does move outwards, but not because everyone is paid more: it is because some become unemployed.

items.q: What is a role of the World Trade Organisation?
o: To set tariff rates and subsidy levels
To organise countries into trading blocs

e.why: The WTO administers the rules of world trade and runs a dispute settlement process for members.

not.B: Low-interest loans come from the World Bank and the IMF.
not.C: Countries set their own tariffs and subsidies; the WTO provides a forum to negotiate limits on them.
not.D: Trading blocs are formed by the countries themselves.

items.q: A hypothetical economy has a small population, a wide export base and a high per capita income. How would this economy be classified?

e.why: High income per person and a diversified (wide) export base are features of an advanced economy. Population size is not part of the classification.

not.A: Emerging economies are industrialising quickly but have middle incomes.
not.C: Developing economies have low incomes and usually a narrow export base.
not.D: An economic forum is a group of countries, such as the G20, not a type of economy.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT contained in the National Employment Standards?

e.why: The national minimum wage is set each year by the Fair Work Commission. It is not one of the National Employment Standards, which cover leave, hours and similar conditions.

not.A: Annual leave is one of the National Employment Standards.
not.B: Public holidays are one of the National Employment Standards.
not.D: The right to request flexible working arrangements is one of the National Employment Standards.

items.q: A government budgets for a deficit but then there is an unexpected decrease in the level of economic activity. Which row of the table shows the most likely change in tax revenue and the deficit that results?

e.why: Lower economic activity means lower incomes, profits and spending, so tax revenue falls. Welfare spending also rises, so the deficit is larger than planned.

not.B: Revenue does fall, but less revenue makes a deficit bigger.
not.C: Tax revenue falls in a downturn; it does not rise.
not.D: Both are the wrong direction.

items.q: Which of the following reflects deliberate changes in fiscal policy?

e.why: The structural component is what the budget balance would be with the effect of the business cycle removed, so it shows the government's deliberate decisions.

not.A: The cyclical component changes automatically with the level of economic activity.
not.C: The headline cash balance is a measure of the total outcome, including both components.
not.D: The underlying cash balance is also a measure of the total outcome, not of policy decisions alone.

items.q: The Gini coefficient of a hypothetical economy has changed from 0.2 to 0.3. An increase in which of the following is most likely to have caused this?

e.why: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality. A consumption tax is regressive: it takes a larger share of income from low-income earners.

not.A: A higher tax-free threshold helps low-income earners most, reducing inequality.
not.C: Training raises workers' skills and wages, which tends to reduce inequality.
not.D: Welfare spending goes mostly to low-income households, reducing inequality.

items.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about an automatic stabiliser?
o: An increase in marginal income tax rates slows economic growth.
An increase in infrastructure spending increases economic growth.
A reduction in unemployment benefit rates slows economic growth.
Taxpayers moving into higher tax brackets slows economic growth.

e.why: Automatic stabilisers work without a new decision. As incomes rise in an upswing, taxpayers move into higher brackets and pay more tax, which slows growth.

not.A: Changing tax rates is a deliberate (discretionary) decision.
not.B: Infrastructure spending is a discretionary decision.
not.C: Changing benefit rates is a discretionary decision. The stabiliser is the number of people receiving benefits.

items.q: Which of the following would lead to an increase in free trade?
o: Decrease in export incentives and increase in tariffs
Increase in export incentives and decrease in subsidies
Increase in size of existing quotas and decrease in tariffs
Decrease in size of existing quotas and decrease in subsidies

e.why: A larger quota allows more imports and lower tariffs make them cheaper: both reduce protection.

not.A: Higher tariffs increase protection.
not.B: Export incentives are a form of protection, so increasing them moves away from free trade.
not.D: A smaller quota allows fewer imports, which is more protection.

items.q: A hypothetical economy has moved from a Current Account Deficit to a Current Account Surplus. Which of the following is most likely to explain this?
o: A decrease in net saving and depreciation of the currency
A decrease in the price of imports and depreciation of the currency
An increase in export prices and an increase in debt servicing costs
An increase in business investment and a decrease in portfolio investment

e.why: Cheaper imports reduce import payments, and a depreciation makes exports more competitive and imports less attractive. Both improve the current account.

not.A: Lower net saving means more borrowing from overseas, which worsens the current account.
not.C: Higher export prices help, but higher debt servicing costs enlarge the primary income deficit.
not.D: More business investment usually means more imports of capital goods and more foreign borrowing.

items.q: The graph shows the business cycle for an economy. Which row of the table shows the combination of changes that would most likely move GDP from X to Y ?

e.why: From X to Y the economy is slowing. Contractionary policy does that: higher taxes (fiscal) and a higher cash rate (monetary) both reduce spending.

not.A: Higher taxes are contractionary, but a lower cash rate is expansionary.
not.B: Both are expansionary and would lift GDP.
not.C: A higher cash rate is contractionary, but lower taxes are expansionary.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. What is the inflation rate for Year 3?

not.A: 5.4% divides by the new index (8 ÷ 148) instead of the previous year's.
not.C: 6.2% does not use the Year 2 index as the base.
not.D: 8 is the rise in index points, not a percentage.

items.q: In a hypothetical economy, there is an increase in the marginal propensity to save (MPS). Which row of the table shows the likely effects on both the national income and the simple multiplier?

e.why: A higher MPS means more of each extra dollar leaks into saving. The multiplier, 1 ÷ MPS, is smaller, and with less consumption national income falls.

not.A: More saving is a larger leakage; neither income nor the multiplier rises.
not.B: The multiplier does fall, but so does income.
not.C: Income does fall, but the multiplier falls too.

items.q: Which of the following statements is most correct in relation to public goods?
o: Each additional user of a public good affects the amount available to others.
Private companies supply public goods because they make a profit from them.
Anyone can benefit from using public goods without paying directly for them.
Low income earners are disadvantaged because they cannot afford public goods.

e.why: Public goods are non-excludable, so people can use them without paying directly. This is why they are funded from taxation.

not.A: Public goods are non-rival: one person's use does not reduce what is left for others.
not.B: Private firms cannot charge users, so they have no profit incentive to supply public goods.
not.D: No one is charged directly, so low-income earners are not shut out.

items.q: Migrant workers in Australia often send money back to their families overseas. How is this recorded in Australia’s Current Account?

e.why: Money sent home by migrant workers is a transfer with nothing received in return, so it is secondary income. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

not.A: Primary income is earnings such as wages, interest and dividends, not gifts.
not.B: It is neither primary income nor an inflow.
not.D: It is secondary income, but an outflow is a debit.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to cause an increase in both the participation rate and the unemployment rate?
o: An increase in the minimum wage
An increase in the age of school leavers

e.why: A higher minimum wage attracts more people into the labour force (participation rises), but employers demand less labour at the higher wage, so more of them are unemployed.

not.B: Higher government spending creates jobs and lowers the unemployment rate.
not.C: Hidden unemployed people have left the labour force, so participation falls.
not.D: A higher school leaving age takes young people out of the labour force.

items.q: A new tollway eliminates 24 sets of traffic lights. Which of the following is NOT an externality as a result of the new tollway?

e.why: An externality falls on people outside the transaction. Faster trips are the benefit drivers pay the toll for, so they are a private benefit.

not.A: Noise affects nearby residents who are not users: a negative externality.
not.B: Traffic diverted to local streets affects third parties: a negative externality.
not.C: Higher land values benefit owners who did not pay for the road: a positive externality.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. Which of the following best describes the changes to the unemployment rate and the participation rate from Year 1 to Year 2?

e.why: Unemployment rate: 2.5 ÷ 13.6 = 18.4% in Year 1, 2.3 ÷ 14.3 = 16.1% in Year 2 (decreased). Participation rate: 13.6 ÷ 25 = 54.4%, then 14.3 ÷ 26 = 55.0% (increased).

not.B: Both are the wrong direction.
not.C: The unemployment rate did fall, but the participation rate rose.
not.D: The participation rate did rise, but the unemployment rate fell.

items.q: The table shows Balance of Payments data for a hypothetical economy. What is the value of the Balance of Goods and Services (BOGS) and the value of Z ?

e.why: BOGS = exports − imports = 125 − 110 = $15 billion. Current account = 15 − 30 − 20 = −35, so the capital and financial account must be +35. With a capital account of −45, Z = 35 + 45 = $80 billion.

not.A: BOGS is exports minus imports, which is positive, and Z must offset the current account deficit.
not.B: Z is right, but BOGS is +15 because exports exceed imports.
not.C: BOGS is right, but −95 adds the deficits together instead of balancing the accounts.

items.q: A hypothetical economy is operating under a managed exchange rate. The exchange rate is to be maintained between $0.60–$0.70 USD. There has been an increase in demand for the domestic currency leading to its value moving outside the central bank’s range. How should the central bank intervene to move the exchange rate towards its range?
o: Increase cash rate to appreciate the currency
Decrease cash rate to depreciate the currency
Sell foreign currency to appreciate the currency
Buy domestic currency to depreciate the currency

e.why: Stronger demand has pushed the currency above the range. Lowering the cash rate makes the currency less attractive to foreign savers, reducing demand and bringing its value down.

not.A: The currency needs to fall, not rise further.
not.C: Selling foreign currency means buying the domestic currency, which pushes it higher.
not.D: Buying the domestic currency raises its value; it does not depreciate it.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. What is the real economic growth rate for this economy in Year 3?

not.A: 8.7% is the inflation rate (125 − 115) ÷ 115, not real growth.
not.B: 9.6% does not use real GDP in Year 2 as the base.
not.D: 20% is nominal growth (250 to 300), with price rises still included.

items.q: Which of the following is responsible for the promotion of global financial stability?
o: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development

e.why: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and lends to countries in financial difficulty to keep the global financial system stable.

not.A: The World Bank funds development projects to reduce poverty.
not.B: The United Nations deals with peace, security and development, not financial stability.
not.D: The OECD researches and coordinates economic policy among its members.

items.q: A jobless person has now stopped looking for work due to the lack of suitable job vacancies. Which row of the table shows how this person would now be counted in official labour force data?

e.why: To be unemployed a person must be actively looking for work. Someone who has given up looking is a discouraged (hidden unemployed) worker: not counted as unemployed and not in the labour force.

not.B: The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed; this person is neither.
not.C: A person cannot be unemployed without being in the labour force.
not.D: They are no longer actively seeking work, so they are not counted as unemployed.

items.q: Which of the following will NOT contribute to the process of globalisation?
o: Trade policies which are less protectionist
Decrease in significance of transnational corporations

e.why: Transnational corporations drive trade and investment across borders, so a decline in their significance would slow globalisation.

not.A: Migration moves labour between economies, which is part of globalisation.
not.B: Larger financial flows link economies more closely.
not.C: Lower protection increases trade.

items.q: Full employment is said to occur when the unemployment rate is
o: low and unemployment is only cyclical.
low and unemployment is only structural.
low and consistent with a non-accelerating rate of inflation.

e.why: Full employment is the lowest rate of unemployment that does not cause inflation to accelerate (the NAIRU). Some frictional and structural unemployment remains.

not.A: There are always people between jobs, so unemployment is never zero.
not.B: At full employment there is no cyclical unemployment.
not.C: Frictional unemployment also remains, not only structural.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to result from a depreciation in a nation’s currency?
o: Its imports become cheaper and its inflation decreases.
Its imports become more expensive and its inflation increases.
Its exports become cheaper and its inflation decreases.
Its exports become more expensive and its inflation increases.

e.why: A lower currency means more local currency is needed to buy the same imports, so import prices rise and feed into inflation.

not.A: Imports become dearer, not cheaper.
not.C: Exports do become cheaper for foreign buyers, but dearer imports and stronger demand add to inflation.
not.D: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers, not more expensive.

items.q: Farmers purchase and trade permits for water use along a river. This is an example of environmental management through the use of

e.why: Tradable permits create a market for the right to use water, so the price of permits rations use. That is a market-based policy.

not.A: A target is a goal, such as an emissions level by a set year.
not.B: A regulation is a direct rule or ban, with no buying and selling.
not.D: This is a domestic scheme, not an agreement between countries.

items.q: An Australian company buys shares in a European bank to the value of $1 million. Where would this be recorded on the Capital and Financial Account?

e.why: Buying shares worth $1 million in a large bank is well under 10% of the company, so it is not direct investment. NESA accepted both portfolio investment and other investment for this question.

not.A: Direct investment needs a holding of 10% or more, giving a say in running the company.
not.C: Financial derivatives are contracts such as futures and options, not shares.

items.q: The diagram shows a shift in aggregate demand for an economy. All other things being equal, which of the following factors is NOT likely to have caused this shift?

e.why: AD has shifted to the left. Exports are an injection: an increase in exports would shift AD to the right, so it cannot be the cause.

not.B: More imports are a leakage that reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.
not.C: Lower business investment reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.
not.D: Lower government spending reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.

items.q: Why might a government look to end a short-term wage subsidy?
o: To reduce the government budget deficit
To reduce the government budget surplus
To discourage employers from hiring new employees

e.why: A wage subsidy is government spending. Ending it lowers spending and so reduces the budget deficit.

not.A: Removing support is contractionary; it does not expand the economy.
not.C: Ending a spending program would increase a surplus, not reduce it.
not.D: Discouraging hiring is a side effect a government would want to avoid, not a reason.

items.q: A government denies a proposed merger between two airlines. What is this an example of?
o: Regulation being used to enhance competition in a factor market
Regulation being used to enhance competition in a product market
Deregulation being used to enhance competition in a factor market
Deregulation being used to enhance competition in a product market

e.why: Blocking a merger is a rule applied by government (regulation), and airlines sell a service to consumers, so the market is a product market.

not.A: Factor markets are for inputs such as labour and capital, not air travel.
not.C: Stopping a merger is regulation, and this is not a factor market.
not.D: It is a product market, but the government is intervening, which is regulation rather than deregulation.

items.q: The table shows selected information for the balance of payments for a country with a floating exchange rate. Account?

e.why: Current account = net goods + net services + primary income + secondary income = 80.5 + 10.2 − 63.8 − 4.3 = $22.6 billion (a surplus).

not.B: The size is right but the sign is wrong: the positive goods and services balance is larger than the income deficits.
not.C: $30.7 billion is the size of the capital and financial account (13.2 + 17.5).
not.D: −$30.7 billion is the capital and financial account, not the current account.

items.q: What would be the likely impact of a change in a goods and services tax (GST) from 10% to 15%?
o: Decreased Gini coefficient and greater income equality
Decreased Gini coefficient and greater income inequality
Increased Gini coefficient and greater income equality
Increased Gini coefficient and greater income inequality

e.why: The GST is regressive: lower-income households spend a larger share of their income, so a higher rate takes proportionally more from them. Inequality rises, which is a higher Gini coefficient.

not.A: A higher GST widens inequality; it does not reduce it.
not.B: A lower Gini coefficient means more equality, so this option contradicts itself.
not.C: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality, so this option contradicts itself.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase the labour force participation rate?
o: A decrease in the tax-free threshold
An increase in the childcare subsidy
An increase in the highest marginal tax rate
An increase in the minimum school leaving age

e.why: Cheaper childcare makes paid work worthwhile for more parents, so more of them join the labour force.

not.A: A lower tax-free threshold means tax is paid on more income, reducing the reward for working.
not.C: A higher top marginal rate reduces the incentive to work.
not.D: Keeping young people at school longer takes them out of the labour force.

items.q: Which row of the table shows the combination of shifts in the aggregate demand (AD) and aggregate supply (AS) curves that is most likely to lower gross domestic product (GDP)?

e.why: AD shifting left and AS shifting left both reduce output, so GDP falls for certain.

not.A: Both shifts to the right raise GDP.
not.B: AD right raises output while AS left lowers it: the result is uncertain.
not.C: AD left lowers output while AS right raises it: the result is uncertain.

items.q: Which of the following would most likely cause the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) to fall?
o: Increased government spending on welfare payments
Increased government spending on vocational training

e.why: The NAIRU depends on structural and frictional unemployment. Training gives the unemployed the skills employers want, lowering structural unemployment.

not.A: Interest rates affect cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.B: Higher company tax discourages investment and hiring.
not.C: Higher welfare payments can reduce the incentive to seek work, which may raise the NAIRU.

items.q: In Year 1, four countries each had real GDP of $20 billion. The figures for Year 2 for each country are shown in the table. Which country experienced negative economic growth in real terms in Year 2?

e.why: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ CPI × 100. Country C: 23 ÷ 118 × 100 = 19.5, below the $20 billion of Year 1, so real growth is negative.

not.D: 27 ÷ 130 × 100 = 20.8: positive growth.

items.q: The table shows data for a three-sector economy. What will be the level of income in Year 3 if investment falls by $30 million?

e.why: Income rose by 400 and consumption by 320, so MPC = 0.8 and the multiplier is 5. A $30 million fall in investment lowers income by 5 × 30 = 150, to 2400 − 150 = $2250 million.

not.A: $1970 million does not come from the multiplier of 5.
not.C: $2370 million just subtracts the $30 million with no multiplier.
not.D: $2400 million assumes income does not change.

items.q: The table shows selected information for a hypothetical economy. Which row of the table below shows the change in terms of trade (ToT) from Year 2 to Year 3 and a corresponding possible reason for this change?
o: Improves Reduction in foreign labour costs
Improves Increase in global demand for exports
Deteriorates Decrease in global demand for exports
Deteriorates Increase in the supply of foreign raw materials

head: ToT
Reason
rows: Increase in global demand for exports
Decrease in global demand for exports
Increase in the supply of foreign raw materials

e.why: Terms of trade: Year 2 = 115 ÷ 105 × 100 = 109.5; Year 3 = 110 ÷ 85 × 100 = 129.4, an improvement. It came from a large fall in import prices, which lower foreign labour costs would explain.

not.B: The terms of trade do improve, but export prices fell (115 to 110); stronger global demand would have raised them.
not.C: The terms of trade improved; they did not deteriorate.
not.D: A greater supply of foreign raw materials would lower import prices, but that improves the terms of trade.

items.q: The diagram shows the market for a good in a particular economy. This economy initially had a tariff of $6 placed upon the world price of $8 for this good. The government has now reduced the tariff from $6 to $4. All else remaining unchanged, what is the impact of this change in tariff on government revenue?

e.why: With the $6 tariff the price is $14, the no-trade equilibrium, so there are no imports and no revenue. With the $4 tariff the price is $12: supply 30 million, demand 50 million, imports 20 million. Revenue = 20 million × $4 = $80 million, up from zero.

not.B: Revenue was zero before, so it cannot decrease.
not.C: $240 million is total spending on imports at the new price (20 million × $12), not tariff revenue.
not.D: Revenue rises, and $240 million is import spending, not revenue.

items.q: The diagram shows the market for a good in a particular economy. This economy initially had a tariff of $6 placed upon the world price of $8 for this good. The government has now reduced the tariff from $6 to $4. All else remaining unchanged, by how much does the revenue of foreign producers of this good change as a result of this lower tariff?

e.why: Before, there were no imports. After, 20 million units are imported and foreign producers receive the world price of $8 each: 20 million × $8 = $160 million.

not.A: $40 million does not match any area on the diagram for the new imports.
not.B: $80 million is the tariff revenue, which goes to the government.
not.D: $240 million is what consumers pay for imports including the tariff (20 million × $12).

items.q: What is the role of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)?
o: To provide interest-free loans to developing economies
To promote sustainable growth and employment for member countries
To boost global financial liquidity during financial crises and global downturns
To provide a forum for leaders and finance ministers of the seven largest economies

e.why: The OECD is a group of mostly advanced economies that share research and coordinate policy to support sustainable growth, employment and living standards in its members.

not.A: Low-interest and interest-free development loans come from the World Bank.
not.C: Supporting liquidity in a financial crisis is the role of the IMF.
not.D: A forum of the seven largest advanced economies is the G7.

items.q: Which of the following is the largest export industry in terms of value for Australia?

e.why: Mining (iron ore, coal, gas) is by far Australia's largest export earner by value.

not.A: Manufacturing is a small and declining share of Australia's exports.
not.C: Rural exports are significant but far smaller than mining.
not.D: Services (education, tourism) are important but well below mining in value.

items.q: An economy’s labour force participation rate falls from 65% to 60%. What is a possible reason for this change?
o: An increase in this economy’s GDP
An increase in funding for childcare places
The official school leaving age has been increased from 16 to 18 years
The official retirement age of workers has been increased from 65 to 68 years

e.why: Keeping 16 and 17 year olds at school removes them from the labour force while they are still counted in the working age population (15 and over), so the participation rate falls.

not.A: Higher GDP creates jobs and draws people into the labour force.
not.B: More childcare places make it easier for parents to work, raising participation.
not.D: A later retirement age keeps older workers in the labour force, raising participation.

items.q: The diagram shows the aggregate demand and supply curves for an economy. What may have caused the shift from AD1 to AD2?

e.why: AD has shifted to the right. Lower taxes raise disposable income and consumption, increasing aggregate demand.

not.B: Imports are a leakage: more imports reduce aggregate demand.
not.C: Lower consumption shifts AD to the left.
not.D: Capacity constraints limit aggregate supply; they do not shift AD to the right.

items.q: To protect its domestic farmers, Country A has increased tariffs on imports of agricultural products from Country B. Which row of the table shows the effect of the higher tariff on each country?

head: Consumer prices for agricultural products in Country A
Producer’s income in Country B

e.why: A tariff raises the price of imported farm products for Country A's consumers. Country B's farmers sell less to Country A, so their income falls.

not.A: Prices do rise in Country A, but exporters in Country B lose sales and income.
not.C: A tariff makes imports dearer, not cheaper, and it does not help Country B's producers.
not.D: Country B's producers do lose income, but prices in Country A rise.

items.q: What is a likely effect on Australia of signing a multilateral free trade agreement?
o: An increase in trade with non-member countries
An increase in tariff revenue for the government
An increase in long-run real gross domestic product
Lower levels of short-term structural unemployment

e.why: Free trade lets resources move to industries where Australia has a comparative advantage and opens larger markets, lifting productivity and long-run real GDP.

not.A: Agreements favour members, so trade can be diverted away from non-members.
not.B: Removing tariffs reduces tariff revenue.
not.D: Less competitive industries shrink at first, which raises structural unemployment in the short term.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a public good?

e.why: A public good is non-excludable and non-rival: no one can be stopped from breathing clean air, and one person's use does not reduce another's.

not.B: Public housing is excludable and rival: a home given to one family is not available to another.
not.C: Internet access is excludable (you pay for a connection).
not.D: Bus travel is excludable by fare and seats are rival, even when the government provides it.

items.q: Which of the following represents a contractionary change in fiscal stance from Year 1 to Year 2?

e.why: A contractionary stance takes more out of the economy than before. Moving from a $10 million to a $20 million surplus does that.

not.A: A smaller surplus means the budget is taking less out of the economy: expansionary.
not.B: The outcome has not changed, so the stance is unchanged.
not.C: A larger deficit is more expansionary.

items.q: The table shows data for Country A. It is likely that Country A has experienced
o: greater access to transport and communication.
decreased levels of international financial flows.

e.why: A rising HDI means better health, education and income. Greater access to transport and communication is a mark of development and of integration with the global economy.

not.A: More protection cuts an economy off from trade and usually slows development.
not.B: Less access to technology would hold back education and income.
not.D: Lower financial flows mean less investment, which slows development.

items.q: A country has decided to decrease its import quota on a particular good. What is the most likely reason for this decision?
o: To reduce dumping on domestic markets
To reduce its current account surplus in the long term
To increase the standard of living and income of its citizens
To encourage specialisation in the industry in which it has a comparative advantage

e.why: A smaller quota lets in fewer imports. One reason to restrict imports is to stop foreign firms dumping goods at below-cost prices on the local market.

not.B: Fewer imports would increase a current account surplus, not reduce it.
not.C: Protection raises prices and reduces choice, lowering living standards.
not.D: Protection shelters less efficient industries; it works against specialisation by comparative advantage.

items.q: The following diagram shows a foreign exchange market for Australian dollars. Which of the following is most likely to have caused the shift in supply of $A from S1 to S2?
o: A decrease in interest rates in Australia
A decrease in Australia’s demand for imports
A decrease in investment opportunities in Australia

e.why: The supply of Australian dollars has decreased (S1 to S2 is a shift left). Australians supply dollars when they buy imports, so lower demand for imports reduces supply.

not.A: Higher commodity prices increase the demand for Australian dollars; they do not reduce supply.
not.B: Lower Australian interest rates send funds overseas, which increases the supply of dollars.
not.D: Fewer investment opportunities reduce foreign demand for dollars, and may increase supply as Australians invest abroad.

items.q: If the Reserve Bank of Australia adjusts the interest rate corridor to decrease the cash rate target, which of the following is most likely to occur?

e.why: A lower cash rate lowers borrowing costs. Cheaper credit raises demand for assets such as houses and shares, lifting their prices, and makes more business investment worthwhile.

not.A: Both are the wrong direction: these are the effects of a higher cash rate.
not.B: Investment does rise, but cheaper credit pushes asset prices up, not down.
not.C: Asset prices do rise, but lower borrowing costs increase investment.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for Country X. X?

e.why: Net foreign liabilities = all foreign liabilities minus all foreign assets. Liabilities: loans owed to foreigners 1200 + Country X assets owned by foreigners 500 = 1700. Assets: loans owed by foreigners 300 + foreign assets owned 200 = 500. 1700 − 500 = $1200 billion.

not.A: $600 billion does not come from the four items: all the liabilities must be added before all the assets are taken away.
not.B: $800 billion subtracts items that should be added: foreign-owned assets in Country X are a liability.
not.C: $900 billion is net foreign debt only (1200 − 300). Net foreign equity (500 − 200) has been left out.

items.q: A government imposes a tax to reduce a negative externality of production. How does this seek to correct the market failure?

e.why: Producers ignore the external cost they impose on others. A tax adds that cost to their own costs, raising marginal private cost towards marginal social cost so that less is produced.

not.B: Lowering private cost would encourage even more production.
not.C: The tax is on producers' costs; it does not change the benefit buyers receive.
not.D: The problem is on the cost side of production, not the benefit side.

items.q: A country has experienced a significant deterioration in its terms of trade (ToT). What combination of events could have caused this?

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Export prices falling while import prices rise makes the ratio fall sharply.

not.B: If both fall by the same percentage the ratio does not change.
not.C: Export prices up and import prices down is an improvement.
not.D: If both rise by the same percentage the ratio does not change.

items.q: The diagram shows the fixed exchange rate for a hypothetical economy. What action will the central bank of this economy need to undertake to maintain this rate?

e.why: The rate is fixed at 0.50, below the market equilibrium of 0.75. At 0.50 demand for the currency exceeds supply, so the central bank must supply more of its own currency by selling it and buying foreign currency.

not.A: Higher interest rates would attract funds and push the currency further above the fixed rate.
not.C: Buying the domestic currency adds to demand and pushes its value up.
not.D: Restricting outflows reduces the supply of the currency, pushing its value up.

items.q: The table shows CPI data for an economy. Which expenditure group made the greatest contribution to inflation?

e.why: Contribution = weight × price rise. Education 15 × 15 = 225; Food 35 × 10 = 350; Health 20 × 25 = 500; Housing 16 × 30 = 480. Health is the largest.

not.A: Education has the smallest contribution (225).
not.B: Food has the largest weight but the smallest price rise (350).
not.D: Housing has the largest price rise but a smaller weight than Health (480).

items.q: The table shows national income data for a hypothetical economy. If the government increased its level of expenditure by $50 million in Year 3, what would be the new level of national income?

e.why: Income rose by 100 and consumption by 80, so MPC = 0.8 and the multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5. Extra income = 5 × 50 = 250, so national income = 1100 + 250 = $1350 million.

not.A: $1150 million just adds the $50 million with no multiplier.
not.B: $1200 million uses a multiplier of 2.
not.D: $1600 million uses a multiplier of 10.

items.q: The graph shows the demand and supply for T-shirts in Country X at the world price of $5. Country X would like to reduce the number of imported T-shirts by 50 000. What subsidy would Country X need to pay its domestic producers per T-shirt to achieve this reduction in the number of imports?

e.why: At the world price of $5, domestic supply is 50 000 and demand is 150 000, so imports are 100 000. A subsidy does not change the price consumers pay, so to cut imports by 50 000 domestic supply must rise to 100 000. Producers supply 100 000 only at $15, so the subsidy is $15 − $5 = $10.

not.A: A $5 subsidy gives producers $10, at which they supply 75 000: imports fall by only 25 000.
not.C: $15 is the price producers need to receive, not the subsidy on top of the $5 world price.
not.D: A $20 subsidy would lift supply to 150 000 and end imports altogether.

items.q: The table shows trade weightings for five of Australia’s trading partners. Which pair of movements would cause a decrease in the Trade Weighted Index?

e.why: The TWI weights each currency by its share of trade. A 10% fall against the yen (weight 13) outweighs a 10% rise against the US dollar (weight 8), so the index falls.

not.A: The rise against the renminbi (31) far outweighs the fall against the euro (9): the TWI rises.
not.B: The rise against the yen (13) outweighs the fall against the won (7): the TWI rises.
not.C: The rise against the euro (9) slightly outweighs the fall against the US dollar (8): the TWI rises a little.

items.q: Which of the following has improving quality of life in developing countries as its main role?
o: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)

e.why: The World Bank lends for development projects to reduce poverty and raise living standards in developing countries.

not.B: The WTO sets and enforces the rules of world trade.
not.C: The IMF looks after the stability of the international financial system and helps countries in financial crisis.
not.D: The OECD is a forum of mostly advanced economies that researches and coordinates policy.

items.q: Which of the following is a benefit of a centralised wage determination system?
o: Provision of a safety net for workers

e.why: Centralised wage fixing sets minimum pay and conditions for everyone, which protects workers with little bargaining power.

not.A: Uniform wages make it harder for labour to move to growing industries, so structural change is slower.
not.B: Wage flexibility is a feature of decentralised bargaining, not a centralised system.
not.D: Centralised systems compress wage differences, and greater inequality would not be a benefit.

items.q: Which TWO economic objectives conflict with one another in the short term?

e.why: In the short term, stronger demand lowers unemployment but pushes prices up, and slowing inflation costs jobs (the Phillips curve trade-off).

not.B: Economic growth creates jobs, so growth and low unemployment go together.
not.C: There is no direct short-term trade-off between these two.
not.D: Inflation is not an objective (price stability is), and it has no clear short-term conflict with sustainability.

items.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of free trade for a domestic economy?

e.why: With open markets, foreign firms can sell goods below cost (dumping), which can drive efficient local firms out of business.

not.A: Greater competition is usually counted as an advantage: it lifts efficiency and lowers prices.
not.B: Free trade lowers domestic prices by letting in cheaper imports.
not.D: Access to bigger markets lets firms gain economies of scale, an advantage.

items.q: A foreign investor buys a 5% share in an Australian company. How is this recorded in Australia’s capital and financial account?

e.why: A holding below 10% of a company is portfolio investment. Foreign money flowing into Australia is a credit on the financial account.

not.A: Direct investment needs 10% or more of the company, and an inflow is not a debit.
not.B: It is a credit, but 5% is too small to be direct investment.
not.C: It is portfolio investment, but money coming in is a credit, not a debit.

items.q: The following information is for a hypothetical economy. What is the labour force participation rate for this economy?

e.why: Labour force = employed + unemployed = 7 + 2 = 9 million. Participation rate = 9 ÷ 11 (working age population) × 100 = 82%.

not.A: 44% is employed people as a share of the total population (7 ÷ 16).
not.B: 56% uses the total population (9 ÷ 16) instead of the working age population.
not.C: 78% is employed ÷ labour force (7 ÷ 9), the employment rate.

items.q: The table shows data for national income and savings for a hypothetical economy. What is the value of marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

e.why: Income rose by 100 (375 to 475) and savings rose by 40 (160 to 200), so MPS = 0.4 and MPC = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.

not.A: 0.34 does not come from the changes in income and saving; the marginal propensity uses changes, not levels.
not.B: 0.40 is the MPS, the share of extra income saved.
not.D: 0.8 would need savings to rise by only 20 for each extra 100 of income.

items.q: Which of the following has the shortest implementation time lag?

e.why: The Reserve Bank Board can decide and announce a change in the cash rate on the day it meets. The lag for monetary policy is in its effect, not its implementation.

not.A: Fiscal changes usually wait for the Budget and must pass Parliament.
not.C: Environmental policies need legislation, negotiation and long phase-in periods.
not.D: Microeconomic reforms take years to legislate and put in place.

items.q: The improved efficiency of job search agencies is most likely to reduce which of the following?

e.why: Frictional unemployment is people between jobs. Better job matching shortens the time it takes them to find work.

not.A: Better job search services would, if anything, encourage people to look for work, raising participation.
not.B: Faster matching would not reduce full-time employment.
not.C: Cyclical unemployment is caused by weak demand in a downturn, not by slow job matching.

items.q: Which of the following actions by the Reserve Bank of Australia would appreciate the value of the Australian dollar?

e.why: A higher cash rate attracts foreign savings, raising demand for the dollar, and buying Australian dollars in the foreign exchange market also raises demand. Both push the dollar up.

not.A: Selling Australian dollars increases their supply and pushes the dollar down.
not.C: Both actions push the dollar down.
not.D: Buying dollars supports the currency, but a lower cash rate reduces demand for it.

items.q: The diagram shows the aggregate demand and supply curves for an economy. What would most likely cause the shift from AS1 to AS2?
o: Increase in the goods and services tax to 15%
Reduction in migrants arriving in the economy
Increase in government spending on aged pensions

e.why: Lower university fees lead to more people gaining skills. A more skilled workforce raises productive capacity, shifting aggregate supply to the right.

not.B: A higher GST raises prices and reduces spending; it does not increase productive capacity.
not.C: Fewer migrants means a smaller labour force, which would shift aggregate supply left.
not.D: Pension spending adds to consumption, which is aggregate demand, not supply.

items.q: The table shows selected information for the balance of payments for an economy with a floating exchange rate. What is the value of the exports of goods?

e.why: Capital account + financial account = 24 + 66 = 90, so the current account must be −90. Current account = (X − 36) + 12 − 120 − 6 = X − 150. Setting X − 150 = −90 gives X = $60 billion.

not.A: −$60 billion has the right size but exports of goods cannot be negative.
not.B: −$12 billion is not possible for exports and ignores the balancing of the accounts.
not.C: $54 billion leaves out net secondary income (−6).

items.q: The government of an economy is planning to increase the local content rules of television streaming services. Which row in the table shows the effect of the increase in local content rules on imports and short-term employment opportunities for this economy?

e.why: Local content rules require more locally made programs, so fewer foreign programs are imported and more local production jobs are created in the short term.

not.A: More local content replaces imported content, so imports fall rather than rise.
not.B: Imports fall, and local production needs more workers, not fewer.
not.D: Imports do fall, but short-term job opportunities in local production rise.

items.q: The income Gini coefficient for a hypothetical economy increases from 0.35 in Year 1 to 0.46 in Year 2. What combination of changes in government policies is most likely to have caused the increase in the income Gini coefficient?

e.why: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality. Cutting childcare subsidies and lowering the tax-free threshold both take proportionally more from low-income households.

not.B: Raising the tax-free threshold helps low-income earners most, which reduces inequality.
not.C: Higher childcare subsidies help lower-income families work and earn more.
not.D: Both changes would reduce inequality, lowering the Gini coefficient.

items.q: Which of the following cyclical and structural factors are the most likely to affect the net primary income account?
o: Government budget outcomes Domestic business cycle

e.why: Net primary income is mostly interest and dividends paid overseas. Interest rates move with the cycle and change the cost of servicing foreign debt. Low national savings is the long-term (structural) reason Australia borrows from overseas at all.

not.A: The terms of trade mainly affect the balance on goods and services, and are not a structural factor.
not.C: The domestic business cycle is a cyclical factor, not a structural one.
not.D: A narrow export base and competitiveness are both structural, and they affect the goods and services balance.

items.q: In a hypothetical economy, the headline inflation rate is rising faster than the underlying inflation rate. Which of the following is most likely to have caused this situation?
o: A rise in the global production of oil
An increase in capital city house prices
The opening of a new international shipping route
A cyclone in domestic tropical fruit-producing locations

e.why: A cyclone that destroys fruit crops pushes fruit prices up sharply. Fruit is a volatile item: it is counted in headline inflation but removed from underlying inflation.

not.A: More oil production lowers fuel prices, which would pull headline inflation down.
not.B: Rising house prices are not a temporary, one-off price shock of the kind underlying inflation strips out.
not.C: A new shipping route lowers transport costs and prices.

items.q: The cost of imported intermediate goods is rising in Australia. All other things being equal, what is the most likely impact on Australia’s exchange rate and domestic prices?

e.why: Paying more for imports means more Australian dollars are sold to buy foreign currency, which depreciates the dollar. Dearer inputs also raise firms' costs, so domestic prices rise.

not.A: Prices do rise, but a bigger import bill increases the supply of dollars, which lowers their value.
not.B: Both are the wrong direction.
not.D: The dollar does depreciate, but higher input costs raise prices, not lower them.

items.q: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. Which of the following statements is correct about this economy?
o: Net foreign liabilities as a percentage of GDP has decreased, leading to a deterioration in external stability.
Net foreign liabilities as a percentage of GDP has increased, leading to an improvement in external stability.
Current Account Balance as a percentage of GDP has decreased, leading to an improvement in external stability.
Current Account Balance as a percentage of GDP has increased, leading to a deterioration in external stability.

e.why: The current account deficit was 35 ÷ 1200 = 2.92% of GDP in Year 1 and 36 ÷ 1250 = 2.88% in Year 2. A smaller deficit as a share of GDP is an improvement in external stability.

not.A: Net foreign liabilities did fall (900 to 850, or 75% to 68% of GDP), but that is an improvement, not a deterioration.
not.B: Net foreign liabilities as a share of GDP fell; they did not rise.
not.D: The deficit grew in dollars but shrank as a percentage of GDP.

items.q: The table shows information for a hypothetical economy. Which of the following best explains the reason for changes in the Trade Weighted Index and terms of trade from Year 1 to Year 2 in this economy?
o: An increase in domestic interest rates
A decrease in global demand for this economy’s exports

e.why: Weaker world demand for exports lowers export prices (terms of trade fall from 110 to 100) and lowers demand for the currency (TWI falls from 65 to 60).

not.A: Lower global inflation would make imports cheaper, which improves the terms of trade.
not.B: Higher domestic interest rates attract foreign funds and push the TWI up.
not.C: Domestic unemployment does not directly change export or import prices.

items.q: The following shows nominal GDP and price data (CPI) for an economy. Which of the following statements is true for this economy?
o: Real economic growth in Year 2 is 3.1% and inflation is 10%.
Real economic growth in Year 2 is 3.1% and inflation is 9.1%.
Real economic growth in Year 2 is 12.5% and inflation is 10%.
Real economic growth in Year 2 is 12.5% and inflation is 9.1%.

not.A: Growth is right, but 10 is the rise in index points; as a percentage of 110 it is 9.1%.
not.C: 12.5% is nominal GDP growth, and 10 is index points, not the inflation rate.
not.D: Inflation is right, but 12.5% is nominal growth with price rises still included.

items.q: Country A and Country B agree to share a common currency. What is this an example of?

e.why: A monetary union is a group of countries that share one currency and one monetary policy, as the euro area does.

not.B: A free trade area removes trade barriers between members; each keeps its own currency.
not.C: A bilateral trade agreement is about trade between two countries, not their currency.
not.D: A multilateral trade agreement involves three or more countries and is about trade, not a shared currency.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to accelerate globalisation?
o: A decrease in the global price of energy
An increase in tariffs by advanced economies

e.why: Cheaper energy lowers the cost of transport and production, which makes trading goods across borders cheaper and speeds up integration.

not.A: Less labour mobility means fewer workers moving between countries, which slows globalisation.
not.B: Dearer communication makes it harder to trade and invest across borders.
not.D: Higher tariffs are protection: they reduce trade.

items.q: The table shows the health and education aspects of different types of economies. Which row of the following table correctly identifies the indicators X and Y?
o: Low literacy rates Low life expectancy
High literacy rates High life expectancy
High literacy rates Low life expectancy
Low literacy rates High life expectancy

e.why: X is the education indicator for a developing economy (low literacy) and Y is the health indicator for an advanced economy (high life expectancy).

not.A: Low literacy fits X, but an advanced economy has high, not low, life expectancy.
not.B: High life expectancy fits Y, but a developing economy has low literacy.
not.C: Both are the wrong way around.

items.q: Which component of the government budget outcome is likely to decrease during an economic downturn?

e.why: In a downturn households spend less, so revenue from taxes on spending such as the GST falls automatically.

not.A: Interest rates are set by the Reserve Bank and are not a component of the budget outcome.
not.C: Unemployment benefit payments rise in a downturn as more people lose work.
not.D: Lower revenue and higher welfare spending push the budget towards deficit, so borrowing rises.

items.q: Why is public transport considered a private good?
o: It is non-excludable and is paid for from taxation.
It is excludable by price and is rival in consumption.
It is rival in consumption and is non-excludable by price.
It is excludable by price and is provided by the government.

e.why: A private good is excludable and rival. A fare excludes people who do not pay, and a seat taken by one passenger cannot be used by another.

not.A: Public transport is excludable: you need a ticket. Being funded from tax does not decide the type of good.
not.C: It is rival, but it is excludable by price, not non-excludable.
not.D: Who provides a good does not decide whether it is public or private; excludability and rivalry do.

items.q: Which of the following is the main rationale for the use of macroeconomic policy?
o: Increasing economic growth and aggregate supply
Managing stabilisation and shifts in aggregate demand
Achieving environmental sustainability and lower costs

e.why: Macroeconomic policy (fiscal and monetary) works on aggregate demand to smooth the business cycle.

not.A: Productivity and efficiency are the aim of microeconomic policy.
not.B: Shifting aggregate supply is the rationale for microeconomic policy.
not.D: Environmental sustainability is pursued through environmental policies, and it is not the main rationale for macroeconomic policy.

items.q: An initial increase of government spending of $10 million leads to a final increase in national income of $50 million. What is the value of the marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

e.why: The multiplier is 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), 1 − MPC = 0.2, so MPC = 0.8.

not.A: 0.2 is the MPS (1 ÷ 5), not the MPC.
not.B: An MPC of 0.4 gives a multiplier of about 1.7, not 5.
not.C: An MPC of 0.5 gives a multiplier of 2, not 5.

items.q: What is a key characteristic of a regional business cycle?
o: Economic fluctuations that occur in rural areas
Economic stability between countries across the globe
Consistent growth rates in all states within an economy
Integration of economic activity across neighbouring countries

e.why: A regional business cycle is the pattern of economic activity shared by neighbouring countries whose economies are closely linked by trade and investment.

not.A: Regional here means a region of the world, not rural areas within a country.
not.B: It describes fluctuations, not stability, and a region rather than the whole globe.
not.C: It is about a group of countries, not the states inside one economy.

items.q: The table shows selected data for a hypothetical economy. Based on the information in the table, which of the following is correct?

e.why: Injections are I + G + X = 20 + 80 + 60 = 160. Leakages are S + T + M = 10 + 70 + 50 = 130. Injections are greater.

not.A: Exports (60) are greater than imports (50), so there is a trade surplus.
not.B: Government spending (80) is greater than taxation (70), so the budget is in deficit.
not.D: Leakages (130) are less than injections (160).

items.q: How is unconditional foreign aid provided by the Australian government recorded in the Balance of Payments?
o: A credit in the current account
A debit in the current account
A credit in the capital account
A debit in the capital account

e.why: Aid with no conditions attached is a transfer with nothing received in return, recorded in secondary income on the current account. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

not.A: The money is leaving Australia, so it is a debit, not a credit.
not.C: Only conditional (capital) aid goes in the capital account, and an outflow is not a credit.
not.D: It is a debit, but unconditional aid belongs in the current account. The capital account records conditional aid for capital projects.

items.q: Which component of the federal budget is directly affected by automatic stabilisers?

e.why: Automatic stabilisers (progressive income tax and unemployment benefits) change with the business cycle without any new decision, so they move the cyclical component.

not.B: External is not a component of the budget outcome.
not.C: The structural component reflects deliberate policy, with the effect of the cycle removed.
not.D: Discretionary changes are deliberate decisions by the government, the opposite of automatic.

items.q: Which of the following policy options could use market forces to reduce negative environmental outcomes?
o: Introducing a new tax on electric and hybrid cars
Ceasing the operation of coal-fired power stations
Imposing fines for harmful emissions from households

e.why: An emissions trading scheme puts a price on pollution and lets firms buy and sell permits, so the market decides where emissions are cut.

not.B: A tax on electric and hybrid cars would discourage cleaner cars and make outcomes worse.
not.C: Closing power stations is direct regulation, not the use of market forces.
not.D: Fines are a penalty set by regulation; they are not a market in which prices are set by trading.

items.q: The table shows selected information for the Balance of Payments for an economy with a floating exchange rate. What is the value of the financial account?

e.why: Current account = (150 − 130) + (60 − 50) − 50 + 10 = −10. With a floating rate the current account and the capital and financial account sum to zero, so capital and financial must be +10. With a capital account of 70, the financial account is 10 − 70 = −60.

not.A: −80 comes from treating the current account as +10: the two sides must offset, not match.
not.C: $10 billion is the whole capital and financial account, before taking out the capital account of 70.
not.D: $280 billion comes from adding items together rather than balancing the accounts.

items.q: The table shows selected data for a hypothetical economy. Which row in the table shows the most likely reasons for changes in inflation rates from Year 1 to Year 2?
o: Drought in food-producing areas Decrease in freight costs
Increase in import tariffs Rise in minimum wage
Microeconomic reform Conflict in oil-producing countries
Temporary discount in fuel excise tax Increase in textile imports

head: Reason for change in headline inflation
Reason for change in underlying inflation
rows: Temporary discount in fuel excise tax

e.why: Headline inflation rose (4.5% to 5%) while underlying fell (3.8% to 3.4%). A drought raises food prices, a volatile item that affects headline but is removed from underlying. Lower freight costs reduce prices across the economy, lowering underlying inflation.

not.B: Higher tariffs and a higher minimum wage raise costs broadly, so underlying inflation would rise, not fall.
not.C: Microeconomic reform lowers costs, so it does not explain higher headline inflation, and an oil conflict would not lower underlying inflation.
not.D: A fuel excise discount lowers fuel prices, which would reduce headline inflation.

items.q: The following table shows selected data for a hypothetical economy. What is the rate of real economic growth from Year 1 to Year 2 in this economy?

e.why: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ CPI × 100. Year 1: 18 ÷ 90 × 100 = 20. Year 2: 22 ÷ 110 × 100 = 20. Real GDP did not change, so growth is 0%.

not.B: 4 is the rise in nominal GDP in dollars ($22b − $18b), not a growth rate.
not.C: 20 is the level of real GDP in both years, not its growth.
not.D: 22% is the growth in nominal GDP (and in prices). Once inflation is removed nothing is left.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for country X. What is the net foreign liability for this economy?

rows: Assets owned by country X overseas
Assets in country X owned by foreigners
Debts owed by country X to foreign lenders
Debts owed by foreigners to country X

e.why: Net foreign liabilities = what the country owes the world minus what the world owes it. Liabilities: 3.0 + 1.8 = 4.8. Assets: 1.2 + 0.5 = 1.7. 4.8 − 1.7 = $3.1 million.

not.A: $6.5 million adds all four items together instead of subtracting assets.
not.B: $4.8 million is the liabilities only; foreign assets have not been subtracted.
not.D: $500 000 is just one line of the table.

items.q: The graph shows the effect of a quota on imported machinery in the domestic market, with the initial equilibrium at X. The government chooses to reduce, but not eliminate, the quota. From the prices shown on the graph, which is the most likely new price of machinery?

e.why: A smaller quota lets in fewer imports, so supply falls and the price rises above X. Because the quota still exists, the price stays below P1, the price with no imports at all. P2 is the only price between X and P1.

not.A: P1 is the price with no imports at all. The quota is reduced, not eliminated in favour of a total ban.
not.C: P3 is below X. A tighter quota raises the price; it does not lower it.
not.D: P4 is the world price, which applies only with no quota at all.

items.q: The graph shows a recently imposed tariff on imported beef. Assume that the world price for beef is $20 and the tariff is $10 per unit of beef. By what amount does the revenue of foreign producers of beef decrease as a result of the tariff?

e.why: Before the tariff the price is $20: demand 600, domestic supply 200, imports 400, so foreign revenue is 400 × $20 = $8000. With the tariff the price is $30: demand 500, domestic supply 300, imports 200. Foreign producers still receive only the world price, so revenue is 200 × $20 = $4000. The fall is $4000.

not.A: $2000 is the tariff revenue collected by the government (200 × $10).
not.C: $8000 is foreign producers' revenue before the tariff, not the decrease.
not.D: $16 000 is too large: total import spending was only $8000 to begin with.

items.q: The table shows hypothetical data for an economy. Which row of the table shows the export price index of this economy in Year 1 and Year 2?

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Year 1: 110 × 100 ÷ 100 = 110. Year 2: 90 × 110 ÷ 100 = 99.

not.A: 90 and 110 are read straight off the table (the Year 2 terms of trade and import price index), not calculated.
not.B: 99 is the Year 2 export price index, not Year 1.
not.C: 110 is right for Year 1, but 90 is the Year 2 terms of trade, not the export price index.

items.q: The graph shows market failure as a negative externality of production. What is the per unit tax required to correct the market failure shown on the graph?

e.why: The tax must equal the external cost: the vertical gap between the social cost and private cost curves. At Q3 that gap runs from P1 (private cost) up to P3 (social cost). The same gap can be seen at Q2, from P0 to P2.

not.A: P0 to P1 is only part of the gap between the curves.
not.B: P1 to P2 is the rise in the market price after the tax, which is smaller than the tax because producers bear part of it.
not.C: P2 to P3 is only part of the gap between the curves.

items.samp: Globalisation has both negative and positive effects on environmental sustainability. Globalisation has increased trade and Gross World Product. It has also resulted in an increase in industrialisation and urbanisation in both developed and developing countries. The demand for resources to support this growth has resulted in a depletion of natural resources, environmental degradation and increased pollution and carbon emissions. The combination of these has meant a significant decline in global environmental sustainability. However, increasing development has also resulted in a growing global awareness of the need to improve the sustainability of economic growth and brought attention to issues such as global warming. International agreements such as the Kyoto and Montreal Protocol and research into green technologies have been possible through globalisation and hold the key to improve environmental sustainability for future generations.

items.samp: The participation rate can decline as a result of an economic slowdown as a reduction in the number of available jobs discourages people from seeking work. These discouraged workers are not counted in the labour force; they are hidden unemployed. The participation rate can also decline if young people decide to spend longer in full-time study, rather than seeking paid employment. In both cases, once an unemployed person stops actively seeking work (for whatever reason), they are no longer officially counted as part of the labour force and hence the participation rate (other things being equal) declines.

items.samp: The limitations of fiscal policy include political constraints – taxation and spending decisions are the outcome of political compromise rather than being economically optimal. Implementation of fiscal policy is also subject to time lags due to the time required to pass necessary legislation through parliament. Monetary policy is subject to shorter time lags than fiscal policy since it is managed by the politically independent Central Bank. Nevertheless, changes in official interest rates take time to affect the real economy as consumers and businesses do not change their spending and borrowing behaviour immediately. Monetary policy is subject to global influences to a greater extent than fiscal policy. For example, low global interest rates will put upward pressure on a country’s exchange rate if the local Central Bank does not reduce local interest rates.

items.samp: Two methods of financing a budget deficit are borrowing from the Reserve Bank or borrowing from the private sector. Borrowing from the RBA involves the RBA creating an increase in the money supply and loaning these funds direct to the government. Borrowing from the private sector involves “selling” new Commonwealth Government securities to the private sector. Borrowing from the private sector does not directly impact interest rates. However it may increase interest rates indirectly. This is because of increased competition for limited funds available in the domestic market. In contrast, borrowing from the RBA may have inflationary consequences due to the additional money supply in the domestic economy. This could lead to increased interest rates as the RBA seeks to maintain the inflation target.

This is often referred to as imported inflation.

This means any policy which aims to increase aggregate demand (eg expansionary fiscal policy) will increase inflation without reducing unemployment. Therefore, a government that aims to reduce unemployment must reduce structural or frictional unemployment. Government can do this by labour market reforms, which increase flexibility, mobility and skills in the labour market. This is potentially difficult for governments due to limitations such as time lags and political constraints.

items.samp: The international division of labour is when different nations specialise in different types of production and labour skills. For example, developing nations often have low skilled, low paid labour markets, which are part of global markets through transnational corporations and global production webs. These low skilled workers depend upon income and investment from developed nations, which in turn depend upon the supply of low cost manufactured products. This is a key part of the increased integration and interdependence between economies.

items.samp: There are many reasons for different levels of economic development between nations. One reason for different levels of economic development is natural resource endowment. Economies with larger quantities of resources use these resources to generate export income, which can be used to fund education and health. Economies with limited quantities of natural resources are unable to generate income to fund this development. Another reason for different levels of development is the differences in the quality of political and economic institutions. Some economies are supported by well-developed institutions, which protect property and investments and minimise corruption. In contrast, other economies have weak political institutions, which discourage the private and public investment necessary to fund development.
