items.samp: Subsidies can impact on both the revenue and expenditure side of the government budget. Removal of the subsidy will reduce government expenditure and, other things being equal, increase a budget surplus or reduce a budget deficit. However, in removing the subsidy, the government may decide to allocate funds to help workers who lose their jobs retrain and find new jobs in other industries. Removing the subsidy, therefore, may increase government spending in the short term. On the revenue side, to the extent that the removal of the subsidy encourages more private sector investment in more efficient industries, this should result in an increase in government taxation revenue over the long term. More efficient industries will generate greater profit and, therefore, pay more company tax.

items.samp: The MPC measures the amount of each extra dollar of income that is spent. A decrease in the MPC means that an economy will tend to be saving more and spending less. A decrease in the MPC also represents an increase in leakages in an economy that results in a reduction in the size of the economy’s multiplier. Each dollar spent in an economy is someone else’s income, which they then re-spend. Therefore, if people spend a lower proportion of each dollar of income, they will spend less, and someone else’s income will be lower and they too will spend less (not just because they are saving more but also because they have less income). A lower MPC therefore means that other things being equal, any increase in the components of aggregate demand will result in a smaller increase in national income.
could: policy implications of change in MPC impact on investment, implications for efficiency, productive capacity and, hence, future growth prospects.

items.title: RBA expected to hold at 4.85% despite inflation surprise

items.guide: When inflation expectations rise, the short-run Phillips curve shifts up, so both inflation and unemployment rise: raising rates fights inflation but pushes unemployment higher still. The split vote shows the policy trade-off and is evidence of the limitations of monetary policy.

Requiring a share of gas production to be sold locally rather than exported.

items.title: RBA: small businesses squeezed by weak demand and rising costs

Assess the potential of AI adoption to improve productivity in Australia.

items.guide: Small businesses feel tight monetary policy through the cash-flow channel (higher loan repayments) and weaker household spending; with about half of small business credit secured on housing, a weak housing market can also restrict finance. Financial stress is expected to rise most in construction, hospitality and retail (hospitality has the highest insolvency rate).

terms.def: Costs rise faster than the prices firms can charge.
When a business cannot pay its debts as they fall due.

Explain how the AI and data-centre investment boom can add to inflation in the short run but raise economic growth in the long run.

items.guide: Construction feeds into GDP through investment (I). More dwellings over time should ease rent and price pressures, though housing and data centres are meanwhile competing for scarce tradespeople and materials (adding to inflation now but expanding capacity later).

Spending on new homes and renovations (part of I).
The maximum sustainable output of the economy (LRAS).
Shortages of labour or materials that push up prices when demand grows faster than supply.

items.title: Data centre boom drives the biggest investment jump since 2011
items.lede: Business investment surged in the September quarter as firms poured money into data centre equipment. But because most of that equipment is imported, the boost to Australia's GDP is much smaller than the headline.

terms.def: Business spending on buildings, machinery and equipment.
Spending that flows to imports rather than domestic production.

items.title: Inflation jumps to 4.9%, its highest in three years

Reliance on a few raw-material exports for income.

A sudden rise in costs, such as oil, that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
Non-essential purchases, which households cut first.

figs.value: US$88.50 a tonne (Friday), lower again Monday

figs.label: BHP South Australian copper plan
figs.value: Double output to 650,000 tonnes by 2040 (US$14.2-18.1 billion); decision due first half of 2027

qs.q: Explain how a fall in iron ore prices affects Australia's terms of trade and current account balance.

items.guide: Weaker Chinese steel demand shifts the iron ore demand curve left, lowering price and quantity. With oil import prices high, the terms of trade worsen, reducing export income and pressuring the AUD; link to the current account and to company tax receipts in MYEFO.

terms.def: The index of export prices divided by import prices, times 100.
Reliance on a narrow range of resource exports whose prices swing widely.

items.title: Philippines pushes to cut US tariffs while signing new trade deals
items.lede: The Philippines is negotiating with the United States to lower the tariff on its exports from 12.5% to 10%. At the same time it is spreading its risk with new agreements with Chile, Canada and the EU.

figs.label: US tariff on covered Philippine goods
figs.value: 12.5% (imposed July 2026, replacing an earlier 10%); Manila seeks 10%

figs.label: Philippine exports, September 2026
figs.value: +35.6% (fastest growth in 35 years, per Trade Secretary Roque)

figs.label: New deals
figs.value: Chile (signed 19 Nov at APEC); Canada FTA talks concluded 14 Nov; EU FTA targeted for end-2026 or early 2027

qs.q: With the aid of a diagram, explain the effects of a tariff on consumers, domestic producers and the government in the importing country.

items.guide: Apply the tariff diagram (price rises to Pw+t, imports shrink, deadweight loss) and link to the WTO and the rise of bilateral and regional deals as countries route around protectionism.

terms.def: A tax on imports that raises their domestic price.
Spreading exports across more markets to reduce dependence on any one.

items.title: Behind the 4.9%: the human cost of rising unemployment
items.lede: Unemployment has risen to 4.9% with about 44,000 jobs lost. One worker has been made redundant four times since 2019 and made over 100 applications; General Pants is in administration with 500 jobs in doubt and about 1,500 jobs were lost at David Jones. Cuts have also been reported at NAB, ANZ, Canva, Qantas and Bunnings.

qs.q: Discuss the economic and social costs of rising unemployment.

items.guide: Use the personal cases to discuss the costs of unemployment (lost income, lower output, social costs) and who bears them: young workers and those in retail and corporate roles.

terms.def: Unemployment caused by a downturn in economic activity.
The labour force as a share of the working-age population.

items.title: Sahm rule: a recession in Australia is "entirely possible"
items.lede: Economist Claudia Sahm says a recession in Australia is 'entirely possible', though she is not forecasting one. The Sahm rule compares the three-month average unemployment rate with its lowest level over the prior 12 months; Australia is now 0.6 percentage points above. Saul Eslake says it could trigger in December, while the RBA and Treasury are not forecasting a recession.

figs.label: Trigger thresholds
figs.value: 0.5 points in the US; RBA research suggests 0.75 points for Australia

qs.q: Assess whether rising unemployment is a reliable indicator of a recession in Australia.

items.guide: Use as evidence on how unemployment relates to the business cycle. Note the caution: the rule was built for the US, and Governor Bullock says people may feel a recession before GDP shows one.

terms.def: A recession signal triggered when the three-month average unemployment rate rises by a set margin above its 12-month low.
A sustained fall in economic activity, commonly two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.

items.title: Miners slump drags the ASX and pushes the AUD to an 11-month low
items.lede: The ASX 200 fell 5.4% in the week to 8,592.6, its worst since 2022, led by materials (-12.3%). BHP (-12.7%) was overtaken by CBA as the largest ASX company, Rio Tinto fell 12.8%, copper about 10% and gold about 9%. The AUD fell from about 70 US cents in late October to about 66.5 cents, an 11-month low.

figs.label: AUD / USD
figs.value: About US66.5c (11-month low), from about US70c in late October

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain how lower commodity prices could affect the Australian dollar.

items.guide: Falling commodity export prices lower demand for AUD (D shifts left), so the AUD depreciates and the terms of trade fall. Falling export incomes also reduce national income.

terms.def: The ratio of export prices to import prices.
A fall in the value of a currency in a floating exchange rate system.

items.title: Xi pitches free trade at APEC as tariff tensions linger
items.lede: At the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping promised lower tariffs and wider market access and pledged to resist unilateralism and protectionism, read by commentators as criticism of US tariffs. Albanese said Australia has abolished more than 1,000 tariffs since 2022 and backs paperless trade and the WTO.

figs.label: Australia's annual trade with APEC economies
Australian business investment in APEC economies

qs.q: Using a tariff diagram, explain the effects of protection on consumers and domestic producers.
Assess the effect of rising global protectionism on a small open economy like Australia.

items.guide: Apply the tariff diagram (price rises, imports fall, deadweight loss) and link the pledges to the gains from trade, noting China's own trade practices are often criticised.

terms.def: Measures such as tariffs, quotas and subsidies that shield domestic industries from imports.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of 21 economies promoting freer trade and investment.

items.title: AI stocks crack and global share markets tumble
items.lede: Share markets had one of their worst weeks in years. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 3.7% and the Nasdaq more than 5%, linked to profit-taking in AI stocks after Anthropic's record listing, and Fed minutes showed some officials think more rate rises may be needed. Copper lost about 9% and silver about 12%.

qs.q: Explain how a fall in global share prices can affect Australia's economic growth.
Outline one benefit and one risk of global financial integration.

items.guide: Falling share prices cut wealth and confidence, shifting AD left. Explain the transmission to the ASX and superannuation balances.

terms.def: When asset prices fall, households feel poorer and cut spending.
Shocks in one market spread quickly to others through global financial flows.

items.title: COP31 collapses without a climate deal
items.lede: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Sunday 22 November without a final agreement. It was the longest-running climate summit on record and broke down over whether the text should mention fossil fuels. Australia's Chris Bowen was co-president.

figs.label: Length of talks
figs.value: Two weeks plus two days of overtime; longest summit on record

figs.label: Formal objectors to the final text
figs.value: EU, Panama and the Marshall Islands

qs.q: Using a negative externality diagram, explain why international cooperation is needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

items.guide: Use the MSC/MPC diagram: the market produces Q1 at P1, more than the socially optimal Q*, with a deadweight loss. Agreements need consensus, and nations with fossil-fuel exports can block it, so COP31 is evidence of the limits of international environmental management.

terms.def: A cost imposed on third parties that is not included in the market price.
Each country benefits from others' cuts in emissions without paying the cost itself.

items.title: Xi hails a "full turnaround" with Australia as AI talks are agreed
items.lede: Anthony Albanese met Xi Jinping at APEC in Shenzhen and Premier Li Qiang in Beijing. Business leaders used the visit to press for better access for Australian food exports, years after Beijing's trade restrictions hit Australian goods, and the two governments agreed to hold talks on artificial intelligence.

figs.label: Australian jobs that depend on trade

qs.q: Assess the benefits and risks for the Australian economy of its trade relationship with China.

items.guide: Weigh the gains from China trade against the risk of export concentration: earlier restrictions on barley, wine and beef show the downside. Easing barriers on beef shifts Chinese demand right, lifting export income. The Business Council pushed for access for beef and rice, medical devices and recognition of professional qualifications.

terms.def: The ability of exporters to sell into a foreign market without tariffs or other barriers.
Reliance on a small number of markets, which raises vulnerability to shocks.

items.title: House prices: how far they will fall, and what it will take to recover
items.lede: Capital-city home values have lost more than 8% since peaking in March and forecasters expect total falls of 11-15%, among the steepest on record. Higher interest rates and the investor tax changes are driving the downturn, and the recovery depends on when the RBA starts cutting.

figs.label: Capital-city home values since the March peak
figs.value: Down more than 8% (Sydney about 10%, over $100,000; Perth, Brisbane and Melbourne about 8%)

figs.label: Forecast peak-to-trough falls
figs.value: CBA 15% (capitals); AMP 15%; NAB 14%; Domain up to 13% (Sydney); Westpac nearly 11%

qs.q: Explain how monetary policy affects the housing market, and discuss the effect of falling house prices on the distribution of wealth.

items.guide: Five rate rises cut borrowing capacity and the May CGT and negative gearing changes cut investor returns, shifting housing demand left. Shows monetary policy lags and its effect on the distribution of wealth: owners and investors lose, first-home buyers with finance gain affordability. CBA warns persistent inflation could mean a higher cash rate before any cuts; Domain sees capital-city houses +2.5% by end-2027.

terms.def: The total fall from the highest price to the lowest before recovery.
Falling asset prices make households feel poorer, so they spend less.

items.title: The big tax hit coming for start-up workers
items.lede: From July 2027 the 50% capital gains tax discount will be replaced by an inflation-adjusted method. A proposed carve-out for 'innovative' businesses is hard to qualify for, so many start-up workers paid partly in shares could face a much bigger tax bill.

figs.label: Take-home pay from $50,000 of start-up shares at IPO (top tax rate)
figs.value: $38,173.50 if the firm qualifies; $26,447 if not

figs.label: Extra tax if the firm does not qualify
Employees who would consider swapping pay for equity
Start of the new CGT method

qs.q: Evaluate the effects of removing the 50% capital gains tax discount on equity, efficiency and innovation.

items.guide: For the reform: taxes real gains consistently across assets and reduces a concession that mostly benefits high-wealth taxpayers, helping equity and revenue. Against: hurts assets that start low and grow fast, and complex, uncertain rules may discourage innovation. The innovative business concession bill is in the Senate and needs Greens support.

terms.def: Tax on the profit from selling an asset.
Adjusting the purchase price for inflation so only the real gain is taxed.

items.title: "Quacking like a recession": economists warn the downturn is deepening
items.lede: After the jump in unemployment, leading economists warn Australia is showing the hallmarks of a recession. HSBC's Paul Bloxham says recession is 'clearly a concern' and Betashares' David Bassanese says the economy may already have 'one foot in recession'.

figs.label: Rise in unemployment since Christmas 2025
figs.value: 0.8 percentage points (from 4.1%); rule of thumb: about 1 point signals recession

figs.label: People available and looking for work who could not find it

qs.q: Outline the definition of a technical recession and explain two indicators that suggest the Australian economy may be approaching one.

items.guide: Rate rises, cost-of-living pressure and falling house prices cut consumption and investment, shifting AD left and lowering output; two quarters of falling GDP is a technical recession. Unemployment is usually a lagging indicator, but a sharp rise can signal a downturn is under way. Other risks: a falling AUD, elevated oil prices and global disruption.

terms.def: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
An initial fall in spending leads to further falls as incomes drop.

items.title: Two-thirds of surveyed migrant workers are underpaid, study finds
items.lede: A Migrant Justice Institute study of almost 10,000 migrants surveyed in 2024 found about two-thirds were underpaid. Very few tried to recover their wages, and many feared that complaining would put their visa at risk.

figs.label: Surveyed migrants underpaid
figs.source: Migrant Justice Institute, via ABC News

figs.label: Underpaid workers who tried to recover wages
figs.source: Migrant Justice Institute, via ABC News

figs.label: Feared that action would put their visa or residency pathway at risk
figs.source: Migrant Justice Institute, via ABC News

qs.q: Explain how underpayment of migrant workers affects the distribution of income, and outline one policy that could address it.

items.guide: Visas that depend on the employer weaken bargaining power and discourage complaints, so underpayment goes unreported and law-abiding firms are undercut. Policy options: stronger Fair Work Ombudsman enforcement, visa protections for reporting and low-cost ways to recover wages; limits: enforcement is costly, small businesses are hard to monitor and policies cutting migration can increase insecurity.

terms.def: Paying workers less than their legal entitlements under awards or the minimum wage.
A worker's ability to negotiate pay and conditions; weaker when a visa depends on the employer.

items.title: Jobs shock takes a December rate rise off the table
items.lede: The RBA raised the cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth rise of 2026, in a split 6-3 vote. After October's jobs data, economists now expect it to hold rates until at least February; Moody's said the data 'all but closes the door' on a December rise.

figs.label: RBA cash rate
figs.value: 4.85% (+25 basis points on 3 November; highest since 2008; board vote 6-3)

figs.label: RBA headline inflation forecast
figs.value: Peak 4.5% in the December quarter; above 3% until late 2027; 2.5% by mid-2028

qs.q: Assess the policy dilemma facing the RBA when inflation is around 3.9% and unemployment has risen to 4.9%.

items.guide: Rate rises move the economy along the short-run Phillips curve: inflation eases but unemployment rises. With inflation still well above target and unemployment at 4.9%, the board must weigh the cost of any further rise. Monetary policy works with long and variable lags, so earlier 2026 rises are still flowing through (a key limitation). Bullock said inflation risks are still tilted upward.

terms.def: The unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation; the RBA raised its estimate to about 4.75%.
The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which the RBA sets.

items.title: Economists warn Australia is edging towards recession
items.lede: After October's jobs shock, leading economists warned the risk of recession is rising. AMP's Shane Oliver puts it at 'around 40 per cent' and BetaShares' David Bassanese says the economy may already have 'one foot in recession'.

figs.label: Unemployment rate
figs.value: 4.9% in October; Eslake: 5% could come by early 2027, not 2028 as the RBA forecasts

qs.q: Explain how a fall in aggregate demand could lead to a recession and higher unemployment in Australia.

items.guide: Higher rates and weak confidence cut consumption and investment, shifting AD left, lowering output and raising cyclical unemployment. GDP data come after jobs data, so the labour market can signal a slowdown first. Big job cuts at NAB, David Jones and General Pants are not yet in the official data (AAP).

terms.def: A recession signal triggered when the 3-month average unemployment rate rises 0.5 points above its low of the past year.
Commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.

items.title: Unemployment jumps to 4.9% as 43,500 jobs are lost
items.lede: The ABS Labour Force survey showed unemployment rising from 4.7% in September to 4.9% in October, the highest since 2021, while markets had expected no change and about 25,000 new jobs. Employment fell 43,500, almost all in part-time work.

qs.q: Explain why the unemployment rate rose by only 0.2 percentage points even though 43,500 jobs were lost in October.

items.guide: Unemployment rose by only 17,800 while 43,500 jobs disappeared because many people left the labour force, so participation fell; people who stop looking are not counted as unemployed ('hidden unemployment'), so 4.9% may understate the weakening. Quote both the unemployment rate and the participation rate. Five rate rises slow household spending, firms cut hours and part-time staff, and cyclical unemployment rises.

terms.def: The labour force (employed plus unemployed) as a share of the working-age population.
Unemployment caused by a downturn in the business cycle.

items.title: US Fed signals more rate rises as global shares slide
items.lede: St Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said 'several' rate rises are likely to be needed before spring 2027, and global share markets have fallen. Higher US interest rates draw investment towards the US, putting downward pressure on other currencies including the AUD.

figs.label: Fed view (St Louis Fed President Musalem)
figs.value: "Several" rate rises likely before spring 2027; real policy rate may need to rise about 1 percentage point

qs.q: Explain how rising US interest rates could affect Australia's exchange rate and financial account.

items.guide: When US rates rise relative to Australia's, investors switch funds into US assets, demand for AUD falls and the AUD depreciates: a key channel linking the global economy to Australia's exchange rate through the financial account. Weak Australian jobs data makes further RBA rises less likely, which could widen the rate gap with the US.

terms.def: The nominal interest rate minus inflation.
Money moving between countries to buy financial assets such as shares and bonds.

items.title: China's slowdown deepens as spending, output and investment all miss forecasts
items.lede: October data from China's National Bureau of Statistics showed factory output and retail spending growing more slowly than forecast and investment falling further. China is Australia's largest trading partner and the main buyer of its iron ore.

figs.label: China industrial output, year to October
figs.source: National Bureau of Statistics via Reuters

figs.label: China retail sales, year to October
figs.source: National Bureau of Statistics via Reuters

figs.label: China fixed-asset investment, January-October
figs.source: National Bureau of Statistics via Reuters

figs.label: China urban unemployment
figs.source: National Bureau of Statistics via Reuters

qs.q: Explain how a slowdown in China's economic growth could affect Australia's terms of trade and current account balance.

items.guide: Weaker Chinese property and infrastructure investment means less steel, shifting world iron ore demand left and lowering the price. Chain: slower Chinese growth, lower commodity prices, lower terms of trade, lower export income, weaker AUD and less company tax revenue. Analysts expect 4.5-5% growth for 2026 unless major stimulus is announced.

terms.def: Spending on buildings, infrastructure and machinery; in China it drives demand for steel and so iron ore.
Export prices divided by import prices; it falls when commodity export prices fall.

items.title: Trade barriers pile up faster than ever, warns the WTO
items.lede: The WTO's trade monitoring report, released 17 November, shows governments brought in more trade-restrictive measures in the first half of 2026 than in all of 2025. Import restrictions in force since 2009 now cover a record share of world trade, even as trade-facilitating measures also rose.

figs.label: World imports covered by import restrictions in force since 2009
WTO forecast, 2026 merchandise trade volume growth
figs.value: 3.9% (up from 1.9% in March); services growth cut to 3.3%

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain the effects of a tariff on domestic producers, consumers and the government.

items.guide: A tariff raises the domestic price, lifts local output, cuts consumption and imports, raises revenue and creates deadweight losses. Each measure is small but together they cover over a fifth of world imports: evidence of the limits of the WTO's ability to restrain protectionism.

terms.def: Anti-dumping and countervailing duties used against imports judged unfairly priced or subsidised.
Measures that cut the cost and time of trading.

items.title: Chile's copper scandal: a test of Australia's pull for mining investment
items.lede: Chile's state-owned Codelco overstated its copper output and is struggling financially, and Chile may open its deposits to private miners. AFR columnist Peter Ker argues this gives BHP an alternative to its South Australian copper expansion, so governments here should consider support.

figs.label: Copper falsely added to Codelco output
BHP's copper growth options in South Australia
figs.value: US$17.4 billion (including a US$4.1 billion Olympic Dam smelter expansion)

figs.label: Return on capital: Escondida (Chile) vs South Australia
Chile's share of world copper supply

qs.q: Explain how global competition for investment can affect Australia's mining sector and capital inflows.

items.guide: Electrification lifts world copper demand and prices, so countries compete to host new mines. Australia competes globally for capital inflows, so higher returns abroad can divert investment. Ker suggests government funding for a $5-7 billion desalination plant near Whyalla rather than propping up loss-making assets such as the Mount Isa smelter ($600 million rescue).

terms.def: Investment that gives an investor a lasting interest in a business, such as building a mine.
Profit as a percentage of capital invested; firms invest where it is highest.

items.title: China's iron ore haggling is a price fight, not a trade war
items.lede: China's single state iron ore buyer, China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG), is pushing Australian miners for lower prices. Analyst Jon Yuan Jiang argues Canberra should leave negotiations to the companies rather than turn a commercial dispute into a state-to-state one.

figs.label: Share of Australia's iron ore exports sent to China
Lithium sent to China for processing
Chinese steel profits, first eight months
Effective discounts won by CMRG (Goldman Sachs)

qs.q: Explain why the concentration of Australia's exports in a single market creates economic risks.

items.guide: Chain: China's steel profits collapse, CMRG pushes for discounts, lower iron ore prices, lower export income and Budget revenue. The author recommends letting miners negotiate commercially (BHP settled in April, Rio Tinto in October, Fortescue still negotiating), allowing ACCC-approved collective bargaining, and cutting costs, adding value and finding more buyers.

terms.def: When one buyer dominates a market and can push prices down.
Using trade restrictions to pressure another government, such as China's 2020 barriers on barley and wine.

items.title: Climate change: is the government having a bob each way?
items.lede: SMH economics editor Ross Gittins praises Australia's renewables progress, highlighted at COP31, but argues that approving new coal and gas projects undercuts climate action and exposes the economy when world fossil-fuel demand falls.

figs.label: Global fossil-fuel emissions this year
figs.value: -0.4% (mainly less oil use during the Iran war and Hormuz blockage); total emissions still about +1%

figs.label: Share of Australia's electricity from renewables
figs.value: About 50% (600,000+ home batteries installed in the past year)

figs.label: Time to 1.5 degrees C of warming at current rates

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain why the market overproduces goods that generate negative externalities, and assess one policy response.

items.guide: Fossil-fuel users pay private costs but not climate damage, so the market produces Q1 above the social optimum Q2 (deadweight loss); carbon pricing or the Safeguard Mechanism aim to move output towards Q2. As other countries decarbonise, demand and prices for coal and gas exports fall, making diversification a long-term growth issue.

terms.def: Investments that lose value early because of changing demand or policy, such as coal mines.
When the free market produces an inefficient outcome, such as too much pollution.

items.title: Gender pay gap falls below 20% for the first time
items.lede: The Workplace Gender Equality Agency reports that the average gender pay gap in total remuneration has fallen to 19.7%, the first time it has been below 20%. Women are still paid substantially less than men on average.

figs.label: Average gender pay gap, total remuneration
Women's average total remuneration per $100 earned by men

qs.q: Outline two causes of the gender pay gap in Australia and explain one policy that could reduce it.

items.guide: Total remuneration includes base pay, overtime, bonuses and super, so it captures more than hourly rates. Causes: occupational segregation, more part-time work and career breaks for caring. Policies: pay transparency, award decisions lifting pay in female-dominated sectors, childcare and paid parental leave; limits: structural factors change slowly, higher awards raise employer and Budget costs, and an average hides differences.

terms.def: The difference between men's and women's average earnings, as a percentage of men's earnings.
The concentration of women and men in different industries and jobs, often with different pay.

items.title: Job ads fall and layoffs mount as the labour market cools
items.lede: Ahead of Thursday's Labour Force release, SEEK job advertisements are falling and several big employers are cutting staff. Higher interest rates are slowing demand, and technology is reshaping some jobs.

figs.label: SEEK job ads
figs.value: -0.8% in October; -6.4% over the year (ACT the only region with growth)

figs.label: David Jones jobs expected to go
figs.value: About 1,500 of 1,689 direct jobs at risk

qs.q: Using examples from this week's news, distinguish between cyclical and structural unemployment and suggest one policy response to each.

items.guide: Five rate rises in 2026 have shifted AD left, cutting output and raising cyclical unemployment. David Jones' collapse is cyclical; Bunnings' AI-linked offshoring is structural, so they need different policy responses (macroeconomic policy versus training and labour market programs).

terms.def: Unemployment caused by weaker aggregate demand during a downturn.
A measure, such as job ads, that tends to change before the wider economy.

items.title: Has the rich world passed "peak Boomer"?
items.lede: An analysis by The Economist, republished in the AFR, argues that the long rise in older people's incomes and wealth relative to the young is reversing across most rich countries. Labour markets, inflation and government budgets are shifting the balance towards the young.

figs.label: Rich countries where pensioners' incomes are falling relative to working-age people
US median elderly household income relative to other households
figs.value: 57% (1979) to 90% (2012); no gain on the non-elderly for over a decade

figs.label: Cost-of-living crisis impact on pension-age households (EU study)
US federal spending per older person vs younger people

qs.q: Explain how inflation can affect the distribution of income between workers and retirees.

items.guide: Strong labour demand lifts young workers' wages, inflation erodes fixed pensions and governments contain age-related spending. For Australia: less fiscal pressure from ageing if spending is better targeted, but retirees on fixed incomes become more vulnerable to inflation and older Australians still hold much of the property and financial wealth.

terms.def: Fairness in the distribution of income, wealth and public spending between generations.
A pension paid as a set amount, often based on final salary; it can lose real value to inflation.

items.title: Rental listings fall by 23,000 in five years across Sydney and Melbourne
items.lede: Cotality data show Sydney and Melbourne have tens of thousands fewer homes available to rent than five years ago, and rents are up more than 35% in each city. Strong population growth and slower home building are the main causes.

figs.label: Rent rise over five years
figs.value: Sydney +36.4%; Melbourne +35.1% (about 4-4.5% in the past year)

figs.label: Peak average rent increase for tenants who got one vs CPI rent inflation
New investor loans
figs.value: Down about a third in the September quarter

qs.q: Explain how population growth and housing tax changes could affect rents, and discuss the effect on income inequality.

items.guide: Fewer new homes and investors selling up shift rental supply left while population growth adds demand, so rents rise and the number of homes rented falls. A policy trade-off: tax changes that help first-home buyers may cut investor-owned rental supply, raising rents for lower-income tenants: evidence for a limitations-of-policy paragraph.

terms.def: The share of rental properties that are empty and available; a low rate signals a tight market.
Deducting rental property losses from other income to reduce tax.

items.title: Wages grow at their fastest pace since 2023, but real wages fall for a fourth quarter
items.lede: The Wage Price Index rose 1.1% in the September quarter, driven by the 4.75% minimum wage rise and state public sector pay deals. With inflation at 3.9%, real wages fell 0.4% over the year, the fourth negative result in a row.

figs.label: Real wages over the year
figs.value: -0.4% (fourth negative result in a row; inflation 3.9% as used by the digest)

figs.label: Private / public sector wage growth over the year
Wage growth by industry over the year

qs.q: Distinguish between nominal and real wage growth, and explain how faster wage growth could influence RBA decisions.

items.guide: Separate nominal wage growth (3.5%) from real wage growth (-0.4%). If pay rises faster than productivity, unit labour costs rise and SRAS shifts left (cost-push), which is why a result above forecast is 'uncomfortably high' for the RBA (EY). The minimum wage rise also gave the largest gains to the lowest paid. Economists expect an RBA hold in December; Westpac tips growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 1% in 2027.

terms.def: Measures changes in the price of a fixed quantity and quality of labour.
Wages adjusted for inflation, approximately wage growth minus inflation.

items.title: Backpacker backtrack: the trade-offs in cutting migration
items.lede: After an employer backlash, Immigration Minister Tony Burke has delayed a ballot for third-year working holiday visas. An AFR editorial argues Labor's migration changes have not balanced the politics and economics of migration well.

figs.label: Third-year backpacker visa cap / required regional work
People in Australia on short-stay visas

qs.q: Evaluate the economic effects of reducing net overseas migration on Australia's labour market and housing.

items.guide: Fewer backpackers shift regional labour supply left, raising wages and costs and risking unpicked crops. Lower migration eases housing and services demand but cuts labour supply and headline GDP growth. The editorial argues for a smaller but more skilled intake.

terms.def: Arrivals minus departures of people staying 12 months or more; a key driver of population growth.
When employers cannot find enough workers at the going wage.

items.title: Phantom forests? The fight over Australia's biggest carbon credit method
items.lede: A new study says many 'human-induced regeneration' (HIR) carbon farms, including Glenn McGrath's former property, show almost no new forest despite earning millions in credits. Industry and the government say the method is sound and the satellite analysis is flawed.

figs.label: HIR coverage
figs.value: 429 properties over 38 million hectares; about one-third of Safeguard credits supplied

figs.label: Average tree cover on 50 HIR projects
figs.value: 29% (2017) to 30% (2025) against 50-58% expected from credits issued
figs.source: Macintosh et al. for the Australian Conservation Foundation, via SMH

figs.label: Wancobra (McGrath family farm)
figs.value: 157,000 t of CO2 credited; about $4.2 million

qs.q: Assess the effectiveness of carbon offsets as a policy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

items.guide: If credits are issued for abatement that is not real, credit supply shifts right and the carbon price falls, so emitters buy cheap offsets instead of cutting emissions. Critics say low-integrity credits keep prices low; defenders cite seven independent reviews and LiDAR measurement. Use in a limitations-of-environmental-policy paragraph.

terms.def: The requirement that an offset delivers abatement that would not have happened anyway.
Limits on emissions from Australia's largest industrial facilities, which can use offsets to comply.

items.title: Gas reservation fires up, but don't bank on cheaper energy
items.lede: A federal-state deal gives Western Australia a permanent carve-out from the planned national gas reservation scheme, and the bill still needs to pass the Senate. AFR columnist Jennifer Hewett argues the policy is the latest in a long line of mixed signals, with uncertain effects on prices and investment.

figs.label: Domestic supply requirement
figs.value: Up to 20% of gas each year, from January 2028

figs.label: WA obligation under the national scheme
figs.value: Permanently zero (10-year sunset clause dropped); WA keeps its own rule of about 15% of LNG exports

qs.q: Discuss the short-run and long-run effects of a domestic gas reservation policy on energy prices and investment.

items.guide: Short run: reserving gas adds domestic supply and lowers prices. Long run: producers expect lower returns and delay projects, so supply may fall and prices rise: the opposite of the aim. Hewett notes past east-coast interventions had only a modest effect on prices. Business groups, manufacturers and unions back the scheme; producers say projects become unviable.

terms.def: Requiring producers to sell a share of gas locally rather than export it.
The risk that government policy changes reduce the value of an investment.

items.title: Chalmers loosens the rules on where super funds can invest
items.lede: The Treasurer announced changes to superannuation investment rules at a conference in Melbourne on 18 November. Media reports say about 5% of fund investments would be exempt from APRA's annual performance test, giving funds more room to invest in subsidised housing and renewable energy.

figs.label: Share of fund investments exempt from the performance test (reported)
figs.value: About 5% (about $170 billion of roughly $3.4 trillion APRA-regulated super)

figs.label: Performance test consequence
figs.value: Funds that fail twice in a row must tell members to consider moving their money

qs.q: Discuss the possible economic benefits and costs of encouraging super funds to invest more in housing and renewable energy.

items.guide: Possible benefits: more capital for housing supply and wind and solar, long-term investment that suits retirement savings. Possible risks: lower or riskier member returns, less pressure on poorly performing funds and government steering of private savings. Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson revived the idea of first home buyers using super; Chalmers said the Coalition wanted a 'wrecking ball' for super.

terms.def: APRA's annual check comparing each super fund's returns against a benchmark.
A policy that changes how markets and institutions work to lift efficiency or productivity.

items.title: Is the AI investment boom running out of steam?
items.lede: ABC analyst Ian Verrender compares today's rush of money into AI with the 1840s railway mania, 1920s radio shares and the dotcom crash. He notes Anthropic's planned float now aims to raise US$90 billion at about US$1.5 trillion, down from about US$2 trillion expected weeks earlier, and that APRA will stress-test banks, super funds and insurers against AI scenarios.

figs.label: Anthropic planned float
figs.value: Raise US$90 billion at about US$1.5 trillion (from about US$2 trillion expected weeks earlier)

figs.label: Share of US market in the 10 companies most exposed to AI

qs.q: Explain how a sharp fall in global share markets could affect the Australian economy.

items.guide: A correction on Wall Street can hit Australian super funds and investment through global financial flows, as the dotcom crash and the global financial crisis did. Balance: history does not always repeat, and AI investment is lifting productivity and spending, including Australian data centres. Cheaper Chinese AI models such as Moonshot's Kimi threaten the earnings forecasts behind valuations.

terms.def: Asset prices rising well above what their future earnings justify.
Financial stress spreading from one market or country to others.

items.title: Trade deals realign around the Asian summits
items.lede: Around the ASEAN and APEC summits countries are signing bilateral trade deals partly to protect themselves from US tariffs. Canada and China extended arrangements and cut some tariffs, while Thailand and the US were due to sign a joint statement on progress towards an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.

qs.q: Evaluate the impact of bilateral trade agreements on the multilateral trading system.

items.guide: Bilateral deals made under tariff pressure can divert trade rather than create it and weaken the WTO's MFN principle. Cutting a tariff reverses the effects on the tariff diagram: lower prices and more trade. Australia also negotiates bilateral deals under US tariff pressure and competes with Canada in Chinese markets.

terms.def: A trade deal between two countries.
The WTO rule that a country must offer all WTO members the same tariff treatment.

items.title: US shoppers slow down as high prices bite
items.lede: US retail sales grew only 0.2% in October, down from 0.8% in September, while consumer prices rose 0.4% in the month, so Americans bought less in real terms. Petrol is still almost 20% dearer than a year ago and AI chip demand is lifting electronics prices.

figs.label: US petrol price, year on year

qs.q: Distinguish between nominal and real growth in retail sales, using the October US data.

items.guide: When prices rise faster than spending, volumes fall, so a small nominal rise can mean shrinking real consumption. The US is the world's largest economy, so slower consumption lowers global demand, and risk-off markets can weigh on the AUD and Australian super funds.

terms.def: Nominal values are in current dollars; real values remove the effect of inflation.
Rising input costs, such as oil and chips, passed on as higher prices.

items.title: Australia signs US-led AI supply chain pact
items.lede: Australia is one of 10 countries that signed the 'San Francisco Declaration', part of the Trump administration's Pax Silica initiative which Australia joined in 2025. It aims to cut reliance on unreliable suppliers of the minerals, energy and technology AI depends on, and is not a tariff-cutting trade agreement.

figs.label: China's share of refining for several critical minerals

qs.q: Assess the economic risks and benefits for Australia of aligning its trade policy more closely with the United States.

items.guide: Opportunities: demand for Australian critical minerals and processing, better access to US AI technology and more diverse export markets. Risks: China, the largest trading partner, may retaliate or restrict rare earth processing, and rebuilding supply chains outside China costs more. Balances the largest export market against security ties with the US.

terms.def: Minerals essential to modern technology that carry supply risk, such as rare earths and lithium.
Processing raw materials further before export.

items.title: Data centre boom adds to inflation and sparks local disputes
items.lede: Record spending on data centres to power AI is pressuring building materials, skilled trades, electricity and water, and driving local opposition. RBA Governor Michele Bullock says construction is straining scarce materials and electricians, and about 70% of data centre technology is imported, so much of the spending leaks out of the economy.

figs.label: Capital raised by local data centre operators, 2026
figs.source: Internal RBA note, via ABC News

figs.label: Data centre capacity
figs.value: About 2.3 GW across 79 sites; planned 23-67 GW

figs.label: Data centre technology imported
figs.source: RBA Governor Bullock, via ABC News

figs.label: NEXTDC market value lost in one day (local dispute)

qs.q: Is data centre investment mainly a demand-pull or a cost-push source of inflation? Justify your answer.

items.guide: Data centre construction lifts investment and shifts AD right; near capacity, much of the rise shows up as a higher price level (demand-pull). Competition for electricians and materials adds cost-push pressure. Mention energy and water use as a sustainability cost.

terms.def: Prices rise because spending grows faster than the economy can supply.
Prices rise because input costs such as labour, materials and energy rise.

items.title: RBA board split 6-3 over the hike to 4.85%
items.lede: Minutes of the RBA's 2-3 November meeting, released on 17 November, show six members voted to raise the cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85% and three wanted to hold at 4.60%. The majority pointed to stronger September-quarter inflation, rising services inflation, higher oil prices and the risk that policy is not restrictive enough.

figs.label: RBA cash rate
figs.value: 4.85% (+25 basis points); board vote 6-3 (minority wanted to hold at 4.60%)

figs.label: RBA inflation forecast
figs.value: Above 3% until late 2027; back at the 2.5% midpoint by mid-2028

figs.label: Rise in unemployment over six months (minority view)

qs.q: Using the November RBA minutes, explain the trade-off the board faced between reducing inflation and supporting employment.

items.guide: The disagreement is about timing and lags: the majority judged the risk of policy too loose greater than too tight, while the minority argued 100 basis points of earlier tightening is still working through. Use it for the inflation-unemployment trade-off and the limits of monetary policy (lags, neutral rate uncertainty, oil supply shocks).

terms.def: The cash rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy.
The time before a rate change fully affects the economy.

items.title: Rising cost of essentials puts affordability on the policy agenda
items.lede: Economist Isabella Weber argues that rapidly rising costs of housing, food, energy, water, health care and transport are testing democracies, and that governments should put affordability at the centre of policy. She is open to targeted, temporary price controls, limits on market concentration and changes to how essentials are supplied.

figs.label: Essentials Weber targets
figs.value: 6: housing, food, energy, water, health, transport

figs.label: Earnings calls analysed in cited research
US data cited (2000-2022)
figs.value: Essentials rose faster than non-essentials such as TVs and electronics

qs.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of price controls as a response to rising living costs in Australia.

items.guide: For an evaluate question weigh quick relief for low-income households and a break in price spikes against shortages (quantity demanded above quantity supplied at the ceiling), rationing, weaker incentives to invest and the difficulty of removing controls. Weber's case rests on temporary, targeted use plus action on market concentration.

terms.def: A legal maximum price set below the market equilibrium, which creates a shortage.
When a few large firms dominate an industry and have pricing power.

items.title: Super nears $5 trillion. Who is it serving?
items.lede: Australians' compulsory superannuation savings are about to pass $5 trillion, roughly $178,571 for each of 28 million people and about 20 months of GDP. Yet two-thirds of retirees still draw a full or part age pension, and fees and marketing spending are under scrutiny.

figs.label: Total super savings
figs.value: About $5 trillion (about 20 months of GDP; about $178,571 per person)

figs.label: Retirees drawing a full or part age pension
Marketing vs complaints spend, 10 largest funds, FY25
Fees: index option vs active default

qs.q: Explain how Australia's superannuation system affects the distribution of wealth.

items.guide: Because contributions are a fixed share of wages, higher earners build larger balances, so super can widen wealth gaps while the age pension acts as a safety net. Link to national saving and to reliance on foreign capital in Topic 2. High fees compound over decades, so fee differences matter for final balances.

terms.def: Retirement balance depends on what is paid in and the returns earned, not on a promised payout.
A measure of inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1; A/(A+B) on a Lorenz curve.

items.title: Miners drag the ASX lower as commodity prices soften
items.lede: Weaker Chinese demand weighed on Australia's key commodity exports and the ASX 200 fell 0.4% to about 9,045 on Monday 16 November. Iron ore fell to US$90.95 a tonne, copper is near a four-month low and port stockpiles in China are rising.

figs.label: LME copper
figs.value: US$13,467 a tonne (-1.3%; fifth straight weekly fall)

figs.label: Iron ore stockpiles at 10 Chinese ports

qs.q: Explain the relationship between commodity prices, the terms of trade and Australia's current account balance.

items.guide: Australia is a price taker in world commodity markets, so falling iron ore, coal and copper prices flow straight into export prices and the terms of trade, lowering mining profits, company tax and the current account. Pair with the China October slowdown card for the cause.

terms.def: An index of export prices divided by import prices, multiplied by 100.
Unsold inventory; rising stockpiles suggest supply is running ahead of demand.

items.title: The dollar slides as the gap with US interest rates narrows
items.lede: The Australian dollar lost 1.4% last week, closing Friday at 67.71 US cents and falling to 67.57 US cents on Monday afternoon. Rising US yields and fading expectations of another RBA hike have narrowed the interest rate gap that supported it, and Australian and US 10-year yields are now almost level.

figs.label: AUD / USD
figs.value: 67.71 US cents on Friday (-0.5%; -1.4% for the week); 67.57 at 4:15pm Monday

figs.label: Market chance of an RBA hike in December

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain how a narrowing interest rate gap with the US affects the AUD. Then analyse the effects on the current account.

items.guide: A narrower yield gap means foreign investors want fewer Australian assets, so demand for AUD shifts left and the exchange rate depreciates. Exporters, tourism and import-competing firms gain; importers, travellers and foreign-currency borrowers lose. Higher import prices add to inflation, which the RBA watches closely.

terms.def: A fall in the value of a floating currency against another currency.
The gap between Australian and overseas interest rates, which drives capital flows.

items.title: Japan's economy shrinks in the September quarter
items.lede: Japan's real GDP fell at an annualised 0.1% in the September quarter, against a forecast of +0.3%, as private consumption dropped 0.3%. The June quarter was revised up to +1.7% annualised, so Japan is not in a technical recession.

figs.label: Japan real GDP, June quarter (revised, annualised)

qs.q: Using Japan's GDP figures, distinguish between an economic slowdown and a recession.

items.guide: One negative quarter is a slowdown, not a technical recession. Consumption is the largest part of aggregate demand, so a fall in household spending pulls GDP down directly. Japan is one of Australia's largest export markets, so weaker demand is a risk to exports such as energy and food.

terms.def: A quarterly change scaled up to show what it would be over a full year.
Two consecutive quarters of negative growth.

items.title: Young workers in the firing line as the economy slows
items.lede: ABS data for September put youth unemployment at 11.1%, compared with 4.7% overall, and economists warn it could rise further as the economy softens after five rate rises. CBA economist Harry Ottley says youth unemployment is rising faster than for other groups, though the youth employment-to-population ratio is still above its 2019 level.

figs.label: Youth employment-to-population ratio
figs.source: ABS and CBA via ABC News

figs.label: Youth participation rate
figs.source: ABS and CBA via ABC News

qs.q: Explain why young people are more likely than other groups to become unemployed during an economic slowdown.

items.guide: Higher interest rates and weaker household spending shift AD left, real GDP falls and firms need fewer workers, so cyclical unemployment rises. Young workers, who are often casual and have less experience, are usually the first to lose hours or miss out on jobs, and SEEK says graduate job ads have trended down since their post-pandemic highs. A July DEWR study found AI is not yet causing broad disruption.

terms.def: Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a downturn.
The share of a group's population that has a job.

items.title: Rate rises and tax backlash put the government's economic management under pressure
items.lede: An ABC analysis by Jacob Greber argues the Albanese government is struggling after five RBA rate rises this year and broken election promises on housing tax concessions. It is a reminder that economic policy runs into political limits.

figs.label: Budget changes in May
figs.value: negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions wound back, despite earlier promises not to

figs.label: Next dates
figs.value: MYEFO in December; trusts legislation due in the Senate the week of 16 November; next federal election due 2028

qs.q: Discuss the political constraints that limit the effectiveness of economic policy in Australia.

items.guide: To bring inflation back toward the 2-3% target the RBA tightens policy and the economy moves along the Phillips curve: inflation falls but unemployment rises. Higher mortgage repayments and job losses are felt by voters, which creates political pressure on governments even though the RBA is independent. Reforms with long-run benefits, such as the housing tax changes, often have short-run costs that make them hard to sustain.

terms.def: Achieving one goal, such as lower inflation, at the cost of another, such as jobs.
When a policy is economically sound but unpopular, making it harder to implement.

items.title: Regional flights cost far more than city routes, Productivity Commission finds
items.lede: A Productivity Commission interim report found regional and remote Australians pay much higher airfares than people flying between major cities: long regional flights cost 67% more on average, and short regional flights cost 173% more per kilometre. Several airlines have cut Northern Territory services, so Darwin's flights to Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra are served only by Qantas and Jetstar.

figs.label: Long regional and remote flights compared with major-city routes
figs.source: Productivity Commission interim report via ABC News

figs.label: Short regional flights, per kilometre
figs.source: Productivity Commission interim report via ABC News

figs.label: Airlines left on several Darwin routes

qs.q: Using the example of regional airfares, explain how a lack of competition affects prices and economic efficiency.

items.guide: If reforms encourage new airlines to enter regional routes, or lower costs such as airport charges, supply shifts right: fares fall and more people fly, which improves allocative efficiency. But thin regional routes may be natural monopolies where only one or two airlines can operate profitably, which limits what competition policy can achieve.

terms.def: When a few firms supply most of a market, reducing competition.
Policies that improve efficiency and competition in particular industries.

items.title: Housing turns into a buyers' market as tax changes and rate rises bite
items.lede: After the government wound back negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions and the RBA lifted rates five times, the national median house price is 5.6% below its March peak, auction clearance rates have dropped below 50%, and realestate.com.au says buyers hold the upper hand in 72% of markets. The government says the shift from investors to first home buyers is the point of the reforms, while critics say the 1.2 million new homes target is now likely out of reach.

figs.label: National median house price against March peak
Share of markets where buyers have the edge
Fall in new home loans by type, September quarter (rounded)
figs.value: investors -31%; first home buyers -8%; owner-occupiers -5%; all loans -15%

figs.label: Value of new home loans
figs.value: -15.5% (largest fall since the series began in 2002)

qs.q: Evaluate whether falling house prices are good or bad for the Australian economy.

items.guide: Lower tax concessions and higher rates reduce investor demand, so prices fall and fewer homes change hands. Lower prices help first home buyers but reduce existing owners' wealth, which cuts spending through the wealth effect, and falling prices can also reduce new housing supply because builders start fewer projects.

terms.def: Deducting losses on an investment property from other income to cut tax.
People spend less when the value of their assets, such as housing, falls.

items.title: Microsoft outage exposes Australia's reliance on a few foreign cloud giants
items.lede: A global Microsoft outage on 13 November knocked out Outlook, SharePoint and Copilot for Australian users. University of Melbourne experts say most Australian email runs through Microsoft or Google and most websites sit on Amazon or other big cloud platforms, and that building resilience will cost money.

figs.label: Firms carrying most Australian email
figs.source: University of Melbourne via ABC News

figs.label: France moved government operating systems from Microsoft to Linux

qs.q: Explain one benefit and one cost for Australia of relying on overseas providers for digital services.

items.guide: Relying on global cloud providers is cheaper because of economies of scale and gives access to frontier tools, but one outage hits millions of users and adds to services imports. Building local or regulated back-ups gives more control and resilience, as Toby Murray argues governments could regulate these firms like banks, but it needs significant investment and gives up some benefit of specialisation. On a production possibility frontier, more digital resilience means giving up other goods and services.

terms.def: Payments to overseas firms for services such as cloud computing and software, recorded in the current account.
The next best alternative given up when resources go to one use.

items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin to meet at APEC in Shenzhen
items.lede: The White House has confirmed the first meeting between the US, Chinese and Russian leaders, on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. It follows a tariff war that pushed US-China tariffs into triple digits before both sides cut them.

figs.label: US tariff increase on Chinese goods last year
China's retaliatory levies on US imports
Strait of Hormuz closure
figs.value: More than 100 days; about a third of China's crude oil used to pass through

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain the effects of a tariff on domestic consumers, domestic producers and government revenue.

items.guide: Tariff diagram: the tariff lifts the price to Pw+t, cuts consumption and imports, raises domestic output and government revenue and creates deadweight losses; cutting tariffs reverses this. Australia benefits from stronger Chinese growth and calmer trade but is exposed if protectionism returns (2D.4).

terms.def: A tax on imported goods.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member regional forum that promotes trade and investment; Australia is a member.

items.title: APRA warns house prices are falling and AI risks are rising
items.lede: The prudential regulator's November System Risk Outlook says banks and insurers are well capitalised, but warns that resilience "cannot be taken for granted". National house prices have fallen about 6% since March, and APRA's 2027 stress test will model AI-driven disruption and a sharp fall in technology valuations.

figs.label: Long-term bond yields in advanced economies
figs.value: near their highest in at least 15 years

figs.label: Australian private credit market
figs.value: estimated $250 billion (under 4% of the banking system)

qs.q: Explain how falling house prices can help monetary policy reduce inflation.

items.guide: Higher rates reduce borrowing capacity, so housing demand and prices fall, and the fall in household wealth reduces consumer spending, which helps monetary policy slow inflation. APRA's job is to make sure the fall does not threaten the banks, so financial stability limits how far and how fast rates can rise.

terms.def: Spending changes as household wealth, such as house prices, changes.
Rules that keep banks and insurers financially sound.

items.title: Only four ministers saved money this year, as spending outruns savings
items.lede: An ABC analysis of the May budget papers found that new government spending in 2026-27 exceeded savings by $8.7 billion, and revenue measures added $2.2 billion, leaving the budget $6.5 billion worse off this year. Only four of more than 20 ministers achieved net savings: Catherine King, Jason Clare, Julie Collins and Jim Chalmers.

figs.label: New spending in excess of savings, 2026-27
figs.source: ABC News analysis of budget papers

figs.label: Revenue measures
figs.source: ABC News analysis of budget papers

figs.label: Net impact on the budget this year
figs.source: ABC News analysis of budget papers

qs.q: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy can limit the effectiveness of monetary policy in reducing inflation.

items.guide: Net new government spending shifts AD right, lifting output and the price level. With inflation above target and the cash rate at 4.85% that works against the RBA, which is trying to slow demand, so the RBA may need to raise rates further when fiscal policy is expansionary and monetary policy is contractionary.

terms.def: Deliberate changes to spending and tax decisions by the government.
Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook: the December budget update.

items.title: The chips powering the AI arms race: an HSC Economics explainer
items.lede: An eight-page explainer built on Visual Capitalist's 13 November 2026 'The Chips Powering the AI Arms Race' graphics. Nvidia shipped 2.96 million H100-equivalents in Q4 2025, far more than Google, AMD, Amazon and Huawei combined, and each stage of the chain shows its own concentration of power.

figs.label: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron share of listed memory market value
China share of gallium; Australia share of rare earths
Share of AI models by country
figs.source: Epoch AI via World Bank WDR 2026

figs.label: Generative AI adoption, working-age population, Q1 2026

qs.q: 'Control of chips, memory and minerals gives some countries and firms an economic advantage in the global economy.' Discuss this statement with reference to the global economy and the Australian economy.

items.guide: Use one data point per stage: gallium and rare earths (Topic 2, supply risk and terms of trade), Nvidia versus Google shipments (Topic 1, concentration), profit margins (Topic 3, distribution), compute costs falling from 172% to 57% of revenue (economies of scale) and the US and China building 74% of models (Topic 4, supply-side policy). Adoption is not productivity: test the link before claiming growth.

terms.def: The ability of a firm to influence price or output because it has few rivals.
Average cost per unit falls as output rises, because fixed costs are spread over more output.
A sudden change in supply, such as an outage or export restriction, that moves the price.

items.title: Bank chiefs urge Canberra to cut spending to bring rates down
items.lede: At a parliamentary inquiry, ANZ chief Nuno Matos and Westpac chief Anthony Miller argued that high government spending is adding to inflation and keeping interest rates higher for longer. Matos called the AI data-centre boom an "unprecedented inflation danger" and noted Commonwealth spending is at its highest in four decades outside the COVID years.

figs.label: RBA cash rate
figs.value: 4.85% (the latest 25 basis point hike flows into variable mortgages from Friday)

figs.label: Commonwealth spending
figs.value: highest in four decades outside the COVID years (ANZ's claim)

qs.q: Discuss the view that contractionary fiscal policy would allow the Reserve Bank to lower interest rates sooner.

items.guide: Lower government spending shifts AD left and eases the price level, which would let the RBA lower the cash rate sooner, but the short-run cost is lower output and possibly higher unemployment. When fiscal policy is expansionary while monetary policy is contractionary the RBA must lift rates higher; a coordinated mix spreads the burden.

terms.def: How fiscal and monetary policy are combined.
Cutting spending or raising taxes to slow aggregate demand.

items.title: ANZ boss: "dangerous" markets, but no recession for Australia
items.lede: ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos told a parliamentary inquiry that record share prices combined with rising interest rates are a "dangerous situation" for the world, but he expects Australia to slow noticeably rather than shrink, in line with the RBA, which is not forecasting a recession.

qs.q: Distinguish between an economic slowdown and a recession, and explain one risk to Australia's growth outlook.

items.guide: Higher interest rates slow household spending, so actual growth falls below trend: a slowdown. A recession would mean real GDP actually falling. Judge whether the RBA can reach a soft landing, inflation back to 2-3% without a large rise in unemployment, and note that a global shock such as a share-market fall could change the outlook.

terms.def: A fall in real GDP, commonly two consecutive negative quarters.
Bringing inflation down without causing a recession.

items.title: Westpac warns of a housing construction drought
items.lede: Westpac CEO Anthony Miller told a parliamentary committee that the bank funds 30% fewer housing construction projects than about 18 months ago, because each dollar is now "delivering fewer houses", mainly due to cost pressures. The HIA forecasts new home starts falling from 199,520 in 2026 to 191,040 in 2027, well short of the Housing Accord goal.

figs.label: Housing construction projects funded by Westpac
figs.source: Westpac CEO via Yahoo Finance AU

figs.label: Housing Accord target
figs.value: 1.2 million new homes over five years

qs.q: Explain how higher interest rates can make a housing shortage worse in the short run.

items.guide: Higher building and finance costs make fewer projects viable, shifting supply left: fewer homes are built and prices are pushed up, which worsens affordability for future buyers even if high interest rates hold demand back today. Housing supply links distribution of wealth with microeconomic reform on planning, construction productivity and tax settings.

terms.def: New dwellings on which construction has begun.
The national target of 1.2 million new homes over five years.

items.title: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico over a migrant caravan
items.lede: On 12 November (US time) President Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods unless a migrant caravan heading north is stopped. Reuters reported more than 1,000 migrants in a caravan that left Tapachula, near the Guatemalan border.

figs.label: Threatened tariff increase on Mexican goods
figs.value: double (current rate not stated in the digest)

figs.label: USMCA
figs.value: US declined in July to extend it beyond its 2036 expiry; trade talks with Mexico under way

figs.label: US-Canada
figs.value: USTR Jamieson Greer says the US has spoken with Canada in recent days and is working towards a trade deal

qs.q: Using a diagram, analyse the effects of a tariff increase on US consumers, US producers and Mexican exporters.

items.guide: A tariff lifts the US price from Pw to Pw+t, so US producers gain, US consumers lose, imports shrink and hurt Mexican exporters, the government collects revenue and there is a deadweight loss. Using tariffs for non-economic goals such as migration is a modern twist on protectionism: weigh the political aim against the efficiency costs and the risk of retaliation.

terms.def: A tax on imports that raises their domestic price.
Output and consumption lost because resources are used less efficiently.

items.title: Hot US inflation puts a December Fed rate hike on the table
items.lede: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point above forecasts, and markets now fully price a 25 basis point rise by the Federal Reserve in December. Fed Governor Chris Waller backs a 25bp hike in December and could favour 50bp.

figs.label: US CPI / core CPI, October (month on month)
Market pricing for a December Fed hike

qs.q: Explain how a rise in US interest rates could affect financial flows into Australia and the value of the Australian dollar.

items.guide: Strong US spending lifts the price level (demand-pull); a Fed hike raises borrowing costs so AD shifts back left, easing price pressure at the cost of slower growth. Higher US interest rates pull global capital towards the US, which links this to the AUD story: the AUD fell as the US dollar rose.

terms.def: CPI excluding volatile items such as food and energy.
Prices rising because spending outpaces the economy's capacity.

items.title: Why COP31 wants 35% of the world's energy to be electric by 2035
items.lede: COP31's "35-by-35" pledge, led by Chris Bowen and Türkiye's Murat Kurum, asks countries to get 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today. Analyst Anita Talberg says the figure is the median across the ten lowest-warming climate scenarios, and the IEA projects current policies deliver just under 30%.

figs.label: Electricity share of global final energy
figs.source: Climate Resource (2026) analysis of climate scenarios

figs.label: Share of new cars sold globally in 2025 that were electric
Best-case peak warming
figs.value: about 1.7°C in the 2040s, back to 1.5°C by 2100

figs.label: Energy demand that could be electrified with existing technology

qs.q: Explain how government policies could speed up electrification, and assess one economic cost of doing so.

items.guide: A subsidy on heat pumps or electric vehicles shifts supply right, lowering the price and raising take-up, so it displaces gas appliances. It has a budget cost and an opportunity cost, so it is justified only if climate and energy-security gains are larger. Cheaper finance helps developing economies electrify, which links environmental goals with development.

terms.def: Energy reaching users such as households and factories.
Warming temporarily exceeding 1.5°C before being brought back down.
A government payment that lowers producers' costs.

items.title: Why Australia's inflation is so stubborn, and why rates can't fix it alone
items.lede: Underlying inflation in Australia is stuck around 3.5-3.6%, while in the US, UK and Canada it has fallen towards 2-2.5%. Finance academic Jak Kakhkharov argues the cause is now mainly supply constraints, such as housing, energy and skilled labour shortages, which interest rates can only partly address.

figs.label: Australia's trimmed mean inflation (US, UK, Canada about 2-2.5%)
RBA rate rises in 2026 against one rise in the past two years in each of the US and UK
Policy rates: RBA / Bank of England / US Fed / Bank of Canada
When the RBA expects inflation back in its 2-3% band

qs.q: Discuss the limitations of monetary policy in reducing inflation caused by supply constraints, and identify other policies that could help.

items.guide: Shortages and higher input costs shift SRAS left, raising prices and cutting output. Rate rises work on demand, lowering the price level but cutting output further and raising unemployment. Rates cannot build houses, generate electricity or train workers, so supply-side (microeconomic) reform and fiscal restraint are needed alongside them. Most Australian home loans are variable, so rate rises hit households faster than where fixed rates dominate.

terms.def: The RBA's preferred underlying inflation measure.
Costs or shortages that stop output keeping up with demand.
Prices rise because production costs rise.

items.title: Budget tax changes push investors out of the housing market
items.lede: Investor home loans fell by almost a third in the first full quarter after the May budget's tax changes: the number of new investor loans fell 30.6% to 35,301 and their value fell 32.3%. Owner-occupiers' share of new home loans rose to 68%, from 59% before the budget.

figs.label: Owner-occupiers' share of new home loans
Brisbane median dwelling value
figs.value: -2% in October (steepest fall in the country)

qs.q: Evaluate the use of tax policy to improve housing affordability in Australia.

items.guide: Reducing tax concessions lowers investors' after-tax return, so demand for investment property falls and the price falls, improving affordability. The limitation: if fewer investors buy, fewer homes may be offered for rent, which could push rents up, and lasting affordability needs more housing supply.

terms.def: The use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy.
How easily households can buy or rent a home relative to their income.

items.title: Has the RBA reached its peak? Economists weigh up the fifth hike
items.lede: The RBA raised the cash rate by 0.25 points to 4.85% on 3 November, the fifth hike of 2026 and the highest since late 2008. A week later, ANZ expects a pause but warns another rise in December cannot be ruled out, and the RBA does not expect inflation below 3% until late 2027.

figs.label: RBA cash rate
figs.value: 4.85% (highest since late 2008; fifth hike of 2026; board vote 6-3, three members wanted to hold at 4.60%)

figs.label: When the RBA expects inflation below 3%
figs.value: late 2027 (about three quarters later than previously forecast)

qs.q: Analyse the transmission mechanism of monetary policy, using recent data on lending and consumer sentiment.

items.guide: Higher rates raise mortgage repayments and reduce borrowing, shifting AD left: the price level eases but output falls. The 6-3 split shows the board is divided over how much tightening is already in the pipeline, a key limitation given time lags of up to two years.

terms.def: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, set by the RBA as its main policy tool.
The channels through which a cash-rate change affects spending, output and inflation.

items.title: CBA's profit is up, but more borrowers are falling behind
items.lede: Commonwealth Bank lifted its first-quarter cash profit about 8% to roughly A$2.8bn, but home loan arrears rose 7 basis points to 0.8% and home loan applications fell 16% over the year. CEO Matt Comyn said higher inflation and interest rates are hitting some households and businesses much harder than others.

figs.label: CBA unaudited first-quarter cash profit
figs.value: about A$2.8bn (+8% on a year earlier)

figs.label: Home loan applications
figs.value: -16% over the year (home lending still +6.6%, business lending +13.6%)

qs.q: Discuss how rising interest rates affect the distribution of income and wealth in Australia.

items.guide: Rising rates redistribute income from borrowers to lenders and savers, which is one reason monetary policy is described as a blunt instrument. Existing loan books are still growing but new demand is falling fast, a leading sign that credit growth will slow.

terms.def: Loan repayments that are overdue (here, 90+ days).
One-hundredth of a percentage point; 7 basis points is 0.07 percentage points.

items.title: New home lending suffers its biggest fall on record
items.lede: The value of new home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, the steepest drop since the ABS series began in 2002, and investors led the retreat. It was bigger than the falls during the GFC (-13.3% in 2008) and COVID (-12.9%).

figs.label: Value of new housing loan commitments

qs.q: Explain how a fall in housing lending can affect economic growth and the distribution of wealth in Australia.

items.guide: Two forces are at work: higher interest rates reduce how much people can borrow, and the sharper investor fall points to the budget's tax changes and falling-price expectations. J.P. Morgan calls the investor decline a structural drag steeper than in past hiking cycles. Falling lending and prices can cut spending through the wealth effect and slow dwelling investment.

terms.def: An ABS release measuring new loan commitments for housing, personal and business finance.
When asset values such as house prices fall, households feel poorer and spend less.

items.title: COP31: arguments over a global electricity target
items.lede: At the UN climate talks in Antalya, a push to lift electricity's share of world energy use from about 23% to 35% by 2035 has divided countries over whether that power must be clean. The draft wording does not require clean electricity, and analysts estimate a clean-only version could cut projected warming by 0.3°C from at least 2.6°C.

figs.label: Electricity's share of world energy use, now / proposed by 2035
figs.value: 23% / 35% (about four times the current pace of electrification)

figs.label: Projected warming on the current path
figs.value: 2.6°C or more (clean-only version could cut about 0.3°C)

figs.label: Rooftop-solar households targeted by 2030 (Australia-backed voluntary pledge)

qs.q: Assess the effectiveness of voluntary international agreements in addressing global environmental problems.

items.guide: Firms set output on private costs, but burning fossil fuels imposes climate costs on others, so the market overproduces. Clean electrification shifts energy use away from that market, but if the power comes from coal or gas much of the climate benefit is lost. Because each country can free-ride, the strength of the wording (binding or voluntary, clean or any electricity) matters.

terms.def: A cost imposed on third parties that is not reflected in the market price.
A non-binding commitment with no penalty for missing it.

items.title: China's trade surplus tops US$1 trillion, again
