items.lede: China's trade surplus for the first ten months of 2026 reached US$1.04 trillion, a month earlier than last year, as Beijing relies on exports to reach its growth target. October exports rose 35.2% year on year to US$412.3bn, and exports to the US rose 32.9% despite US tariffs.

figs.label: China trade surplus, January-October 2026
figs.value: US$1.04 trillion (2025 full-year record: US$1.2 trillion)

figs.label: China's surplus with the EU, January-October

qs.q: Explain how China's reliance on export-led growth could increase protectionism in the global economy.

items.guide: A surplus means China produces more than it spends at home. With weak household demand and low inflation, Chinese firms push output into world markets, which helps China's GDP but squeezes import-competing industries elsewhere and raises protectionist pressure in the US and EU. For Australia, Chinese industrial output underpins iron ore demand, but a growth model built on exports is more exposed to tariffs.

terms.def: The value of exports is greater than the value of imports.
A strategy that relies on selling to foreign markets, not domestic demand, to drive GDP.

items.title: Albanese at COP31: climate policy meets political reality
items.lede: Anthony Albanese has arrived at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, the first Australian prime minister at a COP since 2021, as Australia oversees the negotiations without the United States at the table. The US has withdrawn from the UN climate process under President Trump.

figs.label: Estimated cost of hosting COP31 in Adelaide
figs.value: well over $1 billion on government estimates (Türkiye pays most under the deal)

qs.q: Explain why the withdrawal of a major economy weakens international cooperation on climate change.

items.guide: Both countries are better off if both cut emissions, but each does even better by free-riding, so the likely outcome is that neither acts. When a large emitter such as the US leaves, the gains from cooperation shrink and others have less reason to keep their own pledges. International agreements are hard to enforce because pledges are largely voluntary.

terms.def: Countries benefit from others' emissions cuts without paying the cost themselves.
A benefit, such as a stable climate, that no country can be excluded from enjoying.

items.title: $88m to train an AUKUS workforce amid a skills shortage
items.lede: The federal government will spend $88 million over six years to train workers for nuclear-powered submarines under the 2026 Nuclear-Powered Submarine Workforce Strategy, targeting up to 275 apprentices and trainees in WA and SA. ASPI, citing BuildSkills Australia, estimates a shortfall of about 110,000 skilled trades workers, with AUKUS competing against infrastructure and energy projects.

figs.label: Nuclear-Powered Submarine Workforce Strategy
figs.value: $88 million over six years; up to 275 apprentices and trainees

figs.label: Estimated shortfall of skilled trades workers
Investment in HMAS Stirling
figs.value: $8 billion (hosts one UK and up to four US nuclear subs from 2027)

qs.q: Assess the effectiveness of education and training policies in addressing skills shortages in Australia.

items.guide: Big projects lift demand for tradespeople and, with supply fixed in the short run, wages jump, a source of cost inflation. Training and skilled migration shift supply right and ease wage pressure, but 275 places over six years is small next to a 110,000-worker shortfall, so migration and fewer competing projects also matter.

terms.def: Employers cannot find enough workers with the required skills at current wages.
Joblessness caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs available.

items.title: A weaker Australian dollar complicates the RBA's inflation fight
items.lede: The Australian dollar fell to a seven-month low of 68.42 US cents after hotter-than-expected US inflation data, making imports dearer just as the Reserve Bank is trying to bring inflation down. RBA modelling suggests exchange-rate moves account for up to two-thirds of the effect of rate changes on inflation, so a weaker dollar weakens that channel.

figs.label: Australian dollar
figs.value: 68.42 US cents low in New York (seven-month low); about 68.78 on Wednesday

figs.label: Share of the effect of rate changes on inflation that works through the exchange rate
Market odds of a sixth RBA hike by early 2027
figs.value: about 1 in 4 (would take the cash rate above 5%)

figs.label: CBA AUD forecasts
figs.value: 68 US cents by year-end; 66 by March 2027

qs.q: Explain how a depreciation of the Australian dollar could affect inflation and the RBA's monetary policy decisions.

items.guide: Higher expected US rates make US assets more attractive, so demand for AUD falls and the exchange rate depreciates, and imports cost more in AUD. A full answer shows both sides: a depreciation helps export competitiveness and the trade balance but adds to imported inflation, which matters most when inflation is already above the 2-3% target.

terms.def: A fall in the value of a currency against another under a floating exchange rate.
Rising domestic prices caused by dearer imports, for example after a depreciation.

items.title: Bracket creep bites hardest at the bottom and near the top
items.lede: Analysis by the e61 Institute and Richard Holden finds that, without tax cuts, a $45,000 earner's average tax rate would rise from 11% to 16% over a decade from 2028, and a $190,000 earner's from 29% to 34%. In both cases more than half of real income growth is taxed away.

figs.label: Average tax rate, $45,000 earner, with no tax cuts for a decade from 2028
figs.source: e61 Institute / Richard Holden, via ABC News

figs.label: Average tax rate, $190,000 earner, with no tax cuts for a decade
figs.source: e61 Institute / Richard Holden, via ABC News

figs.label: Budget balance without bracket creep (PBO)
figs.value: deficit of 0.7% of GDP by the end of the decade, not the projected 1% surplus
figs.source: Parliamentary Budget Office via ABC News

figs.label: Opposition pledge
figs.value: Angus Taylor to index tax brackets to inflation from 2028

qs.q: Explain how bracket creep affects the budget outcome and the distribution of income in Australia.

items.guide: Tax brackets are fixed in dollars, so as wages rise with inflation more income is taxed at higher marginal rates and average tax rates rise even when real pay is barely higher. It is a hidden contractionary force and a source of revenue growth; indexing brackets would protect equity but cost the budget.

terms.def: Inflation pushes nominal incomes into higher tax brackets.
Rising tax revenue that automatically slows the economy.

items.title: Cost-of-living anger reshapes politics, with spillovers for Australia
items.lede: ABC analysis by Ian Verrender argues the US midterm result and New Zealand's too-close-to-call election matter for Australia through financial flows and migration. US government debt is about 126% of GDP against about 33% for Australia, and Australian super funds have up to 20% of their investments on Wall Street, mostly in tech.

figs.label: US government debt, share of GDP
Australian government debt, share of GDP
US share of the world's US$112 trillion of government debt
Share of Australian super fund investments on Wall Street
New Zealanders who moved to Australia, three years to mid-2026
New Zealand cash rate / inflation / unemployment

qs.q: Explain how an increase in migration from New Zealand could affect Australia's labour market.

items.guide: An inflow of New Zealand workers shifts labour supply right: employment rises but, if wages are sticky and labour demand is weakening, the extra workers show up as higher unemployment in the short run. Migrants also spend, which lifts demand later. Link migration to both aggregate supply and aggregate demand.

terms.def: Buying shares or bonds overseas, such as super funds on Wall Street.
The number of people willing and able to work.
The stock of government borrowing, often shown as a % of GDP.

items.title: Consumer mood sinks to a four-year low
items.lede: The Westpac–Melbourne Institute index of consumer sentiment fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November, its third monthly fall in a row and the lowest since late 2022. High petrol prices, 4.3% inflation and the RBA's fifth rate rise this year are weighing on households.

figs.label: Sentiment compared with a year earlier
Expectations for the economy over the next 12 months
Consumers expecting mortgage rates to rise further

qs.q: Explain how a fall in consumer confidence could affect economic growth and unemployment in Australia.

items.guide: Consumption is about half of aggregate demand. When households feel worse off and expect higher mortgage repayments they save more and spend less, shifting AD left, and the multiplier amplifies the fall. Falling confidence shows the transmission mechanism working, but raises the risk of slower growth and higher unemployment.

terms.def: An index of how households feel about finances and the economy; below 100 means pessimists outnumber optimists.
An initial cut in spending leads to further falls in income and spending.

items.title: Business conditions slump to a six-year low as costs keep rising
items.lede: NAB's October survey shows business conditions at their weakest since August 2020 and forward orders falling sharply, yet purchase costs are still rising. Underlying inflation was 3.6% in September, above the RBA's 2-3% target.

qs.q: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain why rising business costs make the RBA's job harder.

items.guide: Higher input costs shift SRAS left, raising the price level and cutting output, while weak orders point to falling demand. That creates a policy conflict: raising rates fights inflation but deepens the slowdown in growth and jobs. Retail was weakest and construction is softening.

terms.def: A leading indicator of future demand.
Rising prices combined with weak growth.

items.title: Oil's slide starts to reach the bowser, slowly
items.lede: Brent crude fell about 16% last week, its steepest weekly drop since COVID hit, after President Trump signalled a pause in strikes on Iran, and was about US$93 a barrel on 10 November. Australian petrol prices are only starting to follow: the national average unleaded fell 2.9c to 234.5c a litre, well above its 12-month average of 196.4c.

figs.label: Brent crude
figs.value: about US$93 a barrel (30 October high US$118)

qs.q: Explain why petrol prices in regional areas may take longer to fall than prices in capital cities.

items.guide: More OPEC supply and a smaller war-risk premium shift crude supply right; because short-run demand for oil is inelastic, modest supply changes produce large price swings. On an AD/AS diagram cheaper oil shifts SRAS right, lowering inflation and raising output, the reverse of a supply shock. Cuts should reach capital cities in days but regional areas in weeks.

terms.def: Quantity barely responds to price, so supply shifts cause big price swings.
How quickly cost changes reach retail prices.

items.title: Qantas sends 850 corporate jobs offshore
items.lede: Qantas will cut about 850 corporate roles over the next few years under an outsourcing deal with Accenture, with most of the work moving to India. Its shares rose about 5.6% on the news, and Coles announced a similar plan in August to move up to 1,000 roles to India via Accenture.

figs.label: Qantas share price on the day
Roles Coles plans to move offshore via Accenture (August plan)

qs.q: Evaluate the impact on the Australian economy of firms offshoring service jobs.

items.guide: When firms can buy the same services more cheaply from overseas, demand for local back-office workers falls and wage pressure eases. Winners include shareholders and workers in India; losers include displaced staff, communities and the government through lower tax receipts. It is a case for labour market policies such as retraining and redeployment.

terms.def: Moving work to another country to cut costs.
Job losses caused by long-term change in the economy, not the business cycle.
Services bought from abroad count as imports.

items.title: Opinion: "Blame Canberra and the RBA, not oil, for inflation"
items.lede: In the AFR, economist Dimitri Burshtein (Eminence Advisory) argues that the oil shock is a convenient excuse: underlying inflation has been rising since mid-2025, before the Strait of Hormuz was closed in late February 2026. He blames heavy government spending, made worse by an RBA that cut rates too early in 2025.

figs.label: Cash rate
figs.value: 4.85% after the fifth rise in 2026 (three cuts in 2025 to 3.6%)

figs.label: Broad money growth, year to June 2026 / by September / "needed" rate
Federal spending as a share of GDP
Author's measure of the real cash rate

qs.q: Evaluate the claim that Australia's high inflation in 2026 is caused mainly by government policy rather than global oil prices.

items.guide: His argument is about demand: spending, cost-of-living payments and cheap credit push AD right, a demand-pull inflation that persists however oil moves, while oil is a supply (SRAS) shift. Critics would say the RBA sets interest rates, not money, the money-to-prices link is loose when velocity is unstable, private demand such as the data-centre boom matters, and oil feeds into second-round costs and expectations.

terms.def: Inflation with the most extreme price moves removed.
The RBA's widest measure of the money supply.
The cash rate minus inflation.

items.title: Regulators target dodgy discounts and opaque private credit
items.lede: With Black Friday to Cyber Monday spending forecast to hit a record A$7.2 billion, the ACCC is watching for fake "discounts". Separately, ASIC's second review of the A$250 billion private credit sector found poor disclosure to investors and firms resisting its instructions.

figs.label: Forecast Black Friday to Cyber Monday spending (27-30 November)
Combined fines on six retailers for misleading discounts, over two years
Size of the private credit sector

qs.q: Explain how regulators such as the ACCC can improve the efficiency of markets.

items.guide: A fake "was" price inflates demand from D1 to D2, so consumers buy more at a higher price than they would with accurate information and resources go to goods people would not have chosen. Consumer law aims to keep demand at D1 by keeping price claims honest. Competition and consumer protection is part of microeconomic reform that improves allocative efficiency.

terms.def: One side of a deal (the seller) knows more than the other.
The regulator that enforces competition and consumer law.
The regulator of financial markets and products.

items.title: Business groups back a simpler capital gains tax model
items.lede: Peak industry groups, economists and business leaders are urging the government to adopt independent MP Allegra Spender's alternative to the May budget's capital gains tax changes, which they say would raise as much revenue with far less complexity. The budget replaced the 50% CGT discount with an inflation-based discount on all assets and a minimum 30% CGT rate.

figs.label: Budget model
figs.value: inflation-based discount on all assets; minimum 30% CGT rate

figs.label: Spender model
figs.value: inflation-based discount for passive assets; flat 40% discount for active assets; scraps the start-up carve-out (IBCC)

figs.label: Business owners backing the Spender model
Taxable gain on a $1m gain from a zero-cost stake: old 50% / Spender 40% / budget indexation

qs.q: Evaluate the trade-off between equity and efficiency in recent changes to Australia's capital gains tax.

items.guide: Taxing gains more like wages improves vertical equity, since capital gains flow mainly to high-wealth households, but critics say it reduces the incentive to take risks and invest, which matters for productivity. A start-up founder with a zero-cost stake has nothing to index, so the whole gain is taxable.

terms.def: Tax on the profit made when an asset is sold for more than it cost.
Active assets are businesses, shares and options; passive assets are such as investment property.

items.title: China's factory-gate inflation jumps to 5.7%
items.lede: China's producer price index rose 5.7% over the year to October, up from 5.0% in September and above the 5.3% forecast, while consumer price inflation slowed to 0.7% from 0.9%. The widening gap suggests firms face higher costs while household demand stays weak.

figs.label: China producer price index, year on year (forecast 5.3%)
China consumer price index, year on year (forecast 0.8%)

qs.q: Distinguish between the producer price index and the consumer price index, and explain how rising producer prices in China could affect inflation in Australia.

items.guide: Rising producer prices can be an early sign of future consumer inflation, both in China and in countries that import Chinese goods. Firms' costs are rising, but weak consumer demand stops them passing those costs on to shoppers in full. China is Australia's largest trading partner, so its prices and growth matter for Australian imports and resource exports.

terms.def: Measures changes in prices received by producers (factory-gate prices).
Inflation caused by rising prices of imported goods.

items.title: How exposed is household wealth to an AI share crash?
items.lede: RBA researchers Iris Chan and Marcus Miller estimate that 5.3% of household financial wealth was exposed to AI-related shares in June 2026, up from 2% at the end of 2022. A 30% fall in AI share prices would cut household financial wealth by only about 1.6%, but the effect on consumer spending would now be about twice as large as in 2022.

figs.label: Share of household financial wealth exposed to AI-related shares (end 2022: 2.0%)
Fall in household financial wealth if AI share prices fell 30%
Nasdaq fall in a single session (S&P 500 fell 4%)

qs.q: Explain how a fall in global share prices could affect consumption and economic growth in Australia.

items.guide: Globalisation of financial markets means a sell-off on Wall Street can quickly reduce Australian household wealth through super funds and share portfolios. A crash would still hit only a small part of total wealth, but exposure has more than doubled since 2022, so the effect on consumption would now be about twice as large: AI shares fall, household wealth falls, the wealth effect cuts spending, aggregate demand falls and growth slows.

terms.def: Households spend more when their assets rise in value, and less when they fall.
When a shock in one financial market spreads to others.

items.title: ANZ makes $7.3b profit and will stop financing new oil and gas
items.lede: ANZ posted a $7.3 billion full-year profit that beat expectations, but its shares closed down 3.2% on Monday. In its annual report the bank said it will no longer finance new or upstream oil and gas projects, including LNG plants, and will not finance coal-fired power, expecting its existing coal power loans to run off by September 2030.

figs.label: ANZ share price at Monday's close (down as much as 4.3% to $38.59 during the day)
Year ANZ expects its coal power loans to run off

qs.q: To what extent can private-sector decisions, such as banks refusing to finance new fossil fuel projects, help achieve environmental sustainability?

items.guide: A conceptual diagram: when major banks withdraw lending, the supply of finance for new oil and gas projects shifts from S1 to S2, the cost of finance rises from r1 to r2 and the amount of finance used falls, so fewer projects go ahead and future emissions are lower. Other lenders may fill the gap, so one bank's decision may have a limited effect on its own.

terms.def: A cost imposed on third parties (such as pollution) that is not reflected in the market price.
What firms must pay to borrow or raise funds for investment.

items.title: Oil shock speeds up Australia's switch to electric vehicles
items.lede: Battery electric cars outsold petrol cars in Australia in both September and October 2026, and EVs now make up close to a quarter of new car sales. Researchers say high oil prices from the Iran war are pushing consumers toward electric transport.

figs.label: Electric vehicle share of new car sales in Australia
Electric vehicle share of cars on Australian roads
Crude oil costs saved by the global EV fleet in the six months after the war began
Share of the growth in global electricity demand supplied by solar
Share of world final energy use still supplied by coal, oil and gas

qs.q: Using a demand and supply diagram, explain how a rise in petrol prices affects the market for electric vehicles. Discuss one environmental implication.

items.guide: Price signals can drive environmental change: higher fossil fuel prices act like a carbon price, encouraging people to switch to cleaner substitutes without new regulation. Petrol cars and EVs are substitutes, so dearer petrol shifts demand for EVs from D1 to D2, raising quantity sold and, other things equal, the market price.

terms.def: Goods that can replace each other; when one gets dearer, demand for the other rises.
The price of one good compared with another.

items.title: Are there any good alternatives to raising interest rates?
items.lede: The RBA raised the cash rate from 4.60% to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008, with three of the nine Board members wanting to hold. ABC money correspondent Jessica Irvine asks whether there is a better way to bring inflation down and concludes rate hikes are crude, but they are the tool we have.

figs.label: RBA cash rate after the 3 November rise (highest since 2008)
Board members who wanted to hold on 3 November
Time for a rate rise to have its full effect
Projected budget deficit over the forward estimates
Housing debt as a share of income (CBA's Ashwin Clarke)

qs.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of monetary policy in reducing inflation that is partly caused by a global oil supply shock.

items.guide: Use it to evaluate monetary policy: the transmission mechanism, time lags, limitations and the importance of credibility. Each step takes time and the effect depends on how indebted households are; lower debt-to-income and borrowers who kept repayments high after the 2025 cuts mean weaker transmission this time. Irvine compares rate hikes (an independent RBA can act quickly, but they are crude and hit mortgage holders hardest) with temporary taxes set by an independent body (which would spread the burden more widely, though no country uses this today) and adjusting the 12% super guarantee, which she says needs more investigation.

terms.def: The channels through which cash rate changes affect spending and inflation.
The delay between a policy change and its full effect.

items.title: RBA: the AI boom could keep interest rates higher for longer
items.lede: RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter told a UBS conference that the global rush to invest in AI and data centres may keep interest rates higher, that productivity gains are likely to come later, and that the technology has so far had little effect on overall jobs. Data-centre investment is up tenfold in three years and the RBA expects $115 billion of it by 2028.

figs.label: Expected data-centre investment by 2028 (excluding energy infrastructure)
RBA forecast for business investment growth this year
Rise in data-centre investment over three years
Share of households' roughly $9 trillion of financial wealth in AI-related companies

qs.q: Explain how a surge in data-centre investment could affect inflation and interest rates in Australia in the short run and the long run.

items.guide: The same investment is inflationary now and potentially disinflationary later. In the short run data-centre construction shifts AD right against fixed capacity (LRAS1), lifting the price level so the RBA keeps rates higher; in the long run, if AI lifts productivity, LRAS shifts right and output can grow with less inflation pressure. Firms worldwide compete for scarce savings, so the RBA's neutral rate estimate has risen, as in the late-1990s internet boom.

terms.def: The rate that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy.
An innovation, like electricity, that transforms many industries.
Productivity dips or stalls before rising as firms adapt.

items.title: Chalmers asks Treasury for a productivity plan before the mid-year update
items.lede: The Treasurer has reportedly asked Treasury's structural reform officials to develop new productivity policies for December's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook. Australia's productivity growth over the past decade has been among the weakest in the OECD.

figs.label: Australia's productivity growth over the past decade
figs.value: among the weakest in the OECD

qs.q: Explain how microeconomic reform can lift productivity and reduce inflationary pressure in the Australian economy.

items.guide: When demand grows against fixed capacity (LRAS1) the result is only a higher price level. Productivity-raising reform shifts capacity out to LRAS2, so real GDP can grow with less price pressure. Supply-side policy complements monetary policy, since the RBA manages only demand, but reform takes years to pay off.

terms.def: Output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked.
Policies that improve how efficiently individual markets and industries work.

items.title: China extends its trade truce with the US to January
items.lede: China will keep its extra 24% tariff on US goods suspended for another two months, while a 10% tariff remains, buying time before Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet at APEC on 18-19 November. Waivers on some critical mineral export controls are extended to 10 January 2027.

figs.label: Extra tariff on US goods, suspended / tariff still in place
Suspended penalties and export-control waivers extended to
figs.value: 10 January 2027 (11 US firms on the unreliable entities list; 16 on the export control list; port fees on US-linked ships)

figs.label: Proposed reciprocal tariff cuts (not finalised)
figs.value: US$60bn, including about US$17bn of US farm goods

qs.q: Using a tariff diagram, explain the effects on Chinese consumers and US exporters if the suspended 24% tariff were reimposed.

items.guide: A tariff raises the domestic price to Pw+t, so farmers supply more, consumers buy less, imports shrink, the government collects revenue and deadweight loss appears. Suspending the extra 24% keeps the price wedge smaller. A US-China farm deal could also cause trade diversion: if China buys more US farm goods it may buy less from other suppliers, such as Australia.

terms.def: A tax on imported goods that raises their domestic price.
A temporary pause in retaliatory trade barriers while negotiations continue.

items.title: AI data centres: an economic opportunity or a political problem?
items.lede: Data centres became a cost-of-living and local planning issue in the US midterms, and with multibillion-dollar projects planned across Australia the government must weigh investment and growth against energy, water and community costs. Labor's draft national AI standards would require operators to bring their own energy, manage water and consult communities, while Senator David Pocock wants a 5% levy.

figs.label: Western Downs Digital Park, Queensland (first of four centres leased by Anthropic from 2027)
Possible share of Sydney's drinking water used by the industry by 2035 (Sydney Water warning)
Levy on data centres proposed by Senator David Pocock
Share of planned US data centre capacity in Texas

qs.q: Identify two negative externalities of data centres.
Using a diagram, explain how a 5% levy could correct the market failure caused by data centres.

items.guide: Use it as evidence for environmental management policy. Compare regulation ('bring your own energy') with a market-based levy, and link it to ecologically sustainable development: balancing growth now against resources for future generations. On a diagram, operators base decisions on marginal private cost, so output at Q1 is more than is socially efficient; a levy or rule makes them bear the social cost and moves output to Q2 at a higher price.

terms.def: A cost imposed on third parties that is not reflected in the market price.
A levy or price that changes incentives.
Rules such as 'bring your own energy'.

items.title: Should the budget be tightened in December's update?
items.lede: With the RBA raising rates, some commentators want the government to cut spending in the December mid-year economic update, and ABC political editor Jacob Greber argues it is the right prescription at the wrong time. Minister Clare O'Neil has confirmed a savings package for the update that she called a 'mini budget', with priorities of lower spending, cost-of-living relief that does not add to inflation, and productivity.

figs.label: Government spending as a share of GDP (before the pandemic: under 25%)
RBA cash rate after the 3 November rise

qs.q: Evaluate whether both fiscal and monetary policy should be contractionary in Australia in late 2026.

items.guide: The policy mix matters: if fiscal and monetary policy both tighten into a slowdown, the combined effect on growth and jobs could be larger than intended. Higher rates already reduce consumption and investment, and spending cuts would reduce G as well, shifting AD from AD1 to AD2, so the price level eases but real GDP falls and unemployment rises. Case for cutting: spending is above pre-pandemic levels, it would help the RBA reduce inflation, and fiscal policy could share the load with mortgage holders. Case against (Greber): the deficit is already narrowing faster than forecast, the RBA expects business investment to collapse in the second half of 2027, and house prices have fallen more than Treasury expected.

terms.def: Whether the budget is adding to demand (expansionary) or subtracting from it (contractionary).
The Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, a mid-year update of the federal budget.

items.title: Wesfarmers, Telstra and BHP urge Canberra to move fast on AI
items.lede: Business leaders want rules on AI, copyright and data centres settled before Christmas, warning that slow decisions will push investment to rival countries. Wesfarmers' Rob Scott calls AI one of the few levers big enough to fix Australia's productivity problem.

figs.label: Extra annual output at BHP in WA from AI computer vision
Companies and CEOs represented by the BCA
Share of data-centre power from renewables (industry claim)

qs.q: Explain how regulatory uncertainty can reduce business investment.
Discuss the potential economic benefits and costs of rapid AI adoption in Australia.

items.guide: Balance the dynamic efficiency gains from new technology against externalities (energy, water) and structural unemployment risks. Investment is flowing to Singapore, India and Japan, and Meta says the midterms will make US data-centre building harder.

terms.def: Output per unit of input, such as per hour worked.
Clear, stable rules that let firms plan long-term investment.

items.title: Productivity chief says Labor's workplace laws should be reviewed
items.lede: Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood says the government should check whether its industrial relations changes, including multi-employer bargaining and same-job-same-pay, are holding back productivity. Meanwhile ABS data show federal public service wages rose 7% last financial year.

figs.label: Possible gain in a worker's income from small productivity improvements over a decade

qs.q: Explain the link between wage growth, productivity growth and inflation.
Evaluate the effects of recent industrial relations reforms on the Australian economy.

items.guide: Wages can only rise sustainably in line with productivity without adding to inflation. Critics (Coalition, business groups) say the reforms add cost and complexity; supporters (Labor, unions) say they lifted wages and improved bargaining power for the low paid.

terms.def: Enterprise agreements negotiated across several employers at once.
The laws and institutions that govern pay, conditions and bargaining.

items.title: Democrats take Congress, but America's tariffs are likely to stay
items.lede: Voters punished President Trump over the cost of living, with Democrats winning both houses on 3 November, but trade lawyers say the tariff wall will not come down because the powers now used do not need Congress each year. A bill to roll tariffs back could be vetoed, and overriding a veto needs two-thirds of the Senate.

figs.label: US Senate count (Democrats-Republicans), early
figs.value: 54-44, with 2 seats still to be called

figs.label: Senate majority needed to override a veto
Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs
figs.value: February 2026: the emergency powers law does not allow tariffs

qs.q: Using a tariff diagram, explain who gains and who loses from a US tariff on imported goods.
Explain why US protection could stay high even after the midterm result.

items.guide: Use the midterms as evidence that protection has political as well as economic costs, then explain why tariffs persist: legal authority (Sections 122, 232, 301 and, for the first time, 338), the veto and bipartisan support on China. Expect hearings and oversight rather than repeal.

terms.def: Government measures that shield domestic producers from import competition.
A tax on imports that raises their domestic price.
The efficiency loss when a tariff stops mutually beneficial trade.

items.title: US voters say no to data centres in their backyard
items.lede: About 41 data-centre ballot measures were held across 10 US states and all but one were heading for defeat, with an NBC exit poll finding three-quarters of voters opposed a data centre in their own community. In Australia on the same day, NextDC shares jumped about 48% after a Goodman-backed group bought a stake of up to 9.9%.

figs.label: Data-centre ballot measures
figs.value: about 41 in 10 US states; all but one heading for defeat

figs.label: Voters opposed to a data centre in their community
figs.source: NBC via ABC News live blog

figs.label: NextDC share price
figs.value: +48% (Goodman-backed group bought up to 9.9% at $9.50 a share)

qs.q: Identify one negative externality of data centres and explain a policy that could correct it.
Explain how data-centre investment can affect both aggregate demand and aggregate supply.

items.guide: The costs raised by voters are power prices, water, land use, noise and emissions; investors point to investment spending in AD, productivity gains that shift LRAS outward, and jobs. Link to policies such as pricing, regulation or renewable-supply conditions.

terms.def: A cost borne by third parties that is not reflected in the market price.
Community acceptance a project needs to proceed in practice.

items.title: Diesel squeeze: Australia pays more to find new suppliers
items.lede: Australia is the world's largest buyer of seaborne diesel, importing about 28 billion litres last year, and war in the Gulf and drone strikes on Russian refineries have redrawn the global diesel trade. Diesel peaked at A$3.20 a litre and is still about A$2.79, almost $1 higher than a year ago, with an extra $9 billion paid for imports between March and August.

figs.label: Diesel imported by Australia
figs.value: about 28 billion litres (almost 8% of seaborne diesel)

figs.label: Diesel price
figs.value: A$2.79 a litre (peak A$3.20; almost $1 higher than a year ago)

figs.label: Russia's share of global diesel arrivals
Share of Australia's diesel imports from South Korea
figs.value: 29% to almost half (Indian supply has not arrived since July)

qs.q: Explain how higher world diesel prices affect Australia's terms of trade and current account balance.
Using a supply and demand diagram, explain why diesel prices rose so sharply in 2026.

items.guide: Higher import prices for fuel worsen Australia's terms of trade and add to the import bill in the current account. They also feed into cost-push inflation (Topic 3) and show a risk of globalisation: reliance on a few suppliers threatens fuel security. South Korean refiners still rely on Middle Eastern crude, so the diversification is only partial.

terms.def: Relying on foreign suppliers for an essential good.
The ability to keep reliable fuel supplies flowing during disruptions.
Quantity demanded changes little when the price changes, because there are few substitutes.
The index of export prices divided by import prices, multiplied by 100.

items.title: Farrell: Trump's defeat proves tariffs hurt consumers
items.lede: Trade Minister Don Farrell will use the midterm result to press Washington to drop its tariffs on Australia, calling it a vindication of the view that tariffs mainly raise prices for ordinary consumers. The Coalition says it will vote against the Australia-EU FTA early next year, arguing it falls short on agriculture and ties Australia to climate commitments.

figs.label: Existing US tariff on Australian imports
Australia-EU FTA
figs.value: to parliament early next year; Coalition says it will vote against

figs.label: Summits Trump is due to attend that the PM may raise tariffs at

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain why tariffs raise prices for consumers.
Assess the potential benefits and costs for Australia of a free trade agreement with the EU.

items.guide: The tariff diagram shows consumers losing more than producers and the government gain together, which is Farrell's argument. When evaluating an FTA, weigh gains from trade against adjustment costs and conditions attached, here the climate commitments.

terms.def: A deal that lowers trade barriers between member countries.
Reducing tariffs and other barriers to trade.

items.title: Goods trade surplus jumps to $2.8 billion as imports fall
items.lede: The seasonally adjusted goods surplus rose $2,642m to $2,826m in September, from a revised $184m in August. Exports rose 2.3% to $48.4b, led by other mineral fuels and metals, while imports fell 3.3% to $45.6b, with non-monetary gold making up $1,096m of the fall.

figs.label: Other mineral fuels / metals excluding gold exports

qs.q: Outline the main factors behind the larger goods surplus in September 2026.
Explain how a larger goods surplus affects Australia's current account deficit.

items.guide: A larger goods surplus narrows the current account deficit, but the primary income deficit is usually much bigger. Falling imports of capital and consumer goods may also signal weaker domestic demand as interest rates rise.

terms.def: Exports of goods minus imports of goods; part of the current account.
Gold traded as a commodity; volatile flows that can swing the monthly balance.

items.title: US tech giants push for trade retaliation over Australia's news levy
items.lede: Meta, Google and other platforms claim Australia's News Bargaining Incentive breaches the Australia-US Free Trade Agreement, and their lobby group CCIA has asked US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to investigate. The incentive makes big platforms strike deals with publishers or pay a levy of 2.5% of their Australian digital advertising revenue.

figs.label: Levy rate if no deals are struck
Existing US tariff on Australian imports

qs.q: Explain how a trade agreement can constrain a country's domestic economic policy.
Discuss the risks to the Australian economy of the US retaliating over the news levy.

items.guide: Contrast the platforms' view (a discriminatory tax that breaches AUSFTA) with the government's (it funds public-interest journalism, a merit good, and is a domestic policy choice). Canada dropped its digital tax last year under similar US pressure.

terms.def: The Australia-United States Free Trade Agreement, in force since 2005.
Trade measures imposed in response to another country's policies.

items.title: Woodside cuts 500 jobs and its dividend as energy prices slide
items.lede: Woodside will cut at least 500 jobs, about 10% of its global workforce with around 80% in Australia and mostly in WA, and cut its dividend payout as energy prices slide. Its shares fell as much as 6.6% on the same day oil prices plunged.

figs.label: Structural savings targeted from 2028
figs.value: about US$400m a year (AFR: about A$570m)

figs.label: Dividend policy
figs.value: from 50-80% of underlying profit to 20-40% of adjusted operating cash flow (first 20% guaranteed)

qs.q: Explain how a fall in world energy prices affects Australia's terms of trade.
Discuss the effects of a declining terms of trade on Australian economic growth and employment.

items.guide: A falling terms of trade reduces national income and usually weakens the AUD, but cheaper fuel imports also help households, so the net effect depends on Australia's mix of exports and imports.

terms.def: The ratio of export prices to import prices; it rises when commodity export prices rise.
Liquefied natural gas, one of Australia's largest export earners.

items.title: Cost of living decided the US midterms. Is Labor next?
items.lede: AFR political editor Phillip Coorey argues the Republican defeat was about prices, not ideology, with petrol prices from the Iran war and tariff-driven price rises hurting voters. He says the Albanese government, facing another rate rise, could face a similar backlash in 2028 unless conditions improve.

figs.label: Diesel price cited by Joe Hockey
figs.value: over US$6 a gallon (about A$2.27 a litre)

qs.q: Explain why real wages fall when inflation exceeds nominal wage growth.
Discuss how political pressures can limit governments' ability to fight inflation.

items.guide: Low-income households spend more of their budget on fuel and food, so price shocks are regressive. Pressure for quick fixes may clash with fighting inflation, a political limit on policy.

terms.def: The cost of the goods and services households need; it rises when prices outpace incomes.
Wages adjusted for inflation, which measure actual purchasing power.

items.title: David Jones collapses after 188 years as spending slows
items.lede: Australia's oldest department store has gone into administration after rent talks with Scentre Group, the landlord of 17 of its 38 stores, broke down. All stores keep trading while a sale or recapitalisation is sought, and rival Myer's shares rose 10.9%.

figs.label: Roles Canva is cutting (4 November report)
figs.value: more than 1,200, about a fifth of its workforce

qs.q: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain how higher interest rates can lead to retail business failures.
Assess whether job losses at department stores are mainly cyclical or structural.

items.guide: Weak spending is cyclical, but the long-run shift to online shopping is structural, and the best answers mention both. Five rate rises this year shifted AD left as more household income went to mortgage repayments.

terms.def: An insolvency process where an administrator takes control to try to save or sell the business.
Joblessness caused by a downturn in aggregate demand.

items.title: Home-grown inflation: the RBA says the problem is here, not just overseas
items.lede: The RBA raised the cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November by six votes to three, and Governor Bullock said Australia has a domestic home-grown inflation problem that was visible before oil prices jumped. The Treasurer points to the Middle East war while business, the RBA and AFR columnists point to demand the economy cannot supply and weak productivity.

figs.label: Inflation that is domestic (Business Council analysis of ABS data)
figs.value: 3.0 of 4.3 percentage points (about 70% of the surge)

figs.label: Spending growth now / Business Council wants cut by more than half
Construction pipeline in 2027 / mining boom peak (2012)

qs.q: Distinguish between demand inflation and cost inflation, using the RBA's November decision.
Assess the view that Australia's inflation is mainly home-grown.

items.guide: The label matters because it decides which policy can work. If inflation is mostly imported, the RBA can do little about the cause and risks over-tightening; if it is mostly domestic demand and weak productivity, higher rates and tighter fiscal policy are aimed at the right target, but work with a lag. The test: the Fed, ECB and RBNZ held while Australia hiked.

terms.def: Demand pressing against what the economy can produce.
Expectations of higher inflation that feed into wage and price setting.
Spending that leaves the domestic economy, such as on imports.

items.title: NAB profit falls as bad debts surge and 2,500 jobs go
items.lede: NAB's net profit for the year to September fell 9.1% to $6.14b, short of the $6.45b analysts expected, and its bad and doubtful debts charge rose 86% to $1.55b. A restructure will cut up to 2,500 jobs by mid-2027.

qs.q: Explain why rising bank bad-debt charges may signal a slowing economy.
Outline the role of commercial banks in transmitting a change in the cash rate.

items.guide: Banks raise bad-debt provisions when they expect unemployment and business failures to rise, and tighter bank lending can then amplify a slowdown. Bendigo Bank passed on the RBA's 0.25-point rise to variable home loans the same day.

terms.def: Money a bank sets aside for loans it expects will not be repaid.
How a cash rate change flows through to lending, spending and inflation.

items.title: Data centres could use twice the power of every home in Sydney
items.lede: A NSW parliamentary inquiry warns the $50b of data centres planned in the state could use up to 25,719 GWh a year, about twice the 11,400 GWh used by Greater Sydney's 1.9 million households. It also found nobody knows the true demand because of phantom connection requests.

figs.label: Possible annual use of planned NSW data centres
Greater Sydney households' use (1.9 million households)
Data centres' share of NSW electricity

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain how rapid data-centre growth could affect electricity prices.
Evaluate a requirement for data centres to supply 100% renewable energy.

items.guide: Evaluate the options: regulation (100% renewable supply on an hourly basis, a public register, less diesel backup) versus market-based approaches such as connection charges and carbon pricing, and note the risk of discouraging investment.

terms.def: Speculative grid-connection requests that will never be built and distort forecasts.
Meeting current needs without degrading resources for future generations.

items.title: How the squeeze lands: mortgages, investors, shop floors and tech jobs
items.lede: With the cash rate at 4.85% and average variable mortgage rates at 6.75%, repayments would take 37.4% of a typical household's income, just under the record 37.5% set in December 1989. New housing loan commitments are 27% below their November 2025 peak, with Bullock saying the May tax changes explain the extra drop in investor loans.

Forecast fall in Sydney prices

RBA outlook
figs.value: GDP growth 1.3% by late 2027; real wages fall until at least late 2027; unemployment 5.1% by late 2028

qs.q: Explain how rising interest rates and falling house prices can reduce consumer spending.
Analyse the effects of high inflation and falling real wages on different groups of households.

items.guide: Monetary policy works by shifting AD, and the May changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount amplify the rate rises, so AD falls further than rates alone would cause. HSBC's Paul Bloxham calls the mix a double whammy: the rates and housing part is cyclical, the tax part structural.

terms.def: Spending changes as household wealth, such as house prices, changes.
Deducting investment property losses from other taxable income.
Changes that reverse with the economic cycle compared with persistent changes.

items.title: ACCC steps in to set prices for Armaguard's cash transport
items.lede: The Cash Distribution Framework Act, passed in August, lets the ACCC regulate Armaguard, and talks with its eight biggest customers broke down. The ACCC has set interim prices for the first time, rejecting Armaguard's cost-plus proposal because its costs were not transparent.

figs.label: Increase above CPI for the eight largest customers, until June 2027
Losses Armaguard says it made on big-bank contracts since 2021
Extra funding banks and retailers have already contributed

qs.q: Explain why cash distribution may be a natural monopoly.
Discuss the challenges a regulator faces when setting prices for a monopoly.

items.guide: Price regulation must balance viability (a price too low means the firm exits) against monopoly pricing (too high hurts customers). Mention information asymmetry: the ACCC could not verify Armaguard's costs. Armaguard must keep supplying services and must not favour its own ATM business over rivals.

terms.def: A market where one firm can supply at lower cost than several competitors.
A regulator setting or capping prices where competition cannot.

items.title: Budget versus inflation: when fiscal and monetary policy pull in different directions
items.lede: The RBA is raising rates to cool demand while an estimated $11 billion hole has opened in the federal budget since May, largely because a surge in bond yields pushed up the interest bill. The Treasurer and Finance Minister will not promise net savings in December's mid-year update, and every minister has been told to find savings.

figs.label: Estimated hole in the budget since May

figs.label: Other named contributors
figs.value: Senate carve-outs on capital gains and trust tax, refugee intake and veterans' payment backdowns, a private health rebate compromise, a $680m charity wage subsidy

figs.label: Spending growth now / Business Council target
Federal spending as a share of GDP
Home battery subsidy cost: original / after loophole / after rebate cut

qs.q: Explain how higher interest rates can worsen the federal budget balance.
Evaluate the effectiveness of fiscal policy in reducing inflation in the current context.

items.guide: A deficit is not only a government choice: persistent inflation lifts bond yields and interest costs, widening the hole. Price stability, a smaller deficit and low unemployment cannot all be won at once, and if fiscal policy does not tighten, monetary policy may have to do more and keep rates higher for longer.

terms.def: More saved than spent in a budget update.
A policy whose benefits or costs fall more heavily on lower-income households.
Using policy to smooth the business cycle.

items.title: RBA deputy denies pre-empting the board's rate decision
items.lede: Some external members of the RBA's monetary policy board reportedly felt senior staff's public comments made November's rate rise look decided in advance, but Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser says he was only explaining the data. Market odds of a hike rose from about 20% to 60% after his 21 October speech and to 80% after the 28 October CPI.

figs.label: Market odds of a November hike
figs.value: about 20% to 60% after Hauser's speech, then 80% after the CPI

figs.label: Board vote to raise the cash rate to 4.85%

qs.q: Explain how central bank communication can influence inflation expectations.
Discuss one benefit and one risk of RBA officials commenting publicly before a board meeting.

items.guide: Communication is part of the transmission mechanism, but it creates a tension with board independence. Hauser says he followed the 2023 RBA Review's advice to explain policy publicly and wants the RBA to explain how it would react to new data without promising a path for rates.

terms.def: A central bank signalling the future path of interest rates.
What people expect inflation to be; these feed into wages and prices.

items.title: Productivity inquiry barred from looking at tax and workplace laws
items.lede: The Productivity Commission's interim report on business dynamism focuses on red tape, management and insolvency, but the Treasurer kept tax, industrial relations and mergers out of scope and business groups are angry. Red tape costs business about $160b a year.

figs.label: Annual cost of regulatory compliance to business
Productivity gap between Australian and US management
Firms using an AI tool: Australia / US / UK

qs.q: Explain how reducing regulation could improve productivity.
Using an AD/AS diagram, explain how productivity growth reduces inflationary pressure.

items.guide: Higher productivity raises the economy's speed limit: with LRAS shifted out, output can grow without extra price pressure, so the RBA does not have to hold rates as high. The limitation is that reforms take years to work.

terms.def: How easily firms enter, grow and exit, which drives reallocation and productivity.
Policies that improve efficiency and productivity in particular markets.

items.title: Albanese wants backpacker rules in the UK free trade deal changed to help cut migration
items.lede: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the working holiday arrangements in the Australia-UK Free Trade Agreement should change so that fewer people arrive and net overseas migration falls. British backpackers can currently stay up to three years without doing the specified work, such as regional farm work, that other working holiday makers must do.

Harvest workers who come from overseas
Proposed cap on second-year working holiday visas

qs.q: Assess the economic costs and benefits of including labour-mobility provisions, such as working holiday visas, in a free trade agreement.

items.guide: Migration affects both sides of the economy: it adds to aggregate demand (housing, consumption) and aggregate supply (labour). Cutting it may ease demand pressure but worsen labour shortages in farming, tourism and hospitality.

terms.def: A deal that lowers barriers to trade in goods and services between countries and can also cover the movement of people.
Arrivals minus departures of people staying 12 months or more.
The number of workers willing and able to work at each wage.

items.title: Household spending rose 0.6% in September, but much of it was higher prices rather than more goods
items.lede: ABS data show household spending rose 0.6% in September, led by fuel (+5.4%), transport and health, after a revised -0.1% in August. Capital Economics says nominal spending rose 2.1% over the September quarter but volumes rose only 0.7%, and KPMG notes inflation is above 3% in 45% of the 87 items in the CPI basket.

figs.label: Household spending, monthly
figs.source: ABS Monthly Household Spending Indicator via ABC News

figs.label: Transport and health / recreation and culture

qs.q: Distinguish between nominal and real growth in household spending, using the September quarter figures. Explain why the difference matters for the RBA.

items.guide: Rising nominal spending is not the same as rising living standards, so use real figures when discussing growth. Link fuel prices to cost-push inflation: households pay more at the bowser, so spending rises in dollars while real consumption barely grows.

terms.def: Nominal values are in current dollars; real values remove the effect of price rises and measure volume.
Inflation caused by rising production costs, such as fuel, shifting SRAS left.
Price rises spread across many items rather than a few.

items.title: Job vacancies fall to 325,000, now 31% below their peak, and few businesses blame AI
items.lede: ABS data show job vacancies fell 0.9% in the three months to August 2026 to 325,000, which is 31.2% below the May 2022 peak, with the fall concentrated in the private sector. About 82% of businesses said AI did not affect their vacancies and 4% said it reduced them.

figs.label: Job vacancies
figs.source: ABS Job Vacancies via ABC News

figs.label: Businesses saying AI did not affect vacancies
Businesses saying AI reduced / increased vacancies
Information media and telecommunications citing AI for fewer vacancies

qs.q: Explain why job vacancies are a useful leading indicator of unemployment. Refer to the August 2026 data.

items.guide: Vacancies falling while unemployment rises signals cyclical weakness: higher rates shift labour demand left. The AI survey suggests technology is not yet a major source of structural unemployment.

terms.def: An unfilled job that an employer is actively trying to fill; a leading indicator of unemployment.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs, for example from technological change.
Unemployment caused by a downturn in the economic cycle.

items.title: Analysis: after years of inflation pain, the political debate over the economy needs a reset
items.lede: After the RBA's fifth rate hike of 2026, Labor and the Coalition returned to familiar arguments about who is to blame for inflation. ABC economics reporter Tom Crowley argues both scripts are worn out and that only a bold policy shift may break the cycle.

figs.label: Cash rate after the 3 November hike
Government spending

figs.label: Chalmers' press conferences after RBA decisions

qs.q: Evaluate the claim that fiscal policy is "working against" monetary policy in 2026. Explain one political and one economic limitation on using the Budget to fight inflation.

items.guide: A strong answer weighs both causes: the Government points to supply shocks (the Middle East war and an AI investment boom) while the Opposition says government spending is driving demand. If fiscal policy adds to demand, monetary policy has to work harder.

terms.def: Inflation caused by aggregate demand growing faster than the economy's capacity.
How fiscal and monetary policy work together; if the Budget adds to demand, the RBA may need higher rates.
A constraint on policy because of voter and party pressures.

items.title: RBA raises the cash rate to 4.85%: the factors the Board weighed
items.lede: On 3 November 2026 the RBA's Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, by six votes to three. The Statement on Monetary Policy says inflation is broadly based, capacity pressures are a little tighter than assessed in August, and the inflation outlook has been revised materially higher on fuel and other conflict-related costs.

qs.q: Explain TWO factors that the RBA's Monetary Policy Board considered in deciding to raise the cash rate to 4.85% in November 2026.
Assess the limitations of monetary policy in responding to inflation that is partly caused by higher global energy prices.
Explain how developments in the global economy influenced the RBA's decision to raise the cash rate in November 2026.

items.guide: Use the decision to show how the Board weighs inflation, capacity and expectations against slowing growth, falling house prices and rising unemployment. Monetary policy works on demand and with a lag, so it answers an energy supply shock by slowing the whole economy. The 6–3 vote shows the judgement involved, and the Statement stresses uncertainty about the neutral rate and the NAIRU. Topic 1 link: Australia is a small open economy and a price taker, so world energy prices, partner growth and global interest rates reach domestic inflation and the cash rate; the exchange rate has not added tightening because other central banks also raised rates.

terms.def: The RBA board that sets the cash rate target.
The non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment: the unemployment rate consistent with low and stable inflation.
The difference between actual GDP and potential GDP; a positive gap means demand is running ahead of supply.
The interest rate that neither stimulates nor dampens demand once temporary shocks have passed.

items.title: Rates rise worldwide as government debt piles up
items.lede: An ABC analysis argues investors are demanding higher returns to lend to governments, pushing up interest rates around the world, and that deficits, not just the size of spending, add to inflation. US interest payments on federal debt now exceed US$1 trillion a year and the Bank of England is tipped to raise its rate to 4.0%.

figs.label: US interest payments on federal debt
figs.value: more than US$1 trillion a year

figs.label: Bank of England rate if Thursday's hike goes ahead
Capital raised by data centre operators this year

qs.q: Discuss how rising global interest rates could affect Australia's economy and federal budget.

items.guide: Higher global yields raise borrowing costs for households, firms and governments, shifting AD left and easing the price level but cutting real GDP. Separate the level of spending from the budget balance when judging whether fiscal policy adds to inflation.

terms.def: Government spending exceeds revenue in a year.
Borrowing by a national government, usually through bonds.
The return investors earn on a bond; a higher yield means a higher cost of borrowing.

items.title: House prices fall at the fastest pace in 40 years
items.lede: National home values fell 1.2% in October, the seventh straight monthly fall, and are 6.7% below the March peak, about $63,400 off the median dwelling. Capital cities are down 8.1% in seven months and set to pass the 2017-19 record fall of 8.2%, and AMP now expects a 15% fall.

figs.label: Capital cities, fall over seven months

qs.q: Explain how rising interest rates affect house prices and consumer spending through the wealth effect.

items.guide: Higher rates cut borrowing capacity and investors have pulled back after property tax changes, shifting housing demand left. Falling prices hit recent buyers with small deposits hardest, which matters for wealth distribution as well as spending.

terms.def: Spending changes as household wealth, such as house prices, changes.
The channels through which the cash rate affects spending and inflation.
How net worth is shared across households.

items.title: Banks see slower growth and higher unemployment, but still expect a hike
items.lede: NAB cut its 2027 GDP growth forecast to 1.0% and expects unemployment to reach 5.4% by the end of 2027, while CBA cut growth to about 1% by mid-2027 from 1.8% and raised its unemployment forecast to 5.1% from 4.8%. CBA expects trimmed mean inflation to stay at or above 3.5% until at least mid-2027.

figs.label: CBA trimmed mean forecast
figs.value: 3.5% or more until at least mid-2027

qs.q: Explain why policymakers find it difficult to achieve internal balance when inflation rises while growth slows.

items.guide: Higher fuel and construction costs shift SRAS left, so prices rise while output falls. Raising rates to fight supply-driven inflation deepens the slowdown, a key limitation of monetary policy.

terms.def: High inflation combined with weak growth or rising unemployment.
Sustainable growth with full employment and low, stable inflation.
An underlying inflation measure that removes extreme price changes.

items.title: Inflation pressures persist as factories contract
items.lede: The Melbourne Institute Inflation Gauge rose 0.5% in October (September 0.3%), its fourth straight monthly rise, while the manufacturing PMI fell to 49.6, its second month of contraction. The ABS reported headline CPI of 4.3% and trimmed mean of 3.6% for the year to September.

qs.q: Distinguish between headline and underlying inflation, and explain why the RBA focuses on the trimmed mean.

items.guide: If people expect higher inflation, the short-run Phillips curve shifts out, so inflation rises even as unemployment rises and getting back to 2-3% becomes more costly. This is why the RBA targets underlying inflation and acts early to anchor expectations.

terms.def: The price change of the ABS's full basket of goods and services.
Removes the largest price rises and falls; the RBA's preferred underlying measure.
What people expect inflation to be, which feeds into wages and price-setting.

items.title: Could government spending cuts do the RBA's job?
items.lede: With a fifth rate rise for the year expected, economists and politicians are debating whether the budget should do more of the work of bringing inflation down. Chris Richardson estimates that $7-10 billion a year in spending cuts would have about the same effect as one rate rise.

figs.label: Spending cuts equal to one rate rise (Chris Richardson)
Cash rate before the decision / if the hike is delivered

qs.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of contractionary fiscal policy, compared with monetary policy, in reducing inflation.

items.guide: Evaluate both arms: fiscal policy can be targeted but is slow and political, while monetary policy is flexible but blunt and falls mainly on borrowers. If the budget does more, the RBA may need to do less.

terms.def: Using government spending and taxation to influence the economy.
Settings that reduce aggregate demand.
The combination of fiscal and monetary policy settings.

items.title: Big banks hold about $332 billion that earns savers no interest as rates rise
items.lede: The RBA has raised the cash rate four times this year to 4.60%, but the big four banks lifted their top savings rates by only 0.20-0.25 percentage points and only on products with strict conditions. Savers who miss the conditions earn a base rate of 0.10%, and the four banks hold about $332 billion in deposits that earn no interest.

qs.q: Explain how weak competition in banking can reduce the effectiveness of cash rate rises in curbing spending.
Evaluate whether stronger competition policy in banking could improve both consumer outcomes and the transmission of monetary policy.

items.guide: If banks pass on only small rises, much of the incentive to save is lost and their interest margins widen instead, so transmission is weaker. Stronger competition, easier switching and ACCC scrutiny could make monetary policy work better.

terms.def: How much of a change in the cash rate banks pass on to their savers and borrowers.
The way higher interest rates reward saving and discourage spending.
Laws and regulators (the ACCC) that promote rivalry between firms.
The ability of firms to set prices or conditions without losing customers.

items.title: OPEC+ holds December output targets steady while the Iran war keeps supply tight
items.lede: Seven core OPEC+ members agreed on 1 November to leave December production targets unchanged. The decision makes little difference because war disruptions have already pushed most producers well below their quotas, and the IEA warns of possible oversupply in 2027 if Gulf flows return to normal.

figs.label: Core OPEC+ members in the decision
Other cuts still in place to end-2026

qs.q: Explain why an OPEC+ decision to hold output steady may have little effect on oil prices when members are already producing below quota.
Discuss how a world oil oversupply in 2027 could affect Australia's inflation rate and terms of trade.

items.guide: Quotas only matter when members can produce up to them. With Gulf exports disrupted, the price is set by the physical shock in Hormuz, not OPEC+. If the strait reopens, prices could fall sharply in 2027, easing Australian fuel inflation but lowering LNG export prices.

terms.def: A group of producers that coordinates output to influence price.
A limit on the amount a member may produce.
A sudden change in production costs or capacity.
Supply exceeding demand, which pushes prices down.

items.title: China's factories slow as export orders fall
items.lede: China's official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 in October from 50.1, with new export orders dropping to 48.7 from 50.0, while the private RatingDog PMI held at 52.0. China's trade surplus was about US$800 billion by August, on track to beat 2025's record of US$1.2 trillion.

qs.q: Explain how a slowdown in China's manufacturing sector could affect Australia's terms of trade and current account.

items.guide: If Chinese steel mills cut output, demand for iron ore shifts left, lowering Australia's export prices, terms of trade and national income. Link China's growth to Australia through export revenue, company tax receipts and the AUD. The two PMIs disagree, so avoid overstating one month.

terms.def: A business survey where above 50 means expansion and below 50 means contraction.
Exports exceed imports in value.
Export prices relative to import prices.

items.title: Who should get extra help with health insurance? Age versus need
items.lede: The government has reintroduced a bill to scrap the extra private health insurance rebate for over-65s. New analysis of HILDA 2022 data (not yet peer reviewed) argues a pensioner exemption would mostly protect comfortable part-pensioners and miss struggling younger families.

figs.label: Private health rebate: lowest income tier under 65 / aged 65-69 / aged 70+

qs.q: Explain why income alone may be a misleading measure of economic wellbeing, using evidence about older and younger Australians.

items.guide: Use this to show the difference between income and wealth inequality, and between targeting help by age and by need. The authors favour concessions for low-income people of any age.

terms.def: Treating people with different abilities to pay differently.
Fairness between age groups.
Targeting a payment by income or assets.
Charging everyone the same premium regardless of age or health.

items.title: Inflation at 4.3%: what is driving it, who says what, and what policy can do (six-page special)
items.lede: September's CPI of 4.3% puts the RBA on track for a fifth rate rise on 3 November. The special compares what the Treasurer, RBA officials, the Opposition and commentators say about the causes of inflation, the cost of fighting it, and the roles of monetary policy, fiscal policy and productivity.

figs.label: Trimmed mean
figs.value: 1.0% in the quarter (RBA forecast 0.8%); 3.6% annual (3.7% quarterly measure)

qs.q: Distinguish between headline and underlying inflation, using September 2026 data.
Using an AD/AS diagram, explain how a rise in world oil prices affects inflation and economic growth in Australia.
Using a Phillips curve, explain why rising inflation expectations make it harder to reduce inflation.

items.guide: Do not pick one cause. The strongest answers identify both cost-push and demand-pull pressures, use the trimmed mean to separate them, then explain why the mix matters for choosing a policy. Includes a 20-mark plan: evaluate the effectiveness of Australia's economic policies in managing inflation in 2026.

terms.def: Inflation caused by rising production costs, such as oil.
Inflation caused by spending outrunning the economy's capacity.
The rate of unemployment below which inflation tends to accelerate.
The combination of monetary, fiscal and microeconomic policy in use.

items.title: Wage watchdog recovers a record $453m for underpaid workers
items.lede: The Fair Work Ombudsman recovered about $453 million for more than 181,000 workers in 2025-26, up 27% on the year before, and received a record 31,596 anonymous reports. Large corporates made up nearly half of recoveries, including a Westpac underpayment of more than $50 million affecting about 47,000 staff.
