qs.q: Explain the role of the Fair Work Ombudsman in Australia's industrial relations system.
Discuss how widespread underpayment of wages affects the distribution of income and labour market outcomes.

items.guide: Setting a minimum wage is not enough: enforcement decides whether the floor is real. Weak enforcement lets non-compliant firms undercut compliant rivals and shifts income from workers to employers.

terms.def: The regulator that enforces workplace laws and awards.
The legal minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation.
Government rules and programs that affect wages, conditions and employment.

items.title: Trust tax, housing claims and talk of grocery price caps
items.lede: The ACTU backed the planned 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts, due from 1 July 2028. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said negative gearing and capital gains tax changes will help 75,000 more Australians buy a home, and Ed Husic floated price caps on bread, milk and eggs, which the government resisted in favour of the Grocery Code and ACCC enforcement.

figs.label: Additional home buyers the government says changes will help

qs.q: Explain how a minimum tax on trusts could affect the distribution of income.
Compare price caps with competition policy as ways to reduce grocery prices.

items.guide: A cap below equilibrium creates a shortage, since producers supply less than consumers want. Competition policy aims to lower prices by increasing rivalry without cutting supply. Use the trust tax and the housing claim to discuss equity.

terms.def: A legal maximum price set below the equilibrium price.
Laws and regulators (the ACCC) that promote rivalry between firms.
A tax that takes a higher share from higher incomes.

items.title: Chalmers rules out a new fuel discount and promises budget savings
items.lede: After inflation jumped to 4.3%, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said a new fuel excise discount is unlikely because the budget cannot afford it forever, and flagged savings in the mid-December MYEFO. The Prime Minister ruled out cuts to hospitals and schools, and the Coalition wants a discount funded by spending cuts.

figs.label: Fuel prices
figs.value: +9.4% in September; almost 24% over the year

qs.q: Explain how a fuel excise cut could reduce measured inflation in the short term but work against the RBA over time.
Assess whether a contractionary fiscal stance would support monetary policy in the current economic conditions.

items.guide: A fuel excise cut lowers measured CPI briefly, but households spend the savings elsewhere, shifting AD right and pushing prices up, so fiscal and monetary policy would pull in opposite directions. A contractionary stance supports the RBA.

terms.def: A per-litre tax on fuel.
The Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, which updates the budget.
Whether the budget adds to (expansionary) or subtracts from (contractionary) aggregate demand.

items.title: Small business sales slow as banks debate how tight the labour market is
items.lede: Xero data show small business sales growth slowed to 5.2% a year in the September quarter from 7.3%, and small business wage growth halved to 1.2%. CBA estimates the NAIRU at 4.8%, above the RBA's 4.6%, which would mean unemployment must rise further before inflation returns to target.

qs.q: Define the NAIRU and explain why a higher estimate implies tighter monetary policy.
Explain why monetary policy may affect small businesses and some sectors more than others.

items.guide: The NAIRU cannot be observed, only estimated, and different estimates explain why economists disagree on how much tightening is needed. A higher NAIRU means the RBA must slow the economy further.

terms.def: The lowest unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation.
Non-essential purchases households can delay.
The relationship between inflation and unemployment.

items.title: Inflation at 4.3%: why there is no painless way out
items.lede: An ABC analysis argues the narrow path to a soft landing promised in 2022 has failed, with a Middle East energy shock and an AI-driven investment boom keeping prices high. The RBA is expected to lift the cash rate to 4.85% on Tuesday; spending cuts and tax rises are politically hard and productivity growth is the root fix that no one knows how to engineer.

qs.q: Explain why reducing aggregate demand is described as the most reliable cure for inflation, and identify its costs.
Discuss the role of productivity growth in achieving both low inflation and sustainable growth.

items.guide: Lower demand reduces the price level but also real GDP and jobs, a conflict between price stability and growth. Only a rightward shift of supply (productivity) could lower prices and raise output. Economist Chris Richardson urges governments at least not to add stimulus.

terms.def: Slowing inflation without causing a recession.
Prices rise because spending outpaces the economy's capacity.
Output per unit of input, such as per hour worked.

items.title: Australia-EU free trade deal stalls in Parliament
items.lede: The Prime Minister says the deal makes 98% of Australian exports to the EU tariff-free and would add about $10 billion to the economy, but the Coalition will not support it in its current form, so there is no vote this week. The Nationals want better access for farmers and the Greens are leaning towards support.

figs.label: Australian exports to the EU that would be tariff-free
Beef / sheepmeat access
figs.value: about 8 times / 4 times current levels; review after five years

qs.q: Explain why agricultural market access is often the hardest part of negotiating a free trade agreement.
Assess the likely costs and benefits of the Australia-EU FTA for Australian producers and consumers.

items.guide: The tariff diagram shows who wins and loses from protection: EU farmers and the government gain; consumers and efficient foreign exporters lose. Agricultural quotas also stalled negotiations in 2023.

terms.def: A tax on imports.
A volume that can enter at a low tariff; imports above it pay a much higher rate.
An agreement between two parties to reduce trade barriers.

items.title: One oil shock, three answers: Canada hikes while Europe and New Zealand hold
items.lede: The Bank of Canada raised its rate 25 basis points to 2.50%, its first hike in three years, while the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% and the RBNZ held at 2.75%, surprising markets that expected a hike. The US Fed held its range at 3.75-4% in a 10-2 vote.

figs.label: Bank of Canada rate
figs.value: 2.50% (+25 basis points; first hike in three years)

figs.label: Canada: inflation / petrol / inflation excluding petrol
Canada expects inflation near 3.5% by year-end and growth of

qs.q: Explain why central banks might respond differently to the same rise in world oil prices.
Distinguish between first-round and second-round effects of an oil price shock.

items.guide: Monetary policy cannot fix a supply shock; it can only stop the first-round price rise turning into persistent inflation. Canada judged the inflation risk larger, while the ECB and RBNZ weighted weak growth more heavily.

terms.def: When an initial price shock flows into wage claims and other prices, making inflation persistent.
0.01 percentage points.
An unexpected change in the supply of a key input that shifts costs across the economy.

items.title: Inflation jumps to 4.3% in September, fuelling the prospect of a Cup Day rate rise
items.lede: The ABS reported headline inflation of 4.3% in September, up from 4.0% in August, with underlying inflation at 3.6%. Petrol, home-building costs and tradeable prices drove the rise, and markets put the chance of a fifth RBA rate rise on 3 November at better than 60%.

qs.q: Explain why the RBA might still raise the cash rate when much of the recent rise in headline inflation comes from petrol prices.
Assess the extent to which fiscal policy has contributed to Australia's recent inflation.

items.guide: Much of the jump is a supply shock (oil), which lifts headline inflation without a rise in demand. The RBA's concern is whether it spreads, which is why underlying inflation (above the 2 to 3% target) and the jump in tradeable inflation matter. For fiscal policy, Treasury argued that deficits have come in well below forecast, so changes in the net fiscal position are hard to blame for inflation; the Coalition and some economists argue for spending cuts, so give both views.

terms.def: A measure of inflation that removes the largest price swings to show the trend.
Goods and services that can be traded across borders, so their prices follow world prices; fuel is an example.
Price rises that start with higher prices for imports, such as oil.
Higher production costs passed on as higher prices.

items.title: Why the EU trade deal is about far more than beef
items.lede: Australia and the EU agreed a free trade agreement in March after nearly eight years of talks, but the laws to bring it into force must still pass a divided Senate. Two trade economists argue rejecting it would cost far more than the beef access farmers say is too small.

figs.label: Australian goods exports covered by tariff cuts

figs.label: Value of new trade: industry wanted / deal delivers

qs.q: Evaluate the potential impacts of the Australia-EU free trade agreement on the Australian economy.

items.guide: The authors' wider argument is diversification: Australia is wedged between a protectionist ally (the US) and a coercive customer (China), and the EU deal adds options in trade, investment and critical minerals.

terms.def: An agreement removing tariffs and other barriers between member countries.
A limit on the volume of imports that receive a lower tariff.
Formal approval by a country's legislature so an agreement takes effect.

items.title: Australian dollar climbs as markets bet on an RBA rate rise, reaching a 13-year high against the NZ dollar
items.lede: After the CPI release the Australian dollar rose about 0.3% to around US70.45c, closing near US70.32c, and jumped about 2% to NZ$1.26, its highest since early 2013, after the RBNZ unexpectedly held rates. Australia's 10-year yield of 5.22% is above the US 5.02%.

qs.q: Explain how a widening interest rate differential between Australia and New Zealand affects the value of the Australian dollar and Australia's external sector.

items.guide: Appreciation is part of the RBA's exchange rate channel: it makes imports cheaper, which helps lower inflation, but reduces the competitiveness of exporters such as tourism, education and agriculture.

terms.def: The gap between Australian and overseas interest rates.
A rise in the value of the AUD against another currency.
A rate set by the supply and demand for the currency in the market.

items.title: Inflation jumps to 4.3% as fuel and travel push prices higher
items.lede: Annual CPI inflation rose to 4.3% in September from 4.0% in August. The trimmed mean rose 1.0% in the September quarter, in line with economists' forecasts but above the RBA's August forecast of 0.8%, which strengthens the case for a fifth rate rise on 3 November.

items.guide: As Gross puts it, a rate rise cannot produce more oil, but it can slow spending and make it harder for firms to pass higher costs on. The trimmed mean at 3.6% is still above the 2-3% target, which shows inflation is broad-based.

Inflation caused by rising production costs such as fuel.
Removing regular seasonal swings so data can be compared across periods.

items.title: No recession in sight, but the jobless rate is heading up
items.lede: At Senate estimates RBA officials said none of their indicators point to a recession, but they still expect unemployment, already 4.7%, to keep rising as higher interest rates slow the economy. NAB suggested unemployment may need to reach 5.5%, not 5%, to return inflation to target.

figs.label: Jobless rate NAB says may be needed

qs.q: Explain why the RBA may need unemployment to rise in order to reduce inflation.

items.guide: If the labour market is tighter than thought, the NAIRU is higher than estimated, so unemployment must rise further to bring inflation down. The cost of disinflation falls on workers who lose jobs or hours.

terms.def: The rate of unemployment below which inflation tends to accelerate.
Unused labour and other resources in the economy.

items.title: Markets all but certain of a Melbourne Cup Day rate rise, with all four major banks tipping 4.85%
items.lede: Market pricing for a 25 basis point rise on 3 November rose from about 60% before the CPI to up to 90% after it, and NAB and CBA have switched from expecting a hold to a hike, joining Westpac and ANZ. A rise would be the fifth of 2026 and take the cash rate to its highest level in 18 years.

figs.label: Market odds of a hike
figs.value: about 60% before the CPI, about 79% straight after, near 90% later

qs.q: Explain how an increase in the cash rate is transmitted through the economy to reduce inflation.

items.guide: Monetary policy works with time lags of up to 18 months, so part of earlier rises has not yet fed through: that is the main argument for a hold, while persistent underlying inflation is the main argument for a hike.

terms.def: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which the RBA targets.
The channels through which a change in the cash rate affects spending and inflation.
The delay between a policy change and its full effect.

items.title: Bullock: supply shocks make taming inflation harder
items.lede: RBA Governor Michele Bullock told Senate estimates inflation is far too high and that repeated negative supply shocks worsen the trade-off the bank faces between bringing inflation down and protecting jobs. She said Australia's inflation problem began before the latest energy shock.

figs.label: House prices relative to early 2020
figs.value: about 50% higher, although recently falling in most capitals

qs.q: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain why a negative supply shock creates a policy dilemma for the Reserve Bank.

items.guide: Monetary policy acts on demand, not supply, so it cannot fix the source of a supply shock: a key limitation to discuss in Topic 4 answers.

terms.def: A sudden change in production costs or capacity, such as an oil price rise.
Rising inflation combined with weak growth.
What households and firms expect inflation to be, which affects wage and price setting.

items.title: Missile strike on Saudi refinery keeps oil near US$115
items.lede: Yemen's Houthis claimed a missile hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery, which can process 550,000 barrels a day; Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the strike. Brent crude rose about 1% to US$115.02 a barrel on 28 October and eased to about US$113.90 on Thursday.

qs.q: Draw an AD/AS diagram to show how a sustained rise in world oil prices affects output and the price level in an oil-importing economy.
Explain why a supply shock creates a policy dilemma for central banks.

items.guide: In the short run oil demand is inelastic, so a small fall in quantity brings a big rise in price. For an oil-importing economy the shock shifts SRAS left: higher prices and lower output, leaving central banks with a policy dilemma.

terms.def: An unexpected change in the supply of a key input that shifts costs across the economy.
The extra price traders pay because of the chance of future disruption.
Demand that changes little when the price changes.

items.title: Six everyday items are up more than 40% since the pandemic as the CPI tests the RBA
items.lede: AFR analysis of ABS data finds consumer prices rose 21.5% from December 2021 to June 2026 while nominal wages rose 16.8%, and six CPI items (tobacco, insurance, gas, postal services, eggs, oils and fats) rose more than 40%. Wednesday's September quarter CPI is expected to decide whether the RBA lifts the cash rate to 4.85%.

items.title: China grows 4.5% as exports surge 36.3% despite US tariffs averaging 35%
items.lede: China's real GDP grew 4.5% over the year to the September quarter and September exports jumped 36.3%, even though about nine in ten Chinese exports to the US face tariffs averaging 35.2%. The source does not say where the extra exports went.

items.title: The US moves to extend its port-fee truce with China to 9 January
items.lede: The US Trade Representative has proposed a two-month extension, to 9 January, of the pause on port charges the US and China placed on each other's ships. The proposal is in a notice of 26 October and is not yet final.

qs.q: Explain how port fees on foreign ships act as a form of protection. Outline the likely effects of suspending them on global trade.

items.guide: Port fees work like a tariff on transport, not on the goods themselves, so they raise trade costs for everyone using affected ships, including countries outside the dispute such as Australia.

terms.def: A restriction on trade other than a tariff, such as fees, quotas or regulations.
One country answering another's protection with its own.

items.title: Price gouging? ABS figures point to housing, transport and mining
items.lede: Consumer prices have risen almost 30% since 2020 and company gross operating profits by about the same, but the column argues ABS data do not show widespread gouging: housing and transport drove prices and mining accounts for most of the profit rise.

items.title: The Greens pitch a $26,000 tax-free threshold and a matching welfare boost

items.title: New tax break for startup investors and a refocused R&D incentive

items.title: How big is the multiplier? Australian evidence says it depends on the type of spending and the state of the economy
items.lede: A study by Reynolds and Fisher of Australian data from 1984 to 2019 found government consumption spending has a multiplier of 0.94 after six quarters when unemployment is high, and a negligible effect otherwise. items.title: Injections and withdrawals in the June quarter 2026: investment, government and exports against saving, tax and imports
items.lede: In the June quarter 2026, exports of $173.5 billion exceeded imports of $169.2 billion in volume terms, government consumption rose 0.6% and machinery investment fell 6.6%. On the withdrawal side, households paid $112.3 billion in income tax and saved $12.2 billion.

items.title: The Final Budget Outcome: a $22.3 billion deficit in 2025-26, after surpluses of $22.1 billion and $15.8 billion
items.lede: The Final Budget Outcome released on 28 September 2026 showed an underlying cash deficit of $22.3 billion (0.8% of GDP), $6 billion better than the Budget estimate. In 2023-24 the surplus of $15.8 billion helped hold net debt $280.6 billion below the 2022 projection.

qs.q: Distinguish between a budget deficit and a budget surplus.

Assess the effects of a budget deficit on the economy.

items.guide: Contrast the surplus years with the deficit: a surplus reduces borrowing and eases inflation pressure, a deficit adds demand. The official statements do not say the surplus was spent on anything specific.

terms.def: The main budget measure: cash receipts minus cash payments, excluding net investment in financial assets for policy purposes.

Gross debt less financial assets held.

items.title: Who is affected by unemployment: youth rate 11.1%, teenagers 15.9% and almost one in four unemployed out of work for a year
items.lede: The ABS shows an unemployment rate of 4.72% in September 2026 but 11.12% for ages 15 to 24 and 15.92% for ages 15 to 19. Long-term unemployed (one year or more) were 167,700 people, 22.9% of the unemployed.

qs.q: Identify the group with the highest unemployment rate.
Outline TWO costs of long-term unemployment.
Explain why youth unemployment is higher than the average.

items.guide: Name the groups and give a figure for each; link youth rates to casual work and lack of experience, and long duration to structural unemployment and lost skills.

terms.def: Being unemployed for 52 weeks or more.
The labour force as a percentage of the civilian population aged 15 and over.

items.title: Beyond GDP: Australia ranks 7th on the HDI, while the richest 10% own 75% of world wealth
items.lede: The 2025 Human Development Report puts Australia 7th with an HDI of 0.958, behind Iceland and Norway, and South Sudan last at 0.388. The World Inequality Report 2026 found the richest 10% hold 75% of global wealth and the poorest half hold 2%.

items.title: The international business cycle: IMF sees 3.1% world growth in 2026 but inflation at 4.7%
items.lede: The IMF's October 2026 outlook projects world growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, with global inflation of 4.7% this year. items.lede: The Australian dollar closed the week on 23 October at US70.08c. The RBA raised the cash rate to 4.60% on 29 September without mentioning the exchange rate, and its explainer says it can intervene only if the market becomes disorderly; it last did so in 2007-08.

items.title: Vegetable supplier admits price-fixing at Aldi, with a $12 million penalty proposed
items.lede: Perfection Fresh, Australia's second-largest vegetable company, admitted 11 instances of cartel conduct on broccoli, cauliflower and lettuce supplied to Aldi in 2019-20. The ACCC and the company propose a $12 million penalty, which the Federal Court must still approve.

figs.label: Period covered by the wider ACCC case

Laws and agencies (the ACCC) that keep markets competitive and protect consumers.
The loss of benefits from trades that no longer happen because the price is above the competitive level.

items.title: Coalition proposes $31 billion in spending cuts as the fiscal policy debate heats up
items.lede: The Opposition released PBO costings for $31.3 billion of savings over four years to fund a $9.7 billion plan to index income tax brackets and scrap the $250 workers' tax offset. It argues government spending is keeping interest rates high, which the Treasurer rejects.

Joblessness caused by a mismatch of skills as technology and industries change.

The shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy and storage.
What else the money spent on a project could have funded.

items.title: Chalmers flags weaker growth and higher unemployment ahead of the mid-year update
items.lede: Treasurer Jim Chalmers says December's mid-year budget update (MYEFO) will show softer growth and slightly higher unemployment as higher interest rates and inflation take their toll. The Opposition highlighted an RBA letter confirming that lower government spending would reduce inflation pressure.

figs.label: Business investment growth this year, Treasurer's estimate
Extra business investment over three years

qs.q: Discuss whether fiscal policy should be tightened to support the RBA's efforts to reduce inflation.

items.guide: Even with no new decisions, slower growth weakens the budget automatically, so the underlying fiscal stance becomes more expansionary.

terms.def: The Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, which updates the May Budget.
Whether the budget is adding to or subtracting from demand.
Tax and welfare flows that move with the cycle automatically.

items.title: Snowy 2.0 is now expected to cost up to $25 billion: a warning for other megaprojects
items.lede: An official report confirmed Snowy 2.0 could cost up to $25 billion, more than 12 times the original $2 billion estimate, and will not be finished until late 2029. Dominic Ahiaga-Dagbui (Deakin University) argues both major parties have approved projects before understanding their costs and calls for an independent authority to validate estimates.

qs.q: Explain how cost overruns on large public projects can be an example of government failure.
Outline why an independent cost-benefit analysis may improve decisions about public infrastructure.

items.guide: Government spending and resource allocation: a project can be strategically necessary yet badly managed. Use it for government failure, transparency and the case for independent appraisal, alongside the 23 Oct renewables record on the energy-transition side.

terms.def: A comparison of the full costs and benefits of a project to decide whether it is worth doing.
When the final cost of a project exceeds its original estimate.
When government intervention produces a worse outcome than intended, such as poor planning or wasted resources.
Storing energy by pumping water to a higher dam and releasing it to generate electricity when demand is high.

items.title: RBA deputy warns the inflation outlook is 'materially worse'
items.lede: RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser says inflation is tracking materially worse than forecast, lifting the odds of a fifth rate rise on 3 November. RBA business contacts show a growing share of firms now see 3–3.5% inflation as normal, which he called a central banker's nightmare.

figs.label: Market odds of a rise to 4.85% on 3 November
Inflation rate some firms now see as normal
figs.source: RBA business contacts via ABC News

qs.q: Explain why the RBA is concerned about rising inflation expectations and how monetary policy can respond.

items.guide: The RBA may raise rates even as unemployment rises, to anchor expectations before they become self-fulfilling.

terms.def: What households and firms think inflation will be; they shape wages and prices.
How a change in the cash rate flows through to spending and prices.
Policy that slows aggregate demand.

items.title: Canada spends billions to shield steel and autos from US tariffs
items.lede: On 21 October Canada's Prime Minister and Ontario's Premier announced a package of roughly C$9 billion to support steel and auto firms hit by 50% US tariffs. It follows US tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, failed talks and dollar-for-dollar Canadian retaliation.

figs.label: US tariff on Canadian goods (about US$20b of trade)
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US goods
Fall in Canadian auto exports to the US
Fall in US exports to Canada

qs.q: Using a diagram, explain the effect of a tariff on domestic producers, consumers and government revenue in the importing country.
Explain why the costs of the US–Canada trade war fall more heavily on Canada than on the US.
Assess the effectiveness of industry subsidies as a response to a trading partner's tariffs.

items.guide: Use the first diagram for the effect of a tariff on producers, consumers and government revenue, the second for the cost and benefit of subsidies, and the 'Who bears the cost?' section to show that the costs of a trade war are uneven.

terms.def: Policies such as tariffs, quotas and subsidies that shield domestic producers from foreign competition.
A tax on imports that raises their domestic price.
Counter-tariffs imposed by a targeted country in response to another country's tariffs.
The loss of total welfare when a tariff causes inefficient production and reduced consumption.

items.title: Unemployment hits a five-year high as big employers cut jobs
items.lede: Australia's unemployment rate rose to 4.7% in September, its highest in nearly five years. NAB plans to cut up to 2,500 jobs and BHP has confirmed cuts at its WA iron ore operations, and economists warn the risk of recession is rising.

figs.label: Forecast unemployment rate, former NAB chief economist
figs.value: 4.8% by early 2027 (5% if rates rise again)

qs.q: Explain the relationship between inflation and unemployment, with reference to the Phillips curve.

items.guide: The RBA is aiming for a soft landing; the risk is a loop of job cuts, weaker spending and more job cuts.

terms.def: Joblessness caused by weak demand in a downturn.
The unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation.
The short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

items.title: The Economy This Week, 20 October 2026
outlets: The Economy This Week (HSC Economics digest)
items.lede: Oil is above US$111, China grew 4.5 per cent on exports, NAB is cutting 2,500 jobs and petrol has passed 240 cents a litre. The RBA, which has raised the cash rate four times this year to 4.60 per cent, meets on 3 November.

figs.label: China GDP growth, year to September quarter

qs.q: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain how a rise in global oil prices affects inflation and growth in an oil-importing economy.
Evaluate how effective monetary policy can be in reducing inflation caused by rising global oil prices.

items.guide: A single exam-ready stagflation case: a supply shock lifts prices and cuts growth, which makes the RBA's inflation and unemployment objectives conflict.

terms.def: High inflation and weak or falling growth at the same time.
An index of export prices divided by import prices.
The chain of effects through which a change in the cash rate affects demand and inflation.

items.title: Card surcharge ban saves consumers $1.6 billion a year, but could push more trade into cash
items.lede: Surcharges on card payments were banned from 1 October. Md Akhtaruzzaman (Australian Catholic University) says consumers are forecast to save $1.6 billion a year, but businesses still pay card processing fees and some now offer cash discounts, which could widen the shadow economy and tax evasion.

figs.label: Forecast consumer saving from the surcharge ban
Annual tax gap from undeclared income
Net GST collected from cafes, restaurants and takeaway

Explain how a rise in cash transactions could affect government revenue.

terms.def: An extra fee a business adds to the price when a customer pays by card.
Economic activity that is not reported or taxed.
Illegally avoiding tax, such as by under-reporting sales.
A side effect of a policy that its designers did not aim for.

items.title: RBA's Kent asks whether interest rates are high enough
items.lede: RBA Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said monetary policy is working broadly as expected but questioned whether it is 'restrictive enough'. He said the neutral interest rate appears to be rising, so a 4.60% cash rate may slow the economy less than it would have in the past.

figs.label: RBA cash rate
figs.asAt: after 29 Sept 2026 (fourth rise this year; highest in about 15 years)

qs.q: Define the 'neutral' interest rate.
Explain why a rise in the neutral interest rate makes it harder for the RBA to set monetary policy.
Explain TWO channels through which higher interest rates reduce inflation.
Assess whether the RBA should raise the cash rate again in November 2026.

items.guide: Kent supplies the evidence that channels work (housing, wealth, exchange rate) and the limitations: uncertainty about the neutral rate, long lags, and supply shocks rates cannot fix.

terms.def: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, set by the RBA as its policy target.
The cash rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy.
A cash rate above neutral, designed to slow demand and reduce inflation.
The ways a change in the cash rate affects spending, output and inflation.

items.title: Oil hits US$110 as Hormuz crisis drags on, then eases
items.lede: Brent crude reached about US$110 a barrel on 16 October, its highest since May, as fighting kept the Strait of Hormuz partly closed. It fell to about US$107 after the US waived threatened tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. Australian diesel is up more than a dollar a litre since February.

figs.label: Rise in Brent crude since the start of 2026

Average petrol price, five largest cities

Assess whether the oil price shock is likely to have a net positive or negative effect on Australia's economy.

items.guide: Draw the SRAS shift and explain cost-push inflation and stagflation risk, then balance it: higher coal and LNG prices lift export income and the terms of trade.

terms.def: The main international benchmark price for oil, measured in US dollars a barrel.
Inflation caused by rising production costs, such as fuel or wages.
Rising inflation combined with slowing growth or rising unemployment.
A group of oil-producing countries that coordinates output to influence prices.

items.title: Grattan Institute calls for a 15% GST; Labor rules it out
items.lede: The Grattan Institute's report 'Budget reboot' proposes raising the GST from 10% to 15% and applying it to all food, raising about $76 billion a year. Most of the money would fund income tax cuts and higher welfare payments, with the rest going to the states. The federal government says a GST increase is not on its agenda.

figs.label: Proposed GST rate (extended to all food)
Extra revenue from Grattan's GST proposal
Use of the $76b: tax cuts / welfare and rent / states
Tax collected as a share of GDP

Explain how the Grattan proposal attempts to offset the regressive effects of a higher GST.
Evaluate the economic and political arguments for and against raising the GST in Australia.

items.guide: Use the plan to discuss allocation, distribution and stabilisation together, with the limitations: political constraints, the WA GST deal and federal–state relations.

terms.def: A tax on most goods and services, collected federally and paid to the states.
A tax that takes a larger share of income from low-income earners than from high-income earners.
A tax whose average rate rises as income rises.
The balance between different types of tax, such as income, consumption and property taxes.

items.title: Fuel costs push inflation and the 'misery index' higher
items.lede: ACCC data show petrol averaged 241.9c and diesel 278.5c a litre in the five largest cities on 14 October. Fuel was a major reason headline inflation rose to 4.0% in August, and the 'misery index' that adds inflation and unemployment is at its highest since 2023. The September quarter CPI is due on 28 October.

figs.label: Headline CPI inflation, year to August
Trimmed mean inflation, year to August
Automotive fuel prices in the CPI
Average petrol price, five largest cities

qs.q: Distinguish between headline inflation and underlying (trimmed mean) inflation.

Explain how rising fuel prices can affect the distribution of income.
Evaluate the effectiveness of monetary policy in responding to inflation caused by a global oil price shock.

items.guide: Cost-push from energy, plus a policy cause (the end of fuel excise relief on 3 August); fuel takes a larger share of spending for low-income and regional households.

terms.def: A measure of the change in prices of a basket of goods and services bought by households.
The change in the whole CPI, including volatile items such as fuel.
An underlying inflation measure that removes the largest price rises and falls each period.
A federal tax charged per litre of fuel.

items.title: China's growth beats forecasts, but investment slump deepens
items.lede: China's economy grew 4.5% over the year to the September quarter, faster than forecast, carried by factories, high-tech exports and electric vehicles. Property investment fell 20.6%, households are spending little, and the EU plans to cap Chinese hybrid imports from 2027.

figs.label: China GDP growth, year to Sept quarter 2026

China consumer prices, year on year

qs.q: Outline what is meant by a 'balance-sheet recession'.

Explain how a slowdown in Chinese property construction could affect Australia's terms of trade and exchange rate.
Assess the extent to which Australia's economy depends on China's economic performance.

items.guide: Use China's falling property investment to explain weaker demand for Australian iron ore, then link to the terms of trade, export income, the current account and the AUD.

terms.def: A downturn in which firms and households cut spending to repay debt, even when interest rates are low.
Spending on buildings, infrastructure and equipment; a key driver of China's demand for steel.
Export prices divided by import prices; it rises when prices for Australia's commodities rise.
Policies such as tariffs or quotas that restrict imports to protect domestic industry.

items.title: Grattan researchers say a higher, broader GST would repair state budgets and fund income tax cuts
items.lede: Matthew Bowes and Erin-Lea Brown of the Grattan Institute argue the GST no longer delivers what it was designed to for the states. Their package lifts the rate from 10% to 15% and covers all food, raising about $76 billion a year, with $33 billion for income tax cuts and $25 billion for welfare increases.

figs.label: Use of the revenue: income tax cuts / welfare
GST share of total tax revenue

GST revenue received by the states, share of the economy

items.guide: An argument for broadening the tax base while compensating low-income households: test it on equity, efficiency and political feasibility. Pair it with the 19 Oct Grattan record, which carries the government response.

terms.def: A broad tax on consumption, collected by the federal government and passed to the states.
The things a tax applies to; a broader base taxes more of spending, income or wealth.
A tax that takes a larger share of income from low-income earners than from high-income earners.
The gap between the revenue the states raise themselves and the spending they are responsible for, filled by federal transfers.

items.title: IMF and World Bank meetings close amid war, debt and AI worries
items.lede: The IMF's World Economic Outlook lifts 2026 world growth to 3.1% but warns that growth is narrow, inflation is rising again because of the Strait of Hormuz energy shock, and debt is a growing danger for poorer countries. A new debt framework for low-income countries was released and G20 members disagreed over China's trade surplus.

figs.label: Low-income countries' debt service, share of revenue

Explain how a global oil supply shock can lead to both higher inflation and lower economic growth.
Discuss the effectiveness of international organisations in addressing debt problems in low-income countries.

items.guide: Surveillance (the forecast and its risk warnings), development (the debt framework) and the limits of co-operation (growth in only 32 economies, G20 splits) give both sides of an 'evaluate' answer.

terms.def: The IMF's twice-yearly report on global growth and inflation forecasts.
Interest and principal repayments a government must make on its debt each year.
When payments to the rest of the world for goods, services and income exceed receipts.
A forum of 19 countries plus the EU and the African Union that coordinates global economic policy.

items.title: Rich-country borrowing squeezes the developing world
items.lede: The IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok ended with a warning but no new plan. Debt repayments now take about 14% of low-income countries' government revenue while official aid falls to its lowest level since 2014.

terms.def: Interest and principal repayments a government must make on its debt each year.
The return on a government bond; it rises when investors demand more to lend.
Government aid given to developing countries to promote economic development.
The difference in living standards and economic development between advanced and developing economies.

items.title: Housing slowdown deepens as new home sales slump 17.5%
items.lede: New home sales by large builders fell 17.5% in the September quarter to their lowest in 18 months, and home prices have now fallen for six months in a row. Higher interest rates and the Budget's changes to investor tax concessions are reducing demand, while auctions are at their weakest run since 2011.

items.guide: Show the transmission mechanism working (prices −5.2%, sales −17.5%), then give the limitation: less construction deepens the housing shortage, so long-run affordability needs supply reform.

People spend less when the value of their assets, such as homes, falls.
Deducting losses on an investment property from other income to reduce tax.
The share of homes taken to auction that sell; a gauge of housing demand.

items.title: Government introduces a minimum 30% tax on discretionary trust income
items.lede: The government introduced legislation this week for a minimum 30% tax rate on income from discretionary trusts, first announced in the May budget. Robert Whait (Adelaide University) and Connie Vitale (Western Sydney University) explain why trusts are used, who benefits, and how families could restructure to avoid the new rules.

The principle that people in similar circumstances should pay similar amounts of tax.

items.title: Coal mine methane: the emissions at home we are undercounting
items.lede: A Grattan Institute analyst argues methane from Australian coal mines, about 5% of national emissions, is badly measured: aircraft found open-cut mines released about 3.6 times what they reported. Because every mine moves to the same Safeguard target, low-reporting open-cut mines earned about 700,000 credits (around $26 million) in 2024-25.

items.guide: Market-based environmental policy only works if emissions are measured accurately and baselines are set sensibly. If methane is undercounted, polluters also avoid paying the full external cost.

terms.def: A federal baseline-and-credit scheme that sets a falling yearly emissions limit for big emitters; those that beat it earn credits and those that exceed it must buy them.
A cost imposed on third parties that the producer does not pay.
Emissions released when a product, such as exported coal, is burned elsewhere.

items.title: Unemployment at five-year high of 4.7% as jobs fall
items.lede: The ABS Labour Force survey showed employment fell by 39,300 in September against forecasts of a 20,000 rise. Unemployment was 4.7%, the highest since the pandemic, and the weaker data cut expectations of another RBA rate rise.

Evaluate the economic and social costs of rising unemployment in Australia.

The labour force as a percentage of the working-age population (aged 15+).
Employed people who want, and are available for, more hours of work.
Unemployment caused by a downturn in aggregate demand.

items.title: Property prices are 5.2% below their March peak: how far could the downturn go?
items.lede: National property values were 5.2% lower in September than at their March peak, the sixth straight monthly fall. items.title: Australia must double down to meet our climate targets: a fossil fuel phase-out pathway
items.lede: Bill Hare of Climate Analytics argues a Paris-aligned pathway needs net emissions 55% below 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050, while current policies will barely meet the 43% target. items.title: Australian economy data dashboard for Year 11, September 2026

items.title: When petrol prices rise, do petrol thefts follow? BOCSAR Bulletin 280 summary

items.q: The Reserve Bank cuts the cash rate by half a percentage point, and households and firms borrow and spend more. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect on the economy.
items.ans: Lower interest rates raise consumption and investment, which are components of aggregate demand, so AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level rises from P1 to P2.

items.q: The Federal Government cuts its spending and raises taxes to return the budget to surplus. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect on the economy.
items.ans: Government spending is a component of AD and higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, so AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2 (in practice, inflation slows). This is contractionary fiscal policy.

items.q: Conflict in the Middle East closes a major shipping route and the world price of oil rises sharply. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect on the Australian economy.
items.ans: Higher fuel and energy costs raise production costs across the economy, so aggregate supply shifts left from AS1 to AS2. The price level rises from P1 to P2 while real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2: cost-push (and imported) inflation together with slower growth, or stagflation.

items.q: Microeconomic reform raises labour productivity and lowers firms' unit costs. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect.
items.ans: Lower unit costs mean firms will supply more at each price level, so AS shifts right from AS1 to AS2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2: growth without inflationary pressure.

items.q: A recession in China cuts its demand for Australian iron ore and coal. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect on the Australian economy.
items.ans: Exports are a component of AD, so lower export demand shifts AD left from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2. The international business cycle is transmitted to Australia through trade.

items.q: Consumer confidence jumps after a run of good economic news, and households spend more of their income. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the effect.
items.ans: Consumption is the largest component of AD, so AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level rises from P1 to P2.

items.q: Wages rise much faster than labour productivity across the economy. On the diagram, show the effect on the price level and real GDP.
items.ans: Unit labour costs rise, so firms supply less at each price level and AS shifts left from AS1 to AS2. The price level rises from P1 to P2 and real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2: cost-push inflation.

items.q: The Australian dollar depreciates by 15 per cent against the currencies of Australia's trading partners. Draw an AD–AS diagram to show the main effect on the Australian economy.
items.ans: Australian exports become cheaper overseas and imports dearer, so net exports rise and AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level rises from P1 to P2. A strong answer also notes that dearer imported inputs push AS left a little (imported inflation), which adds to the rise in prices.

items.q: The Reserve Bank raises the cash rate to bring inflation back to its 2–3 per cent target. On the diagram, show the effect of higher interest rates.
items.ans: Higher interest rates reduce consumption and investment, so AD shifts left from AD1 to AD2. The price level falls from P1 to P2 (inflation slows) and real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2, which is the trade-off of tighter monetary policy.

items.q: The world price of oil falls by a third, cutting transport and energy costs. On the diagram, show the effect on the Australian economy.
items.ans: Lower input costs let firms supply more at each price level, so AS shifts right from AS1 to AS2. The price level falls from P1 to P2 and real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2.

items.q: Investment in education, training and new technology increases the economy's productive capacity. Draw an AD–LRAS diagram to show the effect.
items.ans: Higher productivity and more skilled labour raise potential output, so LRAS shifts right from LRAS1 to LRAS2. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and the price level falls from P1 to P2, so the economy can grow faster without adding to inflation.

items.q: A housing boom and strong government spending push aggregate demand beyond the economy's productive capacity. Draw a diagram with LRAS to show why this causes inflation.
items.ans: AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 along SRAS. Because the economy is already near capacity (LRAS), most of the extra demand raises the price level from P1 to P2, with only a small rise in real GDP from Y1 to Y2: demand-pull inflation. Name the upward-sloping curve SRAS because LRAS is also on the diagram.

items.q: The world price of iron ore rises by 30 per cent. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian dollars to show the effect on the exchange rate.
items.ans: Overseas buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for the same exports, so the demand for A$ shifts right from D1 to D2. The exchange rate rises from e1 to e2 (an appreciation) and the quantity of A$ traded rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Central banks overseas raise interest rates while the Reserve Bank keeps the cash rate unchanged. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian dollars to show the effect.
items.ans: The interest rate differential narrows, so Australian assets offer a smaller relative return and foreign investors buy fewer A$. Demand for A$ shifts left from D1 to D2, the exchange rate falls from e1 to e2 (a depreciation) and the quantity traded falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Australian superannuation funds move more of their money into overseas shares. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian dollars to show the effect.
items.ans: The funds sell Australian dollars to buy foreign currency (a capital outflow), so the supply of A$ shifts right from S1 to S2. The exchange rate falls from e1 to e2 (a depreciation) and the quantity traded rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Far fewer international students enrol at Australian universities. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian dollars to show the effect.
items.ans: Education for overseas students is an export of services, paid for in Australian dollars. Fewer students means less demand for A$, so demand shifts left from D1 to D2 and the exchange rate falls from e1 to e2 (a depreciation).

items.q: Australian households cut their spending on imported goods and overseas holidays. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian dollars to show the effect.
items.ans: Fewer Australian dollars are sold to buy foreign currency, so the supply of A$ shifts left from S1 to S2. The exchange rate rises from e1 to e2 (an appreciation) and the quantity traded falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: The Reserve Bank raises the cash rate while rates overseas stay the same, and foreign investors buy more Australian government bonds. On the diagram, show the effect on the exchange rate.
items.ans: A wider interest rate differential attracts capital inflow, so demand for A$ shifts right from D1 to D2. The exchange rate rises from e1 to e2 (an appreciation). This is the exchange rate channel of monetary policy: the appreciation also slows inflation by making imports cheaper.

items.q: Speculators expect the Australian dollar to fall and sell it now. On the diagram, show the effect.
items.ans: Selling ahead of an expected fall increases the supply of A$, so supply shifts right from S1 to S2 and the exchange rate falls from e1 to e2. The expectation is self-fulfilling: the dollar depreciates.

items.q: A global downturn reduces world demand for Australia's commodity exports. On the diagram, show the effect on the Australian dollar.
items.ans: Lower export volumes and prices mean overseas buyers need fewer A$, so demand shifts left from D1 to D2 and the exchange rate falls from e1 to e2. The depreciation cushions the downturn by making Australian exports cheaper.

items.q: The economy falls into recession and firms cut production. Draw a diagram of the labour market to show the effect.
items.ans: The demand for labour is derived from the demand for goods and services, so it shifts left from D1 to D2. Employment falls from Q1 to Q2 and the wage rate falls from W1 to W2 (in practice wages are sticky, so more of the adjustment shows up as cyclical unemployment).

items.q: Net overseas migration of working-age people rises. Draw a diagram of the labour market to show the effect.
items.ans: More people are available to work at each wage, so the supply of labour shifts right from S1 to S2. Employment rises from Q1 to Q2 and the wage rate falls from W1 to W2 (or grows more slowly).

items.q: Strong economic growth lifts the demand for goods and services. On the diagram, show the effect on the labour market.
items.ans: Firms need more workers to produce more output, so the demand for labour shifts right from D1 to D2. Employment rises from Q1 to Q2 and the wage rate rises from W1 to W2.

items.q: A large share of the workforce reaches retirement age and leaves the labour force. Draw a diagram of the labour market to show the effect.
items.ans: The supply of labour shifts left from S1 to S2 as the participation rate falls. The wage rate rises from W1 to W2 and employment falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: The minimum wage for unskilled workers is set above the wage the market would set. Draw a diagram of the market for unskilled labour to show the effect.
items.ans: At the minimum wage (Wmin) the quantity of labour supplied (Qs) is greater than the quantity demanded (Qd), so the gap between Qd and Qs is unemployment. Employment falls from Qe to Qd. In practice the effect depends on how far the minimum wage sits above the market wage and on productivity.

items.dia: sd D left good=Australian wine in China
items.q: China places anti-dumping duties of up to 218 per cent on Australian wine. Draw a diagram of the market for Australian wine sold in China to show the effect.
items.ans: The tariff raises the price Chinese buyers pay, so demand for Australian wine in China shifts left from D1 to D2. The price falls from P1 to P2 and the quantity sold falls from Q1 to Q2. Australian wine exports to China fell from about $1.3 billion to under $1 million by 2023 before the duties were removed in March 2024.

items.q: A state government speeds up planning approvals so more new homes can be built. Draw a diagram of the market for new housing to show the effect.
items.ans: Faster approvals lower costs and delays for builders, so supply shifts right from S1 to S2. The price falls from P1 to P2 and the quantity of new homes rises from Q1 to Q2: a microeconomic policy acting on one product market.

items.q: A state government caps rents below the market rent. Draw a diagram of the rental housing market to show the effect.
items.ans: At the maximum rent (Pmax) the quantity demanded (Qd) is greater than the quantity supplied (Qs), so there is a shortage between Qs and Qd. Fewer homes are offered for rent than at the market rent (Qe), even though renters who find a home pay less.

items.q: The government imposes a tariff on imported steel. Draw a diagram of the domestic steel market to show the effects of the tariff.
items.ans: The domestic price rises from the world price Pw to Pw+t. Domestic production rises from Q1 to Q2 and consumption falls from Q4 to Q3, so imports fall from Q1–Q4 to Q2–Q3. The government collects revenue (the shaded rectangle), producers gain surplus, consumers lose surplus, and the two shaded triangles are deadweight losses.

items.q: The government limits imports of cheese with a quota. Draw a diagram of the domestic cheese market to show the effects of the quota.
items.ans: With imports limited to the quota, the domestic price rises from Pw to P1 until the gap between domestic demand (Q3) and domestic supply (Q2) equals the quota. Domestic production rises from Q1 to Q2 and consumption falls from Q4 to Q3. Unlike a tariff, the government collects no revenue: the importers keep the extra revenue from the higher price (the shaded rectangle). The two triangles are deadweight losses.

items.q: The government pays local makers of solar panels a subsidy for each panel produced. Draw a diagram of the domestic solar panel market to show the effects.
items.ans: The subsidy lowers producers' costs, so domestic supply shifts right from S1 to S2. Consumers still pay the world price Pw, so consumption (Q3) does not change. Domestic production rises from Q1 to Q2 and imports fall. Producers receive Pw+s; the shaded areas show the producer surplus gain and the deadweight loss, and the government pays the subsidy on every unit produced (Q2).

items.q: Coal-fired power stations emit carbon dioxide and no policy makes them pay for the damage. Draw a diagram to show why the market produces too much electricity.
items.ans: Producers base supply on their private costs (MPC), but the social cost (MSC) is higher by the external cost. The market produces Q_m where demand meets MPC, more than the socially efficient Qs where demand meets MSC, and the price is too low. The shaded triangle is the deadweight loss: market failure.

items.q: The government puts a price on carbon equal to the external cost of each unit of electricity. On the diagram, show the effect.
items.ans: The carbon price makes producers pay the full social cost, so supply shifts up from MPC to MSC. Output falls from Q_m to the socially efficient Qs and the price rises from P_m to Ps: the externality is internalised and the deadweight loss disappears.

items.q: The government makes income tax more progressive and raises income support payments. Draw a Lorenz curve diagram to show the effect on the distribution of income.
items.ans: Higher earners pay a larger share of their income in tax and low-income households receive more in transfers, so disposable income is spread more evenly. The Lorenz curve moves towards the line of equality, from L1 to L2, and the Gini coefficient falls.

items.q: Share and property prices boom while wages grow slowly. Draw a Lorenz curve diagram to show the effect on the distribution of wealth.
items.ans: Assets are owned mostly by the highest quintiles, so their wealth grows fastest. The Lorenz curve moves further from the line of equality, from L1 to L2, and the Gini coefficient for wealth rises.

items.q: Unemployment rises sharply in a recession. On the diagram, show the likely effect on the distribution of income.
items.ans: Job losses fall mainly on lower-income households, whose market income falls, so income becomes less equal. The Lorenz curve moves away from the line of equality, from L1 to L2, and the Gini coefficient rises (transfer payments such as JobSeeker offset part of the change).

items.q: Expansionary policy pushes unemployment below the NAIRU. Draw a Phillips curve diagram to show the short-run effect.
items.ans: The economy moves up along the short-run Phillips curve from A to B: unemployment falls from U1 to U2 and inflation rises from π1 to π2. This shows the conflict between the objectives of full employment and price stability.

items.q: After several years of high inflation, workers and firms expect prices to keep rising. Draw a Phillips curve diagram to show the effect of higher inflationary expectations.
items.ans: Higher expectations are built into wage claims and price setting, so the Phillips curve shifts right (up) from PC1 to PC2. Each unemployment rate now comes with higher inflation; the economy may move from A to B with both inflation and unemployment higher. This is why central banks act early to keep expectations anchored.

items.q: New technology and investment in capital raise the economy's productive capacity. Draw a production possibility frontier to show the effect.
items.ans: The economy can now produce more of both capital goods and consumer goods, so the PPF shifts outward from PPF1 to PPF2: long-run economic growth.

items.q: A recession leaves many workers and machines idle. Draw a production possibility frontier to show where the economy is producing.
items.ans: The economy produces at a point inside the frontier, such as A, because resources are unemployed. Output could rise without giving up anything else: the cost of unemployment is the output lost.

items.q: Evaluate the impact of globalisation on economic growth and development in emerging and developing economies.
pts: Defines globalisation, growth and development, and treats emerging and developing economies separately
Trade and foreign investment: export-led growth, technology transfer and jobs, with evidence (e.g. China, India, Vietnam)
Development: poverty reduction and HDI gains, but uneven distribution and rising inequality within countries
Costs: volatile capital flows, commodity dependence, environmental damage, exposure to the international business cycle
A sustained judgement: large benefits for emerging economies; smaller and less certain gains for many developing economies
plan: Judgement: globalisation has driven growth in emerging economies but its benefits for developing economies are uneven
Trade and TNCs as engines of growth (evidence and a diagram such as a PPF shift)
Development outcomes: poverty, HDI, inequality within countries

Effects on the protecting economy: higher prices, inefficient resource allocation, retaliation
Global effects: lower world trade and growth, trade diversion, retaliation and trade wars (e.g. US tariffs from 2025)
Effects on developing economies and on third countries such as Australia
Links throughout to efficiency and living standards

Tariff diagram and its effects on one economy

Effects on foreign liabilities, the exchange rate and external stability

items.q: Discuss the effects of fluctuations in the value of the Australian dollar on the Australian economy.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how a rise in the cash rate affects the economy."
items.text: When inflation is above the target band, the RBA raises the cash rate to [[stimulate => slow]] the economy. Banks pass the increase on, so borrowers face higher interest rates on loans. Higher interest rates [[encourage => discourage]] borrowing for houses, cars and business investment, so consumption and investment fall. Aggregate demand shifts [[right => left]], which eases demand inflation. The higher return on Australian assets also attracts foreign capital, so the Australian dollar [[depreciates => appreciates]], making imports cheaper and further reducing inflation.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the effects of a tariff on an imported good."
items.text: A tariff is a tax on imports, so the domestic price rises from the world price to the world price plus the tariff. Domestic producers respond to the higher price by producing [[less => more]], while consumers buy less. Imports therefore [[rise => fall]]. The government's revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the quantity of imports [[before => after]] the tariff. Consumers [[gain => lose]] consumer surplus, and part of that loss is a deadweight loss to society.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the multiplier effect of a rise in government spending."
items.text: An increase in government spending is an injection into the circular flow. The people who receive it spend part of it, so it becomes someone else's income, and so on. The simple multiplier is k = [[1 ÷ MPC => 1 ÷ (1 − MPC)]]. If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the multiplier is [[1.25 => 5]], so a $10 billion increase in spending raises national income by $50 billion. If households decide to save more of each extra dollar, the multiplier becomes [[larger => smaller]], because more income leaks out of the circular flow in each round.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how unemployment is measured in Australia."
items.text: The ABS Labour Force Survey counts a person as unemployed if they had no paid work in the survey week, were actively looking for work and were available to start. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the [[working age population => labour force]], multiplied by 100. The labour force is the employed plus the [[underemployed => unemployed]]. A discouraged job seeker who has stopped looking for work is [[counted as unemployed => not counted in the labour force]], which is why this group is called hidden unemployment.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the relationship between the current account and the capital and financial account."
items.text: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows. Interest paid on Australia's foreign debt is recorded in the [[financial account => primary income section of the current account]]. When Australia runs a current account deficit, it must be financed by a capital and financial account [[deficit => surplus]], as foreigners lend to Australia or invest here. In theory the two accounts sum to [[one => zero]], although in practice net errors and omissions are needed to make them balance.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain two factors that could cause the Australian dollar to appreciate."
items.text: First, if the world price of iron ore and coal rises, overseas buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for our exports. Demand for the Australian dollar rises and the dollar [[depreciates => appreciates]]. Second, if Australian interest rates rise relative to interest rates overseas, Australian assets offer a higher return. Foreign investors buy Australian dollars to invest here, which [[reduces => increases]] the demand for the dollar and pushes its value up. A higher Australian dollar means one Australian dollar buys [[less => more]] foreign currency.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how the budget can stabilise the economy."
items.text: A budget deficit is [[contractionary => expansionary]] because the government injects more into the circular flow through spending than it withdraws through tax. In a recession, automatic stabilisers work without any new decisions: tax revenue [[rises => falls]] and payments such as JobSeeker rise, which supports aggregate demand. To finance a deficit, the government sells Commonwealth Government Securities. If this borrowing competes with private borrowers, it can [[lower => raise]] interest rates and reduce private investment, which is called crowding out.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Distinguish between headline and underlying inflation."
items.text: Headline inflation is the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index over a year, so it includes every item in the basket. Underlying inflation [[includes => removes]] the most volatile price changes, such as those for fuel and fruit, so it shows the trend in prices. The RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation is the [[GDP deflator => trimmed mean]]. The RBA aims to keep inflation between [[1 and 2 => 2 and 3]] per cent on average over time.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient measure inequality."
items.text: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentage of households against the cumulative percentage of income they receive. The further the curve bows away from the line of equality, the [[more equal => less equal]] the distribution. The Gini coefficient is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the line of equality. A Gini coefficient of 1 means perfect [[equality => inequality]]. Progressive taxes and transfer payments move the Lorenz curve [[away from => towards]] the line of equality.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain why a negative externality is an example of market failure."
items.text: When a power station pollutes the air, it does not pay for the damage it causes to others. Its private costs are therefore [[higher => lower]] than the social cost of its output, so the marginal social cost curve lies [[below => above]] the private supply curve. The market produces [[less => more]] than the socially efficient quantity, at a price that is too low. A [[subsidy to => tax on]] the polluter, equal to the external cost, would make it pay the full social cost.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the basis of free trade."
items.text: Free trade is based on comparative advantage. A country should specialise in the good it can produce at the [[highest => lowest]] opportunity cost, and trade for other goods. Even if one country has an absolute advantage in producing both goods, trade [[cannot => can still]] benefit both countries, as long as their opportunity costs differ. Specialisation raises total world output, so [[only the more efficient country gains => both countries can consume beyond their own production possibility frontiers]].

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the J-curve effect of a depreciation."
items.text: After a depreciation, the price of imports in Australian dollars rises straight away. Because import and export volumes take time to respond, the trade balance at first [[improves => worsens]]: Australia pays more for roughly the same imports. Over the next year or two, buyers switch away from dearer imports and overseas buyers buy more of our cheaper exports, so the trade balance [[worsens => improves]]. Drawn over time, the path of the trade balance looks like the letter J. The effect only works if exports and imports are [[completely inelastic => responsive enough to price]] over time.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the conflict between full employment and price stability."
items.text: The short-run Phillips curve shows a [[positive => negative (inverse)]] relationship between inflation and unemployment. If expansionary policy pushes unemployment below the NAIRU, firms compete for scarce workers and wages rise faster, so inflation tends to [[fall => rise]]. To bring inflation back to target, the RBA may raise interest rates, which [[lowers => raises]] unemployment. This shows that policymakers cannot always achieve both objectives at the same time.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how quality of life is measured."
items.text: The Human Development Index combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (years of schooling) and a decent standard of living, measured by [[the inflation rate => gross national income per person at purchasing power parity]]. The index runs from 0 to 1, and a higher score means [[lower => higher]] human development. Economic growth [[always => does not always]] lead to economic development, because the extra income may be spread unevenly or come at the cost of the environment.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline how minimum pay and conditions are set in Australia."
items.text: The National Employment Standards set minimum conditions, such as annual leave and maximum weekly hours, for employees in the national system. Modern awards set minimum pay and conditions for particular industries and occupations and are [[negotiated between each employer and its workers => made and reviewed by the Fair Work Commission]]. Enterprise agreements are negotiated at the workplace level and must pass the better off overall test, which compares the agreement with the relevant [[National Employment Standards => modern award]]. The national minimum wage is reviewed [[every five years => each year]] in the Annual Wage Review.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how a change in the terms of trade affects Australia."
items.text: The terms of trade is the export price index divided by the [[GDP deflator => import price index]], multiplied by 100. When the world prices of iron ore and coal rise, Australia's terms of trade [[deteriorate => improve]], so each unit of exports buys more imports. Export income rises, so the balance on goods and services tends to [[worsen => improve]], and the extra demand for Australian dollars tends to make the dollar appreciate.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how the Federal Government finances a budget deficit."
items.text: The Federal Government finances most of its deficits by [[borrowing from the Reserve Bank => selling Commonwealth Government Securities, mostly to the private sector]]. When these bonds are bought by foreign investors, the borrowing adds to Australia's [[net foreign equity => net foreign debt]] and future interest payments add to the primary income deficit. When the budget returns to surplus, the government can use the money to [[increase => reduce]] public debt or invest in funds such as the Future Fund.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Outline Australia's approach to free trade agreements."
items.text: Australia takes part in multilateral, regional and bilateral trade agreements. A bilateral agreement involves [[many => two]] countries, such as the Australia–United States Free Trade Agreement. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a [[bilateral => regional (plurilateral)]] agreement that includes China, Japan, Korea and the ten ASEAN members. A risk of preferential agreements is trade [[creation => diversion]], where imports switch from the lowest-cost supplier to a higher-cost member of the agreement.

Which of the following best describes the global economy?
o: The economies of the G20 countries
The sum of the world's national economies and the links between them through trade, finance and people
The total value of world exports in a year
The economies that belong to the World Trade Organization

e.why: The global economy is all the world's national economies together, linked through trade, financial flows, investment, technology and migration. Exports (C) are only one link; A and D are subsets of countries.

items.q: Gross World Product grew by 3.2 per cent in real terms in a year in which world population grew by 1 per cent. Which statement is correct?
o: Real output per person rose by about 2.2 per cent
Real output per person rose by about 4.2 per cent
Nominal output must have grown by less than 3.2 per cent

e.why: Growth in real output per person is roughly real growth minus population growth: 3.2 − 1.0 ≈ 2.2 per cent. Nominal output (D) would usually grow faster than real output because of inflation.

items.q: Which of the following would most likely increase world trade in goods and services?
o: Lower tariffs and the spread of digital trade platforms
More import quotas on farm products

e.why: Lower trade barriers and cheaper ways to buy and sell across borders raise trade. Higher costs and barriers (A, B, D) reduce it.

items.q: Which of the following is an example of a global financial flow?
o: An Australian winery exports wine to the United Kingdom
A Japanese pension fund buys Australian government bonds
A German tourist visits the Great Barrier Reef
A worker migrates from India to Australia

e.why: Buying bonds overseas is a movement of financial capital. Wine exports and tourism are trade in goods and services; migration is a movement of labour.

items.q: Why can a financial crisis in one country spread quickly to other economies?
o: Exchange rates are fixed between most major economies
Financial markets are closely integrated, so investors move funds and losses across borders very quickly
Most countries ban foreign investment during a crisis
Governments must keep their budgets balanced

e.why: Integrated financial markets let capital move instantly, so falling asset prices, losses and loss of confidence in one market spread to others (contagion), as in the 2008 global financial crisis.

items.q: A transnational corporation is best described as a business that
o: is owned by a foreign government.
has production or operations in more than one country.
trades only with members of a free trade agreement.

e.why: A TNC produces or operates in more than one country, usually with its headquarters in one country. It may sell at home and abroad.

items.q: Which development has done most to lower the cost of trading services across borders?
o: Fast, cheap internet and digital communication

e.why: Services such as finance, education and software can now be delivered online. Containers (A) cut the cost of moving goods rather than services.

items.q: A smartphone is designed in the United States, uses parts made in Korea and Japan and is assembled in Vietnam. This is an example of

e.why: Different stages of production are done in different countries according to their comparative advantage: the international division of labour, organised through global supply chains.

items.q: A sharp slowdown in China would most likely affect Australia through
o: higher demand for Australian iron ore.
lower export volumes and prices, and a lower Australian dollar.
a higher Australian terms of trade.
lower unemployment in Australian mining regions.

e.why: China is Australia's largest export market. A slowdown reduces demand for resources, lowering export volumes and prices (the terms of trade fall) and the dollar, which spreads the downturn to Australia.

items.q: In one day, Country X can make 10 shirts or 5 bikes, and Country Y can make 6 shirts or 2 bikes. Which statement is correct?
o: Country X has a comparative advantage in shirts
Country Y has a comparative advantage in bikes
Country X has a comparative advantage in bikes and Country Y in shirts
Neither country can gain from trade, because Country X is better at both

e.why: For X, 1 bike costs 2 shirts; for Y, 1 bike costs 3 shirts. X makes bikes at a lower opportunity cost, so Y has the comparative advantage in shirts (1 shirt costs Y ⅓ bike but costs X ½ bike). Both gain from specialising, even though X has an absolute advantage in both.

items.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of free trade for an economy?
o: Consumers can choose from a wider range of goods
Resources move to industries in which the economy is most efficient
Jobs may be lost in industries that cannot compete with imports
Firms can sell to larger markets and gain economies of scale

e.why: Free trade forces structural change: import-competing industries may shrink, causing job losses in the short term. A, B and D are advantages.

items.q: Which international organisation lends to countries with balance of payments difficulties, usually with conditions attached?

e.why: The IMF lends to countries facing balance of payments crises and sets conditions on their policies. The WTO deals with trade rules; the OECD and G20 are forums for research and coordination.

items.q: Which statement about the G20 is correct?
o: It can impose binding trade sanctions on its members
It is a forum where major advanced and emerging economies coordinate economic policy
It lends money to developing economies
Its members are the 20 richest economies in Europe

e.why: The G20 brings together leaders and finance ministers of major advanced and emerging economies (including Australia) to coordinate policy. It has no power to impose sanctions and does not lend.

items.q: Which of the following is a monetary union?
o: The Australia–United States Free Trade Agreement

e.why: Euro area members share one currency and one central bank (the ECB). The others are trade agreements or forums.

items.q: Australia signs a free trade agreement with Country Z, and Australians switch from buying cheaper TVs from Country Q to slightly dearer TVs from Country Z. This is an example of

e.why: Imports have switched from the lowest-cost producer (Q) to a higher-cost member of the agreement (Z) because Z no longer faces a tariff: trade diversion.

items.q: Which argument for protection is most widely accepted by economists?
o: Protection keeps all domestic jobs safe
Temporary help for an infant industry with real potential to become competitive
Protection improves the trade balance permanently

e.why: The infant industry argument has some support if the help is temporary and the industry can become competitive. Protection raises prices (D is wrong) and does not save jobs overall (A).

items.q: Compared with a tariff that gives domestic producers the same price, an import quota
o: raises more revenue for the government.
lets importers keep the extra revenue from the higher price.

e.why: A quota and an equivalent tariff raise the price by the same amount, but with a quota the government collects nothing: the importers who hold the quota keep the extra revenue. Both have deadweight losses.

items.q: A production subsidy to an import-competing industry will
o: increase domestic production while consumers still pay the world price.

e.why: The subsidy shifts domestic supply right. Consumers keep paying the world price, domestic production rises and imports fall, and the government bears the cost.

items.q: Which change would show economic development rather than only economic growth?
o: Real GDP rises by 4 per cent
Life expectancy and school completion rates rise

e.why: Development is about wellbeing and living standards, such as health and education. Higher output (A, B) is growth, which may or may not improve living standards.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the distribution of global income?
o: Income is spread evenly between countries
