A small share of the world's population, mostly in advanced economies, receives a large share of world income
Emerging economies receive most of the world's income
Developing economies have the fastest growth in income per person

e.why: Global income is very unequal: advanced economies, with a minority of the world's people, receive a large share of world income, although the rise of China and India has narrowed the gap since the 1990s.

items.q: Strong growth in China and India since the 1990s has most likely
o: increased inequality between countries but reduced it within every country.
reduced inequality between countries, while inequality within some of those countries rose.
had no effect on the global distribution of income.
reduced the number of people living in extreme poverty in Africa only.

e.why: Rapid growth in large, poorer economies lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and narrowed the gap between countries. Within China, inequality rose as coastal and urban incomes grew faster.

items.q: Why is GNI per person usually converted at purchasing power parity (PPP) to compare living standards?
o: To remove the effect of inflation over time
To allow for differences in the cost of living between countries
To measure the distribution of income

e.why: PPP adjusts for the fact that a dollar buys more in some countries than others, giving a better comparison of what incomes can buy.

items.q: Which economy is best described as emerging rather than developing?

e.why: India is industrialising rapidly with fast growth and a large middle class: an emerging economy. Malawi, Niger and Mozambique are low-income developing economies.

items.q: Which factor best explains why some nations have much higher living standards than others?
o: Differences in productive capacity: education, technology, capital, infrastructure and institutions
Differences in the number of trade agreements signed

e.why: Productive capacity and strong institutions (rule of law, stable government) drive long-run differences in living standards. Population size alone does not.

items.q: Which of the following is a likely cost of globalisation for an advanced economy?
o: Structural unemployment in manufacturing as production moves offshore
Access to foreign capital for investment

e.why: As labour-intensive production moves to lower-cost countries, workers in advanced economies' manufacturing industries may lose jobs and need to retrain. A, C and D are benefits.

items.q: A critic argues that globalisation has led to a "race to the bottom". This means that
o: countries compete to have the lowest unemployment.
countries lower environmental and labour standards to attract foreign investment.
global interest rates fall to zero.
exporters cut prices below cost to win market share.

e.why: The argument is that to attract TNCs, governments weaken regulation of wages, working conditions and pollution, lowering standards everywhere.

items.q: How can foreign direct investment by transnational corporations help a developing economy?
o: It always increases the government's tax revenue
It brings capital, technology, skills and jobs
It guarantees higher wages for all workers
It reduces the economy's reliance on exports

e.why: FDI can bring new capital, technology and management skills and create jobs. Its benefits depend on conditions; it does not guarantee higher tax revenue or wages for everyone.

items.q: Which statement best describes the link between global economic growth and the environment?
o: Growth in production and consumption has added to greenhouse gas emissions, pollution and resource depletion
Growth has no effect on the environment
Only advanced economies affect the global environment

e.why: Rising output and energy use have increased emissions, pollution and pressure on resources. Cleaner technology can reduce the damage per unit of output, but total impacts have grown.

items.q: Which policy change did most to open China's economy to the world after 1978?
o: Economic reforms that allowed markets, private enterprise and foreign investment, including special economic zones
Fixing the price of all goods

e.why: Under Deng Xiaoping, China introduced market reforms, opened special economic zones to foreign investment and later joined the WTO in 2001, which drove rapid export-led growth.

items.q: Which statement best describes the direction of Australia's trade today?
o: Most exports go to East and South Asia, with China the largest market
The United States buys most of Australia's resources
New Zealand is Australia's largest export market

e.why: Asia takes about three-quarters of Australia's goods exports, and China alone takes close to 30 per cent of all exports. Trade with Europe has fallen in relative terms since the 1960s.

items.q: Which change best describes the composition of Australia's exports over the past 40 years?
o: Manufactured goods have replaced resources as the main export
Resources and services have grown as a share of exports, and rural goods have fallen
Services have fallen to a very small share of exports
Exports have become less concentrated in a few commodities

e.why: Mining exports (iron ore, coal, gas) and services (education, tourism) have grown in importance, while rural goods have fallen as a share. Exports remain concentrated in a few commodities.

items.q: Australia's net foreign liabilities are equal to
o: net foreign debt plus net foreign equity.
net foreign debt minus net foreign equity.
the current account deficit plus the budget deficit.

e.why: Net foreign liabilities are what Australia owes the rest of the world in debt plus the net foreign ownership of Australian assets (equity).

items.q: Which of the following would increase Australia's net foreign equity?
o: An Australian bank borrows from a US bank
A Canadian pension fund buys shares in an Australian airport
An Australian company repays an overseas loan
The government sells bonds to Australian super funds

e.why: Foreign purchases of shares and businesses raise foreign ownership of Australian assets: net foreign equity. Borrowing (A) adds to debt; C reduces debt; D is domestic.

items.q: Where is the payment of interest on Australia's foreign debt recorded in the balance of payments?

e.why: Interest and dividends paid to and received from overseas are primary income, part of the current account.

items.q: Exports of goods $400b, imports of goods $380b, exports of services $90b, imports of services $100b, net primary income −$60b, net secondary income −$2b. What is the current account balance?

e.why: BOGS = (400 − 380) + (90 − 100) = +10. Current account = 10 − 60 − 2 = −$52 billion. B leaves out secondary income; D adds the services deficit twice.

items.q: An Australian superannuation fund buys $5 billion of shares in US companies. In Australia's balance of payments this is recorded as
o: a credit in the current account.
portfolio investment abroad, a debit in the financial account.
direct investment in Australia, a credit in the financial account.
a credit in the capital account.

e.why: Buying overseas shares (below 10 per cent of the company) is portfolio investment by Australians abroad, an outflow recorded as a debit in the financial account.

items.q: Why do persistent financial account surpluses tend to widen Australia's current account deficit over time?
o: They make the Australian dollar depreciate
They add to foreign liabilities, so more interest and dividends are paid overseas, widening the net primary income deficit
They are recorded as exports of services

e.why: Each year's inflow adds to foreign debt and equity. Servicing those liabilities raises payments of interest and dividends abroad, which widens the net primary income deficit in the current account.

items.q: Export prices rise by 10 per cent and import prices rise by 2 per cent. The terms of trade index, starting at 100, becomes about

e.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 110 ÷ 102 × 100 ≈ 107.8. The terms of trade improve.

items.q: Australia recorded current account surpluses from 2019–20 to 2022–23. Which factor contributed most?
o: Very high commodity prices that lifted export income
A rise in Australia's net primary income deficit
A sharp appreciation of the Australian dollar

e.why: High prices for iron ore, coal and gas lifted the terms of trade and produced large trade surpluses, enough to outweigh the primary income deficit. The current account returned to deficit from 2023–24.

items.q: The exchange rate moves from A$1 = US$0.70 to A$1 = US$0.63. What has happened?
o: The Australian dollar has appreciated by 10 per cent
The Australian dollar has depreciated by 10 per cent
The Australian dollar has depreciated by 7 per cent
The US dollar has depreciated against the Australian dollar

e.why: (0.63 − 0.70) ÷ 0.70 × 100 = −10 per cent: the A$ buys fewer US dollars, a depreciation. The US dollar has appreciated.

items.q: The Australian dollar rises against the US dollar but the Trade Weighted Index falls. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The TWI only measures the dollar against the US dollar
The A$ fell against currencies with large weights in the TWI, such as the Chinese renminbi
The RBA lowered the cash rate
The TWI rises whenever the A$ rises against any currency

e.why: The TWI is weighted by trade; the renminbi has the largest weight. If the A$ falls against major trading partners' currencies, the TWI can fall even while it rises against the US dollar.

items.q: Which of the following would increase the supply of Australian dollars on the foreign exchange market?
o: The world price of LNG rises
More overseas students enrol in Australian universities

e.why: To pay for imports, Australians sell Australian dollars for foreign currency, increasing the supply of A$. The other three increase the demand for A$.

items.q: Which group is most likely to be helped by an appreciation of the Australian dollar?

e.why: An appreciation makes imports cheaper in A$. It hurts exporters, tourism operators and import-competing producers, whose prices rise relative to overseas competitors.

items.q: Under a fixed exchange rate, what must the central bank do if there is excess supply of its currency at the fixed rate?
o: Buy its currency with foreign reserves

e.why: To hold the peg, the central bank must remove the excess supply by buying its own currency with foreign currency reserves (and may also need to raise interest rates).

items.q: Since the Australian dollar was floated, the RBA's direct intervention in the foreign exchange market has mainly been to
o: set the exchange rate each day.
keep the A$ at parity with the US dollar.
calm a disorderly market during extreme swings.
make exports more competitive every year.

e.why: The dollar floats. The RBA intervenes only rarely, buying or selling A$ to smooth disorderly markets, as it did during the global financial crisis in 2008.

items.q: A sustained 15 per cent depreciation of the Australian dollar is most likely to
o: lower inflation and improve the current account straight away.
add to inflation and, after a delay, improve the balance on goods and services.
lower the A$ cost of servicing foreign-currency debt.

e.why: Dearer imports raise inflation, while volumes take time to adjust: the trade balance may worsen first and improve later (the J-curve). Servicing foreign-currency debt costs more (C is wrong) and competitiveness improves (D is wrong).

items.q: Which statement best describes Australia's trade policy since the 1980s?
o: Steady increases in tariffs to protect manufacturing
Large cuts to tariffs and quotas, and a focus on free trade agreements
Leaving the WTO to sign only bilateral deals

e.why: Since the 1980s Australia has cut average tariffs to very low levels (most imports now enter tariff-free) and has pursued multilateral, regional and bilateral agreements.

items.q: Which of the following is the best example of Australia still assisting an industry?
o: Removing the tariff on imported cars
Payments and tax incentives for local production of green metals and critical minerals
Abolishing the Export Market Development Grants scheme

e.why: Production incentives, such as those under Future Made in Australia, are a form of assistance (subsidies). Removing tariffs (A) is liberalisation; EMDG still operates (C is wrong); RCEP (D) is a trade agreement.

items.q: Which of the following is a bilateral free trade agreement?
o: The Australia–United States Free Trade Agreement
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership

e.why: A bilateral agreement has two parties: AUSFTA. RCEP and the CPTPP are regional agreements; WTO agreements are multilateral.

items.q: How do Australia's low tariffs mainly benefit Australian households?
o: They raise wages in all import-competing industries
They lower the prices of imported goods and raise real incomes
They reduce the number of goods available

e.why: Low tariffs mean lower prices and more choice, raising households' real incomes. They reduce tariff revenue and can cost jobs in import-competing industries.

items.q: The United States raises tariffs on imports from China. Which is the most likely indirect effect on Australia?
o: Higher demand for Australian iron ore
Slower Chinese growth reduces demand for Australian resources, and diverted Chinese goods may compete with Australian producers
Australia's exports to the US must fall

e.why: Even if not targeted, Australia is exposed: weaker Chinese manufacturing reduces demand for resources, and goods blocked from the US may be sold more cheaply in Australia.

items.q: Which is the largest component of aggregate demand in Australia?

e.why: Household consumption is roughly half of GDP, far larger than any other component.

items.q: In an economy, S = $90b, T = $120b, M = $80b, I = $100b, G = $110b and X = $70b. What will happen to national income?
o: It will rise, because injections exceed withdrawals
It will fall, because withdrawals exceed injections
It will not change, because injections equal withdrawals
It will fall, because the budget is in surplus

e.why: Withdrawals = 90 + 120 + 80 = 290; injections = 100 + 110 + 70 = 280. Withdrawals exceed injections by $10b, so income will fall until they are equal. The budget surplus (D) is part of the story but not the full test.

items.q: The marginal propensity to save is 0.25. Investment rises by $20 billion. By how much will national income eventually rise?
Nominal GDP rose by 6 per cent and the general price level rose by 4 per cent. Real GDP grew by about

e.why: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation = 6 − 4 = 2 per cent.

items.q: Which is a likely cost of rapid economic growth?
o: Greater pressure on inflation and the environment

e.why: Fast growth can push demand above capacity, adding to inflation and import spending, and can increase pollution and resource use. A, B and D are benefits.

items.q: Which would most likely shift aggregate supply to the right?
o: A rise in the world oil price

e.why: Higher productivity lowers unit costs, so firms supply more at each price level. A, C and D raise costs and shift AS left.

items.q: A period of falling real GDP and rising unemployment is called a

e.why: A downturn (contraction) is a period of falling or slowing growth with rising unemployment. Two consecutive quarters of negative growth is a technical recession.

items.q: Employed 14.5 million, unemployed 0.7 million, working-age population 22.8 million. What is the participation rate?

e.why: Labour force = 14.5 + 0.7 = 15.2 million. Participation rate = 15.2 ÷ 22.8 × 100 = 66.7 per cent. A leaves out the unemployed; C is the unemployment rate.

items.q: Which statement best describes unemployment in Australia since the COVID-19 recession?
o: It rose above 10 per cent and stayed there
It fell to its lowest level in about 50 years (around 3.5 per cent in 2022) and has risen gradually since
It has remained above 7 per cent
It has fallen every year since 2020

e.why: Strong demand pushed unemployment down to about 3.5 per cent in 2022–23, the lowest in around 50 years. It rose gradually as growth slowed and interest rates rose (it reached 4.9 per cent in October 2026).

items.q: If unemployment falls below the NAIRU, the most likely result is
o: a rise in the participation rate to 100 per cent.

e.why: Below the NAIRU, employers compete for scarce workers, so wage growth and inflation tend to rise.

items.q: Which group usually has an unemployment rate well above the national average?
o: People who own their own business

e.why: Youth unemployment is usually about twice the national rate, because young people have less experience and are often first to lose jobs in a downturn.

items.q: Which is an economic cost of unemployment rather than a social cost?
o: Lost output and lower tax revenue

e.why: Lost production and lower tax revenue (with higher welfare payments) are economic costs. A, B and D are social costs.

items.q: The CPI was 132.0 last year and is 137.3 this year. What is the inflation rate?

e.why: (137.3 − 132.0) ÷ 132.0 × 100 = 4.0 per cent. C is the change in index points, which is not a percentage unless the earlier index is 100.

items.q: Which statement best describes inflation in Australia since 2021?
o: It has stayed inside the 2–3 per cent target band throughout
It peaked near 8 per cent in late 2022, eased, then rose again in 2026
It has been below 1 per cent since 2021

e.why: Headline inflation peaked at 7.8 per cent in the December quarter 2022 after supply shocks and strong demand, fell back towards the target, then rose again in 2026 with higher energy prices, prompting cash rate rises.

items.q: Workers ask for bigger pay rises because they expect prices to keep rising, and firms raise prices because they expect costs to rise. This is an example of

e.why: Expectations of future inflation feed into wage claims and price setting, which can make inflation self-fulfilling. That is why central banks try to keep expectations anchored.

items.q: Which group is most likely to be harmed by unexpectedly high inflation?
o: Lenders and savers receiving a fixed interest rate

e.why: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed repayments and savings, so lenders and savers on fixed rates lose and borrowers gain.

items.q: Net foreign debt is $1,500 billion, net foreign equity is −$100 billion and GDP is $2,800 billion. Net foreign liabilities as a percentage of GDP are

e.why: NFL = 1,500 + (−100) = $1,400 billion. 1,400 ÷ 2,800 × 100 = 50.0 per cent. C uses debt alone; D adds the equity instead of subtracting.

items.q: Which statement best describes the trend in Australia's net foreign equity in recent years?
o: Foreign ownership of Australian assets has grown much faster than Australian investment abroad
Australian investment abroad, much of it by superannuation funds, has grown so that net foreign equity is negative
Net foreign equity has been unchanged for 20 years
Australia has no foreign equity liabilities

e.why: Large outflows by superannuation funds into overseas shares mean Australians now own more foreign equity than foreigners own here, so net foreign equity is negative and net foreign liabilities are mostly debt.

items.q: Which is a structural cause of Australia's current account deficit?
o: A temporary fall in commodity prices
A short-term boom in domestic spending
National saving that has long been lower than national investment
A temporary recession in our trading partners

e.why: The savings-investment gap is a long-run feature of the economy that has to be funded from overseas, a structural cause. A, B and D are cyclical.

items.q: On a Lorenz curve diagram, the area between the line of equality and the curve is 1,200 and the area under the curve is 3,800. The Gini coefficient is
Which is the main source of income for most Australian households?

e.why: Wages and salaries are by far the largest source of household income. Lower-income households rely more on transfers, and higher-income households receive more capital income.

items.q: Which policy would most directly reduce inequality in disposable income?
o: A rise in the GST rate
Higher income support payments funded by progressive income tax

e.why: Progressive taxes take a larger share of higher incomes and transfers lift low incomes, narrowing the gap. A raises a regressive tax; B and D mostly help higher-income earners.

items.q: Which asset makes up the largest share of Australian household wealth?

e.why: Property is the largest part of household wealth, followed by superannuation. Because older and higher-income households own more property, wealth is less equal than income.

items.q: Which statement about the distribution of income and wealth in Australia is correct?
o: Younger households usually hold more wealth than older households
Women's average earnings are below men's (a gender pay gap)
Income is distributed more unequally than wealth
Occupation has no effect on income

e.why: There is a persistent gender pay gap. Wealth peaks for households near retirement age and is less equal than income; occupation strongly affects income.

items.q: Which is an economic benefit of some inequality?
o: Incentives to work, study and take business risks

e.why: Differences in income reward effort, skills and risk-taking. High inequality has costs, such as lost potential, weaker social cohesion and lower consumption.

items.q: Ecologically sustainable development means
o: stopping economic growth to protect the environment.
growth that meets present needs without reducing future generations' ability to meet theirs.

e.why: ESD balances economic growth with the protection of the environment so that future generations are not left worse off (intergenerational equity).

items.q: A factory pollutes a river used by farmers downstream. Without government action, the market will
o: produce more than the socially efficient output, at a price that is too low.
produce less than the socially efficient output.

e.why: The factory ignores the external cost, so its private costs are below the social cost. It overproduces, and the price does not reflect the full cost: market failure.

items.q: Which is the best example of a public good?

e.why: Defence is non-rival (one person's protection does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be stopped from benefiting), so the market would underprovide it.

items.q: Which environmental issue is an example of the depletion of a natural resource?

e.why: Overfishing uses up a renewable resource faster than it can regenerate. The others are forms of pollution.

items.q: Which statement about economic growth and quality of life is correct?
o: Higher real GDP always means a higher quality of life
Growth can raise living standards, but quality of life also depends on health, leisure, the environment and how income is shared
Quality of life is measured by the inflation rate
Governments do not aim for economic growth

e.why: Growth gives more goods, services and jobs, but quality of life also depends on non-material factors such as health, leisure, the environment and the distribution of income.

items.q: The objective of full employment is best described as
o: an unemployment rate at about the NAIRU, where only frictional, seasonal and some structural unemployment remain.
a participation rate of 100 per cent.

e.why: Full employment allows for people moving between jobs and some mismatch; pushing unemployment below the NAIRU adds to inflation.

items.q: Price stability in Australia means
o: inflation of 2 to 3 per cent on average, the RBA's target.

e.why: The RBA targets inflation of 2 to 3 per cent, aiming for the midpoint. Low, positive inflation is the goal, not zero or falling prices.

items.q: The objective of external stability is best described as
o: never running a current account deficit.
keeping the current account deficit and foreign liabilities at levels that can be serviced, and avoiding big swings in the exchange rate.
having more exports than imports every year.

e.why: External stability means Australia can meet its obligations to the rest of the world over time, so investors stay confident. A deficit is not a problem in itself if it is sustainable.

items.q: Which policy best supports the objective of environmental sustainability?
o: A market-based price on emissions such as the Safeguard Mechanism's tradeable credits

e.why: A price on emissions makes polluters count the external cost. A, C and D encourage more emissions or resource use.

items.q: Which change would most likely make the distribution of income more equal?

e.why: A more progressive tax system takes a larger share from higher incomes, narrowing the gap in disposable income.

items.q: Strong economic growth lifts imports faster than exports. Which two objectives are in conflict?
o: Distribution of income and price stability

e.why: Faster growth raises spending on imports, widening the current account deficit: a conflict between growth and external stability.

items.q: Which policy mix is most suitable when inflation is well above target and unemployment is low?
o: Expansionary fiscal and expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary monetary policy, supported by a tighter budget
Cuts to the cash rate and tax cuts

e.why: With the economy running above capacity, contractionary policy slows demand. Fiscal and monetary policy working in the same direction makes the RBA's job easier.

items.q: Government revenue is $700 billion and government spending is $735 billion. The budget outcome is

e.why: Budget outcome = revenue − spending = 700 − 735 = −$35 billion, a deficit.

items.q: The budget deficit widens because unemployment rises in a downturn, with no change in policy. This change is
o: an increase in the structural deficit.
an increase in the cyclical component of the budget, through automatic stabilisers.

e.why: Lower tax receipts and higher welfare payments in a downturn change the cyclical component automatically. The structural balance reflects policy decisions.

items.q: Which budget change would most directly improve income distribution?
o: Cutting the top marginal tax rate
Increasing the rate of JobSeeker and Commonwealth Rent Assistance

e.why: Larger transfers to low-income households raise their disposable incomes, reducing inequality.

items.q: How does the Federal Government usually finance a budget deficit?
o: By printing money through the Reserve Bank
By selling Commonwealth Government Securities to investors in Australia and overseas
By selling Australian dollars on the foreign exchange market

e.why: The Australian Office of Financial Management sells government bonds and notes. Borrowing from overseas investors adds to foreign debt.

items.q: Which is a common use of a budget surplus?
o: Reducing government debt or investing in funds such as the Future Fund
Buying Australian dollars to raise the exchange rate

e.why: A surplus can be used to repay debt, which lowers future interest costs, or to build up assets in funds such as the Future Fund.

items.q: The main purpose of monetary policy in Australia is
o: to keep inflation at 2 to 3 per cent and support full employment.
to fix the value of the Australian dollar.

e.why: The RBA uses the cash rate to keep inflation within its target and support the maximum sustainable level of employment, which promotes sustainable growth.

items.q: Who decides the target for the cash rate in Australia?

e.why: Since March 2025 the RBA Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy. The RBA then manages money market conditions so the cash rate stays at the target.

items.q: The RBA cuts the cash rate while overseas central banks keep theirs unchanged. Which outcome is most likely?
o: An appreciation of the A$ and lower inflation
A depreciation of the A$, higher spending and more inflationary pressure
Higher mortgage rates and lower spending
Lower investment and a fall in employment

e.why: Lower rates reduce the return on Australian assets, so the dollar tends to depreciate. Cheaper borrowing and a lower dollar lift spending and net exports, adding to activity and inflation.

items.q: Why might a rise in the cash rate take a long time to lower inflation?
o: Banks never pass on changes in the cash rate
Households and firms take time to adjust spending, and many loans have fixed rates for a while
The RBA can only change the cash rate once a year
Higher rates immediately raise import prices

e.why: Monetary policy works with long and variable lags: borrowers on fixed rates are affected only when their loans roll over, and spending plans change slowly.

items.q: Microeconomic reform mainly aims to
o: smooth the business cycle in the short run.
increase efficiency and productivity, shifting aggregate supply to the right.

e.why: Microeconomic policies work on the supply side: they improve how markets and firms use resources, lifting productivity and potential growth.

items.q: The government opens a market for a service to new competitors. In the short run, the most likely effect in that market is
o: lower prices, more choice and possible job losses at the former monopoly.
higher prices and more jobs at the former monopoly.

e.why: More competition pushes prices down and lifts efficiency. The incumbent may cut costs and jobs, a short-term cost of reform.

items.q: Which body enforces Australia's competition laws, such as the ban on price-fixing?
o: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission

e.why: The ACCC enforces the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, including the bans on cartels and the misuse of market power.

items.q: Which statement about Australia's industrial relations system is correct?
o: Each state sets the pay of all private-sector workers in that state
Most private-sector employees are covered by the national system under the Fair Work Act 2009
There are no minimum wages in Australia
All pay is set in individual contracts

e.why: Most states referred their powers to the Commonwealth, so most private-sector employees are in the national system; Western Australia's unincorporated businesses and state public servants remain in state systems.

items.q: Which body decides changes to the national minimum wage each year?
o: The Australian Council of Trade Unions

e.why: The Fair Work Commission's Annual Wage Review sets the national minimum wage and modern award minimum wages. The Fair Work Ombudsman enforces compliance.

items.q: When the Fair Work Commission makes a binding decision to settle a dispute, this is called

e.why: Arbitration is a binding decision by an independent third party. In conciliation and mediation the parties are helped to reach their own agreement.

items.q: Which is an argument for decentralised (enterprise) bargaining?
o: It gives every worker the same pay rise
It lets pay and conditions reflect each workplace's productivity
It reduces wage inequality between industries
It removes the need for minimum standards

e.why: Enterprise bargaining can link pay rises to productivity gains at each workplace. Critics say it can widen inequality where workers have little bargaining power.

items.q: Which policy is best suited to reducing structural unemployment?
o: Funding retraining and apprenticeships in skills that are in short supply
A one-off cash payment to households

e.why: Structural unemployment comes from a skills or location mismatch, so education and training programs address its cause. A and C mainly help cyclical unemployment.

items.q: Which is an example of environmental regulation?
o: A ban on clearing native vegetation near rivers
A rebate for buying an electric vehicle

e.why: A ban is a regulation: a rule backed by penalties. A, C and D are market-based policies that work through prices.

items.q: Australia's legislated emissions targets are
o: a 26 per cent cut on 2005 levels by 2030 only.
a 43 per cent cut on 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050.
no targets, because Australia left the Paris Agreement.

e.why: The Climate Change Act 2022 legislated a 43 per cent cut below 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero emissions by 2050. Australia remains in the Paris Agreement.

items.q: The time between an economic problem starting and policymakers being sure it has started is the

e.why: Data arrive with a delay and are revised, so it takes time to recognise a downturn or an inflation problem.

items.q: Which is the best example of a global influence limiting Australian economic policy?
o: A Senate vote against a tax bill
A global recession that cuts demand for exports even after the RBA lowers interest rates
The time taken to build new infrastructure

e.why: Australia is a small open economy: world events can overwhelm domestic policy. A is a political constraint; C and D are time lags.

items.q: A government delays an unpopular tax increase until after an election. This is an example of

e.why: Political considerations, such as elections or the need to pass laws through the Senate, can stop governments from using the best economic policy at the right time.

items.q: Headline inflation rose to 4.9 per cent in the year to October 2026. Which policy response is most consistent with the RBA's mandate?
o: Cutting the cash rate to support growth
Raising the cash rate to bring inflation back to the 2–3 per cent target

e.why: With inflation well above target, the RBA tightened monetary policy, raising the cash rate several times in 2026 (to 4.85 per cent from 3 November) to slow demand and anchor expectations.

items.q: Which policy would most directly help external stability in the long run?
o: Policies that lift national saving and international competitiveness
Larger budget deficits funded by overseas borrowing
A sharp cut in interest rates to encourage borrowing

e.why: Higher saving narrows the savings-investment gap, and greater competitiveness lifts exports, both reducing reliance on foreign borrowing over time.

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for steel. The world price is $20 a tonne. The government then imposes a tariff of $10 a tonne.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the quantity of steel imported before the tariff.
parts.ans: 80 − 20 = 60 million tonnes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the quantity of steel imported after the tariff.
parts.ans: 70 − 30 = 40 million tonnes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the government's revenue from the tariff.
parts.ans: $10 × 40 million tonnes = $400 million (tariff × imports after the tariff, not before).

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Calculate the change in domestic production and the deadweight loss of the tariff.
parts.ans: Domestic production rises from 20 to 30 million tonnes (+10 million). Deadweight loss = ½ × 10 × 10 (production) + ½ × 10 × 10 (consumption) = $50 million + $50 million = $100 million.

parts.label: (e)
parts.q: Explain who gains and who loses from the tariff.
pts: Domestic producers gain: they sell more (20 to 30 million tonnes) at a higher price, a producer surplus gain of $250 million (1)
The government gains $400 million of tariff revenue (1)
Consumers lose: they pay $30 instead of $20 and buy less, a consumer surplus loss of $750 million, larger than the gains (deadweight loss $100 million) (1)

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for bicycles (quantities in thousands). The world price is $100. The government imposes a tariff of $20 a bicycle.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the number of bicycles imported before and after the tariff.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the tariff revenue.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the loss of consumer surplus, the gain in producer surplus and the total deadweight loss.

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for cheese (million kg). The world price is $4 a kg. The government then limits imports with a quota of 30 million kg.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate imports of cheese before the quota.
parts.ans: 90 − 20 = 70 million kg.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: State the domestic price of cheese once the quota applies.
parts.ans: $6 a kg: the price at which domestic demand (70 million kg) is 30 million kg more than domestic supply (40 million kg).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the extra revenue importers receive because of the higher price, and explain who receives it.
parts.ans: ($6 − $4) × 30 million kg = $60 million. The importers who hold the quota keep it: unlike a tariff, the government receives nothing.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Calculate the deadweight loss of the quota.
parts.ans: ½ × (40 − 20) × $2 + ½ × (90 − 70) × $2 = $20 million + $20 million = $40 million. Check: consumer surplus loss $160 million = producer gain $60 million + importers $60 million + deadweight loss $40 million.

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for sugar (million kg). The world price is $2 a kg. The government sets an import quota of 40 million kg.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate imports before the quota and the domestic price after it.
parts.ans: Before: 100 − 20 = 80 million kg. After the quota the price rises to $3, where demand (80) exceeds domestic supply (40) by the 40 million kg quota.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the change in domestic production.
parts.ans: It rises from 20 to 40 million kg, an increase of 20 million kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the loss of consumer surplus and explain why it is larger than the gain to producers.
parts.ans: ½ × (100 + 80) × $1 = $90 million. Producers gain only $30 million; importers keep $40 million and $20 million is deadweight loss, so the consumers' loss is larger than any one group's gain.

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for canned fruit (million cans). The world price is $50 a can. The government pays local producers a subsidy of $20 a can, which shifts supply from S1 to S2.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate domestic production and imports before and after the subsidy.
parts.ans: Production rises from 40 to 60 million cans. Consumption stays at 120 million cans (consumers still pay $50), so imports fall from 80 to 60 million cans.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the cost of the subsidy to the government.
parts.ans: $20 × 60 million cans = $1,200 million (the subsidy is paid on all domestic production, not just the increase).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why a subsidy has a smaller deadweight loss than a tariff that gives producers the same protection.
pts: Consumers still pay the world price, so consumption does not fall and there is no consumption deadweight loss (1)
The only loss is on production: the extra 20 million cans cost more to make here than to import, ½ × 20 × $20 = $200 million (1)
The cost moves from consumers to taxpayers through the budget, which has an opportunity cost (1)

items.lead: The figure shows the domestic market for solar panels (thousands). The world price is $200 a panel. The government pays local makers a subsidy of $80 a panel, which shifts supply from S1 to S2.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the change in domestic production and the change in imports.
parts.ans: Production rises from 10,000 to 18,000 panels (+8,000). Consumption stays at 40,000, so imports fall from 30,000 to 22,000.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the cost of the subsidy to the government.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the deadweight loss.

items.lead: The table shows labour market data for a hypothetical economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the unemployment rate in Year 2.
parts.ans: Labour force = 14,200 + 760 = 14,960 thousand. Unemployment rate = 760 ÷ 14,960 × 100 = 5.1%.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the participation rate in Year 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why the unemployment rate rose even though employment increased.
pts: The labour force grew faster than employment: it rose by 360,000 (2.5%) while employment rose by 200,000 (1.4%) (1)
More people entered the labour force looking for work (participation rose from 66.4% to 66.8%), so the number unemployed rose (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain ONE policy the government could use to reduce structural unemployment.
pts: Identifies a suitable policy, e.g. education and training or apprenticeship programs (1)
Explains how it addresses the skills mismatch between workers and the jobs available (1)
Explains the effect, e.g. more employable workers, lower long-term unemployment, possibly a lower NAIRU (1)

items.lead: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. The central bank's inflation target is 2 to 3 per cent.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the inflation rate in Year 3.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Outline ONE likely cause of the inflation shown in the table.
pts: Identifies a cause consistent with the data, e.g. demand inflation as unemployment falls to low levels (1)
Outlines how it raises prices, e.g. spending grows faster than capacity and tight labour markets push wages up (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Justify an appropriate monetary policy stance for this economy. Support your answer with reference to the table.
pts: Recommends contractionary (tighter) monetary policy: raise the cash rate (1)
Justifies it with the data: inflation (5.0%) is above the 2–3% target and unemployment is low and falling (3.6%), suggesting excess demand (1)
Explains how higher interest rates reduce spending and inflation, noting the possible rise in unemployment (1)

items.lead: The table shows balance of payments data for a hypothetical economy. Net errors and omissions are zero.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the balance on goods and services.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the balance on current account.
parts.ans: 15 + (−75) + (−2) = −$62 billion (a deficit).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the balance on the financial account.
parts.ans: Current account + capital account + financial account = 0, so −62 + (−1) + financial account = 0: the financial account is +$63 billion (a surplus).

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain the relationship between the financial account surplus and the net primary income deficit.
pts: The financial account surplus shows foreign borrowing and investment flowing in to fund the current account deficit (1)
These inflows add to the economy's foreign debt and equity liabilities (1)
Servicing them (interest and dividends) is recorded as debits in net primary income, so the deficit grows over time and must itself be financed (1)

table.cap: Exchange rates (foreign currency per A$1) and the Trade Weighted Index

items.lead: The table shows the value of the Australian dollar in two years (hypothetical data).

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the percentage change in the value of the A$ against the US dollar.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify the currency in the table against which the A$ appreciated.
parts.ans: The Japanese yen (one A$ buys 104 yen instead of 98).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why the TWI fell by much less than the A$ fell against the US dollar.
pts: The TWI measures the A$ against a basket of trading partners' currencies, weighted by trade (1)
The A$ rose against some currencies (the yen) and fell less against others, so the fall against the US dollar was partly offset (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain how this change in the exchange rate could affect Australian exporters.
pts: Australian exports become cheaper in US dollar terms, so exporters can sell more (1)
Contracts priced in US dollars earn more A$, lifting exporters' revenue and profits (1)

items.lead: The table shows budget data for a hypothetical economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the budget outcome in Year 2, in dollars and as a percentage of GDP.
parts.ans: 690 − 735 = −$45 billion, a deficit of 45 ÷ 2,780 × 100 = 1.6% of GDP.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify the change in the budget stance from Year 1 to Year 2.
parts.ans: More expansionary: the deficit widened from $20 billion (0.7% of GDP) to $45 billion (1.6% of GDP).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain ONE reason the deficit could have widened without any new policy decision.
pts: Automatic stabilisers: a slowdown lowers tax revenue and raises welfare payments (1)
So the cyclical component of the budget moves towards deficit, even though policy settings are unchanged (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain how the government could finance this deficit and ONE possible effect.
pts: By selling Commonwealth Government Securities (bonds) to investors in Australia or overseas (1)
Effect explained, e.g. borrowing competes for funds and may raise interest rates (crowding out) (1)
Or: borrowing from overseas adds to foreign debt and future interest payments in the current account (1)

items.lead: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. The marginal propensity to consume is 0.75.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: State whether national income will rise, fall or stay the same. Give a reason.
parts.ans: It will fall: withdrawals (120 + 200 + 140 = $460b) exceed injections (130 + 210 + 110 = $450b).

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the value of the multiplier.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the change in national income if government spending rises by $10 billion.
parts.ans: $10 billion × 4 = $40 billion increase.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain the implications of the multiplier for fluctuations in economic activity.
pts: Small changes in spending (such as investment or exports) cause larger changes in national income (1)
So shocks are magnified into larger booms and downturns; a larger multiplier means larger fluctuations (1)

items.lead: The table shows the share of income received by each fifth (quintile) of households in a hypothetical economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the ratio of the highest quintile's share of disposable income to the lowest quintile's share.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify which distribution is more equal, and explain why.
pts: Disposable income is more equal: the top quintile's share falls from 52% to 41% and the bottom's rises from 2% to 7% (1)
Because progressive income tax takes more from high incomes and transfer payments add to low incomes (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain how a Lorenz curve for disposable income would differ from one for market income.
pts: The Lorenz curve for disposable income lies closer to the line of equality (1)
Area A (between the line of equality and the curve) is smaller (1)
So the Gini coefficient for disposable income is lower than for market income (1)

items.lead: The table shows external data for a hypothetical economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate net foreign liabilities as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain TWO risks of a high level of net foreign debt.
pts: Servicing costs: more interest is paid overseas, widening the net primary income deficit and the CAD (2)
Vulnerability: lenders may demand a higher risk premium or withdraw funds, causing a depreciation or forcing contractionary policy; a depreciation raises the A$ cost of foreign-currency debt (2)

items.lead: The table shows price indexes for an economy's exports and imports.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the terms of trade in Year 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify the trend in the terms of trade from Year 2 to Year 3.
parts.ans: It deteriorated: Year 3 = 108 ÷ 106 × 100 = 101.9, down from 110.6.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain how the change in the terms of trade from Year 1 to Year 2 could affect the exchange rate and the balance on goods and services.
pts: Higher export prices mean more export income for each unit sold (1)
The balance on goods and services improves (1)
Overseas buyers need more of the domestic currency, so demand for it rises and it appreciates (1)

items.lead: The table shows data for a hypothetical economy. Year 1 is the base year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate real GDP in Year 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the real growth rate from Year 1 to Year 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Outline ONE limitation of real GDP as a measure of living standards.
pts: Identifies a limitation, e.g. it ignores population growth, the distribution of income, unpaid work, leisure or environmental damage (1)
Outlines why it matters, e.g. real GDP can rise while GDP per person falls if population grows faster (1)

items.lead: The table shows the domestic market for a good. The world price is $40, and the government imposes a tariff of $10 a unit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the quantity imported before the tariff.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the quantity imported after the tariff.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Calculate the government's revenue from the tariff.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain the effect of the tariff on the allocation of resources.
pts: Domestic production rises from 30,000 to 45,000 units, drawing resources into a less efficient industry (1)
Consumers buy less and pay more, so resources are not allocated to their most valued uses (1)
The result is a deadweight loss: production and consumption losses that no one gains (1)

items.lead: The table shows development indicators for three countries.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify which country is most likely a developing economy.
parts.ans: Country C: the lowest income, life expectancy and schooling.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain why GNI per person alone is a limited measure of a country's level of development.
pts: It measures average income, not how it is distributed (1)
It leaves out health, education, freedom and the environment, which are part of wellbeing (1)
Two countries with similar incomes can have very different life expectancy and schooling (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Outline how the Human Development Index gives a fuller picture.
pts: It combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living (1)
Each is measured (life expectancy, years of schooling, GNI per person at PPP) and combined in an index from 0 to 1 (1)

items.q: Outline what is meant by the global economy.
pts: All the world's national economies together (1)
Linked through trade, financial flows, investment, technology and the movement of people (1)

items.q: Explain why Gross World Product is usually compared using purchasing power parity rather than market exchange rates.
pts: GWP adds up the output of all economies, which must be converted to a common currency (1)
Market exchange rates do not reflect differences in what money buys in each country (1)
PPP adjusts for price differences, so it gives a better comparison of real output, raising the measured share of emerging and developing economies (1)

items.q: Explain why global financial flows have grown faster than world trade.
pts: Deregulation of financial markets and removal of capital controls since the 1980s (1)
Technology lets funds move instantly and cheaply around the world (1)
Investors seek the highest returns and spread risk, and floating exchange rates create speculation and hedging (1)

items.q: Explain how the international division of labour affects advanced economies such as Australia.
pts: Labour-intensive production moves to lower-cost economies (1)
Advanced economies specialise in skilled services, design and capital-intensive industries (1)
Workers in declining industries may face structural unemployment and need to retrain; skilled migration fills shortages (1)

items.q: Explain the influence of the G20 on the global economy.
pts: The G20 brings together major advanced and emerging economies, which produce most of world output (1)
It coordinates policy, e.g. stimulus during the global financial crisis in 2008–09 and financial regulation reforms (1)
Its influence is limited because its decisions are not binding (1)

items.q: Explain TWO benefits for Australia of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).
pts: First benefit explained, e.g. lower tariffs and common rules of origin across 15 Asia-Pacific economies make it easier for Australian firms to use regional supply chains (2)
Second benefit explained, e.g. better access for Australian services and investment, or a rules-based framework that includes China (2)

items.q: Outline the components of aggregate demand.
pts: AD = C + I + G + (X − M) (1)
Consumption by households and investment by firms (1)
Government spending and net exports (exports minus imports) (1)

items.q: Describe the phases of the business cycle.
pts: Upswing (recovery and boom): rising growth, falling unemployment, rising inflation (1)
Peak, then downswing: slowing growth, rising unemployment (1)
Trough: lowest point; a recession is two consecutive quarters of negative growth (1)

items.q: Explain why young people are more affected by unemployment than other groups.
pts: They have less experience and fewer skills than older workers (1)
They are often in casual or entry-level jobs that are cut first in a downturn (1)
When firms stop hiring, new entrants to the labour force find it hardest to get a first job (1)

items.q: Describe the trend in Australian inflation since 2020.
pts: Low inflation in 2020 during the COVID-19 recession (1)
A sharp rise to a peak of 7.8 per cent in late 2022, from supply shocks and strong demand (1)
A fall back towards the target in 2024–25, then a rise again in 2026 (4.9 per cent in the year to October) (1)

items.q: Describe the trends in Australia's net foreign liabilities over the past decade.
pts: Net foreign liabilities have fallen as a share of GDP (1)
Net foreign equity has turned negative as superannuation funds invest heavily overseas (1)
So the liabilities are now mainly net foreign debt, much of it in Australian dollars (1)

items.q: Explain how the sources of income differ between low-income and high-income households.
pts: Low-income households rely more on social welfare transfers, such as pensions and JobSeeker (1)
Middle-income households rely mainly on wages and salaries (1)
High-income households receive more income from capital (interest, dividends, rent) as well as high wages (1)

items.q: Explain why wealth is distributed more unequally than income.
pts: Wealth accumulates over a lifetime, so older households hold much more than younger ones (1)
Wealth earns income (rent, dividends, capital gains), which is reinvested, so it compounds (1)
Property and inheritance concentrate wealth; housing price rises have favoured existing owners (1)

items.q: Describe TWO dimensions of inequality in Australia.
pts: First dimension described, e.g. gender: women earn less on average (a gender pay gap) and retire with less superannuation (2)
Second dimension described, e.g. age, occupation, ethnic background or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, with an example (2)

items.q: Explain the concept of ecologically sustainable development.
pts: Development that meets the needs of today without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs (1)
Balances economic growth with protection of the environment (1)
Includes intergenerational equity and the precautionary principle (1)

items.q: Explain why preserving natural environments is an economic issue.
pts: Natural environments provide valuable services (clean water, biodiversity, tourism) that are not priced in markets (1)
Because they are public goods or common resources, markets overuse them (1)
Their loss is often permanent, so the cost falls on future generations (1)

items.q: Explain why economic growth is an objective of government policy.
pts: Growth creates jobs and lowers unemployment (1)
It raises incomes and living standards (1)
It increases tax revenue for services such as health and education (1)

items.q: Outline what is meant by full employment.
pts: An unemployment rate at about the NAIRU, not zero (1)
Only frictional, seasonal and some structural unemployment remain (1)

items.q: Explain why governments aim for low and stable inflation.
pts: High inflation erodes purchasing power, especially for people on fixed incomes (1)
Uncertainty about prices discourages investment and distorts decisions (1)
Inflation above trading partners' reduces international competitiveness (1)

items.q: Explain what external stability means for Australia.
pts: A sustainable current account deficit and level of foreign liabilities (1)
Australia can meet its foreign obligations, so investors stay confident (1)
An exchange rate without extreme swings (1)

items.q: Outline the objective of environmental sustainability.
pts: To use resources and the environment in a way that allows growth to continue in the future (1)
E.g. cutting emissions to net zero by 2050 and protecting natural environments (1)

items.q: Explain why governments aim for a more equitable distribution of income.
pts: To reduce poverty and give everyone access to a basic standard of living (1)
High inequality can weaken social cohesion and lower opportunity (1)
Lower-income households spend more of each dollar, supporting demand; equity is also a value judgement (1)

items.q: Explain the rationale for macroeconomic policies.
pts: To stabilise the business cycle by managing aggregate demand (1)
Expansionary policy in a downturn supports growth and employment (1)
Contractionary policy in a boom restrains inflation and external imbalances (1)

items.q: Explain how the government can use a budget surplus.
pts: Repay government debt, lowering future interest costs (1)
Invest in funds such as the Future Fund for future liabilities (1)
A surplus is contractionary, which can help restrain inflation in a boom (1)

items.q: Explain the purpose of monetary policy in Australia.
pts: To keep inflation within the 2–3 per cent target on average (1)
To support full employment (the maximum sustainable level of employment) (1)
Low, stable inflation and employment promote sustainable growth and welfare (1)

items.q: Outline the roles of the national and state industrial relations systems.
pts: The national system under the Fair Work Act 2009 covers most private-sector employees (1)
The Fair Work Commission sets minimum wages and awards and approves agreements; the Fair Work Ombudsman enforces them (1)
State systems cover state public servants and, in WA, unincorporated businesses (1)

items.q: Outline how minimum wages are set in Australia.
pts: The Fair Work Commission conducts the Annual Wage Review (1)
It sets the national minimum wage and modern award minimum wages (1)
It weighs factors such as living costs, inflation, productivity, employment and the needs of the low-paid (1)

items.q: Outline how industrial disputes are resolved in Australia.
pts: Through negotiation between the parties (1)
The Fair Work Commission can help by conciliation or mediation (1)
In some cases it can arbitrate (make a binding decision); protected industrial action is allowed only during bargaining (1)

items.q: Explain how education and training programs can reduce unemployment.
pts: They give workers the skills firms need, reducing the skills mismatch (1)
They help the long-term unemployed and young people become job-ready (1)
A more skilled workforce raises productivity and can lower the NAIRU (1)

items.q: Explain how emissions targets are used in environmental management.
pts: Targets set a goal, e.g. a 43 per cent cut on 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050 (1)
They guide policies such as the Safeguard Mechanism and support for renewable energy (1)
They give investors certainty and meet commitments under the Paris Agreement (1)

items.q: Explain how global influences can limit the effectiveness of Australian economic policy.
pts: Australia is a small open economy, affected by world growth, commodity prices and interest rates overseas (1)
A global downturn can reduce growth despite expansionary policy at home (1)
Global supply shocks (e.g. oil prices) can raise inflation that the RBA can only slow at the cost of jobs (1)

items.q: Explain how political constraints can limit economic policy.
pts: Governments may avoid unpopular measures, such as tax rises or spending cuts, before an election (1)
Legislation must pass the Senate, where minor parties may block it (1)
Promises and pressure from interest groups can lead to policies that are not the best economically (1)

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of government policies in reducing unemployment in Australia.
pts: Macroeconomic policy supported demand during COVID-19, helping unemployment fall to about 3.5 per cent by 2022 (1)
Monetary tightening from 2022 and in 2026 saw unemployment rise gradually (to 4.9 per cent in October 2026) (1)
Labour market programs target structural and long-term unemployment (1)
Judgement: effective in reducing cyclical unemployment, less so for structural unemployment (1)

items.q: Explain how government policies can improve Australia's external stability.
pts: Fiscal consolidation raises national saving and reduces reliance on foreign borrowing (1)
Microeconomic reform improves international competitiveness and export performance (1)
Monetary policy keeps inflation low, supporting competitiveness and investor confidence (1)
A floating exchange rate helps absorb external shocks (1)

items.q: Explain how government policies affect the distribution of income in Australia.
pts: Progressive income tax narrows differences in after-tax income (1)
Transfer payments lift low incomes (1)
The social wage provides services such as Medicare and education (1)
Minimum wages and labour market policies affect market incomes (1)

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of policies to achieve environmental sustainability in Australia.
pts: Policies include the Safeguard Mechanism, renewable energy support, targets and regulation (1)
Emissions have fallen (about a quarter below 2005 levels), largely from electricity and land use (1)
Limits: emissions from transport and industry, political constraints, and dependence on fossil fuel exports (1)
Judgement on whether the 2030 target will be met (1)

items.q: Explain how changes in technology have increased world trade in goods and services.
pts: Containerisation and larger ships have cut the cost of moving goods (1)
The internet and digital platforms let services such as education, finance and design be traded across borders (1)
Lower costs and better information mean more goods and services can be traded profitably, so trade grows faster than world output (1)

items.q: Explain TWO effects of transnational corporations on a host economy.
pts: One positive effect, explained: e.g. foreign direct investment brings capital, technology and management skills, raising productivity and creating jobs (2)
One negative effect, explained: e.g. profits flow back to the home country, local firms may be crowded out, or TNCs may use transfer pricing to reduce tax paid (2)

items.q: Explain how a downturn in the international business cycle can affect the Australian economy.
pts: Weaker growth overseas lowers demand for Australian exports, especially resources (1)
Lower export volumes and prices reduce the terms of trade, national income and investment in the resources sector (1)
Growth slows and unemployment rises in Australia; the dollar may depreciate, which partly cushions the effect (1)

items.q: Explain how free trade can increase living standards in both countries that trade.
pts: Each country specialises in goods in which it has a comparative advantage (lower opportunity cost) (1)
Specialisation raises total output, so world production rises (1)
Through trade, each country consumes beyond its own production possibilities (1)
Consumers benefit from lower prices and more choice; firms gain economies of scale from larger markets (1)

items.q: Distinguish between the roles of the World Trade Organization and the International Monetary Fund.
pts: WTO: sets and enforces the rules of world trade (1)
WTO: runs negotiations to reduce trade barriers and settles trade disputes between members (1)
IMF: promotes international financial stability and monitors members' economic policies (1)
IMF: lends to countries facing balance of payments crises, usually with conditions (1)

items.q: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of bilateral free trade agreements compared with multilateral agreements.
pts: Advantage: bilateral agreements are quicker and easier to negotiate than multilateral deals that need every WTO member to agree (1)
Advantage: they can go further, covering services, investment and other areas (1)
Disadvantage: they can cause trade diversion away from lower-cost non-members (1)
Disadvantage: many overlapping agreements with different rules of origin (a "noodle bowl") raise compliance costs; judgement on balance (1)

items.q: Explain the infant industry argument for protection.
pts: A new industry has higher average costs than established overseas firms because it has not yet reached a large scale (1)
Temporary protection lets it grow and gain economies of scale and experience, lowering costs (1)
Once it can compete, protection should be removed; the risk is that the industry never becomes competitive and protection becomes permanent (1)

items.q: With the aid of a diagram, explain the effects of a tariff on domestic producers and consumers.
pts: Diagram: domestic D and S, world price Pw and Pw+t, Q1 to Q4 (1)
The domestic price rises from Pw to Pw+t (1)
Domestic producers increase output from Q1 to Q2 and gain producer surplus (1)
Consumers pay more and buy less (Q4 to Q3), losing consumer surplus; imports fall (1)

items.q: Distinguish between economic growth and economic development.
pts: Economic growth is an increase in real GDP, the volume of goods and services produced (1)
Economic development is a broader improvement in wellbeing: health, education, living standards and freedom (1)
Growth can occur without development if the gains are not shared or come with environmental damage; development is measured by indicators such as the HDI (1)

items.q: Explain why the global distribution of income has changed since 1990.
pts: Rapid growth in large emerging economies, especially China and India, has raised incomes for billions of people (1)
This has narrowed the gap between countries and greatly reduced extreme poverty (1)
Inequality within many countries has risen, as gains from globalisation and technology went mostly to owners of capital and skilled workers (1)
Many developing economies, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have grown more slowly, so some gaps remain wide (1)

items.q: Outline ONE feature that distinguishes emerging economies from developing economies.
pts: A clear feature, e.g. emerging economies have fast growth driven by industrialisation and rising exports of manufactures (2)
A contrast with developing economies, e.g. which have low incomes and rely mostly on agriculture or commodity exports (1)

items.q: Explain TWO reasons for differences in living standards between nations.
pts: First reason explained, e.g. differences in human capital: education and health raise productivity and incomes (2)
Second reason explained, e.g. institutions and governance (rule of law, property rights, stable government) encourage investment; or access to capital and technology; or geography and resources (2)

items.q: Assess the effects of globalisation on the environment.
pts: Negative: higher world output and trade raise energy use, greenhouse gas emissions and resource depletion (1)
Negative: production may shift to countries with weaker environmental rules ("pollution havens") (1)
Positive: globalisation spreads cleaner technology, such as cheaper solar panels and batteries (1)
Positive: global cooperation through agreements such as the Paris Agreement (1)
Judgement supported by reasoning, e.g. net effect depends on policy and technology (1)

items.q: Analyse the influence of globalisation on the economy of a country other than Australia.
pts: Names the economy and describes how it is integrated into the global economy, e.g. China's trade, foreign investment and WTO entry in 2001 (1)
Effect on growth, with evidence, e.g. export-led growth averaging close to 10 per cent a year for three decades (1)
Effect on development or poverty, e.g. hundreds of millions lifted out of extreme poverty (1)
A cost, e.g. rising inequality between regions, pollution, or dependence on exports and exposure to tariffs (1)
Links the effects back to globalisation rather than describing them separately (1)

items.q: Explain why the direction of Australia's trade has shifted towards Asia.
pts: Rapid industrialisation in Asia, especially China, has raised demand for Australian resources and energy (1)
Rising incomes in Asia increased demand for Australian services such as education and tourism, and for food (1)
Proximity, trade agreements (e.g. with China, Japan and Korea) and Britain's entry to the European Economic Community in 1973 shifted trade away from Europe (1)

items.q: Explain how the purchase of an Australian business by a foreign company affects Australia's balance of payments, now and in the future.
pts: Now: the purchase is a capital inflow, recorded as a credit (foreign direct investment in Australia) in the financial account (1)
It adds to Australia's foreign liabilities (net foreign equity) (1)
In future: profits and dividends paid to the foreign owners are debits in net primary income (1)
This widens the current account deficit over time (1)

items.q: Analyse the relationship between the balance on the capital and financial account and the net primary income balance.
pts: A surplus on the capital and financial account means foreign borrowing and investment flow into Australia (1)
These inflows add to Australia's foreign debt and foreign equity liabilities (1)
Servicing the liabilities requires interest and dividend payments overseas, debits in net primary income (1)
So persistent financial account surpluses lead to larger net primary income deficits, which widen the current account deficit and must themselves be financed: a cycle (1)

items.q: Explain how a rise in the terms of trade affects Australia's balance of payments.
pts: The terms of trade rise when export prices rise relative to import prices (1)
Export income rises, so the balance on goods and services improves (1)
The current account deficit narrows (or a surplus appears, as in 2019–20 to 2022–23) (1)
Profits of foreign-owned mining firms rise, so more dividends flow overseas, widening the net primary income deficit and partly offsetting the gain (1)

items.q: With the aid of a diagram, explain how a rise in Australian interest rates relative to overseas rates affects the value of the Australian dollar.
pts: Diagram of the market for A$ with demand shifting right (D1 to D2), and e1 to e2 (1)
Higher relative interest rates raise the return on Australian assets (1)
Foreign investors buy A$ to invest in Australia, so demand for A$ rises (1)
The exchange rate appreciates from e1 to e2 (1)

items.q: Compare a floating exchange rate with a fixed exchange rate.
pts: Floating: the rate is set by supply and demand; the central bank intervenes rarely (1)
Fixed: the government or central bank sets the rate and defends it by buying or selling currency (1)
Floating: monetary policy can target inflation, and the rate absorbs shocks such as a fall in commodity prices (1)
Fixed: gives certainty to traders, but needs large reserves and can be attacked by speculators (1)

items.q: Analyse the effects of a sustained depreciation of the Australian dollar on the Australian economy.
pts: Exports become cheaper overseas and imports dearer, raising international competitiveness (1)
Net exports and aggregate demand rise, lifting growth and employment (1)
Import prices rise, adding to inflation (imported inflation) (1)
The trade balance may worsen first and then improve (J-curve); the A$ cost of foreign-currency debt rises (1)
Valuation effects: foreign-currency assets are worth more in A$, which can lower net foreign liabilities (1)

items.q: Explain the effects of tariff reductions on Australian firms and consumers.
pts: Consumers pay lower prices for imported goods and have more choice, raising real incomes (1)
Firms that use imported inputs gain lower costs, improving competitiveness (1)
Import-competing firms face more competition; some may close, causing structural unemployment (1)
Resources move to more efficient, export-oriented industries in the long run (1)

items.q: Explain how protectionist policies of other countries affect Australia.
pts: Tariffs or quotas on Australian goods reduce export volumes and prices, e.g. China's duties on Australian wine and barley from 2020 (1)
Export income and employment in the affected industries fall (1)
Subsidies overseas (e.g. EU and US farm support) lower world prices, hurting Australian exporters in third markets (1)
Trade wars between major economies slow world growth and divert goods to Australia, affecting Australian firms indirectly (1)

items.q: Explain how the multiplier affects the impact of a change in government spending on national income.
pts: A rise in government spending is an injection that becomes income for others (1)
Recipients spend part of each extra dollar (the MPC), creating further rounds of income (1)
National income rises by a multiple of the original change: ΔY = ΔG × k, where k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) (1)

items.q: Assess the arguments for and against increasing Australia's rate of economic growth.
pts: For: higher growth creates jobs and lowers unemployment (1)
For: higher incomes and tax revenue fund services and raise living standards (1)
Against: growth above capacity raises inflation and widens the current account deficit (1)
Against: environmental costs and resource depletion; judgement about sustainable growth (1)

items.q: Explain how improvements in efficiency and technology increase aggregate supply.
pts: New technology and better ways of working raise productivity: more output from the same inputs (1)
Unit costs fall, so firms can supply more at each price level (1)
Aggregate supply (and potential output) shifts right, allowing growth without extra inflation (1)

items.q: Distinguish between cyclical and structural unemployment, using an example of each.
pts: Cyclical: caused by a lack of aggregate demand in a downturn (1)
Example, e.g. retail or construction jobs lost in a recession (1)
Structural: caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available, often from technology or changes in industry (1)
Example, e.g. car manufacturing workers after the closure of car plants in 2017 (1)

items.q: Explain the relationship between the NAIRU and inflation.
pts: The NAIRU is the lowest unemployment rate that can be sustained without inflation rising (1)
Below the NAIRU, tight labour markets push wage growth up, raising costs and inflation (1)
Above it, spare capacity keeps wage growth and inflation subdued; structural reform can lower the NAIRU (1)

items.q: Explain TWO costs of unemployment.
pts: An economic cost explained, e.g. lost output and lower living standards, or higher welfare spending and lower tax revenue (2)
A social cost explained, e.g. poorer mental health, family stress, or loss of skills that makes it harder to find work later (2)

items.q: Explain why the RBA pays close attention to underlying inflation as well as headline inflation.
pts: Headline inflation can be swung by volatile or one-off price changes such as fuel, fruit or government rebates (1)
Underlying measures such as the trimmed mean remove extreme price changes, showing the trend in inflation (1)
Monetary policy works with lags, so the RBA responds to the persistent trend rather than temporary changes (1)

items.q: Explain how a depreciation of the Australian dollar can cause inflation.
pts: A depreciation raises the A$ price of imported goods (1)
Consumer goods such as cars and electronics cost more, raising the CPI directly (1)
Imported inputs such as fuel and machinery cost more, raising firms' costs (cost inflation) (1)
Higher import prices can lift inflationary expectations and wage claims (1)

items.q: Explain ONE positive and ONE negative effect of inflation.
pts: A positive effect explained, e.g. moderate inflation lets real wages adjust and avoids the risks of deflation (2)
A negative effect explained, e.g. lower purchasing power for people on fixed incomes, uncertainty for investment, or loss of international competitiveness (2)

items.q: Discuss the effects of a continued current account deficit on the Australian economy.
pts: A CAD allows investment higher than national saving, funding growth (1)
It adds to foreign liabilities, so more income is paid overseas (net primary income), widening the CAD further (1)
A high level of foreign debt can raise the risk premium on borrowing and make the economy vulnerable to a loss of investor confidence (1)
It can lead to downward pressure on the exchange rate and constrain policy (1)
Balanced judgement, e.g. sustainable if borrowing funds productive investment (the Pitchford view) (1)

items.q: Explain how the tax and transfer system reduces inequality in Australia.
pts: Progressive income tax: higher earners pay a higher share of income (1)
Transfer payments, such as JobSeeker and the Age Pension, lift the incomes of low-income households (1)
The social wage (Medicare, public education, housing assistance) gives services regardless of income (1)
Together these make disposable income more equal than market income: the Gini coefficient falls (1)

items.q: Assess the economic costs and benefits of inequality.
pts: Benefit: differences in income create incentives to work, train and invest (1)
Cost: low-income households consume less, which can weaken aggregate demand (1)
Cost: lost potential, as people cannot afford education, and lower social cohesion (1)
Judgement: moderate inequality may encourage effort, but high inequality reduces growth and wellbeing (1)

items.q: Explain why the market fails to protect the natural environment.
pts: Negative externalities: producers ignore external costs such as pollution, so output is too high (1)
Public goods and free riders: clean air and biodiversity are non-excludable, so they are underprovided (1)
Prices do not reflect the full social cost, so resources are overused (1)
Future generations are not represented in today's market decisions (1)

items.q: Explain how a conflict can arise between the objectives of economic growth and environmental sustainability.
pts: Faster growth means more production and energy use (1)
With current technology this raises emissions, pollution and resource use (1)
Policies to cut emissions, such as a price on carbon, raise costs and can slow growth in the short run (1)
Clean technology and structural change can reduce the conflict over time (1)

items.q: Explain how automatic stabilisers in the budget help reduce fluctuations in economic activity.
pts: Automatic stabilisers are parts of the budget that change with the cycle without new decisions (1)
In a downturn, tax revenue falls and welfare payments rise, supporting incomes and AD (1)
In a boom, tax revenue rises and welfare payments fall, restraining AD (1)
So the budget moves towards deficit in downturns and surplus in booms, smoothing the cycle (1)

items.q: Outline how the RBA implements a change in monetary policy.
pts: The Monetary Policy Board decides the target for the cash rate and announces it (1)

The RBA manages the supply of money in the overnight market (exchange settlement balances), through open market operations and the interest rates on its standing facilities, so the cash rate settles at the target (1)
Banks pass the change through to lending and deposit rates (1)
