items.q: Analyse how an increase in the cash rate affects economic activity and the exchange rate.
pts: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and repayments on variable loans (1)
Consumption and investment fall; asset prices and wealth may fall too (1)
Aggregate demand slows, reducing growth and inflation; unemployment may rise (1)
The higher return on Australian assets increases demand for A$, causing an appreciation (1)
The appreciation lowers import prices and net exports, adding to the effect on inflation; note the time lags (1)

items.q: Explain how competition policy can improve the efficiency of a product market.
pts: Competition policy stops anti-competitive conduct such as cartels and the misuse of market power (1)
More competition forces firms to cut costs and prices (allocative and technical efficiency) (1)
Firms innovate to keep customers (dynamic efficiency) (1)
Consumers gain lower prices and more choice; resources go to their most valued uses (1)

items.q: Discuss the arguments for and against decentralised wage determination.
pts: For: pay can reflect each workplace's productivity, which can lift productivity growth (1)
For: flexibility for firms to adjust to their own conditions (1)
Against: workers with little bargaining power may fall behind, widening inequality (1)
Against: can lead to more industrial disputes; safety nets such as the NES and awards remain important (1)

items.q: Compare the use of regulation and market-based policies to reduce pollution.
pts: Regulation sets rules, such as emission standards or bans, enforced by penalties (1)
Market-based policies, such as taxes or emissions trading, put a price on pollution (1)
Regulation gives a more certain result but can be costly because every firm must meet the same rule (1)
Market-based policies cut pollution where it is cheapest, but the outcome of a tax is less certain (1)

items.q: Explain how time lags limit the effectiveness of fiscal policy.
pts: Recognition lag: data are delayed, so problems are identified late (1)
Implementation lag: budget changes need planning and laws passed by Parliament (1)
Impact lag: spending and tax changes take time to affect demand, so policy may take effect when it is no longer needed (1)

items.q: Assess the effectiveness of microeconomic policies in promoting economic growth.
pts: Microeconomic reform raises productivity and shifts aggregate supply right, lifting potential growth (1)
Evidence, e.g. tariff cuts, competition policy and financial deregulation contributed to strong productivity growth in the 1990s (1)
Limitations: benefits take years, there are short-term job losses, and reform can be politically difficult (1)
Judgement: effective for long-run growth, but slower productivity growth since the mid-2000s suggests the pace of reform matters (1)

A tax, regulation or tradeable permits
A subsidy or free provision

items.q: A heatwave hits Sydney over summer. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the market for ice cream.
items.ans: Hot weather changes tastes in favour of ice cream, so demand increases: the demand curve shifts right from D1 to D2. At the old price there is a shortage, so the price rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity bought and sold rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Household incomes fall during a recession. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the market for overseas holidays (a normal good).
items.ans: Lower incomes reduce demand for a normal good, so the demand curve shifts left from D1 to D2. The price falls from P1 to P2 and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Strong population growth adds many new households to a city. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the market for rental housing.
items.ans: More households increase demand for rental housing: the demand curve shifts right from D1 to D2. Rents rise from P1 to P2 and the quantity of rental housing rises from Q1 to Q2 (only a little in the short run, because supply is inelastic).

items.q: Frost destroys a large part of the coffee crop in Brazil, a major producer. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the world market for coffee.
items.ans: Less coffee is available at every price, so supply decreases: the supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2. The price of coffee rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: A new manufacturing technology lowers the cost of making solar panels. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the market for solar panels.
items.ans: Lower production costs mean firms will supply more at every price: supply increases and the curve shifts right from S1 to S2. The price falls from P1 to P2 and the quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Cattle farmers expect beef prices to rise strongly next year, so they hold back cattle from sale. Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect on the market for beef this year.
items.ans: Expected future prices are a non-price factor: holding stock back reduces supply now, so the supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2. The price rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity sold falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: A pizza shop cuts the price of its pizzas. Nothing else changes. Draw a diagram to show the effect on the quantity of pizzas demanded.
items.ans: A change in the good's own price is a movement along the demand curve, not a shift. The price falls from P1 to P2, so the quantity demanded expands from Q1 to Q2 (point A to point B): an expansion of demand.

items.q: The price of strawberries rises. Nothing else changes. Draw a diagram to show the effect on the quantity of strawberries supplied.
items.ans: The higher price is a movement along the supply curve: the quantity supplied expands from Q1 to Q2 as the price rises from P1 to P2 (point A to point B), because growing strawberries is now more profitable.

items.q: To make renting more affordable, the government sets a maximum rent below the equilibrium rent. Draw a diagram to show the effect on the rental market.
items.ans: The binding ceiling Pmax is below the equilibrium price Pe. At Pmax the quantity demanded (Qd) is greater than the quantity supplied (Qs), so there is a shortage of rental housing. Fewer homes are rented than at equilibrium (Qe), and landlords may let homes run down or sell them.

items.q: The government guarantees wheat farmers a minimum price above the equilibrium price. Draw a diagram to show the effect on the market for wheat.
items.ans: The binding floor Pmin is above the equilibrium price Pe. At Pmin the quantity supplied (Qs) exceeds the quantity demanded (Qd): a surplus of wheat, which the government may have to buy and store.

items.q: The government increases the excise tax on each packet of cigarettes. Draw a diagram to show the effect on the market for cigarettes.
items.ans: The tax raises producers' costs, so supply decreases: the supply curve shifts up by the amount of the tax, from S1 to S2. The price consumers pay rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Producers keep P3 (P2 less the tax). The shaded rectangle is the tax revenue (tax × Q2). Because demand is inelastic, consumers bear most of the tax.

items.q: The government places a tax of 50 cents on each bottle of sugary drink. Draw a diagram to show the effect, and shade the tax revenue.
items.ans: Supply shifts up by the tax from S1 to S2. The price rises from P1 to P2 and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Consumers pay P2, producers keep P3 (P2 − 50 cents), and the government's revenue is the tax per bottle × Q2 (the shaded rectangle). The red triangle is the deadweight loss, the consumption and production that no longer take place.

items.q: Coal-fired power stations release emissions that harm people living nearby and the climate. Draw a diagram to show this negative externality in production.
items.ans: The market supply curve reflects only private costs (MPC). The marginal social cost (MSC) is higher, because of the cost of emissions to others. The market produces Q_m, where D (MPB) = MPC, more than the efficient quantity Qs, where D = MSC. The shaded triangle is the deadweight loss from over-production.

items.q: When a person is vaccinated, others also benefit because the disease spreads less. Draw a diagram to show this positive externality in consumption.
items.ans: The demand curve shows private benefits only (D, MPB). The marginal social benefit (MSB) is higher, because of the benefit to others. The market settles at Q_m, where MPB = S, less than the efficient quantity Qs, where MSB = MSC (S). The shaded triangle is the welfare lost through under-consumption; a subsidy or free provision could raise output to Qs.

items.q: Education is a merit good. Draw a diagram to show why, left to the market, too little education would be consumed, and explain ONE policy to correct this.
items.ans: Society gains extra benefits from education, so MSB lies above private demand (D, MPB). The market produces Q_m, less than the efficient Qs where MSB = S (MSC). A subsidy that lowers the price, or free provision of schooling, raises consumption towards Qs and removes the welfare loss (shaded).

items.q: Draw a relatively elastic demand curve and show the effect of a small rise in price on the quantity demanded.
items.ans: A relatively elastic demand curve is flat. A small rise in price from P1 to P2 causes a large fall in quantity demanded from Q1 to Q2, so the percentage change in quantity is larger than the percentage change in price (PED > 1).

items.q: Draw a demand curve for petrol, a good with price inelastic demand in the short run, and show the effect of a rise in its price.
items.ans: The demand curve is steep. A large rise in price from P1 to P2 causes only a small fall in quantity demanded from Q1 to Q2 (PED < 1), because petrol has few close substitutes in the short run.

items.q: Draw a perfectly inelastic demand curve.
items.ans: A vertical demand curve at Q1: the quantity demanded does not change whatever the price (PED = 0).

items.q: Draw a unit elastic demand curve and show a rise in price from P1 to P2.
items.ans: A unit elastic demand curve is a curve (a rectangular hyperbola) along which the percentage change in quantity demanded always equals the percentage change in price (PED = 1), so total revenue does not change when the price changes.

items.q: Draw a supply curve for new housing in the short run, and show the effect of a rise in house prices on the quantity supplied.
items.ans: Supply is inelastic in the short run (a steep curve) because building takes time and land and approvals are limited. A large rise in price from P1 to P2 brings only a small rise in quantity supplied from Q1 to Q2 (PES < 1).

items.q: A clothing maker has plenty of spare capacity. Draw its supply curve for T-shirts and show the effect of a small rise in price.
items.ans: Supply is elastic (a flat curve), because spare capacity lets the firm raise output quickly. A small rise in price from P1 to P2 brings a large rise in quantity supplied from Q1 to Q2 (PES > 1).

items.q: Business confidence rises and many firms plan to borrow to expand. Draw a loanable funds diagram to show the effect on interest rates.
items.ans: More investment plans increase the demand for loanable funds: the demand curve shifts right from D1 to D2. The interest rate rises from r1 to r2 and the quantity of funds borrowed and lent rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Households decide to save a larger share of their income. Draw a loanable funds diagram to show the effect on interest rates.
items.ans: More saving increases the supply of loanable funds: the supply curve shifts right from S1 to S2. The interest rate falls from r1 to r2 and the quantity of funds lent rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Foreign investors become worried about risk and withdraw funds from Australia. Draw a loanable funds diagram to show the effect on interest rates in Australia.
items.ans: Less foreign investment reduces the supply of loanable funds: the supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2. The interest rate rises from r1 to r2 and the quantity of funds lent falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: Draw a long-run average cost (LRAC) curve. Label economies of scale, diseconomies of scale and the technical optimum.
items.ans: The LRAC curve is U-shaped. While it falls, the firm enjoys economies of scale (e.g. bulk buying, specialisation, better technology). Its lowest point is the technical optimum (output Q*). Beyond it, diseconomies of scale (e.g. coordination and communication problems) push average costs up.

items.q: Draw a diagram of the business cycle. Label the trend, a peak, a trough, a contraction and an expansion.
items.ans: Real GDP rises over time along its trend, but fluctuates around it. A peak is a high point, followed by a contraction (downturn) to a trough, the low point, then an expansion (upturn) to the next peak.

items.q: An economy's workers become more skilled and its technology improves. Draw a production possibilities frontier to show the effect.
items.ans: Better skills and technology increase the economy's productive capacity, so the frontier shifts outwards from PPF1 to PPF2: the economy can now produce more of both goods.

items.q: An economy is in recession and many workers are unemployed. Draw a production possibilities frontier and mark the economy's position.
items.ans: The economy is at a point such as A inside its frontier: it could produce more of both goods with the same resources, because labour and capital are unemployed or underemployed.

items.q: Draw a production possibilities frontier. Mark two efficient combinations (A and B), an inefficient combination (C) and an unattainable combination (D).
items.ans: A and B lie on the frontier: all resources are used efficiently. C lies inside it: some resources are unemployed. D lies outside it: it cannot be produced with current resources and technology. Moving from A to B has an opportunity cost: less of the capital good for more of the consumer good.

items.q: Self-service checkouts and AI reduce the number of checkout workers supermarkets need. Draw a labour market diagram to show the effect on the market for checkout workers.
items.ans: Automation reduces the demand for checkout workers: the demand curve shifts left from D1 to D2. The wage falls from W1 to W2 and employment falls from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: The government makes childcare cheaper and more widely available. Draw a labour market diagram to show the effect on the supply of labour.
items.ans: Lower childcare costs encourage more parents to work, so the supply of labour increases: the supply curve shifts right from S1 to S2. The wage falls from W1 to W2 (or rises more slowly) and employment rises from Q1 to Q2.

items.q: A minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage in the market for low-skilled labour. Draw a diagram to show the effect.
items.ans: At Wmin, above the equilibrium wage We, the quantity of labour supplied (Qs) is greater than the quantity demanded (Qd). The gap is unemployment. Workers who keep their jobs earn more, but fewer are employed than at equilibrium (Qe).

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the difference between a change in quantity demanded and a change in demand."
items.text: A fall in the price of a good causes [[an increase in demand => an expansion in the quantity demanded]], which is shown as a movement along the demand curve. A change in a non-price factor, such as income, shifts the whole demand curve. For example, if incomes rise, the demand for a normal good [[decreases => increases]] and the demand curve shifts to the [[left => right]]. If the price of a substitute falls, consumers switch to the substitute, so the demand for the original good [[increases => decreases]].

items.q: This paragraph answers: "A bakery raises the price of a loaf from $5 to $6 and sales fall from 1,000 to 900 loaves a week. Calculate and explain the price elasticity of demand."
items.text: The price rises by [[$1, or 10 per cent => $1, or 20 per cent]] and the quantity demanded falls by 10 per cent. Using the percentage method, PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5. Because PED is [[greater => less]] than 1, demand is relatively inelastic. This means the bakery's total revenue [[falls => rises]] when it raises its price: it rises from $5,000 to $5,400 a week.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain the effects of a binding price ceiling."
items.text: A binding price ceiling is set [[above => below]] the equilibrium price. At this lower price the quantity demanded expands and the quantity supplied [[expands => contracts]]. As a result there is a [[surplus => shortage]] of the good. Some buyers who are willing to pay more cannot buy the good, so queues, waiting lists or black markets may develop.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how a tax can correct a negative externality in production."
items.text: When a firm pollutes, the marginal social cost of production is [[less => greater]] than its marginal private cost, because others bear part of the cost. The market therefore produces [[less => more]] than the socially efficient quantity. A tax equal to the external cost raises the firm's costs, so supply [[increases => decreases]]. The price rises and the quantity falls towards the efficient level, where marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Describe the stages of the business cycle."
items.text: During an expansion, real GDP grows and unemployment [[rises => falls]]. The highest point of the cycle is the [[trough => peak]], when the economy is close to full capacity and inflation is likely to be rising. A contraction follows, during which growth slows or real GDP falls and unemployment rises. The lowest point of the cycle is the trough. Two consecutive quarters of [[rising => falling]] real GDP are often called a recession.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain what a production possibilities frontier shows."
items.text: A production possibilities frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its [[unlimited => given]] resources and technology. A point on the frontier shows that resources are used efficiently. A point [[outside => inside]] the frontier shows unemployed resources. Moving along the frontier to produce more of one good means producing less of the other: this is the [[profit => opportunity cost]] of the choice. An improvement in technology shifts the frontier [[inwards => outwards]].

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain how a rise in household saving affects interest rates."
items.text: When households save more, the [[demand for => supply of]] loanable funds increases. The supply curve shifts to the right, so the interest rate [[rises => falls]] and the quantity of funds borrowed and lent rises. Lower interest rates reduce the cost of credit, so businesses are more likely to borrow to invest. Lower mortgage rates also make housing [[less => more]] affordable for new borrowers, although cheaper credit can push up house prices over time.

items.q: This paragraph answers: "Explain when the circular flow of income is in equilibrium."
items.text: Leakages are income that is not passed on as spending on domestic goods and services: savings, taxation and [[exports => imports]]. Injections are spending that comes from outside the household–business flow: investment, government spending and exports. The economy is in equilibrium when [[S + T + X => S + T + M]] equals I + G + X. If injections are greater than leakages, national income will [[fall => rise]] until the two are equal again.

items.q: The basic economic problem arises because
o: resources are unlimited but people's wants are limited
people's wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are scarce
governments control most of the economy's resources
prices are too high for many consumers

e.why: Scarcity, unlimited wants and limited resources, forces every economy to make choices. A reverses the problem; C and D describe particular situations, not the basic problem.

items.q: Kate could spend Saturday at the beach or work a shift that pays $160. She chooses to work. What is the opportunity cost of working?
o: The cost of travelling to work
The day at the beach she gives up

e.why: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made, here the day at the beach. The $160 is the benefit of working, not its cost.

items.q: Which of the following is an economic decision made by a producer?
o: A family deciding whether to buy a new car
A bakery deciding how many loaves to bake each morning
The Federal Government deciding how much to spend on hospitals
A student deciding whether to save her part-time earnings

e.why: Producers (businesses) decide what and how much to produce. A and D are consumer decisions; C is a government decision.

items.q: A café owner is deciding whether to stay open one extra hour each evening. The extra hour would bring in $300 of sales and add $220 to wages and other costs. Using the cost–benefit principle at the margin, she should
o: stay open, because the marginal benefit ($300) is greater than the marginal cost ($220)
close, because the café already makes a profit during the day
stay open only if the café's total revenue for the day is above its total cost
close, because wages are a cost of production

e.why: A decision at the margin compares the extra benefit with the extra cost of that one choice. The extra hour adds $80 to profit, so it is worth doing; the rest of the day's results (B, C) do not change that.

items.q: A council gives a $50 rebate to households that buy a water-saving shower head. Some of these households then take longer showers. This is an example of
o: an intended consequence of a disincentive
the opportunity cost of saving water
an unintended consequence of an incentive

e.why: The rebate is an incentive to save water; longer showers are a response the council did not intend, which reduces the water saved.

items.q: Many people keep the superannuation fund their employer chose for them, even when another fund would charge lower fees and leave them better off. Behavioural economists explain this mainly as
o: the law of diminishing marginal utility

e.why: People tend to stick with the default option even when switching would benefit them, which challenges the assumption that people always act rationally in their own interest.

items.q: Which of the following is a macroeconomic issue?
o: The price of avocados at a local market
The wage paid to a nurse
A firm's decision to hire one more worker

e.why: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as total output, unemployment and inflation. A, B and D concern individual markets, workers or firms (microeconomics).

items.q: Economic models such as demand and supply often assume ceteris paribus. This means that
o: the government does not intervene in markets
all other factors are held constant while one factor changes

e.why: Ceteris paribus ("other things equal") lets a model show the effect of one change at a time. It is a simplifying assumption, not a claim that nothing else ever changes.

items.q: Which factor income is the reward for entrepreneurship?

e.why: Entrepreneurs organise the other factors and take the risk, and their reward is profit. Rent is paid for land, wages for labour and interest for capital.

items.q: A tractor used on a farm is an example of which factor of production?

e.why: Capital is a man-made good used to produce other goods and services. The soil the tractor works is land.

items.q: In a planned (command) economy, the question "What to produce?" is mainly answered by

e.why: In a planned economy the state owns most resources and a central authority decides what is produced. A and D describe a free market economy; C describes a pre-industrial (traditional) economy.

items.q: Australia is best described as a mixed market economy because
o: the government owns all the major industries
prices are set by a central planning authority
production is decided mainly by tradition
most resources are allocated by markets, while the government provides some goods and services and regulates markets

e.why: A mixed economy combines market allocation with a significant role for government, for example health, education, welfare and regulation in Australia.

items.q: When money acts as a measure of value (unit of account), it
o: is accepted in exchange for goods and services
allows the values of different goods and services to be compared in the same units
can be saved and spent later

e.why: Prices in dollars let us compare the value of very different things. A is money as a medium of exchange; C is money as a store of value.

items.q: The key economic question "How to distribute production?" is about
o: which goods and services to produce
which methods and combinations of resources to use
who receives the goods and services that are produced
what quantity of each good to produce

e.why: Distribution is about who gets the output. A is "What to produce?", B is "How to produce?" and D is "How much to produce?".

items.q: The production possibilities schedule shows an economy that produces only food and machines. What is the opportunity cost of increasing machine production from 20 to 30 units?

e.why: Moving from C to D, food falls from 75 to 55 tonnes, so the 10 extra machines cost 20 tonnes of food (2 tonnes per machine).

items.q: A point inside an economy's production possibilities frontier shows
o: a combination of goods that cannot be produced with current resources
full and efficient use of all resources

e.why: Inside the frontier the economy could produce more of one good without giving up any of the other, so some resources are idle or not used efficiently. A describes a point outside the frontier.

items.q: Which of the following would shift an economy's production possibilities frontier outwards?
o: A new technology that raises productivity in all industries
Moving resources from making consumer goods to making capital goods

e.why: Better technology lets the same resources produce more of both goods. A moves the economy from inside the frontier towards it; C is a movement along the frontier; D moves the economy inside it.

items.q: Which of the following is an assumption of the production possibilities model?
o: Prices are set by the government
Resources can grow without limit during the period
The economy produces two goods with a fixed quantity of resources and given technology

e.why: The model holds resources and technology fixed and assumes they are fully used, so it can show the trade-off between two goods.

items.q: An economy decides to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods this year. The most likely result is
o: no opportunity cost, because capital goods are useful
a point inside the production possibilities frontier
a production possibilities frontier that shifts inwards
lower consumption now but a frontier that can shift outwards in the future

e.why: The opportunity cost is consumer goods today. More machinery and infrastructure raise future productive capacity, so the frontier can shift out later.

items.q: Which of the following is an injection into the circular flow of income?

e.why: Exports bring spending into the economy from overseas. Savings, taxation and imports are leakages from the circular flow.

items.q: In an economy, S = $60b, T = $90b, M = $50b, I = $70b, G = $85b and X = $55b. This economy is
o: in disequilibrium, and national income will fall
in disequilibrium, and national income will rise
in equilibrium, because government spending is less than taxation

e.why: Leakages S + T + M = $200b and injections I + G + X = $210b. Injections exceed leakages, so spending and income rise until the two are equal.

items.q: In the circular flow of income, households provide businesses with
o: the factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise

e.why: Households own the factors of production and sell their services to businesses in return for factor incomes. Businesses provide goods and services to households.

items.q: Households decide to save a larger share of their income. Other things equal, the circular flow model predicts that
o: leakages fall and national income rises
injections rise and national income rises
leakages rise and national income falls
there is no effect, because savings stay in the economy

e.why: Saving is a leakage: money saved is not spent on goods and services, so spending and income fall unless the savings are matched by more investment.

items.q: Which sector's main role in the circular flow of income is to channel savings to businesses for investment?

e.why: Banks, super funds and other financial institutions take in savings and lend or invest them, linking a leakage (S) with an injection (I).

items.q: The stage of the business cycle at which real GDP stops rising and begins to fall is the

e.why: The peak is the high point of the cycle, after which a contraction begins. The trough is the low point, after which an expansion (upturn) begins.

items.q: During the contraction (downturn) phase of the business cycle, we would usually expect
o: unemployment to fall and inflation to rise
both unemployment and inflation to fall
unemployment to rise and inflationary pressure to ease

e.why: Spending and production slow, so firms need fewer workers and have less ability to raise prices.

items.q: An economy's real GDP rose from $2,000 billion to $2,050 billion over a year. Its rate of economic growth was

e.why: Growth = (2,050 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 2.5 per cent. D divides by the new value instead of the original one.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to start a downturn in Australia's business cycle?
o: A large fall in exports because major trading partners are in recession

e.why: Exports are an injection; a large fall reduces spending, production and income. A, C and D would usually lift spending.

items.q: The main reason economies pursue higher GDP is to
o: raise material living standards and create jobs

e.why: Higher output means more goods and services and more income per person, and growing production needs more workers.

items.q: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses is correct?
o: They operate only in the arts
They are not counted in Australia's GDP
They add to GDP through the goods and services they produce, the people they employ and the incomes they pay, across many industries
They are all owned by government

e.why: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses operate in industries such as construction, professional services, tourism, retail, the arts and native foods, and their output is part of GDP.

items.q: During a contraction in the business cycle, the Federal Government's budget usually moves towards deficit because
o: tax revenue rises and spending on unemployment benefits falls
neither tax revenue nor spending changes
both tax revenue and spending rise
tax revenue falls and spending on unemployment benefits rises

e.why: Lower incomes and profits mean less tax collected, while more people qualify for income support.

items.q: When a good becomes scarce and its price rises, the higher price gives firms a reason to produce more of it. This is the price mechanism's

e.why: The higher price makes production more profitable, an incentive to supply more. The signalling function is the price change telling people the good has become scarcer; rationing is limiting who buys it.

items.q: Concert tickets sell out at a high price, so only people willing and able to pay that price can attend. This shows the price mechanism's

e.why: A higher price rations a scarce good among buyers: those who will not or cannot pay that price go without.

items.q: Markets work better when property rights are clearly defined and enforced because
o: firms no longer need to compete
the government can then set all prices
owners can be confident they will keep the rewards of their effort and investment

e.why: Secure property rights and enforceable contracts give people the confidence to invest, produce and trade.

items.q: The market in which businesses hire workers is an example of

e.why: Labour is a factor of production, so it is traded in a factor market. Goods and services are traded in product markets.

items.q: The law of demand states that, other things equal,
o: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded rises
as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls

e.why: The law of demand is the inverse relationship between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, which gives the demand curve its downward slope.

items.q: A fall in the price of coffee leads to
o: an increase in demand for coffee: the demand curve shifts right
a contraction in the quantity of coffee demanded
a decrease in demand for coffee
an expansion in the quantity of coffee demanded: a movement along the demand curve

e.why: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along its demand curve. Only a change in a non-price factor shifts the curve.

items.q: Which of the following would increase the demand for electric cars?
o: A fall in the price of electric cars
A rise in the price of petrol
A rise in the price of electricity

e.why: Dearer petrol makes petrol cars (substitutes for electric cars) more costly to run, so demand for electric cars increases. A is a movement along the curve; C raises the cost of a complement; D reduces demand for a normal good.

items.q: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of tea rises, the demand for coffee will
o: expand along the demand curve for coffee
decrease: the demand curve for coffee shifts to the left
increase: the demand curve for coffee shifts to the right

e.why: Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is demanded at every price of coffee.

items.q: Effective demand is
o: the desire for a good or service
the total quantity supplied in a market
the desire for a good or service backed by the ability and willingness to pay

e.why: Wanting something is not enough; demand only counts in a market when the buyer can and will pay.

items.q: The supply curve slopes upwards because
o: at higher prices production is more profitable, so firms supply more
consumers buy more at higher prices
costs of production fall as prices rise
the government requires firms to produce more

e.why: A higher price covers the higher costs of extra output and gives firms an incentive to produce more (the law of supply).

items.q: The market supply of a good is
o: the quantity one firm will supply at each price
the quantity consumers want to buy at each price
the sum of the quantities all firms in the market will supply at each price
the total stock of the good held in warehouses

e.why: Market supply adds together every firm's individual supply at each price. Supply is effective only when firms are willing and able to produce at that price.

items.q: Which of the following would decrease the supply of wheat?
o: A drought that destroys part of the crop
A fall in the price of fertiliser
More farmers deciding to grow wheat

e.why: The drought reduces the quantity of wheat available at every price, so supply shifts left. A, C and D all increase supply.

items.q: A rise in the price of strawberries causes
o: an increase in the supply of strawberries
the supply curve of strawberries to shift right
a decrease in the supply of strawberries
an expansion in the quantity of strawberries supplied

e.why: A change in the good's own price is a movement along the supply curve (an expansion when the price rises), not a shift.

items.q: Cattle farmers expect the price of beef to rise sharply next year, so they hold back cattle from sale now. The supply of beef this year will

e.why: Expected future prices are a non-price factor: holding stock back for a better price later reduces supply now, shifting the supply curve left.

items.q: Demand for a good increases while supply does not change. The equilibrium price and quantity will

e.why: At the old price there is now a shortage, so the price rises; the higher price causes an expansion of supply, so quantity rises too.

items.q: Demand for avocados increases and, at the same time, a bumper harvest increases supply. What happens to the market equilibrium?
o: Price falls and quantity does not change
Quantity rises, but the change in price depends on the relative size of the two shifts
Price rises, but the change in quantity cannot be known

e.why: Both shifts raise quantity. The demand increase pushes price up and the supply increase pushes it down, so the net effect on price depends on which shift is larger.

items.q: Using the schedule for mangoes, what is the equilibrium price?

e.why: At $3 the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied (600), so the market clears.

items.q: Using the schedule for mangoes, at a price of $2 there is

e.why: At $2, quantity demanded (750) exceeds quantity supplied (450) by 300: a shortage, which pushes the price up towards $3.

items.q: A competitive market equilibrium is said to be efficient because
o: firms earn the highest possible profit
resources are used to produce output up to the point where the value buyers place on the last unit equals the cost of producing it

e.why: At equilibrium, every unit that buyers value at more than its cost is produced, and no unit that costs more than it is worth to buyers is produced (allocative efficiency). It does not mean everyone can afford it.

items.q: The price of a movie ticket rises by 10 per cent and the quantity demanded falls by 25 per cent. Using the percentage method, the price elasticity of demand is

e.why: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = −25 ÷ 10 = −2.5, usually written as 2.5. It is greater than 1, so demand is relatively elastic. A divides the wrong way round.

items.q: Demand for a good is perfectly inelastic. This means that
o: the quantity demanded does not change when the price changes
any price rise causes the quantity demanded to fall to zero
the percentage change in quantity equals the percentage change in price

e.why: Perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0) is a vertical demand curve. B and D describe perfectly elastic demand; C describes unit elasticity.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to have price inelastic demand?
o: One particular brand of soft drink

e.why: Insulin is a necessity with no close substitute, so buyers keep buying when the price rises. A has many close substitutes; B and D are not necessities.

items.q: A business sells a product with price elastic demand. If it raises its price, its total revenue will

e.why: With elastic demand, the percentage fall in quantity sold is larger than the percentage rise in price, so price × quantity falls.

items.q: Demand for petrol is usually more price elastic in the long run than in the short run because
o: over time, people can find substitutes, such as more fuel-efficient or electric cars and public transport
petrol becomes more addictive over time

e.why: The time horizon matters: with more time, buyers can change their habits and find alternatives, so they respond more to a price change.

items.q: Compared with a relatively inelastic demand curve drawn through the same point, a relatively elastic demand curve is
o: flatter, because a small change in price causes a large change in quantity demanded
steeper, because a large change in price causes a small change in quantity demanded

e.why: The flatter the demand curve through a point, the more the quantity demanded responds to a given price change.

items.q: On the morning of a fish market, the supply of fresh fish is likely to be
o: very inelastic, because the day's catch is already fixed

e.why: In the very short run sellers cannot catch more fish, and fresh fish cannot be stored for long, so the quantity supplied barely responds to price.

items.q: Which of the following makes the supply of a good more price elastic?
o: The good perishes quickly and cannot be stored
Production needs specialised workers who are hard to find

e.why: Spare capacity lets firms raise output quickly when the price rises. B, C and D all make supply less elastic.

items.q: Price elasticity of supply matters to a business because
o: a firm with elastic supply can raise its output quickly to take advantage of a price rise
it shows how consumers respond to price changes
it sets the rate of tax on the firm's product

e.why: Firms that can respond quickly to higher prices earn more from a rise in demand. B describes price elasticity of demand.

items.q: The amount of land in a city centre is fixed. Its supply curve is

e.why: However high the price, no more city-centre land can be supplied, so PES = 0 and the supply curve is vertical.

items.q: A market with a single seller, a product with no close substitutes and very high barriers to entry is

e.why: These are the characteristics of a monopoly, which gives the seller strong pricing power.

items.q: Which market structure best describes Australia's supermarket industry?

e.why: A few large firms, led by Coles and Woolworths, hold most of the market, with high barriers to entry and businesses that watch and respond to each other's prices.

items.q: Cafés in a large city are an example of monopolistic competition because
o: there are many sellers offering similar but differentiated products, with low barriers to entry
one café controls the whole market
every café sells identical coffee at the same price
a few large chains dominate and new cafés cannot enter

e.why: Each café differentiates itself (location, quality, atmosphere), which gives it a little pricing power, but it is easy for new cafés to open.

items.q: An increase in market concentration (fewer, larger firms) is most likely to lead to
o: higher prices, lower output and higher profits for the remaining firms

e.why: With less competition, firms have more pricing power: they can charge more and supply less. Quality and innovation may also suffer.

items.q: A social media platform becomes more valuable to each user as more people join it. This is
o: an economy of scale in production

e.why: Network effects make large platforms more attractive and harder for new rivals to challenge, which adds to their market power.

items.q: A negative externality is
o: a cost imposed on third parties who are not part of the transaction
a benefit received by the buyer
a cost paid by the producer

e.why: Pollution affecting nearby residents is an example: the cost is not paid by the buyer or seller, so the market does not take it into account.

items.q: A lighthouse is an example of a public good because it is

e.why: One ship using the light does not reduce its use by others (non-rival), and ships that do not pay cannot be stopped from using it (non-excludable).

items.q: The free rider problem means that
o: people can benefit from a good without paying for it, so private firms will not supply enough of it
the government provides goods free of charge

e.why: If people can use a good without paying, few will pay, so a profit-seeking firm will under-provide it. This is why public goods are usually provided by government.

items.q: A used-car seller knows a car has a faulty gearbox, but the buyer does not. This is an example of

e.why: One side of the transaction knows more than the other, so the buyer may pay more than the car is worth. This can lead to market failure.

items.q: Two petrol stations in a town secretly agree to keep their prices at the same high level. This is

e.why: Collusion is an abuse of market power: firms agree not to compete, so consumers pay more. Predatory pricing is setting prices very low to drive rivals out.

items.q: Education is often called a merit good because
o: left to the market, it would be under-consumed, as people do not take into account its benefits to others
left to the market, it would be over-consumed

e.why: An educated workforce benefits the whole community (a positive externality), so private demand is less than the socially efficient amount.

items.q: Overfishing in international waters is an example of the problem of

e.why: Fish stocks are rival (one boat's catch leaves fewer fish for others) but hard to exclude people from, so each user has an incentive to overuse them.

items.q: Which of the following is a challenge some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses face in accessing capital?
o: Interest rates set specifically for them by the Reserve Bank
Too many lenders competing for their business
A law that bans them from borrowing
Fewer assets that lenders accept as security, such as land that can be mortgaged, which can make loans harder to obtain

e.why: Lenders usually want security for a loan. Land held communally or under native title generally cannot be mortgaged, and lower inherited wealth can mean fewer other assets.

items.q: Income and wealth inequality can be seen as a market failure because
o: markets reward people according to what they own and can sell, which can leave some people socially excluded and unable to meet basic needs
the price mechanism sets the same wage for everyone

e.why: Markets allocate according to purchasing power, not need, so they may not achieve the community's social objectives.

items.q: Which of the following is a limitation of the price mechanism?
o: It allocates goods to people with purchasing power, regardless of need
It responds to changes in consumer preferences
It gives producers an incentive to supply more

e.why: B, C and D are strengths of the price mechanism. Allocating by ability to pay is one reason markets may not meet social objectives.

items.q: The government wants fewer people to smoke. Which policy directly raises the price of cigarettes?

e.why: An excise is a per-unit tax that raises producers' costs and so the price consumers pay, reducing the quantity of cigarettes bought.

items.q: A binding price ceiling, set below the equilibrium price, will cause

e.why: At the lower price, quantity demanded expands and quantity supplied contracts, so demand exceeds supply.

items.q: A price floor is binding only when it is set

e.why: A floor stops the price falling below it. If it is below equilibrium the market price is already higher, so the floor has no effect.

items.q: An industry lobbies the government for a subsidy that benefits its firms but not the wider community. This is an example of

e.why: Rent-seeking is using resources to gain a benefit from government rather than by producing something of value, and it can lead to government failure.

items.q: Placing fruit at eye level and lollies on the top shelf of a school canteen is an example of

e.why: A nudge changes how choices are presented to encourage better decisions, without banning options or changing prices.

items.q: A government subsidises fertiliser to raise farm output, but farmers overuse it and runoff damages a river. This is best described as
o: government failure through an unintended consequence

e.why: The intervention aimed to help but created a new negative externality, so resources may end up less efficiently used.

items.q: A per-unit tax is placed on a good with very price inelastic demand. Most of the burden of the tax will fall on
o: no one, because the price will not change

e.why: When demand is inelastic, buyers keep buying as the price rises, so producers can pass most of the tax on to them in a higher price.

items.q: A household's weekly income rises from $1,000 to $1,200 and its weekly consumption rises from $900 to $1,050. Its marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is

e.why: MPC = change in consumption ÷ change in income = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75. B is consumption ÷ income at the new level, the average, not the marginal, propensity.

items.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the marginal propensity to save is

e.why: Every extra dollar of income is either spent or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1 and MPS = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2.

items.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that
o: total satisfaction falls as more of a good is consumed
utility rises with the price of a good
consumers always buy the cheapest good available
each extra unit consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before

e.why: The third slice of pizza adds less satisfaction than the first. Total utility can still rise; it is the extra (marginal) utility that falls.

items.q: As their incomes rise, people buy fewer packets of generic store-brand noodles. Store-brand noodles are

e.why: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises, because buyers switch to preferred alternatives. Demand for a normal good rises with income.

items.q: Demand for a luxury handbag rises when its price rises, because a high price signals status. The handbag is

e.why: For a Veblen good, a higher price makes the good more desirable as a status symbol, the opposite of the usual law of demand.

items.q: The paradox of thrift suggests that if all households try to save more during a downturn,
o: spending and incomes will fall, so total saving may not rise at all

e.why: One household saving more is sensible, but if everyone spends less, firms sell less and incomes fall, which limits how much people can actually save.

items.q: A subscription service is easy to join online but can only be cancelled by phoning during business hours. This is an example of

e.why: A sludge is friction deliberately put in the way of a choice that is good for the consumer, here cancelling, so that people keep paying.

items.q: Consumer sovereignty means that
o: consumers' spending decisions determine what is produced
the government decides what consumers buy
consumers set the prices of goods

e.why: In a market economy, firms produce what consumers are willing to buy. Marketing and behavioural sludges can weaken this.

items.q: A shopper pays more for free-range eggs because she is concerned about animal welfare. This shows the consumer as
o: an agent who cares only about the lowest price
a socially and ethically motivated agent

e.why: Consumers' choices are also shaped by values, culture and social norms, not only by price and their own satisfaction.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to increase the supply of labour?
o: Higher income tax rates for people returning to work

e.why: Childcare costs and availability are a major barrier to parents working, so making care cheaper and easier to find raises participation. A, C and D reduce labour supply.

items.q: Which of the following is a disincentive to participating in the workforce?
o: A lack of affordable care for children or older relatives

e.why: People with caring responsibilities may not be able to work if care is unaffordable or unavailable. A, B and D make working easier.

items.q: Occupational mobility of labour refers to
o: workers' ability to move between different jobs or occupations
workers moving between cities and regions
workers travelling further to work each day

e.why: Occupational mobility depends on skills and training; B is geographic mobility.

items.q: A business earned revenue of $500,000 and paid $380,000 in explicit costs. Its owner could have earned $90,000 working for another firm. What are the business's accounting profit and economic profit?

e.why: Accounting profit = 500,000 − 380,000 = $120,000. Economic profit also subtracts the opportunity cost of the owner's time: 120,000 − 90,000 = $30,000.

items.q: Australia Post, a business owned by the Australian Government, is an example of

e.why: A public enterprise (government business enterprise) is owned by government but sells goods and services in the market.

items.q: Productivity measures
o: the total output of an economy
output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked

e.why: Higher productivity means more output from the same inputs, which lowers costs and supports higher wages and living standards.

items.q: A large supermarket chain buys stock in huge quantities at a lower price per unit than small grocers pay. This is an example of

e.why: Purchasing economies come from the firm's own size, so they are internal. External economies come from the growth of the whole industry or region.

items.q: Capital deepening means
o: increasing the amount of capital per worker

e.why: Giving each worker more or better equipment raises output per worker, a key source of productivity growth.

items.q: On a long-run average cost (LRAC) curve, the technical optimum is the level of output at which

e.why: Up to the technical optimum the firm enjoys economies of scale; beyond it, diseconomies of scale push average cost up.

items.q: In Australia, the national minimum wage is set each year by
o: the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission

e.why: The Fair Work Commission's annual wage review sets the national minimum wage and the minimum rates in modern awards.

items.q: Which of the following is most likely to reduce businesses' demand for labour?
o: Cheaper automation and AI that can do tasks workers now do
A fall in the cost of labour compared with the cost of capital

e.why: When machines and software become cheaper relative to labour, firms may replace some workers. A, C and D would usually increase the demand for labour.

items.q: Which of the following is a non-wage benefit of a job?

e.why: Non-wage benefits are rewards other than pay, such as flexibility, leave, training or a work car. A, C and D are all forms of wage.

items.q: The main role of the financial sector in the economy is to
o: produce goods and services for households
channel funds from savers to borrowers who want to invest

e.why: By linking savers with borrowers, the financial sector turns savings into investment, which helps the economy grow.

items.q: Which of the following is a financial intermediary?
o: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission

e.why: A super fund pools members' savings and invests them in shares, bonds, property and infrastructure, standing between savers and the users of funds.

items.q: Superannuation supports the Australian economy mainly by
o: building a large pool of savings that is invested in shares, bonds, property and infrastructure

e.why: Compulsory contributions create long-term savings that fund investment, and they also provide retirement incomes.

items.q: From 1 July 2025, the superannuation guarantee requires employers to contribute what percentage of an employee's ordinary time earnings to super?

e.why: The superannuation guarantee rose in half-point steps from 9.5 per cent in 2020–21 to 12 per cent from 1 July 2025 (Australian Taxation Office).

items.q: A company sells new shares to investors for the first time in an initial public offering (IPO). This takes place in the

e.why: New shares are issued in the primary market, which raises funds for the company. Later trading of those shares between investors is the secondary market.

items.q: A shareholder in a company owns
o: a loan to the company that must be repaid with interest
part of the company and a claim on its profits
nothing until the company is sold

e.why: Shares are equity: part-ownership, with a share of profits paid as dividends. A loan is debt.

items.q: The secondary share market, such as the Australian Securities Exchange, helps the economy mainly because
o: companies receive new funds every time their shares are traded
investors can easily sell shares, which makes them more willing to buy new shares when companies issue them
the government sets share prices on it
it removes the risk of owning shares

e.why: Liquidity in the secondary market supports the primary market. Companies do not receive money when existing shares change hands.

items.q: An interest rate can best be described as
o: the price of money: the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving
the rate of tax on savings

e.why: Borrowers pay interest for the use of funds and savers receive it for lending them.

items.q: In the loanable funds market, an increase in the demand for funds, with supply unchanged, will
o: raise the interest rate and the quantity of funds lent
reduce the quantity of funds lent
have no effect on the interest rate

e.why: The demand curve for funds shifts right, so the interest rate rises until the extra borrowing is matched by an expansion in the quantity of funds supplied.

items.q: Which of the following would increase the supply of loanable funds?
o: Households saving a larger share of their income

e.why: More saving means more funds available to lend. B and C affect the demand for funds; D reduces saving.

items.q: A rise in interest rates is most likely to
o: make housing more affordable for new buyers
raise mortgage repayments and reduce how much buyers can borrow

e.why: Higher rates increase the cost of servicing a loan, so existing borrowers pay more and new buyers can borrow less.

items.q: When the Australian Government sells newly issued bonds to raise funds, it is borrowing in the

e.why: New bonds are sold in the primary market. Investors may later trade them in the secondary bond market.

items.q: Riskier borrowers usually pay higher interest rates because
o: lenders want a higher return to compensate for the greater chance that they will not be repaid
interest rates are set by the government

e.why: The interest rate includes a risk premium, so it also acts as an indicator of risk.

items.q: Unemployment benefits and a progressive income tax help the government to

e.why: Taxing higher incomes at higher rates and paying benefits to those on low incomes makes the distribution of income more equal.

items.q: When the government increases its spending during a recession to support jobs, it is carrying out its role of

e.why: Stabilisation means smoothing the business cycle: supporting spending in a downturn and restraining it when the economy overheats.

items.q: A budget deficit occurs when
o: government revenue is greater than government expenditure
government expenditure is greater than government revenue

e.why: The government must borrow to cover a deficit. A describes a budget surplus.

items.q: An energy company sends each household a report comparing its electricity use with that of similar households nearby, to encourage it to use less. This is an example of

e.why: The comparison uses social norms to change behaviour without changing prices or banning anything.

items.q: Which of the following is an argument for privatising a government business?
o: Private ownership and competition may make the business more efficient
Privatisation guarantees lower prices for consumers
Privatisation ensures services reach remote areas

e.why: Supporters argue that the profit motive and competition improve efficiency and service. B and C are not guaranteed; a private monopoly may raise prices or cut unprofitable services.

items.q: Under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap (2020), Australian governments agreed to share decision-making on policy with
o: the Coalition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community-Controlled Peak Organisations (the Coalition of Peaks)
the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission

e.why: The Coalition of Peaks is a party to the National Agreement, which commits governments to formal partnerships and shared decision-making with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisations.

items.q: A law requiring builders to meet safety standards is an example of

e.why: Regulation sets rules that businesses and households must follow, to prevent or reduce harm.

items.q: The largest single source of Australian Government revenue is

e.why: Taxes on individuals' incomes raise more than any other source, around half of the Australian Government's tax revenue.

items.q: A direct tax is a tax that
o: is paid when goods and services are bought
is levied on income or profits and paid by the person or business that earns it

e.why: Income tax and company tax are direct taxes. A and D describe indirect taxes such as the GST.

items.q: The GST is an indirect tax because
o: businesses pay it to the government, but its cost is passed on to consumers in higher prices
it is a tax on wealth
it applies only to imported goods

e.why: The legal incidence falls on businesses, which collect and remit the tax, but most of the economic incidence falls on consumers.

items.q: The legal incidence of a tax refers to
o: who actually bears the cost of the tax
who is legally required to pay the tax to the government
the rate at which the tax is charged

e.why: Legal incidence is who must pay the tax office. Economic incidence (A) is who finally bears the cost, which depends on price elasticities.

items.q: A tax that taxpayers find easy to understand and comply with meets which feature of a good tax?

e.why: Simplicity means a tax is easy to understand, comply with and collect. Fairness concerns who pays; efficiency concerns how little the tax distorts decisions.

items.q: Which of the following is a tax on wealth?

e.why: Land tax is charged on the value of land owned, a stock of wealth. The GST taxes consumption; income and payroll taxes are taxes on income.

items.q: A tax is progressive when
o: everyone pays the same amount of tax
the average tax rate rises as income rises
lower-income earners pay a larger share of their income in tax
everyone pays the same percentage of their income

e.why: Under a progressive tax, people with higher incomes pay a larger proportion of their income. C describes a regressive tax and D a proportional tax.

items.q: Which of the following is a common argument for reform of the Australian tax system?
o: Heavy reliance on income tax may discourage work and investment, and bracket creep raises average tax rates over time
The GST base is too broad
Companies in Australia pay no tax

e.why: Reviews have pointed to Australia's reliance on income taxes and to bracket creep. A common view is that the GST base is too narrow, because of exemptions such as fresh food, the opposite of C.

items.q: The largest category of Australian Government spending is

e.why: Payments such as the age pension, family payments, disability support and unemployment benefits make social security and welfare the largest category, around a third of spending.

items.q: Which of the following is non-recurrent (capital) government spending?

e.why: Capital spending creates long-lasting assets such as hospitals, roads and schools. A, B and D occur every year (recurrent spending).

items.q: Which of the following is a reason given for reform of Australian Government spending?
o: Spending on programs such as the NDIS, aged care, health and interest on debt is growing faster than revenue
The government spends nothing on welfare
Spending never affects the budget balance

e.why: Fast-growing spending pressures, many linked to an ageing population, raise questions about the budget's long-term sustainability and how well spending is targeted.

items.q: International trade raises living standards mainly because
o: countries specialise according to comparative advantage and trade, so more is produced from the same resources
imports always cost more than exports
trade removes the need for money

e.why: Voluntary exchange benefits both sides: each country specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trades for the rest.

items.q: Australia's largest two-way trading partner is

e.why: China has been Australia's largest two-way trading partner since 2007 (Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade), mainly through Australian exports of iron ore and other resources.

items.q: Which statement best describes the composition of Australia's goods exports?
o: They are mostly manufactured goods such as cars and machinery
They are dominated by mineral and energy resources such as iron ore, coal, natural gas and gold

e.why: Resources make up the largest share of Australia's exports. Rural goods such as beef and wheat and services such as education and tourism are also important, but smaller.

items.q: A country's exports of goods and services are worth $480 billion and its imports are worth $510 billion. Its trade balance is

e.why: Trade balance = exports − imports = 480 − 510 = −$30 billion, a trade deficit.

items.q: From at least the 1700s until 1907, fishermen from Makassar (in present-day Indonesia) sailed each year to the Arnhem Land coast and traded and worked with Yolŋu people. The main product they took back, to be sold on to China, was

e.why: The fishermen caught, boiled and dried trepang on the Arnhem Land coast and sold it to Chinese traders. Yolŋu people traded with them for goods such as cloth, tobacco, knives and rice (National Museum of Australia).

items.q: Foreign equity investment in Australia occurs when
o: an Australian bank borrows from overseas lenders
overseas investors buy shares in, or take ownership of, Australian businesses or property
Australians buy shares in overseas companies
the Reserve Bank buys foreign currency

e.why: Equity is ownership. A creates foreign debt; C is Australian investment abroad.

items.q: Which of the following adds to Australia's foreign debt?
o: A Japanese company buying an Australian mine
An Australian company borrowing from a US bank
An Australian buying shares in a US company
A tourist spending money in Sydney

e.why: Borrowing from overseas creates a debt that must be repaid with interest. A is foreign equity in Australia.

items.q: Which country is the largest source of foreign investment in Australia?

e.why: The United States holds the largest stock of foreign investment in Australia (Australian Bureau of Statistics, International Investment Position). China's investment is much smaller than its share of Australia's trade.

items.q: If A$1 = US$0.65, how much does a laptop priced at US$1,300 cost in Australian dollars?

e.why: Australian dollars = US$ price ÷ US$ per A$ = 1,300 ÷ 0.65 = A$2,000. A multiplies instead of dividing.

items.q: Exchange rates are needed for international trade and investment because
o: countries use different currencies, so buyers must convert their currency to pay sellers
every country uses the US dollar
exchange rates set the prices of goods within each country
exchange rates prevent trade between countries

e.why: An Australian importer paying a Japanese supplier must buy yen with Australian dollars, at the exchange rate.

items.q: The Australian dollar rises from US$0.62 to US$0.68. The Australian dollar has
o: been devalued by the Reserve Bank

e.why: Each Australian dollar now buys more US dollars, so its value has risen (appreciated). C applies only to fixed exchange rates.

items.q: The balance of payments is
o: a record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period of time
a record of a country's foreign debt only
the difference between national saving and investment

e.why: It records trade, income and financial flows with the rest of the world, usually each quarter and year.

items.q: Which of the following is recorded in the current account of Australia's balance of payments?
o: A foreign company buying an Australian mine
The Reserve Bank's holdings of foreign currency

e.why: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows. A, C and D are financial account transactions.

items.lead: The production possibilities schedule shows the combinations of cars and wheat an economy can produce when it uses all its resources efficiently.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the opportunity cost of increasing car production from 20,000 to 30,000.
parts.ans: Wheat falls from 170,000 to 140,000 tonnes, so the 10,000 extra cars cost 30,000 tonnes of wheat (3 tonnes per car).

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain why the opportunity cost of producing cars rises as more cars are produced.
pts: Each extra 10,000 cars costs more wheat: 10, 20, 30, 40 and then 60 thousand tonnes (1)
Resources are not equally suited to both goods; as car output rises, resources better suited to growing wheat are moved into cars, so more wheat is given up for each car (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: The economy is producing 20,000 cars and 120,000 tonnes of wheat. Explain what this shows.
pts: This point is inside the frontier: with 20,000 cars the economy could produce 170,000 tonnes of wheat (1)
Resources are unemployed or underemployed (or used inefficiently), so 50,000 tonnes of wheat could be gained at no opportunity cost (1)

items.lead: The table shows the flows in the circular flow of income for an economy over one year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate total leakages and total injections.
parts.ans: Leakages S + T + M = 120 + 160 + 110 = $390 billion. Injections I + G + X = 140 + 150 + 90 = $380 billion.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain what will happen to national income in this economy.
pts: Leakages exceed injections by $10 billion, so less is spent than is received as income (1)
Spending, production and income fall until leakages again equal injections (equilibrium) (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain ONE way the government could keep national income at its current level.
pts: Identifies a suitable change, e.g. increase government spending (G) or reduce taxation (T) by $10 billion (1)
Explains it: injections rise or leakages fall until S + T + M = I + G + X at the current level of income (1)

items.lead: The table shows quarterly growth in real GDP and the unemployment rate for an economy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the two consecutive quarters in which real GDP fell.
parts.ans: Quarters 4 and 5 (growth of −0.3 and −0.5 per cent).

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify the stage of the business cycle in Quarters 4 and 5, and the trough.
parts.ans: Quarters 4 and 5 are a contraction (downturn), the two quarters of falling GDP often called a recession. The trough is around Quarter 5 to 6, after which growth recovers.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why unemployment kept rising in Quarter 6, even though GDP had begun to grow again.
pts: Unemployment lags the business cycle: firms wait to be confident the recovery will last before hiring (1)
Growth of 0.1 per cent is too weak to create enough jobs for the growing labour force (1)
Firms first use their existing workers more fully (more hours) before taking on new staff (1)

items.lead: The table shows the weekly demand schedule for tickets at a cinema.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the change in the quantity of tickets demanded when the price rises from $12 to $16.
parts.ans: The quantity demanded falls from 700 to 500 tickets a week, a contraction of 200 tickets.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Distinguish between a contraction of demand and a decrease in demand, using this cinema as an example.
pts: A contraction of demand is a movement along the demand curve caused by a rise in the good's own price, e.g. the rise from $12 to $16 (1)
A decrease in demand is a shift of the whole curve to the left caused by a non-price factor, e.g. a fall in incomes, so fewer tickets are demanded at every price (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Streaming services raise their subscription prices sharply. Explain the likely effect on the demand for cinema tickets.
pts: Streaming and cinema are substitutes (1)
Some viewers switch to the cinema, so demand for tickets increases: more tickets are demanded at each price and the demand curve shifts right (1)

items.lead: The table shows the market for a good.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Identify the equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.ans: $4 and 800 units, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the surplus or shortage at a price of $5, and explain what will happen to the price.
parts.ans: At $5 quantity supplied (1,000) exceeds quantity demanded (700): a surplus of 300 units. Sellers cut prices to clear unsold stock, so the price falls back towards $4.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Demand increases by 300 units at every price. Identify the new equilibrium price and quantity.
parts.ans: The new quantities demanded are 1,300, 1,200, 1,100, 1,000 and 900. At $5, quantity demanded (1,000) equals quantity supplied (1,000), so the new equilibrium is $5 and 1,000 units: both price and quantity rise.

items.lead: A cinema raises the price of a ticket from $20 to $22. Its weekly ticket sales fall from 2,000 to 1,700.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the price elasticity of demand using the percentage method.
parts.ans: % change in quantity = (1,700 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 × 100 = −15%. % change in price = (22 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 10%. PED = −15 ÷ 10 = −1.5 (1.5): demand is relatively elastic.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the change in the cinema's weekly revenue, and explain it using the price elasticity of demand.
parts.ans: Revenue falls from $40,000 (20 × 2,000) to $37,400 (22 × 1,700), down $2,600. Because demand is elastic, the percentage fall in tickets sold (15%) is larger than the percentage rise in price (10%).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Outline ONE reason why the demand for cinema tickets may be price elastic.
pts: Identifies a reason, e.g. close substitutes such as streaming and other entertainment; not a necessity (1)
Outlines it: when the price rises, many customers switch to the substitute or go less often (1)

table.cap: Responses to a 20 per cent price rise

items.lead: The table shows what happens to the quantity demanded of three goods when each one's price rises by 20 per cent.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the price elasticity of demand for each good.
parts.ans: Petrol: 4 ÷ 20 = 0.2 (inelastic). Restaurant meals: 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 (elastic). Bus fares: 20 ÷ 20 = 1 (unit elastic).

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain what happens to the total revenue of petrol sellers and of restaurants after the price rise.
pts: Petrol: demand is inelastic, so the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the price rise and total revenue rises (1)
Restaurants: demand is elastic, so the fall in quantity outweighs the price rise and total revenue falls (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why the government might prefer to tax petrol rather than restaurant meals if its aim is to raise revenue.
pts: Because demand for petrol is inelastic, a tax barely reduces the quantity bought (1)
So the tax base stays large and the tax raises a lot of revenue with little change in behaviour (1)

items.lead: Before a tax, 10,000 bottles of a sugary drink are sold each week at $3.00 a bottle. The government places a tax of $0.50 on each bottle. Afterwards, 9,500 bottles a week are sold at $3.40.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the government's weekly revenue from the tax.
parts.ans: $0.50 × 9,500 = $4,750 a week (the tax per unit times the quantity sold after the tax).

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate how much of the $0.50 tax is paid by consumers and how much by producers.
parts.ans: Consumers pay $0.40 more ($3.40 − $3.00). Producers now keep $2.90 a bottle ($3.40 − $0.50), $0.10 less than before. So consumers bear $0.40 and producers $0.10 of each $0.50.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why consumers bear most of this tax.
pts: Demand is price inelastic: the price rose by about 13% but the quantity bought fell by only 5% (PED about 0.4), so buyers kept buying at the higher price (1)
So producers could pass most of the tax on in a higher price: the economic incidence falls mainly on consumers, even though producers pay the tax to the government (legal incidence) (1)

items.lead: The table shows a household's weekly disposable income and consumption.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the marginal propensity to consume when income rises from $1,000 to $1,200.
parts.ans: MPC = change in consumption ÷ change in income = (1,080 − 920) ÷ (1,200 − 1,000) = 160 ÷ 200 = 0.8.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the marginal propensity to save.
parts.ans: MPS = 1 − MPC = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2 (the household saves 20 cents of each extra dollar).

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain what happens to the household's saving as its income rises.
pts: Saving (income − consumption) rises from $40 to $80 to $120 a week (1)
The share of income saved also rises, from 5% to about 8% to 10%: as income rises, households can save a larger proportion (1)

items.lead: Mia runs a bakery. Last year it earned revenue of $420,000 and paid $250,000 for ingredients, rent and wages. Mia put $60,000 of her own savings into the business, which could have earned 5 per cent interest in a bank, and she gave up a job paying $85,000 a year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the bakery's accounting profit.
parts.ans: Accounting profit = revenue − explicit costs = 420,000 − 250,000 = $170,000.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Calculate the bakery's economic profit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why economic profit is a better guide than accounting profit to whether Mia should keep running the bakery.
pts: Economic profit also counts opportunity costs: the income from her next best job and the interest on her savings (1)
A positive economic profit ($82,000) shows the bakery earns more than her resources would earn elsewhere, so staying in business is worthwhile (1)

items.lead: The table shows output and hours worked at a factory before and after it installed new machinery.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate labour productivity (output per hour worked) before and after, and the percentage change.
parts.ans: Before: 12,000 ÷ 2,400 = 5 units an hour. After: 15,000 ÷ 2,500 = 6 units an hour. Change = (6 − 5) ÷ 5 × 100 = 20 per cent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how the new machinery raised productivity.
pts: It is capital deepening: each worker has more and better capital to work with (1)
So more output is produced in each hour of work, lowering the cost of each unit (1)

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Explain why higher productivity is important for living standards.
pts: Higher output per hour allows higher real wages without raising unit costs or prices (1)
It raises the economy's productive capacity, so incomes and living standards can rise over time (1)

items.lead: A household has a home loan of $600,000. Ignoring repayments of the amount borrowed, its yearly interest cost is the loan multiplied by the interest rate.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the yearly interest at interest rates of 5 per cent and 6 per cent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Explain how a rise in interest rates from 5 to 6 per cent affects housing affordability.
pts: Existing borrowers pay more interest, leaving less income for other spending (1)
New buyers can borrow less for the same repayment, because banks test whether they can afford repayments (1)
Fewer people can afford to buy, so demand for housing falls, which may slow or reduce house prices over time (1)

items.lead: In a hypothetical income tax system, no tax is paid on the first $20,000 of income, 20 per cent is paid on income from $20,001 to $60,000, and 40 per cent on income above $60,000.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Calculate the tax paid, and the average tax rate, for a person earning $80,000.
parts.ans: 20% × 40,000 = $8,000 plus 40% × 20,000 = $8,000, so the tax is $16,000. The average tax rate is 16,000 ÷ 80,000 = 20 per cent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: Identify this person's marginal tax rate.
parts.ans: 40 per cent, the rate on each extra dollar of income above $60,000.

parts.label: (c)
parts.q: Using a person earning $40,000 for comparison, explain why this tax is progressive.
pts: At $40,000 the tax is 20% × 20,000 = $4,000, an average rate of 10 per cent (1)
The average tax rate rises with income (10 per cent at $40,000, 20 per cent at $80,000), so higher earners pay a larger share of their income (1)
